articles.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
articles.context: With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.

It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit UnrealIRCd Flaw That Enables Server-Level Command Injection
articles.context: The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added a high-severity security flaw impacting UnrealIRCd, an open-source Internet Relay Chat (IRC) server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper neutralization of delimiters that could be used to execute arbitrary commands with server/IRCOp privileges.

"The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 'label' message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority," reads the description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The addition comes nearly a week after UnrealIRCd's project leader, developer, and maintainer, Bram Matthys (aka Syzop), released UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 to address multiple security vulnerabilities identified with the help of artificial intelligence, including CVE-2026-114713.

"We are seeing bad guys exploiting this issue on the internet right now," Matthys said. "Hopefully everyone has hot-patched or updated their server, or at the very least has the spamfilter workaround deployed. If not, do so ASAP!"

Exploitation attempts are said to have commenced a day after the release of the hotfix on November 7, 2026. That said, the exact details of the malicious activity and its end goals are presently unknown. The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 16, 2026, to apply the fixes under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

articles.title: Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Shield Camera and Microphone Data
articles.context: Sensor data is released only once it has confirmed the indicator is on and has been showing for a sufficient period
articles.full_text:
Apple has published a detailed description of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture in its silicon designed to keep camera and microphone data used for ambient sensing isolated from the main operating system.

Ambient sensing lets a device listen for “Hey Siri”. On the recently introduced HomeView smart display, it enables the recognition of user faces and voices.

Secure Exclaves are isolated runtimes that handle camera and microphone data apart from the rest of the device.

“Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple,” the company said.

The design is built around three requirements. The main OS must not be able to pull out or alter data handled in an exclave, and only a narrowly defined set of information may cross over to it. Users must also be able to tell when a sensor session is active, without the main OS interfering.

According to Apple, in background sensing only specific metadata reaches the rest of the system. On HomeView, the recognition result sent to the main OS is a person identifier, position and confidence level, without audio or video data being shared.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

When an app requests full sensor access, a dedicated exclave acts as gatekeeper. Sensor data is released only once it has confirmed the indicator is on and has been showing for a sufficient period.

On devices such as the iPhone, where the indicator is an on-screen dot, another exclave checks which pixels were actually drawn to the display.

Apple said Secure Exclaves protect person recognition on HomeView, along with Siri Recap and Live Rewind. They also protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView.

The exclaves run on a minimal, capability-based microkernel, to which Apple has been applying formal verification. Apple said this turned up hard-to-spot but critical flaws in many kernel subsystems that could have led to full kernel compromise. Many of these issues were caught early in development.

The microkernel is still under active development and changes often, Apple noted. “Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts,” it said.

articles.title: No Signs of Hacking in FAA Ground Stop as FBI Reportedly Probes Software Update
articles.context: No evidence of a cyberattack was found in that case either
articles.full_text:
US officials have found no evidence that hackers caused the outage that led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt flight departures nationwide on Friday, and the FBI is reportedly examining whether a software update was responsible.

The FAA issued the ground stop on November 13 after a communications problem hit its air route traffic control centers. The order was lifted at 8:15 pm ET, more than four hours later, after disrupting thousands of flights. Departures have since resumed, though officials expect delays to continue for several days.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the incident did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack, and that the failure appeared to be mechanical.

On the absence of attack indicators, Mullin said “there’s no chatter, we haven’t seen any footprints.”

He stopped short of dismissing the possibility entirely. “However, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out,” Mullin said.

The NSA, the Department of Defense, CISA and other agencies have been involved in the investigation, according to Mullin.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The FBI does not think a cyberattack or criminal activity was behind the outage, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Investigators are looking at a software update as a potential cause, the source said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed legacy equipment. He said switches and routers in the FAA’s network were flooded with data and began producing inconsistent information, at which point the agency shut the system down.

Officials described the ground stop as a precaution.

Mullin offered a possible trigger. He said it appeared the FAA had been applying patches and installing new equipment and technology, which “was overwhelming the older system.”

CBS News, citing multiple sources, reported that the outage followed an update to the private communications network that links the air traffic control system. The network rebooted and then crashed, and it is operated by L3Harris, according to the report.

Officials said the incident had nothing to do with the Microsoft outage earlier in the week. They also said the FAA’s recently deployed AI systems played no role.

No official root cause has been announced.

The previous nationwide ground stop came in January 2023, after a contractor unintentionally deleted files while working on the system that delivers safety notices to pilots. No evidence of a cyberattack was found in that case either.

articles.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
articles.context: Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their...
articles.full_text: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

Bitdefender researchers have uncovered a malware campaign dubbed Midnight Mimosa that comes preinstalled on low-cost Android devices, compromising phones before users even turn them on.

The malware operates with system-level privileges, allowing attackers to silently install and remove apps, commit ad and click fraud, collect device information, and turn infected phones into residential proxy nodes for botnets. Researchers also identified 13 apps on Google Play sharing the same malicious code and infrastructure, highlighting how the campaign reaches users through both compromised device firmware and seemingly legitimate apps.

articles.title: Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
articles.context: About a fifth of the GitHub accounts used to launch this campaign had already been compromised during the GhostAction attack back in October, GitGuardian said
articles.full_text:
Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials.

Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them.

However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools.

The payload was delivered using at least three methods: modification of existing GitHub Actions workflows, adding a postinstall hook in the package.json file that runs it on any npm install and creating a throw-away branch with a rogue Actions workflow to be run.

“We’ve identified indications that the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories, but this number may understate impact,” the Aikido researchers said in their report. “The run log was deleted in impacted repositories, meaning the threat actor has likely collected the credentials and covered its tracks.”

The npm hook that slipped past GitHub

GitHub’s safeguard against this kind of attack worked as designed for the payloads it could see. The platform has blunted recent workflow-injection campaigns by requiring explicit approval before the malicious workflows run, and GitGuardian found that all seven of the November payload runs still visible in workflow files sat in an action_required state and never started.

“GitHub held the workflow forms, but an npm hook slipped past the hold and ran,” Gaetan Ferry, a security researcher at GitGuardian, said in an analysis.

That’s because the npm hook did not change any workflow file. Instead, the attacker added a hidden script to the repository root and a single line in package.json, which runs on every npm install. The repository’s own unchanged workflows executed npm install as routine build hygiene.

By Thursday the attacker had also changed their exfiltration method. The latest payload sends stolen data only to a Telegram chat, with the HTTP callback now pointing to a dead address. Blocking the previously published IP addresses no longer stops the latest versions.

What the malware steals

Once the script runs, it receives every repository and organization secret through a JSON dump of the workflow’s secrets object. It scans the memory of the runner process, which holds secrets in decrypted form, including ones the workflow never referenced, and collects credential files from well-known paths, shell histories, and API keys for AI services and developer tools such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Copilot, and Cursor.

The script goes further and exchanges OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, mints new long-lived AWS access keys, impersonates GCP service accounts, and replays cached Azure refresh tokens to reach Microsoft Graph and Key Vault.

It packs everything it collects into a gzipped archive and sends it to the attacker then it cleans up. In most repositories the attacker reverted the malicious commit within a minute and deleted the workflow run and its logs.

Backdoors that survive credential rotation

The script also takes actions for attackers to maintain access even if credentials are reset. For AWS it rewrites the assumed role’s trust policy to accept any AWS account, opening the role to anyone, and calls the iam:CreateAccessKey API to create long-lived keys for IAM users.

On Azure it injects federated identity credentials named wfx-ci-* into applications, pointing them back at the compromised repository, so that any workflow in that repository can authenticate to Azure without a stored secret even after every token has been rotated.

If a probe pull request or any of the campaign’s commit strings appear in a repository you control, assume every secret that repository’s workflows could reach is stolen. Rotate repository and organization secrets, package registry tokens, and any cloud keys, and remember that the memory scan means the list of what was taken is wider than what the workflows referenced.

Then hunt for signs of the persistent mechanisms: AWS role trust policies that accept any account, IAM keys created since Nov. 10, and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci-*.

“Ensure all logs are enabled, particularly audit logs on cloud admin behavior,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “Inspect audit logs where possible (specifically in AWS and Azure, as persistence is possible) to ensure the malicious payload did not run.”

The wfx-loot payload also shipped in published packages: the Packagist package neuronai-studio 3.14.3, and the Go modules docker-env and gocurl. In the Go modules the payload sits only in a workflow file that Go tooling never runs, so consumers may not have been affected; machines that installed the Packagist version should be treated as compromised.

About a fifth of the GitHub accounts used to launch this campaign had already been compromised during the GhostAction attack back in October, GitGuardian said. Meanwhile researchers from StepSecurity traced 173 of the probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub App.

Fly.io confirmed that these tokens were leaked when its deploy process left them in .git/config files inside build directories that some apps served publicly, but noted that Fly.io itself was not breached. GitHub’s bulk revocation of the Fly.io app tokens stopped partway, so some of the stolen token pool may still be valid.

articles.title: Out of office, out of service.
articles.context: Check Point patches an actively exploited zero-day tied to wiper attacks. Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability allowing attackers to gain root privileges on vulnerable appliances.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft 365 recovers from a global outage. StingyBasilisk pivots through Windows named pipes to infiltrate isolated networks. The FBI freezes billions after North Korea's Binance heist, while Pyongyang's Sapphire Sleet steals $400 million via spoofed video calls. Cupertino details Secure Exclaves for ambient sensor privacy. Operation TorNado nets 354 arrests in a global dark web crackdown. Check Point patches an actively exploited zero-day tied to wiper attacks. The wfx-loot campaign hijacks thousands of GitHub accounts to harvest cloud secrets. And civil liberties groups warn Congress against slipping Section 702 renewal into the defense bill. Our guests are Lauren Zabierek and Bob Lord, discussing the launch of the Software Safety Institute. United grounds personal AI agents over credential and compliance risks.

Today is Friday November 13th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Microsoft 365 recovers from a global outage.

If you rely on services from Microsoft, I’m betting you are already aware of today’s top story.

A major global outage disrupted Microsoft 365 services for more than twenty hours, and Redmond says a cyberattack is not to blame.

According to BBC, connectivity problems hit Outlook, Teams, and Copilot after a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable, shifting heavy traffic onto remaining infrastructure. Downdetector logged 140 thousand user reports across seventy-four countries, though total impact among Microsoft's more than 430 million users remains unclear. Knock-on disruptions have affected OpenAI, Anthropic, US courts, a Toronto hospital network, and Japanese government systems. Microsoft reports encouraging recovery progress in Europe and North America, noting earlier fixes were not taking as expected.

Prolonged cloud outages create cascading operational friction across critical infrastructure and AI dependencies, even without a threat actor at the keyboard. As Professor James Ferryman of the University of Reading notes, bringing swamped authentication servers back online requires a cautious, gradual approach to avoid triggering a fresh reconnection surge.

StingyBasilisk abuses Windows named pipes and SMB to infiltrate isolated networks.

An espionage group tracked as StingyBasilisk is abusing Windows named pipes and the Server Message Block protocol to move malware across isolated government networks, according to research from Positive Technologies.

According to incident response findings published by Positive Technologies, the group has operated since at least April 2022, masquerading as legitimate security tools. Beginning in February 2026, the attackers spread laterally over SMB and executed memory-resident payloads using Impacket's atexec tool and DLL side-loading via signed SafeNet libraries. To maintain persistence, the threat actors abused Component Object Model hijacking and modified Windows Time service providers, deploying custom implants like SilentCOM, TediousLoader, and CunningDoor. By chaining infected hosts through named pipes, the attackers reach air-gapped or segmented systems lacking direct internet access.

Abusing native Windows inter-process communication allows espionage campaigns to blend into routine administrative traffic and bypass traditional perimeter defenses. Defenders can counter this activity by restricting inter-segment SMB traffic, auditing scheduled task creation, and hunting for anomalous registry modifications.

The FBI freezes billions following the North Korean heist at Binance.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation has frozen over $2.7 billion and obtained court authorization to seize another $1.2 billion following a massive cryptocurrency theft at Binance.

According to the FBI, the October 29 cyberattack resulted in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion, most of it drained within twenty minutes. While the exact intrusion vector remains under investigation, blockchain analysts assess that attackers compromised Binance's transaction-signing infrastructure, enabling unauthorized approvals without stealing private keys. Co-CEO Richard Teng assured users that customer losses will be covered through Binance's Secure Asset Fund for Users and corporate reserves. Investigators linked the stolen funds to a prior Bitget breach, attributing the heist to the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor.

The rapid freeze demonstrates how coordinated public-private action and centralized stablecoin controls can blunt massive cryptocurrency heists intended to fund Pyongyang's prohibited weapons programs.

Pyongyang's Sapphire Sleet steals $400 million using spoofed video calls.

North Korean state-backed hackers have stolen over $400 million in cryptocurrency across eighteen months by secretly recording victims on fake video calls, according to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation.

In a campaign tracked as FaceStealer, the threat cluster known as Sapphire Sleet, or UNC1069, lures targets onto imposter versions of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet using invitations sent from compromised contacts. During the call, a fabricated technical error prompts victims to click a malicious link, infecting their devices and hijacking their accounts to repeat the cycle. Investigators seized more than nine hundred stolen webcam videos and note the group is increasingly generating artificial intelligence deepfakes of prominent cryptocurrency figures.

Weaponizing trusted social graphs alongside synthetic video bypasses traditional perimeter defenses through pure human deception.

Cupertino details Secure Exclaves architecture for ambient sensor privacy.

Apple has published technical details on Secure Exclaves, a hardware-enforced security architecture designed to isolate background camera and microphone processing from the main operating system, third-party apps, and Apple itself.

According to Apple, Secure Exclaves supports features like person recognition on HomeView, Siri Recap, and Live Rewind across new iPhone, MacBook Neo, and HomeView devices. Built on a customized L4 microkernel and enforced by the Secure Page Table Monitor, the architecture processes raw audio and video in an independent execution context before discarding the data. During ambient sensing, only strictly audited metadata—such as an enrolled user's identifier or confidence score—crosses into the main operating system. Full sensor streams are released only in active mode after an Exclave Indicator Controller verifies that on-screen pixels or hardware LEDs meet visibility thresholds.

Enforcing hardware-backed isolation and tamper-resistant indicators helps mitigate silent surveillance risks inherent in always-on ambient artificial intelligence features.

Operation TorNado nets 354 arrests across fourteen countries in dark web crackdown.

Law enforcement agencies across fourteen countries have arrested 354 dark web vendors and buyers in Operation TorNado, a coordinated crackdown spanning May 2025 through October 2026.

According to Europol, investigators targeted users linked to five previously shuttered marketplaces—Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, and Tor2Door—alongside encrypted messaging services and single-vendor shops. The United States led with 132 arrests, followed by the UK with fifty-nine, Hungary with forty-five, and Germany with forty-one. Authorities executed hundreds of searches, seizing over €210 million in combined cash and cryptocurrency, more than two hundred firearms, and nearly six metric tonnes of illicit drugs across the US and Europe, aided by Europol blockchain analysts tracing transactions.

Law enforcement's ability to exploit residual data from defunct sites demonstrates that marketplace takedowns increasingly serve as the starting point for long-term user identification, even as criminals migrate toward specialized platforms.

Check Point patches zero-day flaw exploited for root access and wiper attacks.

Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability allowing attackers to gain root privileges on vulnerable appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, the flaw stems from an unauthenticated local socket in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon. According to Check Point, threat actors compromised Mobile Access portals via the PHP2Shell bug, escalated privileges using this zero-day, deployed backdoors, and pivoted to VMware ESXi hosts to run destructive wiper malware across roughly two dozen customers.

Unauthenticated local inter-process communication exposes perimeter gateways to rapid privilege escalation and lateral destruction.

Campaign dubbed wfx-loot compromises 4,837 GitHub accounts to harvest cloud secrets.

A widespread supply-chain campaign dubbed wfx-loot has compromised 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than sixty-one thousand repositories and steal cloud credentials from at least 1,835 targets.

According to application security firm Aikido, the operation began November 10, targeting accounts linked to Fortune 100 firms, the US General Services Administration, and the French government. Attackers opened fake dependency audit pull requests to test write permissions, then injected a credential-harvesting shell script via GitHub Actions workflows or npm install hooks. The malware exfiltrated cloud tokens, artificial intelligence keys, and developer secrets—and even escalated privileges across Amazon Web Services, Azure, and Google Cloud—before reverting changes and deleting workflow logs in under a minute.

Automating secret theft across continuous integration pipelines turns compromised developer tokens into rapid, multi-cloud privilege escalation.

A Civil liberties coalition warns Congress against attaching Section 702 renewal to defense bill.

A coalition of twenty-seven civil liberties groups is warning congressional leaders against attaching a renewal of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act to the annual National Defense Authorization Act without adding a warrant requirement for searches involving Americans.

According to a letter led by Demand Progress and first reported by CyberScoop, the groups argued that slipping an unamended extension into the must-pass defense bill would circumvent bipartisan debate over constitutional rights, noting that existing court authorization allows intelligence operations to continue through March despite the law's summer lapse. Conversely, House Intelligence Committee ranking member Representative Jim Himes told The Hill that Congress should pass a reauthorization during the current lame-duck session before an incoming Democratic majority potentially imposes stricter limits next year.

The debate highlights the recurring tension between preserving rapid foreign intelligence collection capabilities and enforcing Fourth Amendment privacy safeguards through legislative reform.

United grounds personal AI agents over credential and compliance risks.

United Airlines is grounding artificial intelligence agents, blocking the digital assistants from booking flights or managing reservations on behalf of customers.

In a Wednesday press release, the carrier warned that handing account logins to third-party assistants exposes sensitive data and invites unintended purchases or rogue MileagePlus redemptions. Anyhoo, it turns out that even the smartest algorithm still cannot legally swear to the Federal Aviation Administration that your checked bag is free of explosives. United is updating its ticketing and distribution policies across its own platforms and third-party aggregators, echoing a similar password warning from Bank of America last week.

As enterprises struggle to distinguish legitimate bots from human travelers, Trua CEO Raj Ananthanpillai notes that outright bans merely delay the inevitable shift toward verified identity tokens.

And that’s the CyberWire.

articles.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
articles.context: Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026
articles.full_text: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI. From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse. “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe. “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.” This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching. “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.” What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit. “It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said. AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “super close to my heart.” “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.” Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale. Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance. Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling. Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

articles.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
articles.context: MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads
articles.full_text:
From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon’s MadPot, a globally distributed network of decoy threat sensors, captured requests from AI agents that included operating memory from offensive campaigns that threat actors ran on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.

Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate. Because activity against other organizations could not be confirmed, this post shares the findings and indicators of compromise (IOCs) so that organizations that run the affected technologies can review their own environments.

The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting. Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection. In aggregate, the agent records show that agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention. This post describes how these campaigns operated based on the agents’ own descriptions of the campaigns.

Attribution and instructions

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that ARTEX was used for these campaigns due to prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other technical artifacts referencing ARTEX. Threat actors instructed ARTEX agents through standing instruction prompts that set the mission objectives, targeting rules, and operational constraints. Within those instructions, the agents handled the work themselves. In one credential theft campaign, operators told the agents to work through a fixed sequence of countries, prioritize enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade every stolen credential by whether it worked and what it could reach. Agents were directed to treat credentials exposed publicly for more than 30 days as low-value inventory.

Amazon Threat Intelligence also assess with moderate confidence these are disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups due to use of simplified Chinese language in prompts, China time-zone configurations, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Sample instructions included setting red lines, such as excluding mainland China targets and government domains, and required all outbound traffic to go through proxies.

How MadPot saw inside these campaigns

MadPot presents controlled services to potential attackers and records how they discover, test, and attempt to compromise or abuse them. MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads. In this case, the MadPot sensors presented popular LLM-compatible chat-completions interfaces on various ports. Agentic frameworks sent prompts to these interfaces as part of their offensive workflows, treating them as LLM inference backends.

The resulting telemetry contained the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings that these frameworks ordinarily send to an LLM to make operational decisions. Because agentic frameworks retain the history of past conversations, individual requests often contain the full operational history of a campaign. That history described activity that occurred before and between the captured requests, on systems MadPot does not monitor. Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing.

Most of the activity used ARTEX to divide work among planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. The knowledge graph acts as the operation’s shared memory: every agent reads from it, and writes its results back, so each agent picks up where the others left off. The agents’ records described reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential theft, cloud-privilege expansion, and cryptocurrency fraud attempts across hundreds of targets spanning AI application platforms and other workloads. These records show how threat actors are organizing persistent, financially motivated offensive operations using agentic AI frameworks.

Campaign 1: Stealing AI credentials at industrial scale

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to steal API keys and other credentials that grant access to AI models, most likely so they could use those models while someone else paid for them. The agents’ records show stolen keys being fed into the framework’s own model gateway, where they powered the agents searching for more keys. Beyond AI model access keys, cloud credentials were treated as a doorway to more access. Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities. They prioritized access to premium frontier models over general cloud permissions.

Agents recorded use of different AI gateways, keys, and models, but they all used a shared method: find internet-exposed AI applications, extract the upstream provider keys they hold, validate those keys, and store them in a managed pool. The agents focused on applications that aggregate provider keys, because one weak management interface can expose many downstream accounts. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. A codified vulnerability playbook mapped each fingerprinted product to its known attack chain, including uninitialized installs that could be claimed, anonymous management and provider-configuration endpoints, default administrator credentials, such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files.

To find those keys, discovery drew on internet scanning services, certificate transparency, and public code and artifact sources: GitHub repositories and event archives (targeting secrets that fell outside automated revocation), npm and PyPI tarballs, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. One parallel operation worked through a fixed country sequence, prioritizing enterprise production sites, and graded every credential: L1 for a lead, L2 for a confirmed working API call, and L3 for quantified impact, such as readable data or spendable balance. Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days were treated as low-value inventory.

Campaign 2: Defeating identity verification with deepfakes

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to defeat the identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges with deepfakes. The agents’ records show generating real-time deepfake video to pass live selfie checks and forged ID document photos to pass document checks.

The records describe a methodical approach to the liveness check, which is a security method that confirms a person interacting with a digital system is a real, living human being physically present at the time of capture. The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move. Their best recorded attempt completed the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target. Even so, the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt the agents recorded. In parallel, a separate session built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. By splitting the model and avoiding unnecessary memory copies on the GPU, it reached 11.5 frames per second, close to what a live video check expects.

The agents worked on the ID document as well. Verification vendors look for signs that a document photo was edited or is a picture of a screen rather than a camera capture. To get past those checks, the agents recorded building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that re-saving an edited image would normally replace. The result is an altered image that looks, at the file level, like an untouched camera photo.

This campaign also shows how ARTEX runs several workstreams toward one goal. At least four agent sessions ran at once: one searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass. They shared findings and handed off tasks through cross-session tools.

What this means for defenders

None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker. The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.

Given the speed and persistence of the attackers, organizations should assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate accordingly. They should bring AI applications, model gateways, and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems, and they should watch for misuse of AI services through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

articles.title: Trezor confirms crypto-stealing implants in three wallets, releases fix
articles.context: The findings follow an investigation into a suspected hardware implant first reported in October, when a customer discovered an unauthorized circuit board inside a Trezor Safe 5...
articles.full_text:
Cryptocurrency hardware wallet maker Trezor has confirmed that three Safe 5 devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained malicious hardware implants designed to steal wallet recovery phrases and send them to attackers over cellular networks.

The findings follow an investigation into a suspected hardware implant first reported in October, when a customer discovered an unauthorized circuit board inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis.

At the time, Trezor had not received the device for examination and could not confirm the implant's capabilities.

In a new investigation update, the company says it has now examined the original device in its laboratory and identified two additional compromised wallets using photographs submitted by their owners.

All three compromised devices were purchased from CryptoBilis between August 20 and September 23, 2026.

Trezor says 48 CryptoBilis customers have contacted the company following its October warning, with devices being examined in its laboratory or through photographs of their internal components.

The company has also inspected devices from other resellers in the region and found no evidence of tampering.

So far, the confirmed implants have been limited to Safe 5 devices sold through CryptoBilis, and no affected customers have reported losing funds.

Firmware update blocks hardware implants

Trezor says its engineers analyzed the implant's firmware and confirmed that the malicious hardware can capture sensitive information displayed or entered on the wallet's screen.

The implant consists of an additional circuit board installed between the Safe 5's main board and display, allowing it to monitor screen activity without modifying the device's legitimate firmware or Secure Element.

When wallet recovery words appear on the screen, either during the creation of a new wallet backup or while restoring an existing wallet, the implant collects them.

It can also capture passphrases displayed on the screen, encrypt the stolen information, and transmit it over a mobile network to an attacker-controlled server.

If a connection is unavailable, the implant holds on to the captured data and repeatedly attempts to transmit it until successful.

These reported implants follow confirmed hardware implants previously discovered in Ledger devices sold through CryptoBilis, which have been linked to cryptocurrency thefts.

On November 11, Trezor released firmware version 2.13.1, which includes protections that prevent the implants from capturing information.

"Our latest firmware update 2.13.1, released on November 11th, includes a protection that stops the implants we’ve found from capturing anything on devices that run it, making the current batch of implants useless," Trezor said.

However, the company warns that the update cannot protect wallet recovery phrases that may have already been captured before it was installed.

While no Trezor customers have reported stolen funs, those who purchased Trezor devices from CryptoBilis are still advised to transfer their cryptocurrency to a newly created wallet using a new recovery phrase.

Trezor cuts reseller network by 80%

Due to these supply-chain attacks, Trezor has reduced its global reseller network by approximately 80%, significantly reducing the number of third-party resellers of its hardware wallets.

The company previously announced plans to reduce its reseller network in October, following reports of compromised Ledger wallets sold through CryptoBilis. This was before Trezor had learned of implants in its devices as well.

Trezor says the removed resellers were trustworthy and of no threat, but did not meet the stricter supply-chain security requirements being introduced.

Remaining partners must follow tighter controls governing how devices are sourced, stored, and accessed.

The company is offering replacement devices to anyone who purchased a Trezor wallet from CryptoBilis since March 2026, including customers whose devices have not been confirmed as compromised.

At this time, the company says it has found no evidence of device implants from other resellers and has received no reports of funds being stolen through the compromised Safe 5 wallets.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Crawls Back to Life After a 24-Hour Outage
articles.context: The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page
articles.full_text:
Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.

After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other users around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.

The outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with users reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.

The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.

“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson says in a statement. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.

As Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, users will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.

Microsoft said it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, users may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.

The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.

Ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” says Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

articles.title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
articles.context: Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively...
articles.full_text:
AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

Even in the most high-profile example of an AI powered attack to date, in which Claude Code was abused by Chinese state-sponsored actors to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025, conventional attack techniques and procedures laid the foundation, with AI abused as an enabler to support reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data analysis, and exfiltration during the GTG-1002 campaign.

JadePuffer, a ransomware campaign disclosed in July 2026, witnessed an LLM-driven agent automating most of the intrusion chain. Initial exploitation was through CVE-2025-3248, a year-old missing-authentication flaw in Langflow, a popular open-source framework for building LLM applications and agent workflows.

Vulnerable internet-facing Langflow instances were looted for cloud credentials, API keys, and other secrets before lateral movement, privilege escalation, and ultimately destructive database encryption.

JadePuffer shows AI’s potential for automating conventional attack methods, but it also underscores how vulnerable software is where AI has been giving attackers the biggest edge to date. AI tools can readily find exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders can patch them, a huge problem for the many enterprises carrying years of technical debt. And security experts see software flaws rising as a root cause of breaches as a result.

What AI enables

In addition to enhancing attackers’ flaw discovery prowess, AI is also enabling attackers to fail or succeed faster. Defenders are witnessing improvements in speed, scale, and operational ability from attackers that correlates strongly with increasing capabilities of AI tools.

“Adversaries are realizing the same gains in development velocity and operations that everyone else is getting from implementing AI,” says Darren Meyer, security research advocate at application security tools vendor Checkmarx.

Black Duck’s Lewis sees this expanding attackers’ reach and empowering more attack experimentation.

“An attacker can potentially investigate more opportunities, try more approaches, and move to the next target at a pace that would be difficult for a human team to match,” he says.

That in turn will increasingly alter a pivotal phase of conventional attack patterns that traditional favors defenders, notes Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at cloud security firm Sysdig.“That dwell time, which was often weeks or months, was where detection happened,” she says.

Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait.

‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization

By leveraging agentic AI in their operations, hackers can also draw on a deeper pool of domain expertise — database administration, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — compared to human attack teams where different people tend to specialize in different things such as web app security or malware development.

“Think of it as a database admin, a developer, an IT engineer, a DevOps specialist, a cloud architect, and a hacker combined into a single role,” says Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO and founder of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense. “We call it agentic APT, and the critical shift is that it is no longer exclusive to nation-state actors.”

Tymoshyk adds: “A threat that previously required a coordinated team of specialists can be deployed by a single person with the right prompt and the right model.”

Security researchers, including UnderDefense, report that attackers favor Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, which have significantly fewer content restrictions, rather than their more restricted Western alternatives as a platform to mount attacks.

“Attackers switch between models depending on what the task requires: one for reconnaissance, one for code generation, one for crafting social engineering content,” Tymoshyk says. “The modularity is part of the attack design.”

Attackers often prefer to use local models both because of operational security advantages and because some models may have weaker safeguards against malicious use.

Other experts cautioned that the abuse of particular models is difficult to determine and, in any case, a side issue to the main problem of defending against attacks.

“Attribution of particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation from very thin evidence on the ground,” says Checkmarx’s Meyer. “True attribution can only come from infiltration of threat groups or compromise of threat group infrastructure, both of which are rarely available to public researchers.”

The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining.

AI attack economics

The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI.

“A human attacker builds a playbook per campaign and reuses it, so every new target costs engineering time to make adjustments,” says Sysdig’s Morin. “An agentic threat actor carries context about a whole class of applications and composes its plan live against whatever it finds. There, the only cost is inference budget. And as running a complex attack gets cheaper, the number of attempts will go up.”

Agentic attacks are still flawed, and breadth of expertise is a poor substitute for depth of knowledge.

“Agents hallucinate and are noisy, which is often why they’re catchable,” notes Sysdig’s Morin. “Jadepuffer had flaws in its ransom note, encryption, wallet, and data exfiltration. There are still many areas in which human analysis and skill still outperform agent memory.”

Countermeasures

“The core objectives of the threat actor haven’t really changed, but the timeframe for a successful attack has been compressed dramatically,” says Nathan Smolenski, CISO at vulnerability management and compliance firm Qualys. “Frontier AI tools accelerate vulnerability discovery and weaponization, shrinking the window between disclosure and exploitation to near zero.”

Smolenski adds: “Defenders can no longer rely on traditional, human-speed 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets.”

AI significantly changes the entry dynamic by expanding the attack surface — particularly through end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents.

In response, defending organizations must shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defences while still keeping on top of foundational security defenses such as patching and authentication controls.

“Implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails enables security teams to automate lower-level triage efforts and focus human expertise on governing agents, validating outputs, and making more critical risk decisions,” Smolenski concludes.

articles.title: German military drone operations disrupted by cyberattack
articles.context: In July, another drone manufacturer, the Australian CubePilot, which also openly supports Ukraine, was targeted by a DNS hijacking attack that caused severe operational disruption
articles.full_text:
German defense technology company Quantum Systems confirmed that it detected an incident in late October that was part of an active cyberattack by "hostile actors."

The company responded quickly, working with relevant authorities to resolve the issue swiftly and ensure its unmanned systems could safely resume operations.

Quantum Systems is a German defense technology company that builds reconnaissance and interceptor drones, along with other unmanned systems and the software that controls them.

Its drones are in service with Germany’s military, and in October Germany announced funding to build tens of thousands of Quantum Systems interceptor drones in Ukraine for Ukrainian forces.

Quantum Systems believes it was targeted because of its recent announcement of support for Ukraine and says it is working closely with state authorities to investigate the attack.

“The European defense industry has been facing persistent cyberattacks for years,” Quantum Systems stated without making a specific attribution.

“Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers’ security.”

Update server compromised

According to reports from Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, the compromise occurred via a malicious QBase update file.

QBase is Quantum Systems’ ground-control and mission-planning software, so the point of the compromise was the vendor’s update distribution server.

Der Spiegel identified the Vector reconnaissance drone, known as Falke in German military service, as one of the aircraft whose missions are planned with QBase.

The German outlet reports that the unscheduled update delivered to customers raised alarms within Quantum Systems, but it is unclear how many actually installed it.

Additional reports claim that the German armed forces grounded Quantum Systems drones as a precaution, excluding the company's systems from a recent military exercise.

The response reportedly involves the military counterintelligence (MAD), the domestic intelligence service (BfV), and the federal cybersecurity agency (BSI).

In July, another drone manufacturer, the Australian CubePilot, which also openly supports Ukraine, was targeted by a DNS hijacking attack that caused severe operational disruption.

DNS hijacking could, among other things, be used to deliver malicious updates to downstream users of CubePilot’s drone systems, though such a level of compromise was never confirmed.
