articles.title: The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World
articles.context: “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable
articles.full_text:
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.

Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.

Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.

“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.

Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.

Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

articles.title: The Binance Aftershocks: Tracking the Nearly 130% Spike in Crypto Impersonation Scams
articles.context: Whenever an event of this scale hits, KnowBe4 Threat Labs routinely tracks an immediate surge in secondary attacks that exploit the chaos
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Emily Hanlon, James Dyer

On October 29, 2026, cryptocurrency giant Binance lost approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets in under half an hour. The attack, attributed to the notorious Lazarus Group, stands as the largest crypto heist in history.

But how was an attack of this scale pulled off?

The entire compromise appeared to originate at the human and endpoint layer: a compromised engineer’s machine. Even in high-tech, cryptographically secured ecosystems, targeting humans and their admin permission remains the easiest way into an organisation.

Attacks of this magnitude trigger immediate fallout. In the days following the attack through November 2, KnowBe4 Threat Labs tracked a 128.9% surge in crypto currency impersonation threats. Cybercriminals specifically zeroed in on fake wallet transfers and withdrawal alerts.

The Aftershock: When the Phishing Fallout Hits Inboxes

Threat actors are notorious for riding the wave of major headlines. As we found for the Phishing Threat Trends Report Vol 8., attackers are 5.4 times faster responding to headlines in 2026 than they were in 2022. Whenever an event of this scale hits, KnowBe4 Threat Labs routinely tracks an immediate surge in secondary attacks that exploit the chaos. The sudden influx in cryptocurrency-related phishing is testament to this.

Fallout attacks following a major breach almost always fall across three main vectors:

Brand impersonation:

Impersonation was the main threat vector exploited by attackers following the Binance hijacking. In less than 48 hours, Binance rose from the 73rd most impersonated organization in Defend’s dataset to the 23rd.

High-profile attacks create prime conditions for cybercriminals. Threat actors exploit psychological fallout, specifically availability heuristics and salience bias. Constant media coverage pushes “Binance” to the front of everyone's minds and cuts through inbox noise. Even users who rarely check their accounts suddenly zero in on any message bearing the breached brand’s name. Fear does the rest: worried that their own accounts are compromised, recipients act on impulse. Scammers can ruthlessly capitalize on this anxiety, knowing urgency and fear crush skepticism.

Example:

This phish rolled out mainly to UK and U.S. inboxes, deliberately using the same font colors and styling as typical Binance mail. The attackers likely leveraged generative AI to mimic Binance’s standard email templates. By exploiting brand familiarity, they amplify the urgency and fear that the recipient's account is part of the compromise. The email included embedded hidden characters throughout the text, disrupting linguistic-based detection of Binance brand impersonation. When users click the link, they’re prompted to “login” to authorize the cancelled request, inevitably handing credentials over. This phish deployed only 13 hours after the initial attack.

Shown below is a legitimate email from Binance. The phishing campaign accurately replicates this template that end users are unlikely to spot any visual indicators of compromise:

These impersonation lures extended beyond just “Binance.” In fact, 8.9% of all phishing attacks on Friday, October 30, contained the word “bitcoin” in the email, primarily in the subject and display name.

Top subject lines:

“Bitcoin Deposit Confirmation”

“<name> Update Your Bitcoin Details Now”

“Funds added to your Bitcoin wallet”

“Secure your Bitcoin wallet fast”

Recovery scams

High-profile exchange breaches reliably trigger a predatory second wave: recovery scams. Cybercriminals understand that when news breaks, users scramble in fear. Fraudsters capitalize on this chaos in two ways: first, by blasting fake security alerts that prompt users to "secure" or "re-verify" their wallets, a common credential harvesting lure, and second, by promising users who have lost assets reimbursement or recovery for a fee.

This triggers a cruel cycle of double-victimization. Desperate to recover lost savings, panicked users lower their guard for spoofed "claims portals" and end up signing away whatever assets they had left. Recognizing this pattern is critical: once an attack goes public, assume any unsolicited outreach, no matter how verified or urgent it looks, is an attacker trying to profit from the wreckage.

This campaign has similarly tried to match Binance's branding, pretending to come from the company’s internal insurance or risk division. To slip past automated link scanners, the attackers drop a plain-text URL directly into the body and instruct the recipient to copy and paste it into their browser. The address mimics a legitimate Binance domain at first glance, but swaps the "i" for a "1" and uses a .net extension. Once pasted, the link requests the user pay a small upfront fee to unlock ‘security advice’.

Spear Phishing

Right after a major exchange breach, phishing gets much smarter. Attackers drop the generic spray-and-pray emails and start using the actual details of the incident as bait, knowing everyone is glued to the news waiting for updates.

One of the sharpest vectors targets third-party partners and contractors. Posing as internal incident response teams or forensic investigators, the attackers send emails dangling "Confidential Forensic Reports," "Urgent IoC Feeds," or "Emergency Security Questionnaires." Tucked inside is usually a password-protected ZIP, a poisoned PDF, or a malicious cloud link. The moment an engineer opens it, malware drops quietly onto the machine—setting up a foothold inside partner networks using the exact same playbook that started the breach in the first place.

This phish relied on techniques that work even against alert, well-trained employees. Attackers increasingly go beyond simply avoiding detection and instead they actively limit telemetry from the email itself so detection engines view the emails as “safe.” This email used CEO impersonation to exploit a user’s natural reluctance to question a senior leader, using a spoofed authority figure alongside real organizational stress, pressures staff into skipping normal verification for a payment, access request, or file. This email used PDF-based malware delivery which doesn't require clicking a link inside the document: a crafted PDF can run embedded scripts or exploit the reader itself the moment it's opened.

How Has this Impacted Different Countries and Industries?

In the days following the finance hit, the U.S. was the biggest target for cryptocurrency phish, taking nearly 70% of hits, with the UK behind holding 18%.

Top industry proportions:

Industry

Percentage of the cryptocurrency phish received by industry

Insurance

32.4%

Finance

26.9%

Law

19.4%

Education

12.9%

Dominant attack techniques across industry:

📑 Insurance - 32.4%

They have an average of nearly three tactics per email, aimed to overwhelm both traditional defenses and the user. They blend executive impersonation, BEC, fear-driven extortion, and heavier technical tricks into multi-layered traps designed to slip past defenses. This is a typically aggressive and chaotic technique.

💸 Finance - 26.9%

Finance is completely dominated by brand impersonation, where scammers clone recognizable banking portals and software alerts to harvest login credentials. Because finance teams are conditioned to click through security dashboards and transaction notices all day, attackers simply mimic those routine tools instead of reinventing the wheel.

📜 Law - 19.4%

Legal practices see a lethal mix of personal extortion and high-stakes corporate wire fraud. Attackers know that attorneys deal in tight confidentiality and massive settlement transfers, so they skip fake login pages and go straight for the jugular: personal blackmail or hijacking actual payment chains. It’s less about mimicking big software brands and more about exploiting human panic and professional reputation

🔢 Education - 8.9%

The threat landscape here is about as blunt and generic as it gets, heavily skewed toward automated, copy-paste sextortion blasts. Scammers aren’t burning precious zero-days or drafting elaborate ruses — they're playing an untargeted numbers game across thousands of easily accessible university inboxes.

How To Defend Your Organization

Treat all "recovery" and "refund" outreach as a scam: Real exchanges and insurance divisions will never reach out unsolicited, ask you to pay an upfront fee for "investigation advice," or demand you connect your wallet to an external claims portal. Once an attack goes public, assume any offer to restore lost funds is a predatory second-wave trap.

Never verify accounts through links or copied URLs: Following a massive breach, scammers flood inboxes with fake security alerts using lookalike domains and plain-text URLs to bypass automated scanners. If you receive a warning about unauthorized activity, open a new browser window and navigate directly to your bookmarked login page.

Confirm urgent executive demands: Threat actors weaponize organizational stress and executive authority to rush staff into skipping protocol. If an email claims to come from a senior leader demanding urgent action, wire transfers, or sensitive file downloads, verify it through a separate channel, rather than replying to the email.

Remember, just because it looks real doesn’t mean it is. When major headlines break, always expect the phishing aftershocks to follow.

articles.title: PostgreSQL Patches 52 Flaws, Including 22-Year-Old Bug Enabling Authenticated RCE
articles.context: " The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes
articles.full_text:
A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none.

The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server.

The server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type.

Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week.

His method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command.

He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes.

Red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, says in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code.

Ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015.

He also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status.

The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release.

The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers.

Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output.

What Administrators Should Do

Update the server to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, or 14.25, matching your major version.

Rebuild or update every C-language extension at the same time as the server. Extensions built against older releases still load, but they "may not be protected from the vulnerabilities fixed in this release," according to a repository notice from the project's RPM package maintainers. Some extensions will also need source-code changes.

Extensions rebuilt for the new releases can fail to load on older servers. Extension packages in the project's RPM repositories now require the new minor release.

If PostgreSQL runs outside its package's own service unit, for example under Patroni, restart it right after updating, a maintainer of the RPM packages says in a packaging blog post.

Update client tools such as pg_dump, pg_restore, reindexdb and vacuumdb on every machine that runs them.

Do not use the new composite_type_mismatch setting to turn off the checks. The project says doing so carries security risks.

The project's advisory and release notes offer no workaround for servers that cannot be updated yet.

PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life, and 14.25 is its last release. Older major versions are also affected and received no update.

After updating, follow the reindexing steps in the release announcement. If you use incremental backups, take a new full backup and base later incremental backups on it.

articles.title: New York City votes to ban surveillance pricing
articles.context: Malwarebytes Personal Data Remover finds them and gets your information removed, then keeps watch so it stays that way
articles.full_text:
Two people shopping for the same product shouldn’t have to wonder whether one is paying more because a company knows more about them.

That’s the concern behind a bill passed by the New York City Council on November 12. The legislation targets surveillance pricing, defined as using personal data and algorithms to offer different people different prices for the same goods or services.

Introduction 891-A would prohibit these practices in transactions with consumers in New York City. It would also restrict collecting, selling, or sharing personal data to facilitate surveillance pricing. The bill is at the mayor’s desk and would take effect one year after becoming law.

For consumers, the issue goes beyond an unexpectedly expensive shopping cart. It’s about companies turning information about your life and online behavior into a tool for deciding what to charge you.

Learn more about surveillance pricing in this episode of our podcast Lock & Code:

Large-scale data collection also creates risks beyond pricing, including sensitive inferences about people and unauthorized disclosure of their information.

What exactly is surveillance pricing?

Surveillance pricing uses information about you, or a profile a company has built about you, to help determine the price you see for a specific product or service.

That information can include your location, browsing history, shopping habits, and demographic characteristics. In initial findings published in January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said pricing tools could draw on surprisingly detailed behavior, including mouse movements and the products people leave unpurchased in their online shopping carts.

This is not some conspiracy theory. There is evidence that the tools and data pipelines exist. The FTC’s findings drew on documents from pricing and technology intermediaries. Staff reported that the intermediaries examined worked with at least 250 clients across sectors including groceries and apparel. The published examples were hypothetical to protect confidential business information.

Surveillance pricing should not be confused with dynamic pricing. Dynamic pricing can respond to changing market conditions, such as demand or availability. Surveillance pricing uses personal information to differentiate between customers. While the two can overlap, they aren’t interchangeable.

A personalized price isn’t automatically a higher price. Some shoppers might receive discounts. The concern is that an opaque pricing system gives sellers detailed insight into customers while those customers are unable to see how they’re being assessed.

Another form of unequal pricing that the bill allows is qualifying loyalty and other discounts. The bill preserves genuine discounts, including qualifying loyalty and rewards programs and discounts for clearly defined groups such as veterans, seniors, and teachers. But those exceptions come with conditions.

Surveillance pricing doesn’t necessarily charge wealthy shoppers more and give everyone else a break. Pricing tools can estimate what you’re willing to pay, which may have little to do with what you can comfortably afford. Perceived price sensitivity is a deciding factor, so a wealthy bargain hunter could receive a discount, while someone with less money but an urgent need or few alternatives could be judged willing to pay more.

For consumers, the underlying question about surveillance pricing is straightforward: How much does the price reflect what’s being sold, and how much does it reflect what a company thinks it can get out of you?

New York City’s bill aims to limit how companies use your personal information to make that calculation.

Your name, address, and phone number may already be for sale.

Data brokers collect and sell your personal details to anyone willing to pay. Malwarebytes Personal Data Remover finds them and gets your information removed, then keeps watch so it stays that way.

articles.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay without seeing your card number
articles.context: Luke Gebb, who heads global innovation at American Express, called the wallet the company’s “first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration
articles.full_text:
OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Wallet, which lets ChatGPT agents pay for purchases with a stand-in card number, so the user’s card details are not shared with the agent or the merchant. OpenAI built it with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa. It runs inside dots, where a user’s dot completes the purchase on their behalf.

Merchants will have to do most of the adjusting. OpenAI says some websites may block agent purchases without meaning to, and fraud systems may flag legitimate ones, which ends in declines or cancellations. A retailer that tuned its defenses to stop automated checkout now has to tell wanted bots from unwanted ones.

How a purchase goes through

A user adds a card once. Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, the total, and the chosen card, then approves with Face ID, a fingerprint, or a similar check. The payment network then issues a token, which is a substitute card number with its own security code and expiration date, and the charge lands on the real card behind it. The card keeps its rewards and its protections for eligible disputes.

What sites need to fix

OpenAI published a Commerce Partner Playbook alongside the launch. It asks sites to set their CDN or firewall to recognize Web Bot Auth, a method for verifying signed requests from bots. It also asks them to work with their payment and risk providers on spotting agent purchases. OpenAI is working with the fraud vendors Forter, Riskified, Sardine, and Signifyd, and with the payment providers Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe. The tokens work with existing checkout flows. The risk engines sitting in front of those flows may still say no.

Luke Gebb, who heads global innovation at American Express, called the wallet the company’s “first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration.” For now, access is limited to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US who are 18 or older and hold eligible US-issued cards.

articles.title: KnowBe4 and AWS: Behind Every AI Advancement Is Strong Collaboration
articles.context: What a Strong Foundation Makes Possible The results of the AWS collaboration brings these concrete benefits to our engineering teams and ultimately our customers: 1
articles.full_text:
Delivering AI-native security awareness training through the KnowBe4 Platform to more than 70,000 users means collaboration.

Collaboration takes many forms. Our people working together. Our departments working together. And as KnowBe4 has grown, our infrastructure, DevOps, and site reliability engineering teams have collaborated with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to streamline architectural improvements that support changing demand and simplify data sharing across products.

The Problem

As a recent AWS case study explores, the sheer size of the global employee base using KnowBe4 Security Awareness Training could lead to processing delays and backlogs. Usage peaks came at the start of the week, the month, and the business day, across the United States, Europe, and Southeast Asia.

Our engineers needed a centralized infrastructure channel to manage communication across all components and locations, enabling greater reliability and more robust integration capabilities for our customers.

What a Strong Foundation Makes Possible

The results of the AWS collaboration brings these concrete benefits to our engineering teams and ultimately our customers:

1. Two features reached production three months ahead of schedule.

2. Dozens of AI projects are now in development, each run by teams of two to four engineers supported by AI coding agents.

3. Engineering productivity on net-new development is up to 10x what it was 12-24 months ago.

Long story short: Streamlined infrastructure means lean and recurring innovation directed straight at our customers and their users.

This foundation also supports AIDA Orchestration, our autonomous AI agents that generate and deliver personalized security awareness training and personalized phishing simulations across your entire workforce, without the need for human administration.

"Building on AWS helps us ship new risk indicators faster," says Matt Duren, SVP of Engineering for AI and Data. "We're at 316 today, and the number keeps growing every year."

Keeping AI development within AWS helps our engineers get started quickly and use common development patterns across model providers. The KnowBe4 team also reinforces continuous learning through an internal certification program with incentives for engineers to earn associate-level certification within their first 12 months.

AWS AI Competency: Proof Takes a Team

Results like these are what the AWS AI Competency, recently awarded to KnowBe4, exists to recognize. The designation honors AWS Partners that demonstrate technical proficiency and proven customer success building on foundation models to automate domain-specific work.

Earning it is a collaboration of its own. The process requires a valid AWS Foundational Technical Review, evidence of AI technical controls, including a documented Responsible AI framework, and four production customer examples from the past 18 months, at least two of them public. KnowBe4's engineering, security assurance, alliance marketing, and business development teams pulled that evidence together alongside AWS partner and solutions architect counterparts.

A credential like this is a record of people on both sides asking hard questions and sharing what they know.

The Real Lesson

AWS secures the infrastructure. KnowBe4 helps secure the humans and AI agents operating within it. That is the shared-responsibility model in practice, and it only works when both sides show up.

No single vendor has all the answers, especially as AI changes how attackers and defenders work. The organizations moving fastest pair deep expertise with trusted partners.

articles.title: New Mior and Skyfall Attacks Let Rogue Cloud Hosts Steal Secrets From AMD SEV-SNP VMs
articles.context: Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out
articles.full_text:
Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out.

One of them, Mior, can also modify a VM's memory and fake the signed report confirming which software it runs. Both need control of the server's hypervisor, and Mior also needs control of the server's BIOS. Researchers showed both in lab tests on AMD EPYC server processors.

AMD, which makes the processors, lists SEV firmware for Mior and microcode for Skyfall, both dated August 12. It plans to give server makers platform firmware in November for Skyfall and in December for Mior, and fixes for embedded chips later. Customers are told to get the BIOS update from their server maker.

SEV-SNP brings confidential computing to AMD EPYC server processors. It uses hardware-enforced memory encryption and access control to protect a VM, even from the host's hypervisor.

The ETH Zurich team behind Mior attacked SEV-SNP while it was starting up. During start-up, a security co-processor on the chip, the Platform Security Processor (PSP), fills in a table called the Reverse Map Table (RMP). The RMP records who owns each page of memory and what they may do with it.

The team redirected the PSP's writes to the memory of a graphics card it controlled, instead of to main memory. The team used a card because it believes the PSP reads the values back to check them, and the card could return them. Start-up then finished without errors, but part of the real RMP, including the entry that protects the table itself, stayed uninitialized.

That let the hypervisor rewrite the RMP's protections. The team then enabled debugging on a confidential VM that had it disabled and used the PSP's own debug commands to read and write the VM's memory. This worked in all 1,000 attempts across both test runs.

SEV-SNP also measures a VM's software image when the VM starts, and the PSP signs attestation reports that include this measurement. In a second test, the team copied a harmless VM's measurement into a malicious VM, so the malicious VM's attestation reports described the harmless image instead.

The attack needs control of the hypervisor and the BIOS (also called UEFI), plus a PCIe device such as a graphics card, the Mior paper says. For the tests, the team modified the BIOS to leave the chip's memory-routing settings unlocked.

"We operate in AMD’s threat model defined for SEV-SNP. AMD explicitly distrusts the UEFI, thus an attacker can modify the UEFI," the researchers say.

Ordinary VMs already trust their host and its firmware, so Mior gives an attacker nothing new against them, the team says.

The team ran Mior on one EPYC 9135, a Zen 5 chip. It considers Zen 3 and Zen 4 chips potentially affected but did not test them because it had no setup that allowed it to change their BIOS.

The debugging and attestation tests both worked with ciphertext hiding turned on. That optional SEV-SNP feature stops the hypervisor from even reading encrypted VM memory.

Two earlier attacks by some of the same researchers, the Fabricked attack and the RMPocalypse attack, also corrupted the RMP as SEV-SNP started up. Mior is a separate flaw, unrelated to Fabricked and to the fix for it, the team says. It also worked on older firmware from before that fix.

Skyfall comes from a team at ETH Zurich and Google. It builds on Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA), a group of flaws in AMD processors that can leak data through instruction timing. TSA was first disclosed on July 8, 2025.

The team found that when a hypervisor intentionally causes a VM to fail to start, the processor has already cached part of the VM's saved state. That data is left behind without the usual cleanup, and the hypervisor can read it through TSA.

This way, the team recovered a VM's saved register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM. For the key, it changed the VM's kernel to pause at the moment the key sat in registers. In a real attack, the team says, a hypervisor can instead use a technique called SEV-Step to step through the VM until the key reaches the registers.

Skyfall can also read VM memory, but only three fixed cache lines in a page it targets, at offsets 0x0c0, 0x380 and 0x3c0. The rest of the page stays out of reach.

The attack needs a malicious host or hypervisor, but no tampering with the hardware. The team tested it on an EPYC 7313, a Zen 3 chip, and on EPYC 9124 and 9334 chips, which are Zen 4. It did not show the leak on Zen 5 chips.

Beyond VMs, the Skyfall team read decrypted microcode updates on all three test chips. It also recovered register values stored in System Management Mode (SMM) memory, which even the operating system kernel normally cannot read. Both of these attacks need privileged software on the machine.

The program committee of the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, which accepted the Skyfall paper, said it overlooks what a realistic attack on VMs would need. That includes a processor core free of other activity, failing VM starts and performance-counter reads at high speed, and a VM that does not crash or time out during the attack.

Affected Processors and Fixes

AMD tracks Mior as CVE-2026-0462 and rates it 5.9 on the CVSS 4.0 scale in a security advisory. It tracks Skyfall's VM leak as CVE-2026-40671, rated 4.9, in a second advisory that describes the flaw as exposing VM register data.

For Mior, the company lists only SEV-SNP as affected, not the earlier SEV and SEV-ES versions.

It lists the same five EPYC server lines for both flaws, with these fixes:

As listed in the two advisories

EPYC series

Mior platform firmware (target)

Mior SEV firmware (August 12)

Skyfall platform firmware (target)

7003

MilanPI-SP3_1.0.0.L (December)

1.3A.03

MilanPI-SP3_1.0.0.L (November)

8004

GenoaPI_1.0.0.K (December)

1.3A.4

Genoa_100J Patch 3 (November)

8005

TurinPI_1.0.0.C (December)

1.3A.0A

TurinPI_1.0.0.C (November)

9004

GenoaPI_1.0.0.K (December)

1.3A.4

Genoa_100J Patch 3 (November)

9005

TurinPI_1.0.0.C (December)

1.3A.0A

TurinPI_1.0.0.C (November)

The two advisories give the same TurinPI_1.0.0.C package different target months. Microcode for Skyfall is dated August 12 for each of these lines. The Instinct MI300A accelerator has a Skyfall patch dated September 21, and fixes for embedded EPYC models are due between January and April 2027.

The Mior team says updated firmware that mitigates the flaw is already out, and the Skyfall team says new microcode has been released. The advisories do not say whether those updates work on their own or only as part of the BIOS updates, and they list no workaround.

Supermicro, a server maker, has published a BIOS fix list covering flaws in dozens of its H12, H13, and H14 motherboards. The same pages say the boards also need a BMC firmware update and that the company is still testing affected products.

Because the fixes are implemented in the host's firmware, customers who rent confidential VMs depend on their cloud provider to install them. The advisory covering Mior also lists TCB (trusted computing base) values for SNP attestation next to each fixed firmware version. It does not say how VM owners should check them.

Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been used in attacks. Both teams have published code, and the Mior proof-of-concept code needs a BIOS patched to leave the memory-routing settings unlocked.

The EDK II project assigned Skyfall's SMM leak CVE-2026-18448 and rates it 5.6. AMD's EDK II bulletin traces it to missing TSA mitigations in EDK II firmware code.

The bulletin lists EPYC and Ryzen chips, including embedded models, and recommends the company's earlier TSA mitigations plus an EDK II patch when one is available.

For the five EPYC server lines listed above, the bulletin lists only that patch, due in November. Platform firmware with the fix is already available for other chips, including the EPYC 4004 and 4005 models. The EDK II project's own advisory lists no patched version as of today.

articles.title: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach
articles.context: This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help...
articles.full_text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Ex-FBI agent’s $2.47M crypto theft compromised bureau investigations

Patrick Steven Yaroch, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, faces up to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to wire fraud and money laundering over the theft of roughly $2.47 million in cryptocurrency. Yaroch used wallet credentials stored on FBI systems to make about 100 fraudulent transfers tied to 35 investigations. He took funds from investigation subjects and adversarial nation-state actors, and the thefts compromised multiple investigations and FBI sources and methods.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Baker Tilly client data taken from supplier’s platform

US accounting giant Baker Tilly is informing clients that hackers stole personal information, including Social Security numbers, from a platform operated by one of its service providers. The intrusion dates to early September and also affects clients’ dependents, including children. The firm has not named the vendor or said how many people are impacted in total, but state regulator filings point to more than 10,000 victims in Texas alone.

OpenAI agents concealed unauthorized activity

OpenAI has revealed new details about a July incident in which five AI agents conducting cybersecurity evaluations gained root privileges in CI workloads on the company’s research clusters. The agents used credentials and scripts left by earlier agents to modify evaluation settings, repair broken targets, and access restricted information. Two agents recognized that their activity was unauthorized and omitted it from their final submissions after considering how disclosure might affect their scores.

Prompt injection chain could have backdoored OpenAI’s Codex npm package

Depi researchers have described an attack chain against OpenAI’s Codex repository that started with a prompt injection in a GitHub Actions workflow and could have led to a malicious Codex release on npm. The issue-labeling workflow passed the title and body of any new issue to the Codex agent, so an attacker could execute code in the agent’s sandbox, read tokens from a GitHub runner process’s memory via .NET debug pipes, and poison the cache of a workflow with write permissions. The final step relied on a maintainer deleting a rogue release, which would yield a token trusted by npm. OpenAI has fixed the issue and awarded an initial $1,000 bounty.

Siemens details security advisory policy and planned improvements

Siemens has published a policy document that sets out how its PSIRT deals with product vulnerabilities and what its security advisories contain. Planned improvements include an API for automated lookups of product and vulnerability data, wider coverage of flaws in third-party components, more explicit “not affected” declarations, and getting advisory data into commonly used third-party vulnerability databases.

VulnCheck: Glasswing fixes lag far behind findings

VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity says that seven months after Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, he has tracked 442 CVEs credited to the company (about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year), only two of which are known to have been exploited in the wild. Anthropic’s own ledger listed 37,966 findings as of November 2, but only 7,349 have been made public and 217 are marked as fixed, while more than 1,600 have been flagged as duplicates and 419 withdrawn.

Railway puts unauthorized spend from stolen AI keys at $740,000

Railway has released a detailed incident report on the October attack, in which a threat actor used an undiscovered flaw in its build infrastructure to partially escape isolation, obtained a copy of the company’s code repository, and then abused a misconfigured OIDC binding to reach credentials that let it decrypt customer environment variables. At most 1.85% of workspaces (roughly 100,000) could have had variables decrypted. Linked-account tokens for 1,852 users were also exposed, and unauthorized spending on stolen keys is estimated at about $740,000. Railway believes the attacker wanted AI provider keys to sell for use in distillation, and says it will cover losses that providers do not refund.

Exposed MS SQL servers hijacked to deliver cryptominer and Gh0st RAT

Fortinet has analyzed a campaign in which Go-based malware with the open source Naabu scanner built in looks for internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances, and a companion tool then brute-forces logins using a list of more than 2,700 passwords. After a successful login, T-SQL commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or drop a loader, which installs a Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge update and a Gh0st RAT variant whose features include keylogging and data theft.

Microsoft urges weight audits after ‘Lazarus’ dormant neuron backdoor research

Microsoft researchers have described Lazarus, a technique that backdoors an LLM without any training by rewriting the weights of fewer than 10 dormant neurons, so that an agent built on the model behaves normally until a trigger (such as a date or an error message) makes it emit an attacker’s command. In a demonstration, a modified Nemotron-Terminal-8B model that was debugging a server issued a command to download and run a remote script after seeing a “Connection refused” message. Because the attack needs write access to the weights and can only be reliably detected by comparing them with the originals, Microsoft recommends verifying model provenance and auditing weights the way code is audited.

Connected cars exposed by flaws in automakers’ ForgeRock deployments

Researchers Sam Curry and Shubham Shah have disclosed weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity deployments of unnamed automakers that allowed them to take over customer accounts and send remote commands to connected vehicles, including unlocking doors and starting engines. In one chain, a WAF bypass let them reach an Apache Felix console that still accepted default admin credentials, giving them code execution on production identity servers used by two automakers, which fixed the issue roughly two hours after it was reported.

Palantir CISO LoSapio nominated to fill long-vacant CISA director post

President Donald Trump has nominated Michael LoSapio, Palantir’s CISO since September 2024, to lead CISA, which has not had a Senate-confirmed director since Jen Easterly left in January 2025, Nextgov reports. Should the Senate fail to act before this Congress adjourns, Trump would need to renominate him under an incoming Democratic majority whose members have questioned Palantir’s government work. Sean Plankey, the earlier nominee, pulled out in April following a wait of over a year.

Vanderbilt tells campus to power down devices amid attack claimed by BYOD group

US-based Vanderbilt University this week told everyone in its community to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi as its IT team worked on an active cybersecurity incident that it said could affect devices, systems and cloud-based services. The BYOD group has taken credit for the attack.

articles.title: How one AI agent exposed five critical enterprise security gaps
articles.context: Yet 82% had found agents they didn't know about in the past year
articles.full_text:
Imagine an AI agent being created. Not by an identity team, nor by a security professional. This one is built by someone in accounts at a mid-sized company.

The agent’s job is relatively simple: read an inbox, match invoices against the ERP, and post a daily summary to Slack. And since a frontier model was used to build it, it's a one-shot, 10-minute task.

Nobody in security knows the agent exists.

There's nothing unusual about this. In a survey of 418 IT and security professionals commissioned by Token from the Cloud Security Alliance in January 2026, 68% reported having strong visibility into their AI agents. Yet 82% had found agents they didn't know about in the past year.

The evolution of agents is so rapid that the security playbooks are being written on the go. The people responsible for agent security need to figure things out in production, one problem at a time.

At Token Security, we asked more than 20 of them to write down what they've learned for the Agentic Universe, a free learning hub.

Below, we follow this one agent from the afternoon it was built to the audit after it went wrong, and stop at five points where one of those practitioners could have changed the outcome.

Day One: How the agent got its access

Our agent needs access to three systems: email, the ERP, and Slack. It gets emails via the no-code builder, using an OAuth consent screen. The ERP is trickier, but not by much. The agent’s creator can generate a personal API key in minutes by following the AI's very helpful instructions. Slack comes in through the builder's own Slack connector, with one more consent screen.

That's two of the four access paths John Donovan, former Head of Security, IT and Compliance at Zededa, lays out in How do AI agents access sensitive systems and data?:

Riding a human's session: Browser extensions and in-app copilots that act as the user.

Using a delegated OAuth grant: The user approves scopes once, with a single click, granting the agent access that lasts until someone revokes it.

Utilizing static credentials: API keys and service account passwords, usable by anyone who finds them.

Acting through purpose-built agent identities: Registered, short-lived, and tied to one agent. The ideal and rarest scenario.

Donovan's point is that real agents mix these, and each mix changes what you can see. Say an agent hands a user's OAuth token to a sub-agent, which calls an MCP server that queries a database with a shared service account.

The database log shows the service account. The SaaS audit log shows the user. The identity provider shows nothing at all.

The access path determines what appears in your logs, so ideally you’ll understand it for each agent in the company. Also, be mindful of OAuth grants, as they don’t usually get revoked by the IdP and can remain active long after the person who approved them changes jobs.

The Agentic Universe from Token Security

Here's the thing, nobody's been here before.

In this all-new world of AI Agent Security, take a journey with the practitioners at companies like Roblox, Amex, and more who are actually doing the work to secure AI.

Check out their playbooks

Day Two: The review that never happened

The agent goes live the next morning. Nobody reviews it because nobody was asked to.

Had someone looked, one test would have flagged it. In How do you make an AI agent Secure by Design?, Amber Bennoui, Product Leader for AI and Cybersecurity at DataRobot, builds on the Agents Rule of Two, which Meta's AI security team published in October 2025.

Until prompt injection can be reliably detected and refused, an agent should have no more than two of these in a single session:

A: It processes untrusted input.

B: It can reach sensitive systems or private data.

C: It can change state or communicate externally.

Our agent has all three. It reads email from anyone who knows the address, it sees vendor bank details in the ERP, and the personal API key it runs on can do anything its creator can do in the ERP, including editing those bank details.

Ideally, Bennoui says, you make the safe path the default, then ask builders to answer three plain questions: does your agent read anything from outside the company, can it see private data, and can it act without a person checking first?

Anyone who answers yes to all three has to talk to security before switching the agent on.

Week Three: The malicious email no one opens

The Slack summaries are genuinely useful, and the agent owner is satisfied. They’re thinking about what else can be automated with agents. Just then, an invoice lands in the inbox from the address of a known vendor. Inside the attachment, in white text on a white background, is a note requesting an update to the ERP as the vendor changed its bank.

No person reads that email, but the agent does, including the hidden text, and it makes the change.

In How are AI agents compromised?, a five-minute video, Joshua Copeland, a CISO and cybersecurity researcher, shows how instructions can get into an agent. Some arrive directly from whoever can talk to it. Others ride in on the content it reads, including an email nobody opened.

Either way, the result looks clean in your logs: an authorized tool, a valid credential, permitted work.

Copeland also explains why stealing an agent's credentials can be worse than compromising the agent itself. For this agent, that's the personal ERP key from day one, saved in the builder with no expiry date.

Ideally, you treat every input an agent reads as something that can issue orders to it. Then you make sure no single input can lead to an action you can't undo.

That Thursday: Catching it

The bank change goes through on a Thursday. Whether anyone notices depends on what your detection compares the agent against.

If it compares the agent against its permissions, nothing fires. In The Compromised and Rogue Agent Detection Checklist, Chad Kalmes, CISO and CIO at Benchling, warns against that baseline, because a misbehaving agent can stay inside its grants the whole time.

He baselines on what the agent actually does over a window you can trust, such as the tools it calls and the places it sends data.

Against that baseline, two of his signals fire here:

First use of a tool, even a permitted one. For three weeks, the agent has only read from the ERP. The bank change is its first write.

A new sequence. Reading an email and then changing a payment record is an order of operations the agent has never run.

Kalmes distinguishes a compromised agent, which follows an attacker's instructions, from a rogue one, which causes damage while following legitimate instructions. The signals mostly overlap.

When you act, suspend the agent without destroying it. Revoke the credential, but keep its memory and transcripts. The poisoned invoice may still be in there.

Day Sixty: Who approved this?

Two months later, the auditors pull the bank change from the agent's history and ask who approved it.

In What audit evidence do you need for AI agents?, Rajesh Seshadri Appikulam, Senior Director of Identity Security Services at Simeio, lists the four questions an auditor asks about an agent's action: which agent did it, under what entitlement, with whose approval, and on whose authority.

The first is easy. The last is the hard one, because authority can't be rebuilt after the fact.

Unless the human behind the request and the delegation chain were recorded at the time of the action, they're gone.

For our agent, the record is thin. The ERP log shows the creator's personal API key, so the bank change appears to be their doing. The response team revoked that key, but the agent owner moved to another team last month, and their OAuth grant to the inbox is still live.

Appikulam closes with a ten-question test. Each should take under five minutes. Start with two:

Pick any agent action from 60 days ago. Can you name the human it acted for?

For any agent in production, can you name its owner today?

If either takes longer than five minutes, you know where to start.

One agent out of hundreds

The agent we followed is imaginary, but agents like it aren't. As we've mentioned at the beginning, 82% of respondents in the CSA survey had found ones they didn't know about. Each fix above came from someone who first encountered the problem in production and wrote down a solution.

The Agentic Universe holds the rest of what they wrote.

More than 20 contributors, including security leaders at Roblox, Klaviyo, and Webflow, cover the field from how agents work to how you respond when one goes wrong, in formats from short videos to checklists you can run against your own environment. It's free and ungated.

Explore the Agentic Universe

Sponsored and written by Token Security.

articles.title: Fake GTA 6 download goes after Steam logins and crypto wallet data
articles.context: Cynet researchers followed a “GTA 6 EXE file download” link from a Google Colab notebook to a ZIP archive and found a WARDEN Stealer loader inside
articles.full_text:
Cynet researchers followed a “GTA 6 EXE file download” link from a Google Colab notebook to a ZIP archive and found a WARDEN Stealer loader inside. The malware takes saved passwords, browser cookies, Steam and Roblox credentials, and cryptocurrency wallet data from the machine it runs on.

A Google Colab notebook promotes a fake GTA 6 executable download (Source: Cynet)

Grand Theft Auto VI launches November 19 with no PC version. Any site offering a PC installer is offering something other than the game. People searching for early access or a leaked build are the target, and this sample shows how much work the lure puts into keeping them clicking.

The installer tells you to turn off your defenses

The Colab link led to a page called “Windows Software Hub,” which showed a version number, a download count, and “Virus Free,” “Secure,” and “Verified” badges. The page advertised a 72 MB download. The archive held a 796 KB executable and a 1 KB README. A download page and a file manager measure different things, so the size mismatch proves little by itself. The README proves more: it tells the user to run the file as administrator, click past a security warning, and add an antivirus exclusion if the file is blocked.

The binary contains no game engine, no game assets, and no Rockstar signatures. It checks whether it is running in a virtual machine or sandbox, injects code into browser processes, replaces cryptocurrency addresses copied to the clipboard, and can download more malware.

What to block

Cynet named uroker[.]casa as the probable command-and-control server, which is the machine the stealer reports back to. The company published SHA-256 hashes for the executable and the README. It also listed 104.21.75[.]176 but warned against blocking that address because it is a shared Cloudflare IP.
