articles.title: Gootloader Malware Disrupted After Infecting 25,000 Computers
articles.context: Department of Justice announced that law enforcement has removed Gootloader malware from more than 100 computer servers, seized U
articles.full_text:
International law enforcement disrupts Gootloader, seizing domains and taking down over 100 servers linked to 25,000 infected computers.

The U.S. Department of Justice announced that law enforcement has removed Gootloader malware from more than 100 computer servers, seized U.S. domain names used to deliver and control it, and notified victims worldwide.

“The Department of Justice today announced the successful removal of malware known as “Gootloader” from over 100 computer servers, including compromised WordPress sites, and the seizure of U.S. domain names used by criminals to deliver and control the Gootloader malware. Since 2018, Gootloader malware has infected at least 25,000 computers around the world.” states DoJ. “Gootloader malware has been used in ransomware attacks of at least 44 U.S. based victims which has resulted in approximately $28.8 million in loss.”

Gootloader spreads mostly through compromised WordPress sites and other websites, where victims are tricked into downloading it thinking they’re getting something legitimate. Once a machine is infected it joins a botnet, and the people running Gootloader then sell access to those machines to ransomware groups. The ransomware groups do the rest, and the total losses to US-based victims alone reach roughly $28.8 million across at least 44 victims, including the Department of War and the Defense Industrial Base.

GootLoader runs on an access-a-as-a-service model, it is used by different groups to drop additional malicious payloads on the compromised systems. GootLoader has been known to use fileless techniques to deliver threats such as the SunCrypt, and REvil (Sodinokibi) ransomware, Kronos trojans, and Cobalt Strike. In the past, GootLoader distributed malware masquerading as freeware installers and it used legal documents to trick users into downloading these files.

GootLoader is a part of the GootKit malware family, which has been active since 2014. Mandiant tracked the threat actors behind GootKit as UNC2565.

The law enforcement operation ran under court authorization and in coordination with Operation Endgame, the multinational law enforcement initiative targeting malware criminal services. Partners included Germany’s BKA, the Netherlands National Police, Canada’s RCMP and Ottawa Police Service, Danish Police, France’s Paris Cybercrime Brigade, the UK’s National Crime Agency, the Australian Federal Police and Europol. OpenAI, Fraunhofer FKIE, the Shadowserver Foundation and hosting company Sharktech also provided technical help.

“According to warrants unsealed this week, Gootloader is malware that infects victim computers through a variety of means, often by tricking unsuspecting individuals into downloading it. Once infected, the compromised computers are added to a network of other compromised computers known as a botnet.” continues the report. “The actors behind Gootloader used the botnet to infect other computers, then sell access to those later-infected computers to ransomware actors.”

The Shadowserver Foundation worked with internet service providers and national computer security response teams to find infected machines, tell victims what had happened and help them clean up. Visitors to any of the seized domains now see a law enforcement seizure banner instead of the malicious content. The investigation was led by the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the FBI’s Denver Field Office and Army Criminal Investigative Division.

“Dismantling the Gootloader malware and botnet, which infected over 25,000 systems worldwide, demonstrates the power of unified, international law enforcement operations,” said Director L. Scott Moreland, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division. “Alongside our global partners, Army CID is committed to taking the fight directly to cybercriminals. While disrupting these criminal networks stops ransomware attacks before they can take root, true cyber resilience relies on a combination of global law enforcement action and everyday personal vigilance.”

Since 2020, CCIPS has secured convictions of more than 220 cyber and IP criminals and court orders returning over $500 million to victims. More details on Operation Endgame can be found at operation-endgame.com.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gootloader)

articles.title: FBI Says North Korean Hackers Stole Over $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls
articles.context: Exploit the victim's Telegram account: The attacker impersonates the victim and sends tailored messages to other contacts on their behalf, proposing a Zoom or Teams meeting...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months.

As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized.

In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement.

"North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months."

According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025.

The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff, which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069.

The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust.

"The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust."

A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure.

In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram.

This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles.

The entire attack plays out as follows -

Compromise a victim: This involves harvesting cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, and other valuable access; hijacking their Telegram account or other communication app and locking them out; gaining access to their contacts and chat histories; and secretly recording them during the video chat.

Exploit the victim's Telegram account: The attacker impersonates the victim and sends tailored messages to other contacts on their behalf, proposing a Zoom or Teams meeting under the pretext of discussing an investment opportunity.

Set up the meeting: Should the target express interest, the attacker sends a Calendly invite via Telegram to schedule the video meeting. Shortly before the scheduled meeting time, the victim's Telegram account is used to send a typosquatted link that masquerades as a meeting URL for Zoom ("uu01webzoom[.]us") or Teams ("teams.livemeet[.]us").

Exploit recorded videos: When the target joins the fake Zoom meeting, the attacker plays an already recorded webcam video of the trusted contact and plays other videos, either recorded or deepfake videos, to give the impression that there are multiple participants in the meeting. In addition, headshot images generated using OpenAI ChatGPT are used as static avatar placeholders on the fake calls.

Trick the target into infecting themselves: The attacker sends a message to the target, claiming there is an audio issue or some other technical error (e.g., a deprecated Zoom SDK), and urges them to click on a link to apply an update to address the problem. Alternatively, it can take the form of running a script or copying and pasting malicious code into the command line or Terminal. This results in the deployment of malware that can capture sensitive data from the compromised device, effectively turning the target into the next victim.

Repeat the cycle: With the victim now compromised, the attacker gains control of their device and social media accounts to propagate the attack to their contacts.

Attacks mounted by BlueNoroff are known to specifically single out individuals working in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, along with individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT).

More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume."

In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E.

Deepfake video production pipeline (credit: Arctic Wolf)

"A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority."

The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos.

"Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added. "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves."

BlueNoroff's updated attack flow (credit: Arctic Wolf)

Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation.

"Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said.

From FaceStealer to Contagious Interview

It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview, an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns.

Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart.

"The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said. "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me."

"The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code."

According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries.

The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code -

Embedding malware in coding tests, repositories, or packages that victims are asked to run as part of an assessment process.

Using Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json configuration files to automatically trigger the execution of malicious code when the project is opened in VS Code.

Using .githooks/pre-commit and post-checkout scripts to fire the malicious code on first commit or branch change.

Using trojanized installers for macOS utility apps to deliver OtterCookie by means of a shell script downloader.

Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code.

"The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said. "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload."

The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview.

Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added.

What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step.

"Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page."

articles.title: Trezor Confirms Hidden Implants in CryptoBilis-Sold Wallets That Can Steal Recovery Phrases
articles.context: So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models
articles.full_text:
Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from the reseller CryptoBilis contain an implant, an extra circuit board that can copy their recovery phrases, hardware wallet maker Trezor said yesterday.

The implant reads the phrase from the wallet's screen and sends it over the mobile network to a server controlled by the attackers. The company examined one of the wallets in its lab, identified the other two from photos their owners sent, and has had no reports of lost funds.

A firmware update released earlier this week, version 2.13.1, stops the implants found so far from capturing anything on wallets that run it, the company said, but “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.”

The company has not changed its advice to anyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, including from the reseller's stores on Tokopedia and Shopee:

Move your funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase. Restoring the old phrase on another wallet does not solve the problem.

Do not set up an unused wallet from the reseller, and never type an existing recovery phrase into one.

Keep the wallet and contact Trezor Support, which offers a new Trezor wallet to anyone who bought from the reseller since March. Contact Support too if you are not sure where your wallet came from.

Do not weigh or open the wallet to check it. Neither is a reliable test.

Never share your recovery phrase, as the company will never ask for it. Scammers may pose as the company to offer replacements or refunds.

Version 2.13.1 was released for the Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3 and Model T, according to the company's firmware changelog. The company will not publish technical details that could help attackers or put customers at risk, it said in an investigation update.

Its engineers extracted and analyzed the implant's firmware from the first wallet it reported. The implant sits between the Safe 5's main board and its screen and changes nothing on the wallet itself, including its firmware and Secure Element, the company found.

The implant copies the recovery phrase when the wallet shows it during backup creation, and when someone types it in to restore an existing wallet to the device. It also copies a passphrase if one appears on the screen. It encrypts the data before sending it, and if it cannot connect, it keeps the data and tries again until it succeeds.

The company first warned of a suspected implant on October 30, two days after a buyer reported it and before its lab had seen the wallet.

CryptoBilis served as an official reseller for the company's wallets in Southeast Asia until October 9, when the company removed it. That was the day Ledger, another hardware wallet maker, began investigating losses of funds among the reseller's customers.

Ledger later confirmed an unauthorized implant in a wallet the reseller sold. Attackers had fitted genuine Ledger devices with hidden components designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup, then drained wallets in a single coordinated operation, Ledger said in an incident statement.

Trezor says the implants in its wallets work the same way as those found in Ledger devices, adapted to the Safe 5's display. It has not said who fitted the implants or where in the supply chain that happened.

The three wallets were bought between August 20 and September 23. So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models.

After the October reports, it asked people who bought a Trezor from the reseller to get in touch, and 48 have done so. It is checking their wallets in its lab or from photos of the insides, and has not said how many it has checked so far.

The company says none of the three owners has lost funds. Trezor wallets are self-custodial, so it cannot see anyone's balance.

The company says it has cut its reseller network by about 80%, dropping trustworthy partners that posed no immediate threat but did not fit its stricter new rules. It first announced the reduction on October 13 in a post on X, more than two weeks before the first report of an implant in one of its own wallets.

In a partner letter that day, it told the dropped resellers that they would get no new stock, could sell what they had until January 1, 2027, and would then be removed from its list of authorized sellers.

It is still investigating. It will post an update if it confirms an implant outside the reseller's wallets or the Safe 5, receives a report of lost funds linked to the implants, or releases new protections.

articles.title: Microsoft Struggles to Restore Email and Other Services in a Global Outage
articles.context: “They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack
articles.full_text:
From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue.

Microsoft said the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements,” and that there was “incremental improvement in several workloads.” But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company’s services and anecdotal reports on social media.

Microsoft scrambles to recover services

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.”

The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control.

Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.

An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution.

“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote.

In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”

“Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.”

Governments, businesses from Japan to Australia affected

The British government said it is “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” are in place to minimize disruption.

British police forces said they’re unable to receive crime reports online and are urging people to call emergency responders to make any urgent reports.

The National Pharmacy Association said people could face delays getting their prescriptions because the outage is affecting the email systems of the state-run National Health Service. Hospitals urged patients to attend appointments as usual.

U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.

Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

“They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company could not receive updates from its U.S. customers throughout Outlook. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.

Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

The Philippines’ Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that officials were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

articles.title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
articles.context: "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday
articles.full_text: Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding. The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion. "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday. "Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators." It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years." The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground. The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones. "The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details. Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years. Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

articles.title: Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls
Apify Confirms Customer Data Accessed in Cyberattack
articles.context: The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation
articles.full_text:
Web scraping and automation company Apify has confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack that compromised internal systems and customer accounts.

The Czech company provides a cloud platform for collecting information from websites and automating online tasks. It says it has 91,000 customers worldwide.

The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation.

According to the company, the attacker used a compromised credential to obtain additional credentials and gain access to related Apify accounts.

On November 12, Apify confirmed that some customers had their personal information or stored data accessed during the attack.

The company has contacted customers whose information was exposed. Those who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected so far, although the investigation is continuing. Apify has not disclosed the number of compromised customer accounts.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to an Apify customer who shared a breach notification on Reddit, the exposed information included names, email addresses, billing details, account activity, and IP addresses.

More importantly, the notification listed salted password hashes, 2FA recovery codes and phone numbers, and authentication tokens associated with Google and GitHub sign-ins among the compromised data.

The notification also indicated that payment card information was limited to cardholder names, expiration dates, and the last four digits of card numbers. Full card numbers and security codes were not exposed.

The company has implemented additional monitoring, changed critical internal secrets, and revoked some OAuth connections to third-party services, including GitHub.

Apify said its investigation had not found that the OAuth connections could have been used as an attack vector. Customers building Apify Actors from private GitHub repositories have been instructed to reconnect their GitHub integrations.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Outage Set to Ramp up Security Risks to Organizations
articles.context: ), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted
articles.full_text:
While the global outage of Microsoft 365 services that interact with Exchange Online, significantly Outlook, is not believed to be cyber-related, security teams will need to be on high alert for threats related to the incident.

As the tech behemoth grapples with the fix, cybercriminals will be poised to take advantage of the chaos by launching a surge of convincing phishing campaigns and fake support scams designed to dupe individuals and employees desperate to reconnect to M365 services.

Marie Wilcox, VP of market strategy at digital forensics firm Binalyze, said, “Just because this outage wasn’t caused by a cyber-attack, doesn’t mean attackers won’t seize the opportunity.”

In an update on November 13, the Australian National Cyber Security Coordinator Michelle McGuiness warned people to “remain vigilant and be cautious of unsolicited contact” as cybercriminals often seek to take advantage of the uncertainty.

Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre issued an update recommending everyone exercises caution around unexpected calls and messages, especially those containing links.

It is likely that threat actors will begin to send phishing messages, claiming to be the Microsoft brand in order to trick people in this time of uncertainty.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Jake Moore, Global Cybersecurity Advisor at ESET, said that this kind of disruption is the perfect excuse for cybercriminals to hit organizations with targeted calls posing as IT support.

“Affected employees are literally waiting by the phone (or scrolling on social media!), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted.

Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, said that affected businesses like banks and shops should be particularly vigilant.

“Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email,” he said.

Microsoft is one of the brands most leveraged by threat actors for phishing campaigns. In an October update, cybersecurity firm Check Point noted that in Q3 2026 Microsoft accounted for 33% of all brand phishing attempts, up from 23% in Q2 2026 and roughly four times the share of any other brand.

Read more: Phishing Dominates as Initial Entry Method for Cyber-Attacks, as Hackers Hone Evasion Techniques

Defenders Should Treat Outage as Security Incident

Binalyze’s Wilcox said that many security teams themselves will have been locked out of tools they depend on to prevent trouble, for example Microsoft Defender XDR or important alerts pushed via Outlook.

She noted that when email services return and workers are beginning to clear the day’s backlog, this is when they will be most susceptible to trusting any messages that looks like they came from Microsoft – especially fake security updates.

During the outage period it will also be easy for suspicious activity to go unnoticed while alerts were not being monitored as usual.

“A suspicious sign-in or a new inbox forwarding rule is easy to miss when everyone is focused on getting email back,” she said.

“The wisest approach is for security teams to treat the outage window as an incident in its own right. That means going back over sign-ins, mailbox rules, account changes and endpoint activity from the hours when visibility dropped, and collecting evidence directly from devices rather than relying on the platform that was down,” Wilcox advised.

At the time of writing, Microsoft’s latest update said recovery efforts are ongoing across the impacted infrastructure. “We are seeing early signs of stabilization, but service capacity has not yet returned to normal levels and health remains variable as traffic is carefully reintroduced.”

Image credit: Mijansk786 / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
articles.context: Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting.

As the company explained in a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects users attempting to print documents with images that have zero height or width on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.

"After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said.

"These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present."

The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications.

Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature.

More recently, the company notified customers that the August 2026 .NET Framework cumulative updates broke printing and PDF export in apps that use the Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) UI framework.

This week, Microsoft also confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates trigger Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday cause SQL Server performance and stability issues.

Additionally, the company warned that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

articles.title: SilentAir Hackers Intercept Calls, SMS From Inside Mobile Networks
articles.context: SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators
articles.full_text:
Telecom software and cybersecurity company Enea has detailed the activity of a previously unknown threat actor that intercepts phone calls and text messages through compromised mobile operator infrastructure, with Taiwan as its main target.

The company tracks the group as SilentAir and assesses with high confidence that it’s a new state-level actor.

Enea’s researchers also believe, with low confidence, that SilentAir’s activity is aligned with China-nexus operations. Their reasons include the hackers’ interest in Taiwan, the absence of Chinese targets, and attack timing consistent with a workday in China’s time zone.

SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators. The attacks route a target’s incoming calls and SMS messages through the compromised node and harvest subscriber details.

The hackers can also track a target’s location, but this makes up only a small part of their activity. They send silent SMS messages, which don’t appear on the recipient’s phone, possibly to check whether earlier interception attempts succeeded.

Enea has monitored the attacks since early 2025, and further digging revealed suspicious activity from before that.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The hijacked nodes belong to operators in at least six Asian countries. Besides Taiwan, the group has targeted a dozen other countries and territories, occasionally going after people in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. High-profile political and government figures were among those targeted.

The report also covers 2026 activity from Liminal Panda, a group that CrowdStrike linked, with low confidence, to China-nexus operations. Enea says it’s the only actor known to actively exploit the IPX, the interconnect network that mobile operators use to exchange traffic.

Starting in the first quarter of 2026, Enea spotted and blocked Liminal Panda’s GTPDoor backdoor at several of its mobile operator customers. In total, it caught several hundred attempts to covertly reach command-and-control servers.

Enea says it has seen potential infections at between five and ten operators. It estimates that the total could reach several dozen, particularly in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

According to Enea, SilentAir and Liminal Panda could be connected, although the evidence isn’t strong enough to link them.

articles.title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
articles.context: The last two matter more than the first
articles.full_text:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.

AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.

First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”

The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.

What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.

All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.

A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.

AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.

There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.

Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.

Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.

Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.

These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.

The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.

Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.

This problem shows up often in myth.

In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.

In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.

More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.

The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.

If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.

Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.

In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.

If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.

Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.

We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.

We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.

We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.

I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.

Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.

We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.

A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.

Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.

There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.

Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.

AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.

Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.

Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.

Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.

Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.

Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.

Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.

Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.

Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.

AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.

Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.

Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.

Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.

Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.

These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.

Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.

Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.

Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.

The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?
articles.context: The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect
articles.full_text:
Suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action.

That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls.

An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents.

Turning off the model may not stop the work

An AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect.

The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received.

That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services.

When should a team contain an agent?

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context.

Signals that warrant a closer look include:

The agent calls a tool or accesses a resource outside its assigned task.

It attempts an unusual volume of reads, writes or exports.

A workflow continues after an operator believes it has been paused.

The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect.

Identity, application or network logs show activity that does not match the agent’s normal work.

The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded.

A practical response sequence

1. Pause the affected workflow

Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely.

A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow.

2. Revoke or limit the agent’s access

Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used.

Revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire quickly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it.

3. Restrict tools and network paths

Disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues.

This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations.

4. Preserve evidence and establish what happened

Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs.

Then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions.

5. Contain downstream effects

If the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes.

Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed.

Restore access carefully

Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy.

Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution.

Prepare before the incident

An incident response plan is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know:

Who owns it and who can suspend its runs.

Which identity, credentials, tools and systems it can use.

How to revoke its access and block its network connections.

Which logs show its actions and the results.

How to investigate changes and restore the workflow safely.

Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event.

An effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows.

With Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

articles.title: Apple details Secure Exclaves, isolated runtimes for camera and microphone data
articles.context: In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system
articles.full_text:
Apple published details of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture designed to protect camera and microphone data during background processing. Apple says data processed and analyzed within Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or the company itself.

The company uses Secure Exclaves for person recognition on HomeView, as well as for Siri Recap and Live Rewind. The architecture also protects the on-screen camera and microphone indicators on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView.

Protecting background sensing

Ambient sensing uses the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. It reduces sensor streams to simple signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or an enrolled user was recognized. During ambient sensing, raw audio and video remain protected within Secure Exclaves and are discarded once processing is complete, without reaching the main operating system.

The architecture supports two modes. In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system, with a secure indicator informing the user that this is happening.

Apple built the isolated environment around three requirements. Isolation prevents the main operating system from extracting or modifying data processed within Secure Exclaves. A controlled interface limits what can cross that boundary to a precisely defined set of information. Secure indication lets users see whether an active sensor session is in progress, without interference from the main operating system.

“Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP),” Apple explained.

The microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that identify a resource and authorize access to it.

The exclaves run in a separate processor execution context with an independent operating system. The Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), which runs at a higher privilege level than the main operating system’s kernel, enforces memory isolation.

Exclaves communicate through Secure IPC. Apple audits each interface to the main operating system to limit outgoing information to the metadata needed for ambient sensing.

The Exclave Indicator Controller allows full sensor data to flow to the main operating system only after confirming that the indicator is on and has been visible long enough. On HomeView, it controls the LED directly and ensures that it is bright enough to be visible. On iPhone, a display exclave checks that the pixels used to render the indicator meet a minimum brightness threshold and are not obscured by nearby pixels.

How HomeView recognizes people

At startup, the person recognition exclave loads enrolled face and voice models and an identity database from the secure storage exclave.

Person recognition flow on HomeView (Source: Apple)

The camera exclave detects faces and queues frames for processing, while audio exclaves handle anomaly detection and echo cancellation. They can notify the main operating system that someone may be present without sharing images or audio.

The Neural Engine exclave generates face and voice prints using isolated work queues, clearing its state after each model finishes. An orchestration service matches the prints against the identity database and combines the results into a confidence score.

Only the person’s identifier, position, and confidence level reach the person recognition daemon in the main operating system. These outputs support identity-dependent features in Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, and compatible third-party audio and video apps from an iPhone. No audio or video leaves Secure Exclaves during recognition.

What comes next

Apple said it will continue hardening Secure Exclaves through AI-accelerated vulnerability research and broader formal verification coverage. The company described the architecture as a step toward giving users greater clarity and confidence about how their Apple products respond to the world around them.

articles.title: Google pushes second Chrome update this week
articles.context: Technical details Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability
articles.full_text:
On November 11, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.78 for Linux. It includes 83 security fixes, five of which are rated Critical—the highest severity level. This update came out only two days after the previous one.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.79 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability.

A use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability happens when software accesses memory after it has released that memory for reuse. The program still has a reference to the old location, but the original object is no longer valid, and something else may now occupy that space.

The leftover reference is called a “dangling pointer” and is caused by a mistake in managing how long an object remains available. One part of a program may release it while another still expects to use it. That can happen because of confused ownership, faulty error handling, or a timing issue between tasks running simultaneously.

The consequences range from crashes and corrupted data to information leaks and, in some cases, execution of attacker-controlled code. The dangerous possibility is that an attacker can influence what replaces the freed object, then trick the program into treating that replacement as legitimate data or instructions for what to do next.

That explains why UAF flaws can receive critical severity ratings. However, the label describes a class of memory-management bugs, not a guaranteed outcome: the actual impact depends on the affected component, how reliably an attacker can exploit the mistake, and the protections in place.

Stop threats before they can do any harm.
