articles.title: SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users
articles.context: Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week
articles.full_text:
A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

Mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

For interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

Some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the company saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the company said points to a single controller.

The attacks came in bursts, from one or a few subscribers to several thousand over a month, with gaps of up to several months or longer between bursts.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the company could not see that traffic.

The company spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

The networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

The company then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

Detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

The report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

SilentAir also sent silent SMS on a very large scale, mainly to subscribers in Taiwan. These are texts that the phone does not display or alert on.

During the day, most silent SMS went to subscribers on other networks, such as Southeast Asian networks. One of their main uses appears to have been checking whether a diversion had worked, the company said.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

Most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company said the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

The company's low-confidence link to China rests on several signs. SilentAir focused on Taiwan and did not target Chinese networks or subscribers.

Its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

The company also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

In several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two showed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency said CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea said SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the company's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

The GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The company also found evidence of a new version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries users' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

What Enea Recommends for Operators

The company said any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:

Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls and configure them to share information with their SS7 and Diameter firewalls.

Go beyond the industry's basic recommendations for signaling security.

Treat the whole IPX as untrusted.

Add detection for signaling protocols inside their own networks.

Connect signaling security with the rest of their IT security.

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

articles.title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Operation TorNado
articles.context: Europol’s 2026 Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment names the replacement of shut-down markets as a current trend, with criminals moving fast to new platforms
articles.full_text:
Europol and police in 14 countries arrested 354 dark web vendors and buyers in Operation TorNado, which ran from May 2025 to October 2026. Investigators went after people who had traded on five marketplaces that were already offline: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom and Tor2Door.

Seized money (Source: Europol)

The people who used those markets were still exposed after the sites went dark. Police also went after vendors and buyers on forums, single-vendor shops and encrypted messaging services, and carried out hundreds of house searches.

The US made the most arrests

The United States made 132 of the arrests. The UK followed with 59, then Hungary with 45 and Germany with 41. Finland made one arrest and conducted 159 interrogations.

US authorities seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of drugs, 152 firearms and over €150 million in cash and cryptocurrency. In Europe, police seized 950 kilograms of drugs, 57 firearms, more than one million prescription tablets and over €60 million in cash and crypto. The US drug haul is about five times the size of Europe’s.

Europol traced the money

Europol sent staff to Czechia and Slovenia during the operation. It also coordinated the national cases so investigators didn’t end up chasing the same suspects twice. Its blockchain analysts traced the illegal transactions.

New markets keep appearing

TorNado follows earlier Europol operations, including RapTor in 2025, SpecTor in 2023, Dark Huntor in 2021 and DisrupTor in 2020. Europol’s 2026 Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment names the replacement of shut-down markets as a current trend, with criminals moving fast to new platforms. The same assessment says marketplaces are splitting into platforms that each focus on one kind of crime.

articles.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
articles.context: This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem
articles.full_text: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

articles.title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
articles.context: Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative...
articles.full_text: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively. Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience. The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition. Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns. "Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said. "A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence." As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK. Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made. Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped. The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements. A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals. "The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said. "This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before. "Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused." Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

articles.title: Citrix Patches 10 Critical NetScaler Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs
articles.full_text:
Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs.

The critical flaws stem from memory overflow issues in Packet Processing, SMPP traffic, DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), NetScaler Push, Email OTP authentication, Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS), and ICA proxy, and could lead to unpredictable/erroneous behavior or denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.

They are tracked as CVE-2026-120868, CVE-2026-107407 to CVE-2026-107410, CVE-2026-107412, CVE-2026-107415, CVE-2026-111334, and CVE-2026-120864.

Most of the remaining 19 security defects are high-severity weaknesses leading to similar outcomes. Citrix also patched several medium-severity bugs, including CVE-2026-111338, which exposes sensitive authentication material in a log file.

NetScaler ADC and Gateway versions 14.1-73.57 and later, 13.1-64.39 and later, 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later, and 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later contain the relevant patches.

Citrix urges customers to update their instances as soon as possible, and details CVE preconditions associated with some of the vulnerabilities.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, the company also announced patches for a critical-severity flaw in NetScaler Console. Tracked as CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score of 9.4), it could allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass controls and access restricted resources.

The security defect impacts all NetScaler Console 14.1 releases before 14.1-74.34.

Citrix makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but vulnerabilities in NetScaler are a frequent target for threat actors.

articles.title: Microsoft confirms Windows activation failures after November updates
articles.context: While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates are causing Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes.

According to a Wednesday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation and licensing processes or use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter (SWbemObjectEx), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said.

"Devices that are being configured to use KMS activation might encounter errors when attempting to initiate their activation. KMS-activated devices typically remain activated for up to 180 days following successful activation."

The activation failures occur after executing the 'slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain>' and 'slmgr.vbs /ipk <key>' commands on client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) devices.

However, Microsoft added that customers with the KMS client key installed in their image and who don't use SLMGR for licensing management are unaffected.

"Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted.

While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business.

In January, Microsoft addressed another known issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because affected devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses.

This week, it also confirmed that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues.

articles.title: OpenAI’s Daybreak brings AI agents to security testing and vulnerability fixes
articles.context: Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI is bringing AI agents into more of the software security process with Daybreak, pairing web application penetration testing with tools that investigate vulnerabilities and develop fixes. The two offerings, Red Team and Defense Factory, connect the work of finding security weaknesses with patching and retesting them.

Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes

Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and context, investigate potential attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities. It can validate findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions and vulnerability disclosure reports, giving security teams evidence to help prioritize repairs.

Validate reported vulnerabilities (Source: OpenAI)

Once a patch is ready, Red Team can test whether it blocks the exploit. Assessments run within defined boundaries, using isolated environments and Guardian review to control which applications and endpoints agents can reach, according to OpenAI.

Defense Factory investigates vulnerabilities and prepares patches

Defense Factory handles the remediation side. Agents investigate findings from existing security tools or Red Team, trace vulnerabilities through the code and prepare proposed fixes. Engineers review and test patches before merging them, while Codex lets teams examine evidence, supply additional context and refine changes.

Put your existing security tools to work on fixes (Source: OpenAI)

Teams with access can install and enable the Daybreak Defense Factory (Preview) plugin in ChatGPT and connect a GitHub repository. Cloud scans run in Codex cloud, and each person starting a scan needs a personal GitHub connection. Scans can cover an entire repository’s default branch or selected folders and files.

Choose how to scan a repository (Source: OpenAI)

Teams can monitor new commits on the default branch, schedule recurring scans of that branch and enable security reviews of pull requests before changes merge. The desktop app also supports scans of local checkouts and uncommitted changes, with an optional Deep scan mode that makes multiple passes and uses additional time and tokens.

articles.title: OpenAI Unveils Daybreak Red Team, Defense Factory Security Tools
articles.context: The products, Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, were announced at the company’s Cyber at the Frontier event on November 12
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has introduced two new Daybreak cybersecurity products that use AI agents to test web applications for vulnerabilities and help security teams develop fixes.

The products, Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, were announced at the company’s Cyber at the Frontier event on November 12. Red Team focuses on penetration testing and vulnerability validation, while Defense Factory investigates security findings and prepares patches.

Daybreak Red Team uses multiple AI agents to identify and investigate potential security weaknesses in web applications. “Agents use source code and app context to investigate attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities,” OpenAI says.

The product can examine findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions, and vulnerability disclosure reports.

OpenAI says the agents operate in isolated environments, with Guardian review enforcing testing boundaries and controlling which applications and endpoints they can access.

Daybreak Defense Factory, meanwhile, is designed to help organizations address vulnerabilities identified by their security tools.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Agents trace vulnerabilities through your code and develop patches. Engineers review and test proposed patches before merge,” OpenAI explains.

Defense Factory can investigate findings from Daybreak Red Team and other security products, and supports importing vulnerability information from Wiz, Snyk, and Endor Labs. The product can scan connected GitHub repositories, monitor new commits, and perform scheduled security assessments.

Engineers can examine supporting evidence, modify proposed patches using Codex, and create draft GitHub pull requests. However, patches are not deployed automatically.

OpenAI is accepting requests for early access to Daybreak Red Team. Defense Factory is offered through a preview plugin in ChatGPT for workspaces with Daybreak access.

articles.title: AI Set to Revolutionize Ransomware Following “Stagnant” Few Years
articles.context: However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities...
articles.full_text:
Ransomware will be revolutionized in 2027 due to the influence of AI, with threat actors poised to become more innovative, according TrendAI’s director of cybercrime research, Bob McArdle.

“Ransomware has been pretty stagnant and boring for the past couple of years, at least if you’re a researcher like me,” he told the audience at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11.

To date, ransomware actors have primarily used AI to enhance the speed and efficiency of campaigns. This includes the use of AI tools to identify the most important data once inside an organization’s environment, while some groups have deployed chatbots to carry out the initial negotiation stages on their behalf.

However, the overall process of ransomware attacks, from the use of initial access brokers through to the double-extortion method, have not changed.

“That’s a drop in the ocean compared to where we’re going with ransomware next,” McArdle warned.

Devaluation of the Initial Access Broker Marketplace

One expected change is around how initial access is gained to victim’s environments. In the current ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem, initial access brokers typically sell access to affiliates through techniques like compromised vulnerabilities and stolen credentials.

However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities rapidly.

“Anything that’s connected to the internet and is misconfigured or has vulnerabilities will be compromised,” he commented.

This will devalue the initial access market and, as a result, McArdle expects brokers to adapt their business model towards offering privilege escalation to ransomware groups.

Post initial access, tools like Artex and AI agents will allow attackers to shrink down the “kill chain” to machine speed.

McArdle also observed that many organizations are centralizing their data storage, which is good for business efficiency purposes amid the growing use of AI for data processing.

However, this centralization will provide new opportunities for threat actors. This includes ransomware groups threatening to tamper with the AI orchestration around organizations’ data as a further extortion technique.

Another area in which AI will benefit ransomware groups is its ability to process data effectively, enabling actors to quickly develop datasets of high value data, which will be easier to sell on to other malicious actors. This approach will provide even more profit-making opportunities for these actors.

“Over 2027, we will start seeing an inflection point where you have extortion-based business models of ransomware living side-by-side with the actual data theft and sales models increasing every year,” McArdle explained.

Hostile Takeovers by Ransomware Groups

With AI making ransomware attacks easier to undertake, McArdle expects to see a growth in the number of ransomware groups in the next year.

This further fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem will likely lead to large groups frequently undertaking “hostile takeovers” of smaller actors.

“We will start seeing Conti and LockBit level groups effectively acquiring smaller groups for their technology or even just their affiliate networks,” he added.

articles.title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
articles.context: Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it
articles.full_text:
On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.”

Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure.

The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead?

A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled

Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop.

It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works.

Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue.

That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself.

The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path.

What a fallback has to do

I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover, patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name.

Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then.

The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live.

The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them.

Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals.

The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope.

How I’d build fallback-first today

If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live.

A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident.

A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it.

Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns.

A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it.

Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day.

None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone.

Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull.

Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

What’s affected by the Microsoft 365 outage

What Microsoft has said about the cause and recovery efforts

Where to check for updates and what to keep in mind about security

A widespread Microsoft outage is disrupting Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services, including SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot. Reportedly, the problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued into Friday, affecting people trying to access email, communicate with colleagues, and use workplace applications.

Microsoft initially reported problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas, but disruption subsequently extended beyond that region. CNN reports impacts on businesses, schools, and government services, including in Australia.

There are a lot of questions we’ll try to answer as the day evolves.

What’s affected?

Outlook users have reported being unable to send or receive emails or even load their inboxes. Other affected services include SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot, although availability has varied: some people have been able to use certain applications while others remain inaccessible.

Outage tracker Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

What’s the cause?

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said there was no indication that malicious activity or a cyberattack caused the outage. The underlying cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said some servers became unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks. That left the remaining infrastructure handling extra traffic, contributing to connection problems. The underlying reason for the failures was not immediately clear.

Recovery has not been straightforward. Microsoft restored some servers, but subsequently said they could become unresponsive again when traffic returned. Other attempted changes also failed to deliver the expected improvement.

Update November 13, 10:01 UTC (05:01 EST): Microsoft says it currently has no evidence that malicious activity caused the outage. The company says it will publish a full post-incident report once mitigation is complete, detailing the root cause and additional safeguards to help prevent similar incidents.

How long will it take to restore services?

At the time of writing, Microsoft has not provided a timeframe for full restoration. The company reported partial recovery in some regions, after earlier attempts produced mixed results.

For updates, check Microsoft’s service status page and its Microsoft 365 Status account on X. Both are channels Microsoft is using to communicate about the incident.

Update, November 13, 09:57 UTC (04:57 EST): Microsoft says its latest traffic optimization measures are producing “positive results for service stability and increased capacity.” The company is continuing to restore affected servers and monitor recovery, but full restoration has not yet been confirmed in the updates reviewed. Earlier improvements proved temporary, with Microsoft reporting partial recovery that was not sustained.

Update, November 13, 12:11 UTC (07:11 EST): Microsoft says it has made further progress toward recovery, with traffic gradually being restored across portions of the affected infrastructure. The company is seeing improvements in mailbox access and delayed-email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent problems. Recovery work is continuing across the remaining affected infrastructure. Microsoft has also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect delayed messages while recovery continues. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Update, November 13, 13:46 UTC (08:46 EST): Microsoft says recovery is progressing across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. The company is also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Some users may still experience intermittent access problems or delayed email delivery as recovery work continues across the remaining affected infrastructure. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

What about security?

ABC reports that Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 are both on Microsoft’s list of services that may be affected.

Being unable to log in doesn’t mean attackers are also locked out, or that every security feature has stopped working. If you rely on these services, check which security features are working as access is restored. Follow your IT team’s guidance and check Microsoft’s updates for details.

Be alert for unexpected messages offering to restore access or asking you to sign in through a link. Go directly to Microsoft’s official status pages instead.

Malwarebytes and ThreatDown products are not affected by this outage.

articles.title: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines: Will Your AI System Need an Independent Audit?
articles.context: These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using: Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1
articles.full_text:
Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk.

Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week.

Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom.

The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now.

Key Takeaways

CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users.

Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence.

From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation.

Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger.

AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions.

What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04.

Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page.

The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies.

It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism. Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity.

Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9

There are three narrow exclusions:

Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot.

Purely rule-based automation, such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope.

Consumer personal use, such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope.

Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size.

Is It Mandatory?

The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier.

Three things give it teeth in practice:

It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours.

Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators.

Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next.

For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor.

How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works

Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place.

Factor

What it asks

F1: Impact severity

How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output?

F2: Autonomy and actionability

What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves?

F3: Data sensitivity

How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified?

F4: Scale and exposure

How many users, transactions or systems does it reach?

F5: Reversibility

How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone?

F6: Sector criticality

Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function?

F7: Adversarial exposure

Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment?

F8: Complexity and auditability

How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score.

The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement:

Score

Tier

Minimum audit requirement

8–12

Tier 1 (Low)

Self-assessment or basic internal review, reviewed annually

13–19

Tier 2 (Moderate)

Documented internal audit, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization at least annually

20–26

Tier 3 (High)

Periodic independent third-party audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization, every six months where risk or material change warrants

27–32

Tier 4 (Critical)

Independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization with continuous monitoring

The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state.

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Section 5.4, page 25.

Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority.

The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier

The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines.

Version A answers questions, checks order status through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over help articles and order history, and hands refunds to human agents. Version B is the same bot, but it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 on its own.

Factor

Version A: answers only

Version B: issues refunds

Why it changes

F1: Impact severity

2

A wrong answer or a single bad refund is still limited and recoverable

F2: Autonomy

2

3

Version B initiates consequential actions instead of advising a human

F3: Data sensitivity

2

3

Refunds bring payment and financial data into play

F4: Scale and exposure

3

Large-scale, customer-facing in both cases

F5: Reversibility

2

3

Money paid out to the wrong account is costly and slow to recover

F6: Sector criticality

2

An important business function, not critical infrastructure

F7: Adversarial exposure

3

Internet-facing, so anyone can send it hostile prompts

F8: Complexity

3

A third-party LLM is partially opaque to the deploying company

Total

19 (Tier 2)

22 (Tier 3)

Source: Illustrative scoring · tier bands and minimum audits from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Table 11

Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3.

Two things stand out.

First, even the "harmless" Version A sits at the top of Tier 2. That already means a documented internal audit, a simplified AI impact assessment, AI threat modelling and API security testing, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization at least annually. Many companies running customer-facing LLMs may not realize they're here.

Second, Version B doesn't just cross a score threshold. Its ability to initiate transactions is also a named escalation trigger, and an internet-facing bot that can move money is an obvious prompt-injection target. Moving to Tier 3 adds a comprehensive AI impact assessment, validation independent of the development team, a comprehensive AI security assessment with VAPT, a formal AI Governance Committee, and audits as often as every six months.

Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment.

What Auditors Will Test Your AI For

Section 9 of the guidelines adds dedicated requirements for generative AI, RAG, agentic, multimodal, and multi-agent systems. These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using:

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Table 16, page 63.

Source: Refund chatbot attack surface · threats from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Section 9.2

Mapped onto the refund chatbot, each component becomes a separate test case, and the leaked-credential risk sits outside the system entirely

CERT-In takes prompt injection seriously enough to apply it to auditors too. Audit teams using AI tools must treat auditee documents, logs and tool outputs as untrusted data and test for injection attempts designed to alter audit criteria or suppress findings.

The guidelines also expect AI threat models to draw on MITRE ATLAS, OWASP guidance, CERT-In advisories and "other relevant threat intelligence." That's where many teams have a blind spot.

Threat actors trade stolen AI API keys, discuss jailbreak and injection techniques on underground forums, and leak cloud and model credentials in breach dumps. Cyble's threat intelligence tracks this activity across the surface, deep and dark web, so security teams can build AI threat models on what attackers are actually doing rather than on assumptions.

What to Do in the Next 90 Days

The first step is the one most organizations will find hardest: knowing what AI they actually run. The guidelines treat an incomplete or missing AI inventory as a governance non-conformity in its own right.

Build your AI inventory. List every AI system in use, including vendor APIs, copilots built into SaaS tools, and shadow AI that teams adopted without approval. Record purpose, owner, model source, data processed and deployment status.

Score each system honestly. Apply the eight factors to what each system can actually do today. Flag any system that can act on its own, such as issuing refunds, sending messages, executing code or calling tools, since those are the ones most likely to sit higher than you expect.

Review permissions before you add features. Treat every new agent capability as a potential tier change. Put human approval gates on consequential actions and make sure agents run with least privilege.

Map your AI incidents to the six-hour clock. Define what an AI incident looks like, such as a successful prompt injection, data leakage through a model, or a poisoned knowledge source. Then check that you can detect, classify, and report one within six hours, with 180 days of time-synchronized logs to support the investigation.

Lock down AI secrets and watch for leaks. Move API keys and model credentials into a secrets manager and rotate them. Then monitor for those credentials turning up outside your environment. With Cyble's dark web monitoring, teams get alerts when credentials, keys or data tied to their organization appear in breach dumps, underground markets, paste sites or code repositories, so a leaked key can be revoked before it's abused.

Bring in threat intelligence for your AI threat model. Use current intelligence on attacker techniques, rather than a generic checklist, to decide what your red-team and VAPT exercises test.

Engage a CERT-In empaneled auditor early. If any system scores Tier 2 or above, start scoping the independent audit now rather than when a regulator or customer asks for the report.

How Cyble Helps You Get AI-Audit Ready

Cyble's dark web monitoring watches underground forums, marketplaces, paste sites, and code repositories for leaked API keys, credentials, and datasets linked to your organization, which supports the guidelines' secrets-management and continuous-assurance controls.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines? They are a risk-based framework, issued by CERT-In on 4 November 2026, for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their lifecycle. Each AI system is scored on eight risk factors and placed in one of four tiers that set its audit requirements.

Do the guidelines apply to foreign AI companies? Yes. They cover AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users, not only organisations based in India.

Does using a third-party AI model or API take my system out of scope? No. AI systems stay in scope regardless of model origin or delivery mechanism, and lack of access to vendor evidence is treated as a scope limitation, not as proof of conformity.

Which AI systems need an independent audit? Systems scoring 13 or above (Tier 2 and higher) require an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation, with frequency and depth increasing at Tier 3 and Tier 4.

How quickly must AI security incidents be reported to CERT-In? AI incidents that meet CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, consistent with CERT-In's April 2022 Directions, which also require 180-day log retention.

Sources

articles.full_text:
Authorities arrested 354 suspects in a joint international operation targeting vendors and buyers on the Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces.

Codenamed 'Operation TorNado,' this law enforcement action ran from May 2025 to October 2026 and involved agencies from 14 countries.

"Additionally, law enforcement targeted vendors and buyers active on forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services. National authorities conducted independent investigations with Europol's support, including cross-checks via SIENA and forensic analysis," Europol said.

"The operation highlighted the evolving resilience of dark web marketplaces, which continue to adapt despite takedowns."

They seized over €60 million ($66 million) in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs (including amphetamines, cocaine, ketamine, psilocybin mushrooms, MDMA, and cannabis), and 57 firearms in Europe.

Law enforcement authorities also seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 152 firearms, and over €150 million ($166 million) in the United States.

"Following the takedown of multiple darknet marketplaces and vendor targets in the previous JCODE operation, U.S. and international law enforcement agencies obtained intelligence to identify Dark Web drug traffickers, resulting in a series of complementary, but separate, law enforcement investigations," the US Department of Justice added.

"By leveraging complementary partnerships and surging resources across the U.S. government and Europol, Operation TorNado significantly disrupted the online opioid trade and sends a strong message that criminals operating on the Dark Web are not beyond the reach of law enforcement."

Operation TorNado follows several similar actions over the last six years, including DisrupTor in 2020 (which led to 179 arrests) and Dark Huntor in 2021 (in which 150 more high-volume darknet vendors were apprehended).

In April 2022, US authorities and German police also took down Hydra, the world's largest dark web marketplace at the time, with more than 19,000 seller accounts that were serving over 17 million customers worldwide.

One year later, in 2023, Operation SpecTor led to the arrest of 288 other suspects who allegedly sold illicit drugs on dark web markets and the seizure of €50.8 million ($55.9 million) in cash and cryptocurrency.

More recently, in May 2025, law enforcement also announced the arrest of another 270 dark web vendors and buyers from ten countries as part of Operation RapTor.

articles.title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
articles.context: A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users
articles.full_text:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:

Encourage faster vulnerability remediation

Encourage vendors to reduce “patch gap”

Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors

Our new policy: “Full X”

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Starting today, our policy is “Full 90”, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a “Full 60” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a “Full 30” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

We are also removing most ‘special cases’ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:

Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Google’s application security vulnerability disclosure policy

Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others

Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it

Why reduce remediation time gradually?

Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors aren’t equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and don’t attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.

What about severity?

While our analysis isn’t always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we don’t feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

What about hardware?

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies, as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.

We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.
