articles.title: Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase
The School Bomb Threats Came From Accounts Already in Stolen Data
articles.context: Hudson Rock researchers found that two university addresses tied to Italy’s school bomb threats were in infostealer data
articles.full_text:
Hudson Rock researchers found that two university addresses tied to Italy’s school bomb threats were in infostealer data.

On 11 November, bomb-threat emails hit schools across Europe. ANSA, citing the Education Ministry, reported that about 6,000 Italian schools received them. Some evacuated, others kept teaching after talking to police, so the recipient count tells you nothing about how many buildings emptied.

The emails were signed “Mikhail Andropov” and threatened pupils and school staff. They also mentioned a bomb targeting the prime minister. However, these names and claims came from the sender and do not confirm who was behind the threats. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that searches found no bombs. She described the emails as an attempt to spread fear and chaos, adding that anonymous messages would not change the school calendar.

The same threats were reported outside Italy. Police in Northern Ireland said that more than 300 schools had received the same message, while Police Scotland classified the cases it investigated as hoaxes. In Ireland, The Journal reported threats against schools and newsrooms sent from different email addresses. This means there is no reason to assume that all the messages came from the same person or group.

Hudson Rock now reports that two university addresses tied to the threats appear in its stolen-credential data.

“The bomb-threat emails that disrupted Italian schools on November 11 have a significant credential-exposure connection.” reads the report. “Hudson Rock identified records for both university email addresses highlighted in threat-related material: f0523219@cloud.dyu.edu.tw and Mosaad_Khalifa@den.kfs.edu.eg.”

One belongs to an Egyptian university, the other to a Taiwanese one. The company says only that the credentials were exposed. It doesn’t claim they sent the emails, and it doesn’t blame any person, group or state.

The Egyptian address shows up in a Vidar infostealer record from 1 October 2021, taken from a Windows 7 machine running Chrome. The export holds 112 saved credentials, 20 of them using the university address, and two of those point to Microsoft sign-in pages. The same password habits spill across services, so one infected computer exposed a lot more than one account.

That record is more than five years old, which proves exposure and little else. It doesn’t show continuous access, an unchanged password or an infection nobody cleaned. The address also appeared in a newspaper photo and a public post, and the legitimate account holder shouldn’t be treated as the author of the threats.

“The saved credentials also show password reuse across services. That broadens the consequences of a single device infection: the same stolen collection can expose several accounts, including a university identity used on unrelated websites.” continues the report. “The age of the record is an important part of the finding. It places documented exposure more than five years before these threats. It does not demonstrate five years of continuous attacker access, an unchanged password, or an unremediated infection.”

The Taiwanese address turned up in AlienTXTBASE, a collection of aggregated infostealer data that Troy Hunt added to Have I Been Pwned in February 2025. Hudson Rock dates the record to more than a year before the threats. An Italian school published the address after receiving the email, and Focus Taiwan reports that Da-Yeh University found an alumnus account sending a large volume of mail, appearing compromised, and suspended it.

An infostealer copies what a device holds: saved passwords, session cookies, tokens, system details and sometimes wallet data. A stolen password may still open an account later, and stolen session tokens can skip MFA. Nothing in the files shows token theft in either case.

There is still no proof that the stolen credentials were used to send the emails. Full email headers, provider message logs and sign-in records would help identify which account or session sent them. Even if an email passes authentication checks, this does not prove that a specific stolen password was used.

Hudson Rock also discusses what Microsoft and the universities could have done to prevent the abuse. Entra ID Protection can compare leaked credentials with password hashes in an organization’s tenant and apply security policies based on risk. However, this requires an Entra ID P2 or Entra Suite license and proper configuration. The report does not explain what Microsoft or the universities knew about the exposed passwords or whether they were still valid.

A proper response must address the compromised account, its active sessions and the affected device. Organizations should block the account, reset its password through a trusted process and check whether the same password was used elsewhere. They should also revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, review app passwords, unauthorized sign-in methods, application permissions and mailbox rules.

The affected device must also be checked and cleaned. Otherwise, malware on the machine could steal the new password as well. Organizations should also introduce phishing-resistant authentication and monitor sign-in activity and outgoing emails. A sudden increase in outgoing messages should always raise a security alert.

A password reset alone isn’t enough, because some applications control their own sessions and token revocation takes time. An outbound filter won’t stop every first message either. Nobody should need a bomb threat to notice a password has been on the market for a year.

“The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft.” concludes the report. “An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, school bomb threats)

articles.title: Hackers compromise 4,800 GitHub accounts to steal cloud credentials
articles.context: Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets
articles.full_text:
Tens of thousands of GitHub repositories were targeted in a campaign dubbed ‘wfx-loot’ that uses malicious workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets and cloud credentials.

Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets.

The threat actor used thousands of compromised GitHub accounts to open pull requests against repositories those accounts could access, testing whether they had sufficient write permissions to inject malicious code.

Some of the compromised accounts belonged to Fortune 100 organizations, the US General Services Administration, the French government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO.

According to researchers at application security company Aikido, about 50 of them appear to have publishing rights on other open-source software ecosystems and package indexes such as npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.

Attack details

Aikido says the wfx-loot campaign began around 12:45 UTC on November 10, when the attacker used stolen GitHub credentials from 4,837 compromised accounts to probe 61,764 repositories for write access.

The threat actor opened pull requests titled ‘docs: dependency audit notes,’ disguised as dependency audit notes.

Of those pull requests, 92% remain open, Aikido reports, suggesting the legitimate repository owners did not notice the activity.

They then delivered a 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.

The script attempts to collect the following data:

GitHub Actions and variables, the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC, and Actions runtime tokens.

Cloud credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, including credentials exposed through instance metadata on self-hosted runners.

Developer and infrastructure credentials from Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault, and Terraform.

AI service and developer-tool credentials for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

Other sources of secrets include environment variables, .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, repository files and recent commits, and workflow artifacts.

The script also supports cloud privilege escalation by exchanging GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure, and GCP cloud sessions.

In AWS, it can chain into additional IAM (identity and access management) roles present in the repository "to create long-lived credentials for IAM users." It also uses collected service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP.

Aikido notes that capabilities include establishing persistent access by creating long-lived credentials or modifying cloud identity and trust policies where permissions allow.

The script compressed the collected data into tarballs and exfiltrated it via HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints.

In the final stage, the attacker quickly reverted their changes and deleted workflow runs and logs. Aikido says this was completed in under a minute.

Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist’s digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280.

The researchers believe the threat actor's primary objective was to steal CI secrets, while the package releases were a byproduct of automated publishing.

The researchers also found certain overlaps with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.

Repository owners are advised to look for the ‘wfx-docs’ branch, the probe pull request, and gaps in workflow run numbers.

Where payload execution is confirmed, all secrets and cloud roles available to the affected workflows should be considered compromised and rotated immediately.

articles.title: A patchwork of problems.
articles.context: Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook. Most notably, CVE-2026-124194 is an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw that leaks a user's NTLMv2 authentication hash if they open a malicious message file,...
articles.full_text:
Patch Tuesday. Maersk investigates a legacy system breach. A chip-smuggling probe stalls after Nvidia reaches out to Commerce. A US Army officer is arrested in the UK for alleged Russian espionage. Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents across Central Asia. Opsec blunders unmask an alleged Qilin ransomware boss. Researchers hijack connected cars via Android apps. Our guest is Tim Starks from CyberScoop to discuss what Democratic control of Congress means for cybersecurity. A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Today is Thursday November 12th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Patch Tuesday.

In honor of the Veterans Day holiday here in the U.S. we did not publish yesterday, which means we are playing a bit of catch up for this month’s patch Tuesday.

Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook.

According to SecurityWeek, Redmond addressed one thousand ninety-four vulnerabilities this month. Most notably, CVE-2026-124194 is an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw that leaks a user's NTLMv2 authentication hash if they open a malicious message file, allowing attackers to impersonate them. Windows accounted for seven hundred twenty-six of Microsoft's patches, alongside one hundred seventy-four for Office.

Meanwhile, Fortinet published eighty-nine advisories resolving nearly one hundred flaws, including roughly seventeen critical issues across products like FortiMail, FortiOS, and FortiClient, which researchers note were discovered with the help of frontier artificial intelligence models. Ivanti and Citrix patched nineteen vulnerabilities combined; Ivanti's fixes address critical unauthenticated remote code execution and authentication bypass defects in Endpoint Manager and Cloud Services Application, while Citrix resolved six XenServer flaws and mitigated AMD processor issues. Finally, Zoom patched two unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, and Asus addressed four router firmware bugs.

Attackers rapidly weaponize edge devices and collaboration tools, requiring security teams to prioritize patching Outlook and internet-facing enterprise infrastructure immediately, even where active exploitation has not yet been reported, according to vendor advisories.

Maersk investigates isolated security incident on legacy system.

Shipping giant A.P. Moller-Maersk is investigating a security incident involving potential data theft from an isolated legacy system.

In a Wednesday statement, the Denmark-based logistics firm confirmed it secured the affected platform, a local system from a previous acquisition. Maersk said initial findings strongly suggest no sensitive information was disclosed, and there is no evidence of impact on core operations or customer integrations like APIs and electronic data interchange.

Any cyber incident at Maersk recalls the devastating two thousand seventeen NotPetya attack, attributed to Russia's Sandworm group, which cost the firm roughly three hundred million dollars. While this localized intrusion appears far less severe, it highlights persistent cybersecurity risks within inherited acquisition infrastructure, according to Maersk and reporting from The Register.

The Commerce Department halted a chip-smuggling probe after Nvidia outreach.

Federal investigators at the Commerce Department abruptly paused a monthslong probe into suspected artificial intelligence chip smuggling to China late last year after receiving unusual outreach from Nvidia.

According to The New York Times, the inquiry focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed, led by Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials now believe spied for Beijing and who had an acknowledged intimate relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The case was hastily transferred to the Justice Department after Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter emailed investigators, claiming Commerce official Jeff Kessler authorized the company to inquire about the probe.

The episode highlights growing tension between national security enforcement and corporate influence over semiconductor export controls, raising concerns among officials that executive intervention could compromise federal investigations into illicit technology transfers.

Nvidia shares fell ten percent after CEO Jensen Huang resigned today, naming CFO Colette Kress interim chief executive.

The Wall Street Journal reports the board met following a New York Times report alleging a second affair with executive Kimberly Powell.

A US Army officer is arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia.

British police have arrested a forty-one-year-old US Army lieutenant colonel on suspicion of attempting to steal secret information from a NATO installation for Russia.

According to The Washington Post, the unnamed officer was stationed at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire, England, which houses NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. A joint counterintelligence operation involving Britain's MI5, Metropolitan Police, and the FBI detained the officer before any sensitive files were transferred to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any Russian link to the incident.

US Army Counterintelligence Command noted the arrest is a sobering reminder of persistent insider threats within allied defense infrastructure, as Western nations navigate heightened Russian hybrid operations across Europe alongside ongoing Ukraine peace negotiations.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents in Central Asian espionage.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an autonomous artificial intelligence agent to conduct cyberespionage against Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure, according to Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK.

Researchers uncovered the operation on an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, also tracked as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper. The operator configured an open-source AI agent named Hermes, powered primarily by DeepSeek models, to act as an offensive security specialist. Controlled remotely via a Telegram bot in Russian, the agent automated reconnaissance, data theft, and log erasure.

Using compromised railway credentials, the attackers breached Tajikistan's national electronic document platform, stealing thousands of files linked to the Defense Ministry and security agencies. They also compromised a server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and prepared phishing lures targeting Turkmenistan.

The discovery underscores how threat actors are operationalizing agentic AI to automate complex intrusions, lowering the operational friction required to pillage government networks.

Operational security missteps expose an alleged Qilin ransomware administrator.

Operational security mistakes over the past decade have exposed the alleged real-world identity of the administrator behind Qilin, currently the world's most active ransomware affiliate program.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, Qilin, which claimed at least three hundred sixty-five victims in the past three months, is led by a threat actor using the handle "Haise." Threat intelligence firms IntelHawk, Intel 471, and Flashpoint traced Haise back to older cybercrime forum monikers, including "Rjun," and a Telegram account tied to an email address exposed in a late two thousand twenty-five breach of Russia's state services portal, Gosuslugi. Those records, alongside leaked travel and education data, point to thirty-six-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev of St. Petersburg.

The attribution demonstrates how even sophisticated ransomware operators leave persistent digital breadcrumbs across seized forums and breached databases, aiding defenders and law enforcement in piercing criminal anonymity.

Security researchers exploit Android apps to remotely control connected cars.

Security researchers uncovered critical flaws in Android applications from two major automakers that enabled remote access to connected vehicles in the United States and Australia.

According to research published by Assetnote co-founder Shubham Shah and Sam Curry, the exploit chains targeted weaknesses in the manufacturers' ForgeRock identity platforms. In Australia, hardcoded staging credentials and path traversal flaws allowed account takeovers using just a license plate lookup. In the US, path confusion and factory default credentials on an Apache Felix console yielded shell access to identity servers, letting the pair start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. The unnamed automakers, widely speculated by observers to be Toyota and Lexus, patched the vulnerabilities within two hours of disclosure earlier this year.

The findings underscore how backend identity misconfigurations and hardcoded credentials in connected vehicle ecosystems can turn everyday mobile apps into remote-control attack vectors.

A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Officials in Cranbury, New Jersey, intended to buy land for affordable housing, though they inadvertently subsidized some ambitious cybercriminals instead, wiring twenty-six million dollars straight into fraudsters' hands.

According to The Wall Street Journal, police expect to recover seventeen point three million dollars, leaving roughly nine million missing, an amount comfortably exceeding the township's five-million-dollar insurance policy. Adding salt to the fiscal wound, officials waited until the Friday afternoon after Election Day to announce the heist. While the police chief took responsibility, explaining a gag order prevented thieves from liquidating the stolen funds, residents packed a town meeting expressing skepticism over the timing and marveling that an eight-figure transfer proved easier than logging into an iCloud account.

The episode offers a sobering reminder that business email compromise doesn't spare small municipalities, and that delayed breach disclosures rarely play well with voters, even when investigators have sound operational reasons.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Report: Online Scams Nearly Doubled in 2026
articles.context: A new report from Akamai has found that online scams surpassed traditional phishing attacks for the first time in 2026, nearly doubling from about 3
articles.full_text:
A new report from Akamai has found that online scams surpassed traditional phishing attacks for the first time in 2026, nearly doubling from about 3.2 million to approximately 6.4 million year-over-year. The researchers say this signals a “shift toward higher-return fraud tactics focused on direct financial and consumer deception.”

“Since MFA has become a baseline security measure, attackers are pivoting toward higher-return scams for faster payouts,” the researchers write. “Traditional phishing, however, still grew by 61% by Q2 2026, according to Bolster. Together, these numbers show that while credential theft remains a core driver, threat actors are aggressively expanding into social engineering tactics that can manipulate consumers into direct financial losses.” Threat actors are increasingly using AI to streamline these attacks, allowing them to launch higher volumes of attacks for less effort.

“Attackers are expanding their use of AI to create more varied phishing templates, produce multilingual content at scale, and deploy adaptive evasion techniques,” the report says. “These capabilities reduce the cost and effort required to build convincing scams and make campaigns faster to launch, scale, and modify.”

Attackers are also using AI as a phishing lure, impersonating popular AI services with malicious websites. “Beyond traditional phishing attacks, adversaries are capitalizing on the boom of generative AI in the workplace,” Akamai says. “This has given rise to ‘AI phishing,’ which is defined as attacks that include fake sites impersonating major platforms like OpenAI’s ChatGPT to pilfer employee credentials. Although AI phishing currently represents only 3.3% of observed activity, organizations should monitor it closely as a critical initial access vector. According to our Enterprise AI Usage Risk Report 2026, nearly half of enterprise employees have tried workplace AI tools, though only 18% use them weekly; those figures will likely rise steadily over time. As employee adoption inevitably scales, these low-volume lures will likely transform into high-yield entry points for enterprise compromise.”

Akamai has the story: https://www.akamai.com/lp/state-of-the-internet/digital-fraud-abuse-report-2026

articles.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
articles.context: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use...
articles.full_text: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations. “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team, which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory, automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber. The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models. The lawsuit, filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face, gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics, and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents. “Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

articles.title: Microsoft Cloud Outage Hits Outlook, Teams, Copilot and AI Services
articles.context: However, it later found that increased traffic was not the cause
articles.full_text:
A Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot, also breaking OpenAI and Anthropic connectors to Microsoft 365 accounts.

Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams went down for thousands of US users on Thursday, November 12. Reuters reported that the disruption also hit the connectors OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services use to reach Microsoft accounts.

“Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams were down for thousands of US users on Thursday, ​according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com, with the disruption ‌also hitting connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.” Reuters states

Downdetector, which collates status reports from several sources, logged more than 97,000 Outlook incidents at 2:07 p.m. ET. It also recorded more than 38,000 reports of Microsoft 365 problems and about 4,500 for Teams. Reuters notes the number of affected users may vary. Expers observed complaints surge that afternoon across Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive and the Microsoft Store.

In a Microsoft 365 admin center notice (MO1550821), Microsoft warned that users might have trouble accessing several services, including Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR.

Microsoft said the outage started at 1:26 p.m. ET. However, it had already been investigating problems connecting to Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas earlier that day. The company later confirmed that users worldwide could be affected.

Microsoft initially blamed heavy workloads across several regions. However, it later found that increased traffic was not the cause. In an update on X, the company said it was working to safely bring several unavailable servers back online. Their loss was putting extra pressure on the remaining infrastructure.

Its response so far has been to pause all deployments, redistribute connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure and move additional traffic away from affected systems. It’s also restarting the affected servers to restore capacity. In a statement to Reuters, Microsoft said it was aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.

“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” ​states Microsoft.

“We determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We’re working to safely return them to service,” Microsoft wrote on X.

Microsoft first blamed the disruption on high infrastructure demand across several regions. However, it later found that the issue was caused by servers unexpectedly going offline.

Microsoft also reported a separate Teams outage (TM1550488) that affected users in North and South America from 9:45 to 10:53 a.m. ET. Users experienced delays or failures when sending messages, creating or updating conversations, and retrieving chat messages. Microsoft traced the problem to resource contention within its infrastructure, which increased resource usage and prevented Teams from processing messages properly. The company confirmed that the issue has been resolved.

We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365…

— Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026

At this time the massive outage has yet to be resolved. Reuters says Microsoft later told customers the issue may also affect Microsoft 365 connectivity for users in other regions.

The impact also extended to AI services. OpenAI reported problems with its Microsoft connectors, saying new connections might fail and tools might not work properly. Anthropic also reported an issue with its Microsoft 365 connector caused by a problem at an upstream provider. As a result, Copilot and competing AI services were unable to access users’ inboxes because the underlying Microsoft services were unavailable.

IT teams should check the Microsoft 365 admin center for updates rather than make assumptions about the cause. They should also expect emails and messages to be delayed until services fully recover.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Microsoft)

articles.context: Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated infrastructure load across multiple regions, but has determined that the problem was caused by servers unexpectedly...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is investigating a widespread outage affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams, and Copilot, as users report connectivity problems worldwide.

BleepingComputer has received numerous reports from users experiencing problems accessing Microsoft's services, including complaints that Outlook is down.

According to Downdetector, which tracks user-submitted outage reports, complaints surged Thursday afternoon across numerous Microsoft services, including Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive, and the Microsoft Store.

In a Microsoft 365 admin center advisory tracked as MO1550821, Microsoft confirmed that customers may be unable to connect to multiple services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR.

The company says the Microsoft 365 incident began Thursday at 1:26 PM ET, although it began investigating reports of Exchange Online mailbox connectivity problems in the Americas earlier in the day.

Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated infrastructure load across multiple regions, but has determined that the problem was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable.

"We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," Microsoft said in an update on X.

The company says it has paused all deployments, redistributed connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure, and is moving additional traffic away from affected systems to reduce load.

Microsoft is also restarting affected servers to restore capacity and return services to normal operation.

While the company initially reported Exchange Online connectivity problems in the Americas, it later confirmed that users in any region could be affected.

The outage follows a separate Microsoft Teams incident earlier Thursday that caused an outage for users in North and South America.

That earlier incident, tracked as TM1550488, lasted from 9:45 AM to 10:53 AM ET and caused delays or failures when sending messages, errors creating or updating conversations, and problems retrieving chat messages.

Microsoft attributed the earlier Teams disruption to resource contention within its infrastructure, which led to elevated resource utilization and prevented the service from processing messaging requests normally.

The company says the earlier Teams incident has been fully resolved.

Microsoft has not indicated whether the two incidents are related, and the ongoing Microsoft 365 outage has not yet been resolved.

BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the outage and will update our story if we receive a response.

Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
articles.context: " The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack
articles.full_text: Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ®

articles.title: Major Microsoft Outlook Outage Leaves People With Email Jobs Unable to Email
articles.context: In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it’s...
articles.full_text:
It’s not just you. Microsoft’s 365 business and enterprise services suffered a major outage on Thursday, preventing users of its popular cloud suite from accessing their accounts.

Around 10:40 am ET on Thursday morning, Microsoft posted on its 365 status page on X that it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America.” By just before 1pm ET, it said it was aware of “issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.”

Microsoft later said that its network was also “experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” but that the issue was related to servers going offline, not due to increased traffic.

Around an hour later, Microsoft said it had “begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load” and was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.”

“We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service,” Microsoft wrote.

In an update on its status page, Microsoft said impacted services may include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, and Microsoft Defender XDR.

“We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement. “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."

Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon.

It is currently unclear when the outage may be over or what its cause may be. In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it’s attempting to reboot its systems to hopefully bring them back online.

Outages in cloud services occur frequently, and their causes can vary. Configuration errors, resolution issues with the Domain Name System, and cyberattacks can all cause connection errors. There is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused the current Microsoft outage.

While major Microsoft outages are relatively rare, they are far from unprecedented. In July 2024, a corrupted update from the security firm Crowdstrike knocked out Microsoft Azure services for hours, causing untold millions of dollars in lost revenue due to companies’ inability to function as normal.

Updated 11/12/2026 at 3:05 pm ET: Added comment from Microsoft.

Additional reporting by Matt Burgess.

articles.title: New N-able "4EverAble2Shell" zero-day exploited hours after PoC released
articles.context: Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with...
articles.full_text:
Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with researchers reporting at least 21 affected systems, including 19 running the company's latest security update.

The attacks follow security researcher Sean Bales' release of two new zero-day exploits today, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, which he says allow attackers to gain root-level access to N-central appliances and SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems.

N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely.

The new vulnerabilities were disclosed on November 12, just two days after N-able released emergency security updates to address critical N-central zero-day vulnerabilities that Bales had publicly disclosed earlier this week.

Bales published proof-of-concept exploits for both the 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell vulnerabilities, saying they were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.1.26 HF2, the security update N-able released on November 10.

The 4EverAble2Shell exploit allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root on vulnerable N-central servers. However, the researcher says exploitation requires the platform's Legacy API functionality to be enabled.

The attack combines an Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436, with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to gain root-level access.

The second exploit, Agent2Shell, targets N-central's agent functionality and is claimed to allow attackers to execute commands with SYSTEM privileges on Windows devices.

The disclosures came after N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after Bales published more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities.

Bales has criticized N-able's handling of the vulnerability disclosures and the company's slow response to patching responsibly disclosed flaws.

"It's much much easier for me to just release the research I have and the vendor can decide what they want to do with it, what they do and don't want to fix, etc. :)," Bales told BleepingComputer.

Bales said N-able has not patched two unrelated RCE vulnerabilities in a different N-able product that he previously disclosed to the company in July.

In a November 12 security advisory, N-able said it was implementing additional protections in response to the new disclosures, including restricting certain N-central features and integrations while it develops further fixes.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," N-able said.

"These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The company says it has disabled the Intune integration as a precaution and is urging on-premises customers to ensure Legacy API access is disabled, which is already the default.

The protections have already been applied to hosted environments, but customers are also advised to continue upgrading their Agents and Probes under the previous Hotfix 2 guidance.

In its advisory, N-able said it had seen no signs of compromise using the new flaws, although security researchers have since reported successful exploitation of the vulnerability against production N-central servers.

Hackers already exploiting 4EverAble2Shell

Cybersecurity company Previdian told BleepingComputer that attackers began probing for the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerability on November 12, shortly after the public release of the proof-of-concept exploit.

The company first observed suspicious requests targeting its N-central honeypot at approximately 08:30 UTC, using the same Java class referenced in the publicly released exploit.

While the initial requests were limited to probing for vulnerable servers, Previdian later confirmed that attackers were attempting to execute the complete exploit chain against its honeypot server.

The attacks initially exploit Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 to execute commands as the 'nable' service account, then exploit a separate N-central privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges.

This attack chain matches the POC Bales released on GitHub.

According to Previdian, the privilege escalation stage abuses N-central's privileged setLDFileOwner helper and a symbolic link to make a normally root-owned script writable.

The attacker then modifies the script and invokes N-central's serverControl functionality to execute commands as root, while attempting to restore the modified files afterward.

The payload attempted to download and execute an additional shell script from an attacker-controlled server at 157.20.241[.]16, while sending diagnostic information and command output back to the same IP address.

Previdian is tracking the N-central privilege escalation flaw as VULN-2026-0009 and has added it to its own Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Cybersecurity company Huntback also reports that attackers have already successfully compromised at least 21 production N-central servers using Bales' publicly released exploit chain.

Huntback saw the same attacker IP address as Previdian probing its N-central honeypots at approximately 08:30 UTC on November 12, with the first attempts to execute the complete exploit chain beginning at 09:16 UTC.

The attacks seen by Huntback exploited the 4EverAble2Shell exploit chain to download a shell script that installed an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner.

The miner was configured to use about half of the available CPU cores, likely to make the mining harder to detect.

Huntback identified other compromised systems through the attacker's cryptocurrency mining pool statistics, where infected systems were assigned identifiers beginning with nc_ followed by the server's IP address.

At 12:50 UTC on November 12, the researchers found 21 active miners using this naming convention, all of which had submitted mining shares within the previous five minutes.

The researchers then checked the associated IP addresses and confirmed that all 21 hosted N-central installations, including 19 running version 2026.4.1.26, the latest Hotfix 2 release issued on November 10.

The compromised servers were located across multiple countries, including the United States, Canada, South Africa, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Sweden.

While the attacks observed so far have been primarily used for cryptojacking, attackers could use compromised N-central infrastructure for additional malicious activity targeting managed customer environments.

Organizations running N-central should ensure that Legacy APIs are disabled and investigate suspicious requests to /dms/services/ServerUI, especially those referencing jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings.

Huntback also recommends checking for unexpected xvd.service systemd services, cryptocurrency mining processes, and files created under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd.

Because the 4EverAble2Shell attack grants full root access to exploited servers, organizations that detect these IOCs should treat the breach as a full compromise of the server.

articles.title: Apache HTTP Server patches critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw
articles.context: A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE)
articles.full_text:
A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE).

The Apache Software Foundation has fixed the issue, now tracked as CVE-2026-119618, but a significant number of servers are vulnerable and reachable over the public internet.

Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research teams, the vulnerability is a race condition in the mod_http2 module that can corrupt heap memory.

An attacker successfully exploiting it could run code with the web server process’s privileges in HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Apache describes the problem as “Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.”

Apache HTTP Server is a free and open-source software that handles requests from web browsers and serves pages, images, and other website content. It is a widely used tool estimated to back roughly one out of five websites.

According to telemetry data from cloud security company Wiz, 64% of the cloud environments have vulnerable resources, and roughly half of them have publicly exposed instances.

However, the numbers do not account for server configuration, which requires HTTP/2 to be enabled (default is off).

Researchers at cybersecurity company watchTowr confirmed this condition and recommend technicians to "patch now or drop h2 until you can."

"Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption," Wiz researchers say.

"This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process."

Wiz assesses the severity of the vulnerability to be critical, although no official score is available. The company says that it is currently unaware of any public exploits or attacks targeting the flaw, but this could change soon.

The latest version of Apache HTTP Server also addresses two additional flaws, CVE-2026-106023 - a null pointer dereference in ‘mod_md,’ and CVE-2026-109163 - a low-severity data overwrite flaw in ‘mod_vhost_alias.’

articles.title: Webinar: See How Identity Blind Spots Put Your SOC at Risk and How to Close Them
articles.context: Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation
articles.full_text:
Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access?

A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently.

Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story.

And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem.

Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence.

The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations

Here's the problem.

Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats.

But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities.

When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means.

Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain:

What applications and systems can this account access?

Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network?

How much damage could it cause?

Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process?

These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move.

And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated.

More Identities, More Access, More Risk

Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity.

Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement.

These identities often have access to important systems and data.

If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact.

That's where identity context changes the investigation.

Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations.

📅 Save Your Spot: See how identity context can improve your SOC response in this free webinar.

What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like?

The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts.

It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding.

That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can:

Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved.

See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement.

Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation.

Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals.

The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable.

Learn How to Close the Gap

In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together.

Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems.

It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks.

Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act.

articles.full_text:
Identity Security was built around the front door. Verify who is logging in, grant access, and trust policy to hold from there. That worked when only people logged in. It stops working once service accounts and AI agents authenticate alongside them.

We built Silverfort around that problem. We believe it is why we have been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment (doc# US54116526, November 2026).

What changed in Identity Security

An AI agent can use one identity or session to make hundreds of tool calls: pulling records, calling APIs, moving data. In the environments we work in, how many agents exist, and what each one is allowed to do, is often an open question.

The IDC MarketScape describes the shift in the report’s market definition:

“The breach does not occur when access is granted. It occurs when control fails to follow what happens next.”

What does the IDC MarketScape evaluate?

IDC MarketScape positions vendors into four categories: Participants, Contenders, Major Players, and Leaders. For this study, IDC analyst Emmanuel Figueroa evaluated 18 identity security vendors, including Silverfort.

The report defines the category, the five capability areas IDC assessed, and how each vendor was evaluated. The five areas are:

Identity Coverage

Continuous Risk Scoring

Automated Enforcement

Bidirectional Interoperability

Identity Observability and Delegation Governance

What does enforcement at every access request look like?

Silverfort’s Runtime Access Protection (RAP) operates from within the identity infrastructure, where it sees each authentication. When someone or something requests access, the identity system forwards the request to Silverfort. Silverfort assesses the risk, applies inline controls such as MFA or a block if needed, and returns a verdict. The identity system then grants or denies access. It covers workforce and privileged users, third parties, non-human identities, and it needs no proxies, app changes, or changes to user workflows.

In Active Directory, that means visibility into Kerberos, NTLM, and LDAP authentications in real time, without rewrites or architectural changes.

We also extended our runtime protection to include AI agents. Agents are protected not at the authentication layer, but in the tool call process—each tool call is checked against policy before it runs.

What does IDC MarketScape say about Silverfort?

On how Silverfort works, IDC MarketScape notes:

“Silverfort enforces at the authentication layer, so domain controllers and identity providers become policy points, and legacy protocols such as NTLM, Kerberos, LDAP, and RADIUS receive step-up MFA, access blocks, and service-account fencing without endpoint agents or application changes. In IDC’s view, that is a practical answer to a long-standing hole in the identity stack.”

IDC MarketScape also comments on enforcement:

“Silverfort names automated enforcement as its primary strength, and IDC agrees: it acts before access is granted, not after someone reads a log.”

The IDC MarketScape profile also covers when buyers should consider Silverfort. You can read that in the vendor excerpt.

Where we go from here

We started a few years ago by bringing MFA to systems that had always been out of reach. Since then, we’ve evolved into a complete Identity Security Platform that secures every identity across every environment. Our acquisition of Fabrix Security, which was announced in April 2026, adds an AI decisioning engine and an Identity Knowledge Graph that analyzes access activity, organizational context, and intent—laying the foundation for our autonomous Runtime Identity Security Platform.

Four questions we think are worth asking

These are our questions, not IDC’s. They reflect how we think about Identity Security.

Does it enforce, or only alert? Enforcement decides at the moment of access. An alert tells you what already happened.

Does it cover Active Directory and legacy protocols? These are where attackers look, and they are often the hardest systems to change.

Does it treat AI agents as identities? An AI agent can make hundreds of tool calls during a single session, all under the same identity. Each request—not just the initial sign-in—should be evaluated against policy.

Does it re-evaluate risk on every access request? Risk can change between one request and the next. The decision should change with it.

Thank you

Thank you to the customers, partners, and Silverfort team members who made this possible.

Next steps

Read the Silverfort vendor excerpt for the IDC MarketScape

See a real AI attack, then see it stopped. Book a session in our AI Attack Lab.

FAQ

What is an IDC MarketScape?

The IDC MarketScape is a vendor assessment model for a technology market. IDC’s own description of the methodology appears under the graphic at the top of this post.

What is augmented identity security?

It is the category name IDC uses in this IDC MarketScape. IDC’s definition is in the full report. In our view, it means Identity Security that keeps enforcing after the login, not only at it.

What is Runtime Access Protection?

Runtime Access Protection (RAP) is Silverfort’s patented technology. It operates from within the identity infrastructure, sees each authentication, and enforces a decision at the moment access is requested.

Which identities does Silverfort protect?

Workforce users, privileged users, third parties, non-human and machine identities, and AI agents, across on-premises, hybrid, and cloud environments.

What is the AI Attack Lab?

It is a session with a Silverfort Identity Security specialist, about 30 minutes, that shows a real AI attack and how inline identity controls can stop it.

Where can I read the report?

Silverfort’s vendor excerpt is linked in this post.

Sources

“IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment,” doc #US54116526, November 2026.

articles.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
articles.context: First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess
articles.full_text: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month, eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort. eMudhra has since left the CA racket, saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue. What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of. eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing. By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task. “Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.” The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers. As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work. “It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo. It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads. “The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.” As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself. “I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained. We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

articles.title: The Token Cost of Shell Commands
articles.context: Even if an agent later summarizes its history, the initial ingestion of these massive, unfiltered outputs causes severe token spikes
articles.full_text:
You asked your AI coding agent to debug a simple test failure, and it somehow ended up recursively reading your entire .git/objects history. If your API bills are climbing while your agent seemingly just browses your codebase, you aren’t alone.

Developers often blame the LLM model choice or a poorly written system prompt. But the real budget killer is input context. Your agent isn’t paying to think, it’s paying to re-read a 4,000-line grep output it already understood six turns ago. The biggest culprits are everyday shell commands developers have used for decades without a second thought.

Why Do Shell Commands Break AI Agent Budgets?

Shell commands like ls, find, and grep were built for humans, and human brains filter out terminal noise automatically to find the one line that matters. AI coding agents don’t have that filter. They process raw terminal output as billable context. Even if an agent later summarizes its history, the initial ingestion of these massive, unfiltered outputs causes severe token spikes.

As autonomous coding agents move from simple autocomplete into planning and executing multi-step workflows over a terminal, they call these commands again and again. Each call adds tokens that build up rapidly until the session ends or the agent compacts its history. The gap between a human skimming an output and an agent absorbing every character of it is where your budget gets burned.

The three everyday culprits

Alongside verbose test logs, these three ordinary shell commands are frequent sources of the runaway costs that agentic workflows can rack up. Recognizing them is the first step toward controlling them.

ls, the directory dump: An agent asks what’s in a directory and runs ls -la. In a small folder, that’s harmless. In the root of a monorepo, that single command can dump tens of thousands of tokens of permissions, timestamps, file sizes, and hidden files nobody asked for.

find, the infinite tree: Asked “where is the database configuration?”, an agent runs find . -name "*.yaml". Without depth limits, find recursively walks every hidden folder, cache directory, and build artifact path it can reach.

grep, the context killer: An agent hunting for a function call runs grep -r "processPayment". Left unconstrained, it can return minified JavaScript, binary garbage, and endless test-mock data. Worse, if it matches a 10,000-character line in a generated JSON file, that entire line lands in the prompt.

Each of these commands is safe in isolation and expensive at scale, which is exactly why they slip past code review unnoticed.

Why Doesn’t Blind Truncation Fix the Problem?

Blindly truncating shell output (i.e. just capping every command at 1,000 tokens) sounds like a quick fix, but it quietly breaks the agent’s ability to reason about what it’s looking at.

If you silently truncate a grep output, the agent may not know it received partial results. It may assumes the results don’t exist. From there, it can guess, hallucinate, or spiral. In our internal testing, agents re-ran the same ls command up to six times trying to re-establish where they were in the filesystem.

An optimizer the agent can’t detect is an optimizer you can’t debug. Any compression layer you build has to tell the agent what it’s not seeing, or you’ve traded a cost problem for a correctness problem. This is the exact failure mode a token-compression tool like JFrog Boost is built to avoid. It compresses output and tells the agent when it has done so, so the agent can request the full output.

The Snowball Effect: How One Bad Command Multiplies

This is the most easily missed cost in agentic workflows: a bad command isn’t paid for once. Because of how multi-turn LLM conversations typically work, prior turns’ tokens are resent with each new message until the session ends, the agent compacts its history, or the session hits its context limit.

That resend behavior turns small waste into compounding waste. The value of trimming a command’s output isn’t just the tokens you cut, it’s those tokens multiplied by the number of turns they would otherwise have sat in context. For instance, a 3,000-token log removed at turn four of a 40-turn session isn’t a 3,000-token saving.Before prompt caching or history compaction, it’s more than 100,000 input tokens avoided over the life of that session.

Scenario

Tokens removed once

Turns remaining in session

Cumulative tokens saved

Trim at turn 4 of 40

3,000

Trim at turn 20 of 40

3,000

Trim at turn 38 of 40

3,000

~6,000

Illustrative calculation. Assumes no prompt caching or history compaction.

The earlier a command’s output gets optimized, the more that optimization is worth because it avoids being re-processed on every subsequent turn, not just the current one. Note: Prompt caching can reduce some re-processing costs, but cache lifetimes and discounts vary by provider and model, and cached tokens are still billed. In our view, caching complements output optimization rather than replacing it.

At list prices as of October 2026, 100,000 input tokens cost roughly $0.15 to $0.30 on models such as GPT-5 or Claude Sonnet 5, before caching or batch discounts. That sounds cheap until it repeats. If each of 50 daily debugging sessions wastes about 100,000 input tokens on noise, that adds up to roughly $200 to $300 a month at those rates. Suddenly, a team is burning hundreds of dollars a month letting an AI agent stare at hidden cache directories.

Key insight: Saving 2,000 tokens on an early grep command can save far more than the same cut late in the session, because those 2,000 tokens would otherwise be re-processed on every later turn.

How Can You Stop Shell Commands from Draining Your Token Budget?

If you’re building agentic workflows, MCP servers, or custom developer tools, you need an optimization layer that trims noise without blinding the LLM to what it’s missing. JFrog Boost, a free CLI wrapper currently in public preview, is built around four rules for optimization that any team can adopt even without the tool itself.

Force constraints by default. Where your agent setup allows it, route shell commands through wrapped versions instead of raw commands. Expose wrapped versions or aliases that enforce limits automatically — a safe ls that forces ls -1 (names only) instead of ls -la, and a safe find that enforces depth limits, such as find . -maxdepth 2 -name "*.ts".

Tell the agent what you filtered. If a 10,000-line log has to be truncated, don’t do it silently. Append a system message to the output so the agent knows a summary, not the full picture, is in front of it.

Provide a recovery hatch. Give the agent a specific tool, such as cat_full_file <path>, so it can explicitly request the dropped data instead of hallucinating an answer.

Instrument the recovery path. Track how often the agent actually uses that recovery hatch. In our view, your retrieve rate is a better measure of a tool’s usability than your compression ratio alone.

Applying these rules consistently helps keep an agent’s context lean without leaving it guessing about what it can’t see.

Building a Safer Tool Wrapper That Reduces Injection Risk

To make this concrete, let’s look at how to implement Rule 1 (forcing safe constraints). Instead of letting the AI agent execute grep directly on your operating system, we create a Python function that acts as a “wrapper” around the command.

This wrapper intercepts the agent’s request, makes the command safe, runs it, and then filters the output before sending it back to the LLM. Here’s how JFrog Boost and similar tools build these baseline patterns, broken down step-by-step:

Step 1: Pass the Command Arguments as a List. First, we construct the command. Instead of passing a single string to the shell (which can expose you to command injection), we pass a list of separate arguments. We also force grep to ignore notorious token-wasting directories like .git and node_modules.

import subprocess def safe_grep(search_term: str, directory: str = "."): """"Illustrative agent tool for searching a codebase with output limits.""" # 1. Passing arguments as a list (no shell) reduces command-injection risk cmd = [ "grep", "-r", "-n", "-I", "--exclude-dir=.git", "--exclude-dir=node_modules", "--exclude-dir=dist", "-e", search_term, "--", directory, ]

Step 2: Execute Safely and Capture Output. Next, we run the command. We explicitly set check=False so that if grep finds nothing (which returns a non-zero exit code), it simply returns an empty string rather than crashing our entire agent loop.

try: # 2. Execute without shell=True result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False) output = result.stdout

Step 3: Enforce Limits and Add the Recovery Hatch. Finally, we check the length of the output. If it exceeds our token limit (roughly 8,000 characters), we truncate it. Crucially, we append a [System] note directly to the output. This tells the LLM exactly what happened and gives it the exact tool command (cat_file) it needs to use if it genuinely needs to read the rest of the file.

# 3. Token limit safeguard (~2000 tokens) char_limit = 8000 if len(output) > char_limit: truncated_output = output[:char_limit] # 4. Tell the agent what happened and provide the recovery hatch return ( f"{truncated_output}\n\n" "[System: Output truncated. Use `cat_file` for specific files.]" ) return output except Exception as e: return f"[System Error: {str(e)}]"

This wrapper passes arguments as a list instead of a shell string, which reduces shell command-injection risk, and it pairs each truncation with an explicit note the agent can act on. Production versions should also limit which paths the agent can search and run with the least privileges needed. An agent’s outputs are only as trustworthy and cost-effective as what it’s allowed to consume; don’t let a stray shell command break that trust.

How JFrog Boost Helps: Build and Scale Agents with Confidence

Manually wrapping every shell command is a reasonable starting point, but it doesn’t scale across a team running dozens of agentic workflows a day. JFrog Boost, currently in public preview, is designed to apply these rules automatically: it’s a free CLI wrapper that compresses noisy command output before it reaches agents like Cursor, Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot. JFrog Boost is designed to strip irrelevant noise from test runs and searches while preserving failures, summaries, and other signal agents typically need.

This is why JFrog Boost targets compression at the command level, right where the output first enters context, instead of trying to clean up the conversation after the damage compounds.

Paired with that kind of compression layer, the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform gives teams a single system of record for the artifacts, packages, and binaries their agents touch.
