articles.title: New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access
articles.context: Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver
articles.full_text:
Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop, targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix.

The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare, released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates.

CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025.

To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine.

The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page.

SignDrop targets the creation of that companion file. According to the proof-of-concept code, a standard user prepares a CLFS log and container with paths the user controls. When a privileged process later opens that log, the driver creates the .cnpf file in the privileged process's security context rather than the user's.

The exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect that file creation to a location the attacker chooses. In the published code, the privileged process is the Defender antimalware service, triggered through its update interface.

"Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the researcher wrote.

Because the .cnpf file inherits the original log's permissions, the result is a file created as SYSTEM that the standard user can write to. The researcher says that can be chained into a SYSTEM shell.

The exploit was tested on Windows 11 26H2, a Windows 11 26H2 Experimental build, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, according to the repository. Systems are affected when the CLFS authentication registry mode is set to 0 (enforced) or 1 (learning). Systems older than 90 days typically move from learning to enforcement automatically, so the default configuration on established installations is the one the exploit targets.

A registry value of 2 or 3 means the mitigation is disabled. That takes the system outside the claimed attack surface, but the researcher and the driver's own documentation both warn against it: disabling lets CLFS parse tampered log files, reopening the memory corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent.

Independent Test

Sungyup Nam, head of research at Korean security firm 78researchlab, reported in a published assessment today that researcher Heewon Song of the firm's PurpleHound offensive content team tested the exploit and found that it works. Song assessed that it does not run reliably enough for operational use, Nam wrote.

Defender must be enabled for the published chain to succeed. Running the exploit changes every UAC prompt to open a standard user shell and a SYSTEM shell, blocking other actions and making the attack noticeable to anyone at the machine.

The repository claims the technique can work against any antimalware engine whose process runs with elevated privileges. That broader claim has not been tested.

What Defenders Can Do

No CVE, advisory, or patch for SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog does not list it, and no attacks using the exploit have been reported.

Administrators can check their exposure by reading the CLFS authentication mode at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, where a Mode value of 0 or 1 falls within the researcher's claimed scope. The vendor's mitigation guidance describes the setting and the risks of disabling it.

The researcher has released a series of exploits targeting Windows and Defender since April. The vendor confirmed an earlier Defender exploit called RoguePlanet in June as CVE-2026-50656 and patched it the following month.

The ShieldBreak bypass followed in August and was assigned CVE-2026-69414. Three of the researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks.

SignDrop is a different class of issue. Where the earlier exploits targeted race conditions in Defender's file handling, this one targets the CLFS driver's own authentication feature. The vendor's security update guide is the place to watch for a response.

articles.title: From AI ambition to business impact
articles.context: They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning
articles.full_text:
Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs?

That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries.

Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams.

More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning.

The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together.

What this looks like in practice

Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations.

3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations.

Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees.

Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing. Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service.

KT, one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions.

Saint-Gobain, the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab.

Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same:

Begin with the value, not the technology.

Redesign the process, not just the task.

Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams.

Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one, so scaling doesn’t stall.

This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time.

New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact.

We’re holding ourselves to the same standard

If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to.

The real measure of success

The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build.

Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours.

Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company.

Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world.

articles.title: The Hidden Relay: Inside a Device Code Phishing Kit That Never Shows the Code
articles.context: Where the token was found Length SHA-1 (first 12 hex) Inside decoded 'ctx', attacker relay page 810 9abe6d45ae29 Inside decoded $Config
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Maddhav Grandy, Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

A smart TV or a streaming box throws a short code on screen and tells us to go type it into a website on your phone to finish signing in. It feels almost quaint compared to typing a password.

Microsoft built that same convenience into its own sign-in flow, for devices that cannot easily take a password, handing the user a short `user_code` to approve on a separate screen. Device code phishing takes that convenience and turns it into bait: phishing kits impersonate the device, get handed the code, and trick the victim into approving it on Microsoft's real site instead. Once the victim approves the sign-in and satisfies MFA, Microsoft issues access and refresh tokens straight to the attacker. From there, the attacker can access whatever resources those tokens grant in Microsoft 365, such as email and cloud files.

Device code phishing has risen since August 2024. Microsoft had tracked Storm-2372 using the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID in device code sign-ins, disclosing the campaign in mid-February 2025. The technique abuses Microsoft's authentic flow to steal access tokens. Victims enter real codes on genuine Microsoft sites, authorizing attacker sessions. The EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit has been observed to commercialize this approach.

Every documented variant of the device code phishing has depended on one step: the attacker opens an OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant, their phishing page hands the victim a short code and the victim copies it into a real Microsoft sign-in page.

The phishing URL we observed in August 2026 never sent that code. The victim types their email address, and the next screen is a genuine Microsoft login page. They just log into their account normally. No code, no instruction to go somewhere and enter. But still the attacker's backend was already holding everything it needed to collect the tokens.

Key Takeaways

Zero Code Display: The attack observed was a device code phishing flow. A user code came back in the kit's response, but it was never shown to the victim, and the flow carried on without it, leaving the attacker positioned to collect tokens if the victim finished signing in.

Direct Authentication with Microsoft: The victim types an email address on the kit's relay page, and the browser lands on login[.]microsoftonline[.]com, ending at Microsoft's own device-approval page.

Pre-Staged State vs. AiTM: Unlike Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) reverse proxies, which relay traffic live as the victim interacts with the page, this kit opens a Microsoft sign-in session in advance and embeds that session's tokens into the relay page's HTML before the victim submits anything. The session is already open and waiting, the victim's action only carries it forward. The pre-staged private session tokens are:

1. ctx - a token that identifies which sign-in session you're currently in.

2. flowToken - a token that changes at every step, so Microsoft can tell the sign-in steps are happening in the right order.

3. canary - a token that ties a submitted form to the exact page that issued it, so a mismatched submission gets rejected.

Passkeys and FIDO2 Do Not Stop This: Authentication happens entirely on Microsoft's genuine domain, so FIDO2 and passkey origin checks pass without error. The session state even carries an essential 'ngcmfa' claim; which Microsoft defines as "equivalent to MFA (multi-factor authentication), used for provisioning of certain advanced credential types." A new login session is requested even if there is an existing session. The sign-in must use Microsoft Authenticator push or Windows Hello for Business, and the session is restricted to a strict 10-minute validity window. That leaves the attacker's already open authorization grant positioned to receive the tokens.

How Does the Attack Work?

KnowBe4 ThreatLabs observed a generic phishing email urgently requesting approval of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA). The analysis of the phishing URL led to discovery of this attack.

The attackers used legitimate infrastructure to send these phishing emails, in this case Mandrill, Mailchimp's transactional email service. The message arrived fully authenticated from a sender with a clean reputation, which helped in evading Secure Email Gateways (SEGs).

Anatomy of the Attack Chain

The phishing URL was wrapped in Mandrill's click tracking service, which hides the real destination from email scanners. The URL then redirected through several hops before reaching the final phishing page. Most hops were hosted on serverless infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers page.

Microsoft's sign-in endpoint communicates through TCP protocol, and here the Cloudflare Workers page leads the sign-in to happen over QUIC protocol: “a modern transport layer network protocol that speeds up web connections and reduces latency. It serves as the foundation for HTTP/3”. It operates on UDP port 443 with transport-layer encryption. Since most inspection tools target TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, they see little of an HTTP/3 session, which Cloudflare serves by default.

The final landing page runs two checks in its own JavaScript before it will start the device code flow, and both are looking for an analyst:

A WebGL software-renderer check, which sends anything that looks like a sandbox to microsoft.com.

A sweep for automation globals and headless User-Agent strings, plus a DevTools timing trap. Any hit wipes the page.

Only after those passes does the victim see anything, and what they get is a fake "Microsoft Defender" verification overlay. Clicking verify runs a 950 millisecond spinner, then the overlay fades out. Nothing is verified. It is there to make the page feel like it came from Microsoft. Then the page offers a "Download Attachment" button, and clicking it starts the device code flow.

How Does the Device Code Flow Start?

The flow starts with a POST request sent to the Cloudflare Worker hosted phishing URL and the response has the details on how to proceed with the flow. The JavaScript code uses the response to follow the flow intended by the attacker.

The values sent in POST request are hardcoded, lureType selects the next page template to load, in this case server was instructed to load a fake Outlook-themed login page.The term deviceName is what the victim sees on the next page as the document being requested, in this case Document.pdf.

The response is as shown below (obtained by decrypting the HTTP/3 capture with the sandbox's own TLS session keys).

"userCode": It shows a nine-character uppercase code "EGEGABPRP", with a 900 second lifetime, which is 15 minutes. Both the format and the lifetime line up with RFC 8628, the specification Microsoft's authorization server follows.

"verificationUriComplete": This field is set as “null,” which determines that the user has to manually enter the code into the microsoft[.]com/devicelogin page rather than endpoint sending a URL where code is already embedded, so the user only has to authenticate.

"autoRelay" and "relayMode": These are set as “true” and “redirect,” which determines the next steps that should be taken by Cloudflare Worker hosted JavaScript code.

The JSON response mentioned above is being used by same JavaScript code that has sent the POST request:

AutoRelay and RelayMode, acts as the flags that decides which of these behaviors the JavaScript runs next.

The kit has three ways to run the device code flow:

1. Device code Hidden Relay (through redirect) In this case, autoRelay is set to ‘true’ and relayMode as ‘redirect’, so instead of showing a code, the JavaScript builds a URL from the relayToken in the response and redirects the victim's browser there.

2. Device code Hidden Relay (through popup)If autoRelay is set to ‘false’, the JavaScript writes the userCode into the page, tells the victim where to go and enter it, and starts a loop that polls the backend once a second to ask whether the grant has been approved yet.

3. Normal Device CodeIf relayMode were missing from the response, the JavaScript defaults to create a popup window and proceed with the Hidden Relay flow.

We observed the first of these, the redirect version. A userCode did come back in the response with a 900 second lifetime, so the code existed behind the scenes and it was just never written into the page for the victim to see, and no popup ever opened.

What Does the Victim See Instead of Code?

The browser was sent to the relay page, built from the relayToken in the response, at bandgdruback1[.]workers[.]dev/link/372b56d018b8cbc359b0819e402f11d5.

The page is titled "Verify your identity" and carries Microsoft branding. It shows the filename Document.pdf, the same string the kit hardcoded into the POST body, and it requests for a user email address for validation.

Once the user submits the email address, the browser is handed off to Microsoft.

What comes back is login[.]microsoftonline[.]com. The domain and sign-in page belong to Microsoft, and that is where the password prompt and the MFA prompt appear. Nothing the attacker controls is between the victim and their identity provider at this point.

The application mentioned on the consent screen is Microsoft Authentication Broker, and the attacker is targeting this client for the grant.

Where Did Microsoft's Session Parameters Come From?

The webpage shows one email input box, and the source code reveals four more fields that the victim never sees.

'ctx', 'flowToken' and 'canary' are Microsoft's own sign-in session parameters. Microsoft's authentication pages emit them, and no attacker generates them.

These fields are also observed in a reverse proxy phishing kit because it sits in the middle of a live session passing elements from the Microsoft page. But in this case we observe that the tokens arrived embedded in the HTML before the victim interacted with the phishing webpage. That is what rules out a reverse proxy here. A proxy has nothing to put in the page until the victim acts, because its tokens come from a live session it is relaying.

The 'ctx' token then tells us which session these belong to. It is not encrypted, only encoded, base64url with a six byte header and then a raw DEFLATE stream, so it inflates back to plaintext. Inside it sits an 810 byte Microsoft flow token.

When the 'ctx' from the attacker-served page and the $Config.s'ctx' from the genuine login[.]microsoftonline[.]com page reached after submitting the email were both decoded, the same 810 byte token was present in each, byte for byte.

Where the token was found

Length

SHA-1 (first 12 hex)

Inside decoded 'ctx', attacker relay page

810

9abe6d45ae29

Inside decoded $Config.s'ctx', Microsoft sign-in page

810

9abe6d45ae29

So the attacker's page and Microsoft's page share the same authentication session. The attacker's backend opened that session and was holding its state before the victim did anything at all. If the victim had signed in, the grant would have been approved, and the backend was positioned to collect the tokens it produced.

When the victim submits an email address in the phishing page, the browser posts the data to the attacker's end, not to Microsoft. The response is what sends the browser onward to login[.]microsoftonline[.]com/common/login. That destination is picked server-side, and nothing in any URL the victim could have inspected points at Microsoft. All the calls described here were observed in the network capture. What happened between the attacker's server and Microsoft was never visible from the victim's side.

How Do We Know This Was a Device Code Flow?

The answer rests on the kit's own vocabulary. The endpoint is named device/start and the field is named userCode, and those names are the attacker's own, consistent with what has been observed in EvilTokens kit.

The decoded 'ctx' is what actually settles it, because what inflates out of it is Microsoft's own record of the request its authorization server was handling.

Parameter

Value (this specific request)

client_id

29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e (Microsoft Authentication Broker)

grant/flow-type indicator

OAuth2DeviceAuth

prompt

select_account

resource

https://graph.microsoft.com

tenant

common

claims

{"access_token":{"amr":{"essential":true,"values":["ngcmfa"]}}}

The victim’s consent screen shows the client is Microsoft Authentication Broker (Client ID: 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) and the resource requested is https://graph[.]microsoft[.]com.

Together, the client and resource show what the attacker is after: tokens scoped to Microsoft Graph, Mail, Files and other account data.

In conclusion, three independent pieces of evidence points to:

The response's userCode value, nine uppercase characters with a 900-second lifetime, matches the shape RFC 8628 describes.

The decoded 'ctx' names Microsoft Authentication Broker as the target client.

The grant type recorded in that same 'ctx' is OAuth2DeviceAuth, Microsoft's own string for the Device Code Authentication.

Together, they confirm this is a genuine device code flow and the mitigations that work against real device code grants, blocking the flow, watching sign-in logs for the client ID, apply here too.

What Is Actually New Here?

Device code phishing is not new, and reverse proxy phishing kits are not new either. What’s new here is the flow we observed: the kit opened the authorization grant, and the user_code was never shown to the victim.

The actions observed in this kit's code are similar to those in the EvilProxy kit, where a proxy sits between the victim and Microsoft and relays live session parameters onto the phishing page, as the victim interacts with it, nothing staged beforehand. Here, In contrast: the same parameter values were pre-staged in the phishing page before the victim ever interacted with it, something that was not observed in an EvilProxy-style relayed kit.

This attack is using a hybrid approach associating both AiTM attacks and Device code phishing attacks, which was not observed before.

What Do Defenders Need to Know?

Restrict device code grants for non-essential users, as attackers are unable to alter this grant type. Additionally, track sign-in logs for device code authentication requests targeting the Microsoft Authentication Broker to detect these uncommon events.

The transport layer is notable: Block UDP port 443 and clients fall back to TCP, which Cloudflare serves too, so the traffic still completes and your inspection stack can read it.

Code-entry detections fail: The network log lacks “microsoft[.]com/devicelogin”, “login[.]microsoft[.]com/device” navigations, and the “?otc=” parameter, leaving detection rules with nothing to flag.

AiTM detections miss it for a different reason: AiTM detections look for a proxy relaying the victim's sign-in to Microsoft, such as sign-ins arriving from the relay or tokens replayed from elsewhere. Here the victim signs in directly on Microsoft's site, so that relay never exists for those detections to see.

We recommend keeping the old detections for AiTM and Device code phishing running as the same kit build still contains the classic branch that writes the code into the page and polls for approval.

While these security rules address previously documented scenarios, the critical insight lies in how the attacker orchestrated this chain. The initial email successfully passed domain authentication, and the link was delivered via a reputable email service provider. The user encountered a legitimate CAPTCHA and was ultimately directed to an authentic Microsoft sign-in page. Because users are trained to trust genuine Microsoft authentication portals, the victim made no discernible error. The attacker constructed an end-to-end chain where every user-facing step appeared completely legitimate.

The single most effective defense is evaluating the context before proceeding: "Does this sign-in prompt align with this user, device, and specific action?" An authentication attempt triggered by an unsolicited document approval request inherently lacks context. This contextual mismatch remains visible even when all technical indicators appear benign.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) to Block and Monitor

Indicator

Role in the chain

polwanlo[.]vip

First attacker-controlled domain. Took the click from the tracking link and redirected onward from /.well-known/rr/.

*.merlekw[.]workers[.]dev

Campaign router. Carried the campaign token in ?_k= and issued the victim's transfer token for the next hop.

*.maxjln[.]workers[.]dev

Turnstile challenge stage and the kit page itself. The kit path only becomes reachable once Turnstile issues a pass token.

c30d9e770432bc4-id-gate.bandgdruback1[.]workers[.]dev

Backend. Served /api/device/start, the relay page at /link/<token>, and the email submission endpoint.

The domains rotate. These fingerprints are the more durable half:

Fingerprint

What it is

POST /api/device/start with an X-Worker-Token header

The call that opens the device authorization grant.

/link/ followed by 32 hex characters

The relay page path.

The JSON fields autoRelay, relayMode, relayToken and lureType

The kit's own response contract. relayMode is the field that selects code suppression.

A sessionId shaped ses_<unix_ms>_<8 hex>

Server-generated session identifier.

29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e

Microsoft Authentication Broker. A first-party Microsoft client. Do not block it. Hunt for it paired with a device code grant.

Where KnowBe4 Can Help

Although this email bypasses email gateway controls and avoids triggering AiTM or FIDO2 detection mechanisms, multiple security layers still apply. Rather than relying on session replay tracking or domain reputation, protection depends on evaluating message content and user behavior.

KnowBe4 Defend: Real-Time Behavioral AI

The relevant layer here is content, not sender history, because SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass on this message, so nothing at the reputation layer has a reason to flag it. Defend's behavioral AI and natural language processing read the email itself rather than checking domain history, and the lure text, an unsolicited document-approval request running on an artificial deadline, is the kind of urgent, action-forcing language that analysis is built to flag, independent of how clean the sending domain looks.

Context-Aware Warning Banners

Defend adds a warning banner directly into the email before the recipient opens it, in this case the kind built for urgent action requests, ahead of the recipient doing anything with it. The banner acts at delivery, before a click, provided the classifier reads this specific lure pattern as risky in the first place.

articles.title: New Windows SignDrop zero-day gives hackers SYSTEM privileges
articles.context: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges
articles.full_text:
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges.

Named SignDrop, it exploits mitigations Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to defend against authentication attacks targeting vulnerabilities in the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. Naceri added that attacks exploiting CLFS vulnerabilities dropped sharply after the mitigation, but that Microsoft's mitigation itself introduced this new vulnerability.

According to Naceri, the flaw is in how CLFS handles creating the authentication file (".cnpf") when it creates a new log file. He said that CLFS enforces access checks correctly at the start, but the logic can be abused if a different, privileged process later opens the log file.

He also added that privileged processes such as Windows Defender can be forced to open the files, so the authentication file gets created with SYSTEM privileges, and CLFS creates it with the original file's access permissions.

Naceri noted that Microsoft implemented the mitigation properly but that "the logic allows abuse" and said the technique works against any antimalware engine's self-defense (tamper protection), because the file-creation request appears to come from the engine's own legitimate process.

"If everything is chained correctly, funnily, this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation of privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the security researcher said.

"What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism, as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR."

​While SignDrop can't be used against all Windows machines, Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental and estimates that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable.

Naceri recommends running the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to check if a Windows device is vulnerable to SignDrop attacks or to check the CLFS authentication mode under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry value.

If the PoC exploit spawns a SYSTEM shell, the machine is vulnerable. Additionally, if the registry value is 0 or 1 (learning mode or enforcement mode), the computer is vulnerable.

Naceri added that there is currently no solution except waiting for a patch from Microsoft, since disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose the devices to attacks exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities.

The security researcher, who says he is a former Microsoft employee, has disclosed a long list of other zero-day flaws in Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components since April, including BigDiskBuster, ShieldCrash, ShieldBreak, LegacyHive, RoguePlanet, BlueHammer, RedSun, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, and UnDefend.

Five years ago, Naceri released several zero-day exploits that allowed privilege escalation on various Windows versions.

After Naceri publicly disclosed the zero-days without first attempting to report them privately, Microsoft warned of legal action against anyone engaging in "malicious activity causing real harm" to the company's customers, leading many in the infosec community to see the company's actions as a direct threat to the security researcher.

While Microsoft has fixed some of the security flaws Naceri disclosed since the start of the year (including ShieldBreak, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, and MiniPlasma flaws), the other zero-day bugs still lack an official patch.

articles.title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
articles.context: “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information...
articles.full_text:
Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC, commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain.

In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale.

What the research found

Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters.

Measurement is the next test. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms.

Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks.

Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy.

“Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC.

AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings

Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses.

Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability.

Where scale stalls

66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them.

The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design.

Inside the Frontier Firm

IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause.

What they do differently comes down to five behaviors:

They invest ahead of plan. 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend.

They deploy AI broadly, across most of the business, not just a few teams.

They put agents to work. 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows.

They govern so they can scale. 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters.

They build skills everywhere. 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters.

At Bristol Myers Squibb, the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time.

Four disciplines for scaling AI value

The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off.

I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER. “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.”

Unlock model choice

Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data.

Redesign workflows around agents

Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters.

Govern decisions and actions

Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do.

Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.”

Measure and optimize value

Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest.

Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start.

Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch.

Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite

IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall.

What this means for business

The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation.

First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day.

Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business.

Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI.

The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next.

Get the full picture

Download the global infographic, The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe, Asia Pacific and the Americas. The full InfoBrief will follow.

Alysa Taylor is the Chief Marketing Officer for Commercial Cloud and AI at Microsoft, leading teams that enable digital and AI transformation for organizations of all sizes across the globe.

articles.title: Weak Passwords Expose SQL Servers to Cryptominer and Gh0st RAT
articles.context: Attackers Scan and Brute-Force SQL Servers A brute-force tool then tried usernames including "sa" and "admin" against more than 2700 passwords on each host the scanner found
articles.full_text:
A campaign has been breaking into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances with weak passwords to install a Monero cryptominer and a Gh0st remote access trojan (RAT).

FortiGuard Labs, Fortinet's research team, uncovered the campaign in early October 2026 and rated it high severity, according to new research published on November 12. The report did not say how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign.

The initial Go payload contained the open-source Naabu port scanner. It retrieved an IP range from its server, scanned it for TCP port 1433, the default SQL Server port, and recorded the hosts that responded, before requesting another range and starting again.

Attackers Scan and Brute-Force SQL Servers

A brute-force tool then tried usernames including "sa" and "admin" against more than 2700 passwords on each host the scanner found.

After a successful login, the malware ran Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands on the server. T-SQL is SQL Server's extension of the SQL database language, adding programming features to standard queries.

The commands enabled xp_cmdshell, which runs operating system commands, then downloaded or unpacked a loader. They also scheduled the loader to run daily and placed a copy in the Startup folder so it ran when the server booted.

The loader pulled additional malware from an FTP server and registered each compromised server with the attackers' backend. The data sent back included the public IP address, country, Windows edition, processor and memory details, Windows installation time, user name and host name.

Cryptominer and Gh0st RAT Hide on Servers

One payload was a Monero cryptominer based on XMRig that used the compromised server's processor. It was named to look like a Microsoft Edge update, as were two of the scheduled tasks the malware created, and reported to the attackers when mining began.

Read more on cryptomining: Cryptominer Abuses Linux PAM to Hide From SOC Analysts

The second payload was a Gh0st RAT variant named after a Windows system process. Its command-and-control (C2) server had shut down before Fortinet's analysis, so researchers examined its code without running it.

The RAT supported keylogging, data theft and over 30 control commands, with plugins providing screen capture and remote desktop. It could also clear event logs, check for 78 security products by process name and steal data from the QQ messaging app.

For persistence, it used a registry Run key, a Windows service and a scheduled task that ran every 30 minutes.

In effect, the search had no built-in end, continuing for as long as the attackers’ server kept handing out new address ranges.

articles.title: Citrix Patches 12 NetScaler and Secure Access Client Flaws, Including Authentication Bypass
articles.context: Citrix has released patches for multiple critical security flaws impacting NetScaler ADC, Citrix NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console that could lead to denial-of-service...
articles.full_text:
Citrix has released patches for multiple critical security flaws impacting NetScaler ADC, Citrix NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console that could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or an authentication bypass.

The critical vulnerabilities that impact NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway are listed below -

CVE-2026-120868 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Packet Processing can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments)

CVE-2026-107407 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in SMPP traffic can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured with a Load Balancing or Content Switching virtual server of type SMPP)

CVE-2026-107408 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured for DNS load balancing and recursive DNS resolution)

CVE-2026-107409 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured with DNS Load Balancing over HTTPS)

CVE-2026-107410 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow in NetScaler Push can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as Load Balancing virtual server of type PUSH)

CVE-2026-107412 (CVSS score: 9.5) - Multiple memory overflow vulnerabilities can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior and DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway or an AAA virtual server)

CVE-2026-107415 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Email OTP authentication can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway configured with an Email Action)

CVE-2026-111344 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a VPN virtual server or an authentication (AAA) virtual server with Endpoint Analysis)

CVE-2026-120864 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in ICA proxy can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway VPN virtual server, an AAA virtual server, or a CR virtual server of type HDX)

All the issues have been patched in the following versions -

Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.57 and later releases

Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.39 and later releases of 13.1

Citrix NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPS

Citrix NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP

Also addressed by Citrix are a number of flaws in NetScaler Console and Secure Access Client for Windows and Linux -

CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score: 9.4) - An improper authentication vulnerability in NetScaler Console can allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication controls to access restricted resources on the appliance. (Fixed in NetScaler Console 14.1-74.34 and later)

CVE-2026-118268 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Windows can allow a low-privileged user to escalate privileges to SYSTEM. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Windows 26.11.1.6 and later)

CVE-2026-118269 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Linux can allow a low-privileged user to gain root privileges. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Linux 26.10.4 and later)

The security updates, Citrix said, follow a deeper review of its codebase by integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted code analysis to detect and resolve vulnerabilities with an aim to harden the products before potential threats could materialize.

The company said it's not aware of any exploits for any of the announced vulnerabilities, but urged customers to apply the updates as they are designed to "enhance the security posture of NetScaler."

articles.title: 186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers
articles.context: Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking malware, and a set of extensions that hijack user searches.

This delivery pattern has been codenamed TypoPrompting by Island.

"AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else," the cybersecurity company said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

In all, the campaign spans 186 bogus domains spanning 27 AI brands, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), Microsoft Copilot, SpaceXAI Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.

While one category leads to a ClickFix lure that serves a PowerShell command via a fake Cloudflare verification page, the second route takes unsuspecting users to "Security Check" pages that deliver a browser-hijacking malware called Net Guard. The third pathway sends users to a search-hijack extension family with 16 live Chrome Web Store listings and 972,000 declared users.

Some of the AI lookalike domains are listed below -

cloude[.]ai

cluade[.]ai

clsude[.]ai

chatlgpt[.]com

geimini[.]com

notebookklm[.]com

griok[.]com

preplexity[.]ai

deepceek[.]com

elevenlebs[.]io

copiot[.]com

midj0urney[.]org

An analysis of registration records shows that some of these domains, like cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 13, 2023.

The use of parked domains for malware delivery is not new. In December 2025, Infoblox highlighted how domains without a current web page can be monetized to redirect visitors to sites that serve scams and malware after profiling the host and the device they are visiting from.

"When a domain owner opts into direct search, traffic to the domain is sold to advertisers who bid on keywords and traffic characteristics," the DNS threat intelligence firm noted at the time. "In practice, the site visitor is usually funneled through a series of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) operated by third-party advertising platforms, creating a complex web where a legitimate business model is weaponized for abuse."

In the case of the ClickFix route, the parked page initiates a redirect chain that fingerprints the web browser and collects the public IP address before displaying the fake Cloudflare verification page.

Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.

These domains serve three types of lures -

Fake verification pages on Windows that are designed to run a clipboard command

Terminal or security updates on macOS that are designed to run a shell command

Archive download pages that instruct users to extract and run an executable

Separately, eight typosquat domains for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs, and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages that ultimately deliver Net Guard.

While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."

"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."

The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.

"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."

Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.

"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."

(The story was updated after publication to include a response from Island.)

articles.title: Palo Alto tracks a massive Chinese AI attack that sadly lives up to industry fears
articles.context: ” He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval
articles.full_text:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said.

The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems.

It even gained unauthenticated access to cloud storage and overwrote a live ballot for a vote on an industry standard. Through separate flaws, the attackers logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions.

“What a nightmare,” said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “This campaign is impressive, in the worst way.”

He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval.

Unit 42 “took the machine apart and showed how it thinks: the shared blackboard, the facts, the intents, the human hints, and even the exact prompts the attackers used,” he said. “The expensive part of an intrusion was always the labor: the reconnaissance, the trial and error, and the patience. That labor is now a line item on an API bill. Unit 42 believes one person or a handful of people ran all of it, hitting 19 organizations in two weeks. Some operations ran for more than 50 hours.”

Andy Piazza, senior director of threat research at Unit 42, said the monitored campaign showed that the massive scope of a global AI-fueled assault is every bit as frightening as predicted.

“We are now starting to see the evidence” because the monitored campaign “can now interact with 1,000 organizations at the same time,” Piazza said. “I think we need to throw out the risk model for the perimeter. This also completely breaks our attribution models. The fingerprinting of attack uniqueness is going to be a hell of a lot harder now.”

Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that he was concerned about this campaign because of the scope of activities that AI is now able to handle.

“This is significant because AI is taking on the coordination of an intrusion, using each result to decide what to try next and reducing the hands-on effort required to pursue multiple targets,” he said. “That changes the economics of targeting. An attacker can sustain pressure across more organizations without personally directing every step. An organization’s risk can rise even when its vulnerabilities haven’t changed.”

Greis noted that the altered ballot deserves attention because it shows how an intrusion can undermine the information people rely on to make decisions. “Alongside detecting data theft, CISOs should monitor unauthorized changes to critical records and privileged access and test their ability to verify and restore trusted information after an incident,” he said. “Resilience includes knowing that the information you are using to run the business can still be trusted.”

The model’s process

The report included a detailed description of the campaign’s methodology. “Cairn coordinated its activities through a shared blackboard,” it said. “Agents read the blackboard and wrote their ﬁndings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject hints at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Conﬁrmed ﬁndings accumulate as immutable facts and the agent queues its next actions as intents. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the US.”

The model produced a different plan for each target, each running between three and seven stages, the researchers explained. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Chinese AI Models Cairn is model-agnostic, they noted, and the attackers ran their operations on the Chinese models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro.

The report also described attackers’ efforts to negate systems attempting to prohibit the unauthorized activities.

“Cairn’s stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task,” it said. “The attackers reinforced this with an authorization pretext of their own. Each operation also generated an authorization.md file. This file declared the operation authorized, treating the attackers’ act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement. The attackers seeded each task with an organization’s root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface.”

“We knew attackers would get here. We hoped it was not now,” Dickson said. “AI attack agents have graduated from failed experiments to real breaches, and they did it in about three months.”

articles.title: WhiteArmor gang claims responsibility for latest cyber attack on shipping giant Maersk
articles.context: In 2017, the company was hit by the NotPetya malware attack which forced the firm to reinstall more than 4000 servers and 45,000 workstations, and ended up costing it up to US...
articles.full_text:
Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that one of its systems was broken into by hackers who have stolen data.

In a statement published yesterday on its website, the company said that it had detected the unauthorised access to a "local legacy system". The Danish company has not said which system was hit, what data was taken, or when the security breach occurred.

The firm has, however, said that it has seen no sign that the breach involved other Maersk systems, or that shipments have been impacted. To date, Maersk says that it has not seen any evidence that any sensitive information has been breached.

Responsibility for the attack has been claimed by the WhiteArmor cybercrime group, which has listed Maersk on its dark web leak site. There it demanded a ransom equivalent to US $5 million be paid within 30 days, for the 100GB worth of data it claims to have stolen from a platform built by LF Logistics, a firm that Maersk acquired in 2022.

WhiteArmor is a relatively new cyber-extortion group, having emerged late last month, but it is already claiming more than a dozen victims on its leak site including Chinese electronics and home appliance manufacturer Hisense.

According to WhiteArmor, its data haul from Maersk includes nearly 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords, purchase orders, advance shipping notices, signed delivery receipts, and 27,842 mobile device records containing phone numbers, email addresses, and IMEI numbers.

While Maersk has not confirmed the veracity of the hackers' claims, it is advising customers and partners to treat unexpected messages about the security breach with caution, and to always verify with a trusted contact at the company before taking any action.

Regular readers of the Hot for Security blog will be well aware that this is not Maersk's first brush with cybercrime.

In 2017, the company was hit by the NotPetya malware attack which forced the firm to reinstall more than 4000 servers and 45,000 workstations, and ended up costing it up to US $300 million.

On this occasion the breach appears to have happened because of IT systems inherited from an acquisition. As such it serves as a salutary reminder that when you buy a company you also buy its IT systems, and any security problems which may lurk within them.

articles.title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
articles.context: Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released
articles.full_text: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned. Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)." And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server. This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves. According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®
