articles.title: Predator, Pegasus and Graphite: Governments Accused of Spyware Abuse Face Little Accountability
articles.context: In 2025, Citizen Lab found Italian phone numbers among those targeted by Paragon Solutions, an Israeli company that was later acquired by a US investment fund
articles.full_text:
Europe’s spyware victims face years of legal battles and few answers as governments shield surveillance behind national security.

Greek journalist Thanasis Koukakis waited almost five years for a court to confirm what happened to him. His phone was infected with the infaous spyware Predator that gave whoever was watching access to his contacts, documents and messages, and even let them switch on his camera and microphone. IrpiMedia’s journalist and researcher Rosita Rijtano interviewed him and four other victims in a long investigation, and the picture it paints is bleak.

On February 26, a court in Athens convicted four executives linked to Intellexa, the company behind the Predator spyware. They include its founder, Tal Dilian, a former Israeli military intelligence commander. They face prison sentences of up to eight years for illegally accessing computer systems, violating data protection rules and breaking telecommunications privacy laws. Their sentences are suspended while they appeal, and investigators have not identified who ordered the surveillance. This is the first conviction of its kind in Europe, highlighting how rare such cases are.

The scandal began in 2021, when an international investigation led by Forbidden Stories revealed that dozens of European activists, politicians and journalists had been targeted with Pegasus spyware, developed by NSO Group. The company says it sells its products only to government intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Other spyware companies later came under scrutiny. In 2025, Citizen Lab found Italian phone numbers among those targeted by Paragon Solutions, an Israeli company that was later acquired by a US investment fund. Except in Greece, none of these cases has led to a criminal conviction.

“Yet, with the exception of Greece, none of these cases has resulted in a criminal conviction. In Spain and Hungary, victims say they have been unable even to obtain basic information about the surveillance they were subjected to, with authorities citing “national security.”” reads the report published by IrpiMedia.

In Spain and Hungary, victims say they can’t even get basic information about the surveillance, because authorities cite national security. Rebecca White, a researcher at Amnesty International’s Security Lab, calls it double victimization: first you’re hit by one of the most invasive technologies in the world, then you find one dead end after another when you seek justice. Courts and bodies like the European Court of Human Rights take years and cost a lot, and the search wears people down psychologically.

Europe’s own recommendations haven’t helped. After the Pegasus scandal, the European Parliament’s PEGA inquiry committee adopted recommendations on June 15, 2023, including an EU fund for victims’ legal costs and an independent laboratory offering free legal and technical help and forensic analysis. Member states were asked to strengthen safeguards, notify people who were surveilled, guarantee effective remedies and let independent bodies access the data needed to investigate abuses. Three years later, Green MEP Saskia Bricmont says nothing has been done by the Commission or the member states, and that governments hide behind national security.

Sophie in ‘t Veld, the former PEGA rapporteur, says the situation has become worse. She argues that governments realised they would face no consequences and that more spyware cases have emerged since the inquiry, especially in Italy. She also criticises the European Commission for supporting national governments instead of protecting victims. Polish MEP Krzysztof Brejza says the system does not help victims because there is little transparency and no clear process for seeking justice.

Brejza was also a victim of spyware. His phone was infected with Pegasus while he was leading the election campaign against Poland’s then-ruling Law and Justice party. He says attackers accessed 85,000 messages covering ten years and changed some conversations.

“They gained access to 85,000 messages, covering the last ten years of my private and professional life. Because they found nothing against me, they went further and manipulated my conversations. Altered exchanges were broadcast by national television to discredit me. The aim was to interfere in the election by weakening democracy,” Brejza tells IrpiMedia.

National television later broadcast these messages to damage his reputation. Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau had requested the surveillance as part of an investigation into his father, a mayor. Prosecutors in Gdansk later found no grounds for that investigation.

In October 2026, a Polish parliamentary inquiry concluded that Pegasus had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents. So far, Brejza has won only civil cases: the broadcaster was forced to apologise and pay damages. Criminal investigations are still ongoing and progressing slowly.

“In October 2026, a parliamentary inquiry committee set up in Poland after Donald Tusk took office to investigate the use of Pegasus under the previous government concluded that the spyware had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents.” states the report.

Poland’s justice minister also serves as prosecutor general, while the former justice minister received asylum in Hungary before moving to the US.

Koukakis says they identified the Predator spyware and its operator but not who ordered the attacks. Court records show that nearly one-third of those targeted in 2020 and 2021 were also under Greek intelligence surveillance. He suspects a link. Fake appointment messages and article invitations were used to lure victims. He believes his reporting on legal changes that allegedly benefited people involved in financial crimes may have made him a target.

Greek authorities deny using Predator, arguing that no law regulated it at the time. Although an Athens court referred the case for further investigation, the Supreme Court prosecutor refused to reopen it on April 27. Koukakis challenged the decision and took his case against Greece to the European Court of Human Rights.

In Hungary, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi, who has covered Russian influence on the government of Viktor Orbán, learned from analyses by Amnesty’s Security Lab and Citizen Lab that he’d been spied on with Pegasus for seven months in 2019, with about 100 megabytes of data moving to and from his phone. All he’s found out since is that the civilian intelligence agency holds classified information about him, and every request has been blocked on national security grounds. He says Hungarian law lets anyone be spied on legally, because the justice minister, a member of the government, authorizes it.

Despite Spain’s stricter laws, spyware infected the phones of at least 65 people linked to the Catalan independence movement, mostly between 2017 and 2020, according to Citizen Lab. The victims included four members of Òmnium Cultural. The legal case was dismissed and later reopened on appeal, while the government was asked to declassify related documents.

In 2022, Spain’s ombudsman confirmed that intelligence services had legally monitored 18 independence movement members. However, Òmnium’s Elena Jiménez argues that judicial approval doesn’t automatically make surveillance lawful, warning that even progressive governments can spy on political opponents.

In Italy, Mediterranea Saving Humans founders Luca Casarini and Beppe Caccia, along with activist David Yambio, were targeted with Paragon’s Graphite spyware. The government cited suspected facilitation of irregular immigration, while Casarini believes the real motive was their evidence of abuses against migrants in Libya and Tunisia. Italy’s parliamentary oversight body ruled all three cases lawful.

Citizen Lab founder Ron Deibert warns that spyware creates a worldwide pattern of abuse, silencing victims and weakening democratic accountability. Experts argue that Europe still lacks effective safeguards and oversight. They call for greater transparency and a way to identify who orders and conducts surveillance. As Sophie in ‘t Veld puts it, “It is clear that they feel safe, untouchable.”

“Spyware can be useful in addressing real threats, such as terrorism or crime. But we need tools that allow us to identify the end user of the product, so that, when necessary, we can trace who ordered the surveillance and who carried it out, even in real time,” the journalist Koukakis told IrpiMedia.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Spyware )

articles.title: Cyberattacks Are Skyrocketing in Japan as Researchers Trace AI-Assisted Intrusions
articles.context: Investigators found that attackers exploited software vulnerabilities, stole session information, and abused legitimate CSV export functions to extract customer data
articles.full_text:
Japan is facing an extraordinary surge in cyberattacks, with a record 233 security incidents publicly disclosed in October alone. That's roughly 2.4 times the previous monthly record, according to Trend Micro data reported by TV Asahi. Cyberattacks are rising around the world, but the pace of disclosures in Japan is staggering. Nearly every day has dragged another affected company, service provider, or public institution into the headlines.

The volume of exposed information is growing even faster. An analysis by MM Research Institute estimates that approximately 185 million personal information records were exposed or potentially exposed in incidents disclosed during October, nearly four times the total reported for all of 2025. The number of large breaches has also increased sharply, with 30 incidents involving at least one million records disclosed in October.

The disclosures have implicated major retailers, technology companies, financial services providers, and government agencies. On November 9, Japanese furniture giant Nitori disclosed that unauthorized access to its systems may have exposed up to 37.62 million customer information records. Days earlier, email service provider Arara confirmed an intrusion affecting more than 81 million email addresses and potentially hundreds of corporate customers.

Japan's government has announced emergency cybersecurity measures as researchers dig into why so many attacks are succeeding and what's driving the sudden spike.

Breaches Surge While Ransomware Disclosures Remain Relatively Flat #

In an October analysis of Japanese security incidents, TrendAI counted 607 publicly disclosed incidents from January through September 2026, already exceeding the 594 reported during all of 2025.

Yet ransomware disclosures barely moved in TrendAI's dataset. Researchers counted 82 publicly disclosed ransomware incidents during the first nine months of 2026, compared with 79 during the same period last year.

Unauthorized access accounted for 331 incidents in TrendAI's analysis, more than half of the total. Another 62 involved what TrendAI calls data supply chain incidents, in which an organization entrusted with information suffers an attack and its customers subsequently report their own exposure.

A separate investigation by Japanese cybersecurity firm Macnica illustrates just how dramatically web application breaches have increased. Researchers identified 288 incidents involving unauthorized access to web systems and potential data theft through October 2026, compared with 84 during all of 2025. October alone accounted for 168 disclosures.

Macnica excluded ransomware, credential-stuffing attacks, and duplicate disclosures from customers affected by the same compromised provider. Its research found that attacks have expanded well beyond traditional ecommerce targets to membership portals, business applications, and specialized services.

Some of the targets are surprisingly obscure. Macnica documented breaches involving:

A regional table tennis association's tournament registration system: 185 organizers

A tourist train's seat reservation system: Approximately 1,400 passengers

A funeral company's flower-ordering system: Roughly 10,000 records

An event ticket refund system: Approximately 1,500 records

A fashion magazine's blogger management system: About 2,800 people

These incidents, disclosed between July and October, show how far the attacks have spread beyond major retailers and technology companies. Membership portals and business or administrative systems accounted for roughly two-thirds of the October web-system incidents Macnica tracked.

Researchers also found evidence of successful intrusions continuing into late October, indicating that the spike wasn't simply the result of organizations discovering and reporting older compromises.

Arara Compromise Leads to Hundreds of Affected Companies #

The breach at Japanese email distribution provider Arara demonstrates how an intrusion at a single company can spread through an extensive network of business customers.

In an updated disclosure on November 6, Arara confirmed that attackers had obtained approximately 81.3 million email addresses, with up to 380 corporate customers potentially affected. Depending on the customer, the exposed information may also have included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, addresses, and membership information.

Attackers also used Arara's email distribution service to send as many as 7.13 million fraudulent messages impersonating credit card companies between October 28 and October 30.

The company suspended the affected service on October 31 while investigating the intrusion.

On November 9, Japanese gaming giant SEGA disclosed that approximately 2.2 million newsletter email addresses were exposed through Arara. Other affected organizations include major retailers and service providers that relied on the same email infrastructure.

Arara wasn't the only Japanese email distribution provider hit. On October 19, Ymir Link disclosed an intrusion into its Cuenote FC service. In a November 11 update, the company confirmed that attackers had extracted approximately 47.9 million email distribution records from 49 systems. Investigators found that attackers exploited software vulnerabilities, stole session information, and abused legitimate CSV export functions to extract customer data.

The Arara breach left hundreds of companies dealing with the fallout of an attack on systems they didn't operate. A company whose own systems remain secure may still need to notify customers, investigate potential exposure, and address the consequences of an intrusion at a service provider.

Researchers Find Evidence of AI-Assisted Exploitation #

The reasons behind Japan's sudden increase remain under investigation, but researchers have identified evidence that artificial intelligence is being used to help attackers discover and exploit vulnerabilities.

In an October 21 technical investigation, Japan's Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center, JPCERT/CC, confirmed that attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs.

Investigators examining attack infrastructure found that attackers had analyzed Android application packages to identify API endpoints and test them for weaknesses, including server-side request forgery (SSRF).

On another attack server, researchers found Blutter and jadx, tools used to reverse-engineer Android and Flutter applications. Analyzing these apps can reveal API endpoints and authentication mechanisms, allowing attackers to probe backend services for weaknesses that aren't obvious from the public website.

The attacks go beyond known vulnerabilities. Macnica's investigation found attackers exploiting authentication and access-control weaknesses specific to individual applications. Finding these issues has traditionally required considerable effort, but AI-assisted analysis and automation can accelerate the process across many targets.

TrendAI researchers have also observed suspicious files containing artifacts consistent with AI-generated code and attack attempts that rapidly adjusted after initial failures.

While researchers have confirmed AI-assisted attacks, they haven't established how much AI is contributing to Japan's broader cyberattack surge. JPCERT/CC also found that some of the infrastructure it investigated targeted services outside Japan, suggesting these techniques are not limited to Japanese organizations.

Japan Seeks Earlier Vulnerability Warnings as Attacks Accelerate #

The surge has prompted Japan's government to examine how quickly organizations receive information about software vulnerabilities and can respond before attackers exploit them.

According to a November 5 Reuters report citing Nikkei, Japan plans to seek earlier access to information about undisclosed software vulnerabilities from US AI developers and other overseas technology companies.

The government is exploring arrangements that would give agencies and critical infrastructure operators advance warning of serious vulnerabilities, allowing them more time to prepare patches or other mitigations before public disclosure.

The effort follows a disruptive October incident involving critical vulnerabilities in PHP, which is particularly prevalent in Japan. According to W3Techs, PHP runs on approximately 92% of websites hosted in Japan whose server-side language can be identified, compared with 69% globally. One reason is the popularity of WordPress in Japan. The content management system powers 88% of Japan-hosted websites with an identifiable CMS, compared with approximately 58% worldwide.

Exploitation attempts began before the PHP vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on October 21, and millions of subsequent attempts forced some website operators to patch urgently or temporarily take their systems offline.

The pressure to respond faster extends beyond newly discovered vulnerabilities. On November 5, Japan's National Cybersecurity Office warned businesses that several recent breaches appeared to involve inadequate security practices, including continued use of unsupported software and known vulnerabilities that had not been patched.

The guidance calls on organizations to maintain visibility into their software components, establish priorities and deadlines for fixing vulnerabilities, and prepare procedures for responding when serious vulnerabilities are discovered in open source software and external libraries. It also addresses security weaknesses in APIs and systems operated by outside contractors.

The following day, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration announced a 10 billion yen ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package. The measures include expanded intelligence gathering, AI-assisted vulnerability detection, stronger coordination between government and industry, and additional support for organizations responding to attacks.

Japan is pushing for earlier vulnerability warnings as attackers find and exploit weaknesses faster than organizations can patch them, including vulnerabilities that have already been known for some time.

There has also been speculation about state-backed involvement. Kyodo News reported that GMO Internet Group's investigation pointed to a North Korea-linked hacking group in its October breach, but no public evidence has linked Japan's broader cyberattack wave to a single state-sponsored campaign. The incidents involve different systems, techniques, and circumstances, and many investigations remain ongoing.

For organizations trying to keep pace, patching faster requires knowing which software components and open source dependencies they run, where they're used, and which vulnerabilities need attention first. Japan is now seeking access to vulnerability intelligence before public disclosure, while urging businesses to address known weaknesses more quickly. The pressure is mounting after a month of record breaches, with November already bringing another wave of major disclosures.

articles.title: Hacked Asian Telcos Used to Intercept Taiwanese Calls and Texts
articles.context: Enea, a firm providing software for telecommunications and cybersecurity, named the actor SilentAir in its November 11 research, which also covers Liminal Panda, a group that...
articles.full_text:
A newly identified state-level actor has used compromised mobile operators in Asia to intercept calls and texts, mainly targeting subscribers in Taiwan. Enea has watched it since early 2025.

Enea, a firm providing software for telecommunications and cybersecurity, named the actor SilentAir in its November 11 research, which also covers Liminal Panda, a group that has attacked mobile operators.

The company said it saw a possible but unproven connection between the two groups.

SilentAir Targets Taiwanese Subscribers

Enea is highly confident that SilentAir operated at state level. The actor launched Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) and Diameter attacks from hijacked equipment in operators across at least six Asian countries, hitting targets in a dozen more countries and territories.

The attacks came in waves, from a handful of subscribers to several thousand in a month, with quiet spells of months in between. Interception accounted for 18.30% of SilentAir's activity, against 2.07% for the surveillance companies behind most signaling attacks.

For some targets, two-factor authentication (2FA) codes arrived moments after interception began, which Enea said showed an aim of breaking into their other accounts. Most of its other activity was silent SMS, texts that never show on the phone, sent largely to Taiwanese users around midnight.

Enea linked SilentAir to China-nexus operations with low confidence, citing the Taiwan focus, the lack of Chinese targets, working hours matching China's time zone and lulls over Chinese holidays. Some targets were political and government VIPs.

Read more on telecom espionage: Singapore Takes Down Chinese Hackers Targeting Telco Networks

Liminal Panda Expands GTPDoor

Enea said its firewalls spotted and blocked GTPDoor and other Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators from early 2026, detecting several hundred attempted command-and-control (C2) exchanges.

GTPDoor, a Unix backdoor, hides its C2 traffic in the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP), which carries roaming data.

Enea said it had seen at least five to 10 operators infected by Liminal Panda, directly or through strong indications, and believed the true figure might be several dozen, concentrated in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

It also found a new GTPDoor version that rode on GTP-U, the part of the protocol carrying user data. That traffic is far heavier and, according to Enea, less closely watched, and unlike the control side it carries over into 5G. Enea believed the new version mostly served as a fallback.

CrowdStrike linked Liminal Panda to China-nexus operations in November 2024, also with low confidence.

Enea said it helped customers clear out Liminal Panda and alerted operators hosting SilentAir sources. It said both groups had been set back for now, but warned the conditions remained for them, or others, to return.

In this article

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting unusual activity

The company has not confirmed a hack or whether customer data was affected

Users should watch for suspicious payment requests and avoid reusing passwords

LEGO collectors looking for a missing piece have a bigger problem to contend with: accessing the specialized marketplace BrickLink.

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting what it calls “unusual activity.” The company says it is investigating before bringing the marketplace back, but has not disclosed whether attackers accessed its systems or whether customer information was affected.

BrickLink allows users to buy and sell LEGO parts, sets, and minifigures, making it a useful resource for collectors and a business platform for independent sellers. LEGO acquired the fan-founded marketplace in 2019. Its disruption leaves more than unfinished builds on hold: sellers also depend on access to orders and their storefronts.

The BrickLink website previously said it would remain unavailable until at least Wednesday, November 11. That date has now been removed, with no replacement given.

We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform. Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

This work is still on-going and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible.

Updated: 11th November 2026

According to the BBC, LEGO had not provided details confirming a hack or explaining whether customer data was affected.

Specialist LEGO publications reported that BrickLink went offline around November 5. An article published the following morning described a notice saying the site was unavailable while teams carried out “necessary work.” That report also noted that users could not access storefronts, profiles, order histories, or the Designer Program page.

In November 2023, BrickLink also closed down after it noticed what turned out to be credential stuffing attacks.

The BBC also reported the experience of a BrickLink customer who received repeated payment links for a limited-edition preorder she said she had already paid for. The dispute was subsequently resolved, and LEGO told the BBC it was not aware of wider payment issues. But there is no established connection between that payment problem and the activity that prompted the shutdown.

How to stay safe

Until we know what the issue is, it is hard to provide targeted advice, but users can take a few proportionate precautions:

Watch for unexpected account or payment messages. A request to “restore access,” confirm payment information, or resolve an urgent account problem deserves scrutiny, because these are common phishing themes.

Verify requests through an independent route. Use the official website or an established support channel rather than following links in an unexpected email or text.

Use unique passwords. If your BrickLink password is also used elsewhere, change it on those other services now. Use a password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords. Change your BrickLink password once the site is available again.

BrickLink’s shutdown is disruptive, but the available evidence does not yet justify calling it a confirmed data breach. For now, the priority for users is to follow official updates, check unexpected payment requests carefully, and watch for scams exploiting the outage.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

articles.title: Apple’s HomeView Tries Face Authentication Without FaceID
articles.context: “This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post
articles.full_text:
Apple's HomeView, which debuts on Friday, is a smart home device—think of it as a an iPhone-Apple Watch hybrid sitting on your counter—that can be personalized for up to six people and connected to each of their iCloud accounts. Using ambient face and voice data, it is designed to seamlessly switch between users while maintaining each of their privacy. You can ask HomeView about your schedule for the day and what movie your friend recommended in a text, but you'll be stopped from asking about your roommate's travel plans or her texts from last night. The feature doesn't rely on one of Apple's battle-tested biometric locks, like FaceID or TouchID, though. Instead, it uses new “person recognition” technology built off of an Apple architecture for securing sensor data.

This is a key departure for Apple. On the one hand, the company has still been very careful to think about security and privacy comprehensively. Not only does HomeView check for your face and voice before accessing your data from iCloud, it is also designed like an Apple Watch to check that your iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView and has been recently unlocked (with FaceID or a PIN). On the other hand, expanding the architecture used to process biometric data and authenticate users creates more opportunities for mistakes and potential vulnerabilities. And when it comes to attempting to access users' Apple data, both law enforcement and exploit brokers consistently go to great lengths to attempt to break the company's on-device defenses.

FaceID is built for the use case where a person is staring at their device head-on from less than an arm's length away. It provides reliable security that’s difficult to defeat because it stores your biometric data on a special, physically isolated chip known as the Secure Enclave—first introduced in 2013 for the iPhone 5s. The architecture is so robust that Apple also relies on the Secure Enclave as the foundation of a device's entire encryption scheme. But Apple concluded that FaceID wasn't the best fit for the HomeView, because it needs to bounce quickly between users and relies on AI processing, which can't all be squeezed into the Secure Enclave.

As a result, HomeView uses Apple's recently announced Secure Exclave (note the “x”) to handle the video and audio data the device uses to evaluate who is in a room at a given time. Apple says it has actually been laying the groundwork for the Secure Exclave for a long time—early versions of the architecture were already in place for the iPhone 16 and 17 and MacBook Neo. Instead of being an entirely separately chip, the Secure Exclave is a dedicated, memory-protected space in recent Apple processors. It is in Apple's latest S11 chip for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, as well as the A20 Pro chip for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

Even though the Secure Exclave isn't based on the tried and true Secure Enclave technology, Apple argues that it is robust and expands the company's ability to secure a range of features, including improving the security of existing mechanisms. In a blog post on Thursday, the company even goes into some detail about how it used the mathematical technique known as formal verification to vet the “microkernel” designed for the Secure Exclave.

“This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks.”

HomeView and the MacBook Neo also use the Secure Exclave to govern the indicator light that tells users when their camera or microphone is active. The goal is to isolate this process and the chain of command governing it to make it even more difficult for attackers to try to disable an indicator light when it should be on or stop it from coming on in the first place.

The HomeView's “person recognition” technology is simply not as comprehensive as FaceID, though, and it is possible that the technology is more susceptible to reconstructed 3D depth map attacks—and potentially voiceprint attacks—than FaceID.

Of course, you don't have to have a HomeView in your house. Or if you do, you can use it on guest mode or a less involved “personalized” mode that only incorporates things like your playlists for other users to access as well and doesn't access calendar or Messages data. But as Apple forges deeper into AI integration, HomeView's departure from FaceID provides insight into the scale of the changes Apple is planning.

articles.title: Lego Takes BrickLink Marketplace Offline After Detecting Unusual Activity
articles.context: In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to...
articles.full_text:
Lego Group has taken its BrickLink Marketplace offline after identifying “unusual activity” on the platform.

An update was posted on November 11 by the Danish toy firm which said, “Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.”

The company is currently investigating the activity and said it needs to “fully understand” what has happened before bringing the site back online.

“That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.”

It is not yet known how long the downtime is expected to last and when the service will be reinstated.

BrickLink is an online marketplace owned by Lego Group where independent third-party sellers can buy and sell individual Lego parts – like eBay for Lego. Lego Group acquired the online marketplace in 2019.

The Lego marketplace has previously found itself at the center of security issues. In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to internal production data. Lego resolved the issues after Salt Labs disclosed the issues to the toy firm.

In November 2023 BrickLink was taken offline for a number of days due to a suspected cybersecurity incident.

Professional Lego reviewer Jay Ong, who runs Jay’s Bricks Blog, covered the downtime and noted that users were prompted to update their passwords. However, in an email he received at the time of the incident, he was reassured that his BrickLink account had not been compromised.

articles.title: Hackers abuse SQL Server’s weak passwords to drop cryptominers and Gh0st RAT
articles.context: “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit
articles.full_text:
An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware.

The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems.

The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said. “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.”

The campaign delivers two distinct payloads: an XMRig-based Monero cryptocurrency miner that hijacks the compromised servers’ computing resources, and a Gh0st remote access trojan (RAT) variant that gives attackers remote access and capabilities such as keylogging and data theft.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brute-forcing SQL logins to get Windows commands

The campaign begins with a Go-based payload named “dllhost.exe,” which runs the open-source Naabu port scanner, FortiGuard researcher Xiaopeng Zhang said in a disclosure shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Thursday.

The payload retrieves target IP ranges from an attacker-controlled server, converts them into CIDR ranges, and scans randomly generated addresses for systems with TCP port 1433 open. This is the default port used by Microsoft SQL Server.

Once reachable servers are identified, the malware records their IP addresses and launches a brute-force attack using a separate executable named “dwn.exe.” The tool attempts to authenticate with usernames such as “sa” and “admin,” alongside a predefined password list containing more than 2700 entries.

Successful logins give attackers more than database access, Zhang said. The malware executes a series of malicious T-SQL commands contained in a file named 2018.sql, using SQL Server’s administrative functionality to run commands on the compromised Windows machine.

Among other things, the commands enable xp_cmdshell, a SQL Server feature that allows database administrators to execute Windows command shell operations. The attackers then use it to download or extract executables into the server’s “C:\Users\Public” directory and run them.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo, said the campaign effectively turns a database login into a way to execute malware on the server. “Organizations should remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials,” he said. “Administrative access should be limited to accounts that need it.”

Soroko also recommended keeping xp_cmdshell disabled unless required and monitoring attempts to enable it.

A cryptominer and a Gh0st RAT come along for the ride

The malicious T-SQL commands deploy a loader that retrieves additional executables from the attackers’ FTP infrastructure, including a Monero cryptocurrency miner and a variant of the Gh0st RAT.

FortiGuard observed a payload, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, posing as a legitimate browser update but actually turning out to be an XMRig-based cryptocurrency miner. It uses the compromised server’s CPU resources to mine Monero and communicates with mining pools using a wallet address embedded in its configuration.

The Gh0st RAT variant was delivered through “Winlogon.exe.” The researchers identified functionality for keylogging, file management, data theft, remote shell execution, and process management, alongside more than 30 control commands. Its capabilities also include screen capture and remote desktop access through plugins.

The attack was found using multiple persistence mechanisms to maintain access. The initial payload creates a scheduled task running every 30 minutes, while the downloader establishes another task to repeatedly execute daily at 1 AM. The Gh0st RAT, meanwhile, adds itself to the Windows registry’s Run key, installs a Windows service and creates a scheduled task that launches it every 30 minutes.

Barney said cryptominers may serve as a distraction from the more serious implications of an intrusion. Attackers, he noted, can use mining activity as “a smokescreen for establishing long-term persistence through remote access tools.” FortiGuard said it provides detection coverage for the campaign through its FortiGuard IPS, Web Filtering, and Antivirus services. For those who aren’t its customers, the company shared a list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) to help catch potential infections.

articles.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths
articles.context: The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a...
articles.full_text:
The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a new vulnerability, it has emerged.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), which shared the details with The Hacker News, said the recovered attacker toolkit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that could allow an attacker to file transfer and execute through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation.

The cybersecurity company confirmed that testing against a fully patched ScreenConnect client successfully prevents execution of the exploit's payload.

"Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it," APG researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "That's an important finding for security teams."

"But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session."

Notably, the SCKit malware contains functionality called RelayTrap to reverse-pivot to infect the workstations of technicians who attempt to investigate suspicious activity in a managed endpoint. In other words, the activity abuses trusted functionality and does not rely on a software vulnerability once an attacker obtains a valid session.

The attack sequence makes use of the platform's built-in Run Command functionality to execute commands. This involves first checking for an existing ScreenConnect installation before downloading and running an attacker-controlled MSI installer ("sc.msi"), which then delivers the batch script dropper ("sckit-run.bat").

The batch script dropper subsequently contacts "ns.mo7sen[.]dev" to fetch a PowerShell decoder ("sckit-decoder.ps1") and ultimately deploy various components associated with the SCKit toolkit.

This includes a PowerShell script ("SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1") used to establish persistent remote access by deploying two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients, along with a set of scripts and C# code designed to interfere with existing ScreenConnect Guest sessions, including RelayTrap.

The component attempts a guest-to-host file execution technique associated with CVE-2026-84869 by replacing the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest and sending the SCKit payload back toward the connecting technician for execution.

If this action is successful, the malware tries to recover the technician's authenticated ScreenConnect browser sessions and leverage their existing management permissions to distribute commands across additional endpoints they have access to. As a result, an attacker can move beyond the original compromised system and into other customer environments through the same infrastructure used to administer them.

"Because these commands were executed through existing ScreenConnect agents, the attackers could deploy additional software under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context without needing to establish a separate execution method on each machine," Blackpoint Cyber said.

"The unauthorized Access clients provide attackers with persistent control over the endpoint, while the RelayTrap components position the malware to intercept legitimate support connections. Rather than simply preventing administrators from accessing an infected machine, the toolkit attempts to use their next connection as an opportunity to extend the intrusion directly to the technician's workstation."

The end goal of the attack appears to target technicians, as they regularly connect to managed endpoints belonging to different customers, typically from workstations with access to administrative tools and authenticated management sessions. This enables the attackers to break out of the original endpoint and move the intrusion into an environment with potentially broader access and privileges.

Once the malware gets executed on the technician's machine, it shifts from remote support manipulation to session theft, searching the local browser data and process memory of the machine to recover an existing authenticated management session (i.e., .ASPXAUTH cookies) that can be used to propagate the malware to other endpoints without having to obtain their credentials.

"By first attempting to compromise a technician's workstation, then recover their authenticated ScreenConnect session, SCKit seeks to turn access to a single managed endpoint into an opportunity to reach other systems under that technician's control," the researchers said.

The Hacker News has contacted ConnectWise for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-84869 was previously exploited in a set of attacks in which threat actors leveraged ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious four-stage Visual Basic Script (VBScript) payload to newly connected systems and ultimately serve an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

The vulnerability was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 11, 2026, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by September 14, 2026.

In response to the latest incident, ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments. However, Blackpoint Cyber said it found no technical link between those extensions and SCKit.

As of writing, there is no evidence that the activity has established successful propagation to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch for CVE-2026-84869.

The findings reinforce the importance of patching ScreenConnect clients, and underscore the need for stronger operator-session protections, including tighter session validation and additional authentication for bulk administrative actions, Blackpoint Cyber noted.

"Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions," the researchers said.

"For MSPs, the practical lesson is to investigate the management relationship, not only the endpoint. Rogue Access installations, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions all deserve attention, especially when support personnel have already connected to a suspected system."

RMM+ Authentication Flaw Found

Huntress, in an update, said it has identified a serious authentication flaw in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the five third-party ScreenConnect extensions that has already been blocked by ConnectWise.

"When an administrator had not configured an access key, the extension would accept a blank one, potentially allowing unauthorized commands to execute without going through ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls," the company said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

RMM+ makes it possible for another tool to manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. It authenticates requests with a shared access key ("RMMPlus.AccessKey") stored in the extension's settings. However, in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, the key defaults to a blank value.

Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts, roles, and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands on the device without bypassing multi-factor authentication.

"Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+."

It's worth mentioning here that while the toolkit possesses capabilities to exploit CVE-2026-84869, there is no evidence to suggest that an unpatched ScreenConnect client was the initial entry point for the attack.

"At this time, initial access appears to be linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions, although we do not have sufficient evidence to confirm this," Beal, principal MDR analyst at Blackpoint, told The Hacker News.

"Identifying patient zero would require additional forensic evidence from affected environments. Similarly, while November 11 marks the earliest publicly reported activity, we cannot rule out earlier compromises without further investigation. Our findings confirm the toolkit's capabilities but do not establish when or how the initial compromise occurred."

When contacted for comment, a ConnectWise spokesperson told The Hacker news that it's aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and that it's actively investigating the incident.

"While the initial access method remains unconfirmed, our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," the spokesperson said.

"We have disabled the identified extensions where we can take action as a precaution and are advising on-premises partners to disable them immediately. The presence of these extensions alone does not establish compromise. We encourage partners to review the precautionary guidance in the ConnectWise Trust Center, where we will provide updates as information is validated."

(The story was updated after publication to include responses and insights from ConnectWise, Blackpoint Cyber, and Huntress.)

articles.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
articles.context: Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT...
articles.full_text: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

articles.title: Zoom Fixes Critical Windows Vulnerability Allowing Privilege Escalation
articles.context: If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system
articles.full_text:
Zoom fixes two Windows Workplace flaws, including a critical bug that could let unauthenticated attackers remotely escalate privileges.

Zoom has released security updates to fix two vulnerabilities in Zoom Workplace for Windows. One is critical and could let attackers gain higher privileges on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are:

CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS 9.6): An input validation flaw that could allow an attacker to gain higher privileges through a network connection, without logging in.

CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS 8.1): An origin validation flaw that could also allow an unauthenticated attacker to gain higher privileges remotely.

If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system. Users should install the latest Zoom Workplace updates to protect their systems.

The first flaw was reported by the internal security team, while the second one was reported by the research shmoul.

CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows releases earlier than 7.1.5, while CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions from 7.1.0 up to, but not including, 7.1.8.

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In August, Zoom patched four vulnerabilities, including a critical zero-click flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53413. CVE-2026-53413 is a memory corruption issue found by A Security that could allow a meeting participant to execute code on another participant’s computer.

Due to its impact, the researchers dubbed the flaw “Zoomsday,” it affects Zoom clients on all supported platforms and is linked to the proprietary protocol used by the annotation function. Zoom has now begun rolling out security updates to address the issue.

“Ⓐ Security, the Autonomous Offensive Security and Remediation Platform, discovered a critical flaw in Zoom that let an attacker take complete control of another user’s device during a live call. No click, no download, and nothing required of the victim but being in the meeting.” reads the report published by A Security. “The vulnerability is present in every version of Zoom on every device and operating system: Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android and Linux. The vulnerability exists in all versions up to and including 7.0.5.”

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In July, Zoom fixed another critical Windows vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412 (CVSS score of 9.8), that could allow unauthenticated attackers to hijack user accounts. The flaw affects older versions of Workplace, the Windows VDI Client, and the Meeting SDK for Windows.

At this time, Zoom is not aware of attacks exploiting one of the above vulnerabilities. Users are recommended to apply the latest updates.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-108186)

articles.title: AI found Linux kernel bugs that remained undetected for decades
articles.context: By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local...
articles.full_text:
A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years.

While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive.

The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

“We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post.

From thousands of findings to 59 reports

Microsoft said it scanned selected kernel components covering networking, filesystems, and security modules. The initial findings were reduced to 11,769 candidates through automated screening. AI agents then attempted to reproduce potential vulnerabilities using QEMU, an open-source machine emulator.

This produced 621 cases with proof-of-concept evidence. Human researchers reviewed these cases to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions, the blog post added.

Of the 621 cases, 59 resulted in public upstream reports. Microsoft said another 266 shared root causes with other findings and could be addressed through the same patch. A further 163 were not reported following review, mostly because of limited security impact, while 133 had already been reported or fixed upstream.

Microsoft said its first public report was submitted on June 27, 2026. By September 1, 55 of the 59 reports had been posted to public mailing lists. The remaining four were reported privately during the same period and routed to public lists by mid-October.

Of the 33 CVEs assigned to the findings, 24 carry a High or higher severity rating, based on CVSS v3.1 scores of at least 7.0, according to Microsoft.

Eight vulnerabilities had working exploits

The eight vulnerabilities for which Microsoft developed working local privilege-escalation exploits affect several kernel components, including IPv4 and IPv6 networking, IPsec routing, encrypted-key handling and the resizable hash-table implementation. Some demonstrations required non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations, the researchers said.

One finding, CVE-2026-64563, involves the kernel’s rhashtable implementation, a shared resizable hash-table library used by different kernel subsystems.

Microsoft traced the flaw to a 2018 code change that allowed a table-walk operation to retain a pointer when paused. Under specific conditions involving table resizing and the removal of an entry, the kernel could subsequently access freed memory through that stale pointer.

The researchers identified an exploitable path through Netlink socket diagnostics, which are accessible to unprivileged users. By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local privilege escalation, Microsoft explained.

The company said this vulnerability was exploitable on standard Linux configurations without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces. It also affected Android devices with SELinux enforcing.

Across the 59 reports, the average age of a bug was 8.1 years when Microsoft first reported it publicly. One vulnerability, CVE-2026-74544, had been present in the kernel for at least 21 years, the researchers said.

Patching remains a lengthy process

While AI agents helped identify potential vulnerabilities, generate proof-of-concept demonstrations and draft initial patches, Microsoft said human investigation remained necessary to validate findings and work with Linux kernel maintainers.

“Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential,” the researchers wrote.

Fixes for 38 of the 59 reports had been merged into the upstream Linux mainline at the time of publication. Half were accepted with the initial submission, while the others required between one and four revisions. The median time from the first public patch submission to a mainline release was 41 days, with the longest taking 108 days, Microsoft said. Work with maintainers on the remaining reports was continuing.

Microsoft said the initial scans took about two weeks, but converting the findings into validated reports and patches required more than four person-months of work.

“Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance,” the researchers wrote. “For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck.”

The researchers said the project covered only a small fraction of the Linux kernel and that further tuning of the AI-assisted approach could uncover additional bugs. However, they cautioned that finding more vulnerabilities would not necessarily make systems more secure.

“More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system,” the blog post concluded.

articles.title: Google Cloud Warns Three AMD Turin CPU Flaws Could Leak Data Across Processes in VMs
articles.context: AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory
articles.full_text:
Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week.

The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1."

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:

VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough."

Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available.

Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives.

GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available.

Cloud Run: No action is needed.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

articles.title: Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones
articles.context: The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps
articles.full_text:
Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones

Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police.

The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg.

There’s a nice infographic that explains how the system works at the link.

articles.title: Exploit Attempts for GPUStack Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-102895), (Thu, Nov 12th)
articles.context: CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability
articles.full_text:
CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability. GPUStack is also an attractive target. It is open-source software that manages clusters of GPUs, which are typically used to run AI workloads. All versions of GPUStack prior to 2.2.0, which was released at the end of June. This vulnerability was not made public until the end of July, and the CVE was assigned on November 4th.

The vulnerability stems from a common pattern: proxies add custom headers, and the recipient trusts them. An attacker can spoof these custom headers, thereby bypassing authentication and/or access control. In this particular case, the header in question is "X-Gpustack-Real-IP". Like similar headers (Forwarded, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP), this header is intended to help identify the IP address from which the request originates. This is all nice and safe as long as no security decisions are made. But this is exactly what happens with GPUStack. If the "X-Gpustack-Real-IP" identifies loopback (127.0.0.1) as the source of the request, Gpustack bypasses authentication (after all, the request originates from a trusted source)

The requests we are seeing right now are pretty straightforward:

GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: [redacted] Accept-Encoding: identity User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 X-Gpustack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

The IP address we see as the origin of these requests is 144.91.73.103. In the last couple of days, we have seen this IP look for other AI-related resources:

/v1/models /v1beta/models?key=x /v1/messages /models

https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack/security/advisories/GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|
