articles.title: Calendar Invites and Live Proxies: Inside a Google Session Hijacking Campaign
articles.context: The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire
articles.full_text:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

Why the usual controls stay quiet

Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

What stopping it took

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

One month by the numbers

These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:

68,676 campaign messages blocked

2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed

897 unique domains taken down

8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

Message delivery by time of day

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

Where things stand now

The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

Messages detected by week

Domains registered by interval

That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

articles.title: PTC Patches Critical Windchill and FlexPLM Flaw That Could Enable Remote Code Execution
articles.context: PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution
articles.full_text:
PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0.

It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests.

"A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data."

The CVE record lists the following versions as affected -

PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0

PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website.

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems."

The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation.

Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises.

"PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime."

Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.

articles.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
articles.context: NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to...
articles.full_text: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic. ®

articles.title: Beyond Storage: Your Repository as Software Inventory
articles.context: But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job
articles.full_text:
Repositories give teams a managed source for build inputs. They proxy public registries, host internal components, and cache packages.

That work remains essential. But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job.

A typical build may pull in open source packages, container images, internal libraries, build tools, and models. Those inputs can enter in several ways:

A developer selects a package or library.

A pipeline retrieves a component.

An AI agent adds a dependency while changing code.

A package manager resolves additional components required by another library.

Because many requests happen automatically, teams need to understand what is available through the repository path and manage the inputs that pass through it. A repository used as a common source can provide that operational inventory.

From Artifact Storage to Software Inventory

A repository inventory describes the artifacts available through a managed source: the formats and versions present, and the assets associated with them.

Sonatype Nexus Repository gives teams a shared view of components available through managed repositories.

That view can help answer questions such as:

Which packages, containers, models, and build artifacts are available through managed repositories?

Which versions are hosted or cached?

Do developers, pipelines, and agents have a common route to obtain software?

Can teams apply consistent policies and block known malicious packages before they are served?

Consider a routine library update. An engineer needs to know which versions are available through the team's standard source. When groups rely on separate proxies or caches, that information may be scattered. A shared repository gives teams a common place to check.

Know What the Repository Inventory Covers

A component appearing in Nexus Repository does not necessarily mean it is included in a deployed application. It means the component is managed or available through the repository. Build records or software bills of materials (SBOMs) identify what went into a specific application or release.

These views answer different but related questions. The repository inventory helps teams manage the shared supply path, and build records help them understand a particular application's inputs.

That distinction also gives teams a place to start an investigation. If a package is flagged, they can check whether it is managed or available through Nexus Repository, then consult build records to determine if a specific application included it.

Software Delivery Starts With What Teams Pull

Most applications depend on components their teams did not write. A developer might add a framework, then a package manager resolves its dependencies.

Each component can affect the application in different ways:

Compatibility: Dependencies may conflict or require specific versions.

Maintenance: Older or unsupported components create upgrade work.

Security: A malicious component requires investigation and response after it enters development.

When these issues surface after development begins, replacing a component can mean code changes, retesting, and release delays.

AI tools can add or update dependencies while changing code, increasing the pace of these choices. A faster request does not tell a team whether or not a component is compatible, maintained, or appropriate for the application. Teams need enough context to assess those choices before they create work downstream.

Make Centralized Access the Trusted Default

A shared repository gives teams a consistent place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs their workflows need. Developers and pipelines can use a managed route that supports their existing package managers and build tools, instead of relying on separate collections of external sources.

In day-to-day work, that shared route gives teams a common way to:

Retrieve components and resolve dependencies through the organization's configured source.

Manage the software supply chain used by multiple groups, rather than having each team create its own process.

Route AI agent dependency requests through the same access and intake controls used for other development activity.

Configure supported formats in a shared repository, giving new projects a starting point instead of another one-off source.

Centralizing access does not automatically cover packages downloaded directly from a public registry or through an unconfigured source. Teams need to route the requests they want managed through Nexus Repository. Then it can serve as a common point for understanding the inputs it handles and applying controls to them.

Block Known Malicious Packages Before They Reach the Build

Nexus Repository sits between upstream sources and the developers, pipelines, and agents requesting software. In the Pro+ and Enterprise editions, malicious package protection and configurable policies can block known malicious packages when requests pass through a protected repository path, before Nexus serves them downstream.

If a malicious package reaches a development environment, teams may need to remove it from the repository if it is still available, then:

Identify which developers, pipelines, or agents retrieved and used the package, and assess what systems or data may be affected.

Assess which systems or credentials it could access.

Determine whether builds or releases incorporated it, and assess downstream exposure.

Blocking the package at the repository can prevent that specific input from becoming part of a downstream investigation. Developers also do not have to identify every suspicious package name or track each campaign themselves. Protection applies where component requests already flow.

Repository protection does not address every dependency or application risk. A component can cause compatibility problems without being malicious, so teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. For dependency decisions and remediation, Sonatype Guide brings intelligence into developer and AI coding workflows to inform component choices and help automate dependency upgrades.

Within the broader Nexus One platform, Guide complements repository protection: developers and agents get support for choosing and updating dependencies, while Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can block known malicious packages and packages flagged as suspicious, even before they are confirmed as malicious at the repository request point.

Make the Repository Part of Delivery Infrastructure

A reliable software supply chain depends on more than where artifacts are stored. Teams need a consistent way to find the components their workflows can use, manage the route those components take, and keep known malicious packages out.

Nexus Repository provides a shared source for the software inputs it manages. Its Pro+ and Enterprise editions add protection that can block known malicious packages at the point where components enter the managed path. Together, these capabilities give teams both a clearer view of available inputs and a way to stop a known threat before it reaches a build.

As developers and AI agents make more requests, that combination becomes more useful. Teams can make software available through a common route, apply consistent controls to incoming requests, and understand the limits of what the repository inventory shows.

Know what your teams can get through the repository. Make trusted access the default. Block known malicious packages before they become part of the work.

See how Sonatype Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can help your teams manage software intake and block known malicious packages. Book a demo.

articles.title: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
Why scammers want you to allow push notifications
articles.context: Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware
articles.full_text:
A website asks you to click “Allow” to start a quiz or read an interesting story. A little later, your device starts warning you about viruses, missed payments, or legal trouble.

While every message may look like a new security problem, the cause could be a permission you granted earlier.

For scammers, browser push notifications turn a passing visit into something much more valuable: access to your attention after you have left their website.

Two investigations—including our own research into deceptive quiz sites and HUMAN Security’s investigation of an operation called Pushpaganda—show how that permission can become a tool for repeated advertising, scareware, and fraud.

Ordinarily, a deceptive website has a limited opportunity to influence you. Once you leave, its sales pitch disappears.

A simple browser push notification permission changes that relationship. A website you’ve authorized can send browser notifications even when you’re not visiting it. Depending on the platform and browser configuration, those messages can appear even when the browser is not visibly open.

Just what scammers need

That gives scammers several advantages:

Repeat opportunities to get a click. Instead of relying on one visit, they can send more messages to bring you back to their sites.

A more convincing place to display a lie. Notifications appear through the browser and operating system, while their wording and imagery can impersonate security alerts, financial messages, or people you know.

Distance from the original trick. By the time alarming messages start appearing, you may not remember which website received permission, let alone connect the alerts to an innocent-looking quiz.

More chances to make money. The resulting traffic can feed advertising, affiliate promotions, scams, and unwanted downloads.

Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware. But scammers can use them to trick you into clicking a harmful link or downloading something dangerous. That explains why your device can display frightening warnings while a malware scan finds nothing wrong.

The campaigns

The quiz that came with an unwanted extra

Our investigation, published on March 9, began with customers who thought their devices were infected. Malwarebytes scans came up clean. Screenshots helped our Malware Removal Support team identify the real source of the trouble: web push notifications.

While the quizzes were real, the trick was making people think they had to allow the notifications to take them.

Clicking “Start the quiz” first brought up the browser’s notification permission request. Behind that legitimate browser prompt, the website displayed its own instruction:

“Click ‘Allow’ to continue.”

The page made it seem you had to allow the notifications to take the quiz, when it actually meant agreeing to receive future messages.

From clickbait to a notification loop

On April 14, HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers published a larger example of the same underlying strategy. They called it Pushpaganda.

Instead of quizzes, the operation used sensational articles and images, many showing signs of AI generation. Headlines promised attention-grabbing financial developments or implausible technology bargains. The content appeared in Google Discover feeds, exposing it to Android and Chrome users. Researchers could not establish whether those placements resulted from paid promotion or search optimization.

Once someone visited an associated website, the operation prompted them to enable notifications. The messages that followed had little to do with the article that attracted the visitor. Researchers observed fake arrest warrants, false financial alerts, and notifications mimicking missed calls from “Mom” or other family members.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

Scam Guard stats

The graph shows weekly counts of reports classified by Scam Guard as matching quiz-site notification abuse (red) and Pushpaganda (blue), based on the information provided by users.

The counts show reports over time linked to these campaigns. They don’t represent unique victims, confirmed infections, or total campaign activity.

For context: HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers observed roughly 240 million advertising bid requests associated with Pushpaganda domains in a single seven-day period at the operation’s peak.

A bid request asks advertisers in real-time to bid for an opportunity to show an ad. In a push notification ad auction, the winning ad is sent as a notification to someone who has allowed them.

Note the dip after the reports came out. It takes time to rebuild the infrastructure, but criminals will do so if they think it’s worth the investment.

How to stay safe

Allow notifications only when you want ongoing messages from a site. A few guidelines that may help you:

Don’t click on prompts until you’re sure what they will set in motion.

Treat “Allow notifications to continue” as a red flag, particularly on quizzes, video pages, or unfamiliar websites.

Use web protection. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free tool that can help block malicious websites.

If you’re haunted by unwanted alerts, they might be web push notifications. Here’s how to identify the website sending them and turn them off in several popular browsers.

On supported Android devices, Chrome notifications include an Unsubscribe option. Use that built-in control rather than a link inside a suspicious message. When you receive an unwanted website notification through Chrome on Android:

Swipe down from the top of the screen to open Android’s notification shade.

Look for an Unsubscribe action on the notification.

If it is present, tap it to stop future notifications from that website. Chrome also provides Undo if you unsubscribe accidentally.

If Unsubscribe is not present, open Chrome and go to More > Settings > Site settings > Notifications. Review the allowed websites and block the offending site. You don’t need to follow a link in the suspicious notification to manage its permission.

articles.title: Security Teams Must Shift from Patching to Mitigation in the AI Era
articles.context: This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026
articles.full_text:
Organizations “can’t patch their way out of AI” and should instead focus on mitigation post exploitation, according to Dick O’Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec.

Speaking at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11, he highlighted the rapid closure of the patch window in the past year due to attackers’ use of AI.

This includes AI tools to discover zero day flaws and the ability of frontier models to chain together low severity vulnerabilities together to find an exploit path in a way that humans would not be able to do.

The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard that tracks the collapse of the time-to-exploit (TTE) window from CVE disclosure to confirmed exploitation in the wild, has estimated that the average time to exploitation following public disclosure of a vulnerability fell from one week in 2025 to one day in 2026. The initiative estimates that in 2027, the average time will be a minute.

“Once you get to a minute, what can you do realistically? We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities,” O’Brien said.

This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026. O’Brien noted that the first reporting exploitation attempts occurred just 19 minutes after the bug was made public.

Amazon also reported that it detected an attempted exploitation attempt of PHP2Shell four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

Agentic AI Orchestration of Attacks

Post-initial access, O’Brien expects threat actors to move to an era of “end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks” in the next year, shifting away from using AI as an assistant for various tasks towards AI agents undertaking attacks independently.

This will make it significantly harder for defenders to detect and respond to threats in their organization’s environments.

There have been a few examples of this approach taking place so far. One of these was an attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026, where AI agents executed the post-compromise tasks independently, operating at machine speed.

According to an analysis by Symantec of the DIVD’s assessment report, it took 19 minutes for the attack to be detected, but 19 hours before the response began, and a further nine hours to contain the threat.

“This is what we’re dealing with. It’s an excess of 24 hours and you know you’re not going to be able to compete with something operating at machine speed,” O’Brien commented.

Adopt an Assume Exploit Mindset

In this landscape, organizations should assume exploitation is inevitable and prepare for machine-speed post-compromise activity, where attackers can move from initial access to impact in minutes rather than days.

“Stop measuring your mean time to patch and start measuring your mean time to mitigate. Assume an exploit is going to happen and the plan your preparedness for that,” O’Brien advised.

He set out a number of mitigation tasks security teams can immediately focus on:

Behavior blocking

Default-deny for what runs

Least privilege for every agent and token

Inspect data before it leaves the device

Bind every agent action to a named human

“These are all things you can start doing right now before you become aware of a vulnerability,” O’Brien added.

Longer-term, organizations must integrate detection and protection technologies on multiple different control points, which are able to identify behavioral anomalies of rogue or malicious AI agents.

articles.title: NCSC Launches Cyber Adversary Testing to Boost Resilience
articles.context: The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience
articles.full_text:
The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) first trailed its Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme at the CYBERUK 2025 conference.

It enables participating organizations to choose from a list of vetted suppliers, who then craft realistic attack plans based on reconnaissance of the client’s IT infrastructure, exposure, and threat landscape.

“Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs),” the NCSC said.

Read more on cyber resilience: NCSC: Observability and Threat Hunting Must Improve

The CyAS scheme is designed to complement other NCSC initiatives including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA).

It’s hoped that larger organizations, CNI providers, and government bodies in particular use these frameworks to better understand their security posture and resilience.

“By enabling rigorous, realistic end-to-end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organizations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber-attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience,” said NCSC CTO, Ollie Whitehouse.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.”

Building Resilience for the Future

Andrew Costis, engineering manager of the Adversary Research Team at AttackIQ, welcomed the program's potential to help organizations test how well they can keep essential services running during an attack.

“Building each simulation around an organization’s actual exposure should uncover weaknesses that a generic assessment might miss. Looking back, that approach could have exposed gaps in detection or containment before an intrusion became a prolonged outage,” he said.

“The longer-term opportunity is turning those findings into an ongoing practice through adversarial exposure validation.”

Costis explained that teams must repeat attack behaviors after remediating a weakness to check that the fix has worked, and adapt their testing over time as environments change.

“An assured provider gives organisations confidence in the assessment’s quality,” he concluded. “Keeping those lessons current will determine how much resilience the scheme delivers.”

CyAS will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), so that the NCSC can test demand, refine its methodology, and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

A list of service providers can be found here.

articles.title: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
articles.context: ” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams
articles.full_text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

articles.title: Critical Pre-Auth MongoDB Flaw (CVE-2026-118383) Can Crash Lagging Servers on Failover
articles.context: A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes.

MongoDB, the company that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.

The affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all new writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary.

Researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, is a use-after-free: the server ends up using memory it has already freed. MongoDB rated it 9.5 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The company said it found the flaw itself and was "not aware of any attempts to take advantage of this vulnerability."

Affected members include the shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod, a single server outside any replica set, is not affected.

Each affected branch has a fixed release, listed below and in the CVE record. Every earlier version in a branch is affected, back to the branch's first release.

MongoDB Atlas clusters automatically receive fixed versions during maintenance, the company said in its security announcement. Customers who defer maintenance should apply the upgrade as soon as possible.

Self-managed deployments need the fixed release on every replica set member. After upgrading, check the version each member is running, including members in containers and any that were offline during maintenance.

The 8.2 branch is not among the affected versions listed, and its newest release is 8.2.12. But a proof of concept published on GitHub reports that 8.2.12 still exhibited the bug in a lab test using a test-only setting.

The 8.2 branch reached end of life on July 31, according to the company's lifecycle schedule. Past that date, a version no longer receives fixes, including security fixes.

Until a member can be upgraded, the researchers advise restricting network access to the database to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the two requests but does not fix the flaw.

A member who wins an election first catches up by applying the writes it missed before it accepts new ones. The flaw is in the cleanup that runs when this catch-up step ends, according to the Datadog researchers' technical analysis.

The two requests are ping commands that carry a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each asks the server to wait until replication reaches a certain point, and the server records a pending notification for it, called a waiter.

Planting the waiters does not crash the server. They do not expire, and stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back or steps down from primary.

The crash needs the member who received the requests to win a later election, even though it is behind another member. When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice, reusing memory that was already freed, and the new primary crashes before it accepts any writes. Once those conditions are met, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race, the researchers said.

In the lab, the researchers caused the member to fall behind and forced a failover themselves by using admin access to pause and stop mongod processes. Only the two requests came from a client without credentials, and that client could not write to the database.

On version 8.0.34, the member crashed with a segmentation fault, leaving the lab cluster without a primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

In the fixed version 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as unauthorized at once, and the member kept running. One part of the fix lets only system users use readConcern.afterOpTime.

MongoDB says the flaw may also result in arbitrary code execution in the server process under certain conditions. In the lab, though, "we did not achieve code execution," the researchers said. Their results also do not show how often the attack would work in other setups.

The proof-of-concept code reproduces the bug in a lab replica set, according to its author. Its reliable mode requires a test-only setting that a remote attacker cannot enable. Its stated impact is a crash or memory corruption, with no claim of code execution.

The second part of the fix stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters are already in place, the researchers said. They did not test that part themselves.

In the proof-of-concept lab test, which ran with authentication turned off, the fixed 8.0.37 accepted the planted waiters but ran the cleanup only once.

To look for planting or a crash, check the server's structured logs for these signs from the researchers' vulnerable run:

Log event: a COMMAND "Slow query" entry (ID 51803) for an unauthenticated ping carrying readConcern.afterOpTime that ended with MaxTimeMSExpired.

Log event: a member entering primary catch-up (ID 21359), then exiting it twice (ID 21363) in one transition.

Log event: a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock() after those exits.

A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not point to this flaw. The requests may also arrive before the failover, so check earlier logs from the same member too.

Whether the request fields are logged depends on logging settings, and the attr.remote field may show a loopback address instead of the client's real IP.

articles.title: FBI agent stole $2.47m in crypto from criminal wallets
articles.context: A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet
articles.full_text:

In this article

A former FBI supervisor stole from cryptocurrency wallets involved in 35 FBI investigations

He planned to use the proceeds to finance a new life in Portugal

He turned himself in after confessing to a former colleague

Law enforcement officers are trusted to handle sensitive evidence properly. A 37-year-old former FBI supervisor used that access to steal millions in cryptocurrency.

Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty on November 5 to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million from cryptocurrency wallets linked to FBI investigations.

He stole the money from wallets held by people the FBI was investigating, which included adversarial nation-state actors. Starting no later than December 2024, he made around 100 transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate investigations.

The FBI’s search affidavit says that Yaroch accessed FBI systems containing wallet seed phrases and memorized them. A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone with the seed phrase can potentially control the funds.

He then used the memorized phrases to transfer funds to a personal wallet on his own device. He subsequently swapped assets into different currencies and made further transactions to try and hide their origins.

According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), his actions compromised multiple investigations.

The affidavit also revealed that Yaroch had asked ChatGPT how to invest a million dollars, along with advice on where to live in Europe. It suggested Portugal, and he began the process of setting up a life there.

Caught by a case of cold feet

According to the affidavit, he approached a former DOJ colleague to confess because his actions were “eating him up inside.” The employee urged him to self-report, which he did.

The FBI placed him on leave and then terminated his employment two days later. They showed up at his home with a warrant and seized assets, including his phone, which had access to a Kraken cryptocurrency account. They also seized a piece of paper containing the seed phrases for his own account.

More law enforcement corruption

Yaroch’s justification for his initial actions was frustration that the FBI wasn’t acting quickly enough against the wallets’ criminal owners. So he decided to “take matters into his own hands,” according to the affidavit.

But according to the DOJ, he also used some of the proceeds to cover personal debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

This isn’t an isolated incident. In December 2024, former Secret Service agent Anthony Joseph Evans pleaded guilty to stealing cryptocurrency worth $56,000 from a hardware wallet held in the agency’s secure evidence vault.

In 2015, former Secret Service agent Shaun W. Bridges also pleaded guilty to money laundering and obstruction of justice after stealing bitcoin during the investigation of Silk Road, a dark web marketplace used to sell illegal drugs and other contraband. He used another person’s administrator account to reset users’ passwords and move bitcoin into a wallet he controlled. The stolen bitcoin was worth approximately $350,000 at the time; he later sold it for $820,000.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
articles.context: No vulnerability needs to be exploited
articles.full_text:
For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production. An agent can reach systems that previously required deliberate human intervention, often using permissions granted for an entirely different purpose. Unlike conventional software, an agent may take different actions when presented with the same task because its context and decisions change. CISOs now face a fundamentally different challenge: governing autonomous software that already holds active pathways into production.

The security control we never recognized was human judgment

Where human developers and coding agents diverge most sharply is in judgment, not technical capability.Developers understand what state their code is in, whether it’s something they’re testing or something that’s production-ready. They understand what their credentials permit them to do, but also when and how those credentials should be used. There’s an implicit compartmentalization between having access and exercising it.An AI agent is much more single-minded. If an available credential helps accomplish the task, the agent uses it. Agents don’t recognize the distinction between what is technically possible and what policy permits.Consider an agent asked to troubleshoot a failing application. It discovers production credentials on the developer’s laptop and determines that querying the live database is the fastest way to diagnose the problem. It might modify production data while attempting a fix, even though the developer intended only to investigate a local issue. No vulnerability needs to be exploited. The agent simply uses available authority to pursue its assigned objective.Traditional development pipelines weren’t designed around software that independently decides which systems to access and what actions to take. Security controls must now account for behavior that can’t be fully anticipated from the original request.

A sandbox can contain an agent without containing its authority

Sandboxing has emerged as an obvious response to the risks of autonomous agents. By isolating execution inside a container, virtual machine or microVM, organizations can limit an agent’s ability to interfere with its host or other workloads.Strong isolation is essential, particularly when agents execute untrusted code or interact with potentially malicious tools. A microVM with its own guest kernel can provide a stronger boundary than a conventional container sharing the host kernel. But isolation answers only part of the security question.An agent sandbox that blocks all external access is as useful as a computer encased in cement at the bottom of the ocean.An agent doesn’t have to escape its sandbox to cause a security incident. It can misuse perfectly legitimate permissions, send sensitive information through an authorized network connection or make destructive changes using credentials deliberately provided to it.Isolating execution is useless unless you also precisely control what that workload can reach. A secure sandbox containing unrestricted credentials still leaves an enormous attack surface.

Can you revoke an agent without disabling its developer?

Security professionals are familiar with least privilege, but agentic development exposes the limitations of conventional identity and access management.Consider a developer who authorizes an agent to modify one GitHub repository. If the agent uses the developer’s personal token, it may inherit access to every repository that developer can reach. That could include merge permissions, CI/CD environments and downstream credentials associated with those systems.This is ambient authority: the ability to perform actions beyond the particular task for which access was originally intended. Even a relatively narrow token may authorize repeated actions when the agent only needed permission to perform the action once.When an agent operates under a developer’s credentials, revoking its access can also mean disabling the developer. Security teams need to separate autonomous workloads from human identity.Agents should have independently defined identities, with permissions delegated for specific purposes. That makes it possible to track what each agent did, investigate where something went wrong and revoke an individual agent’s authority without disrupting its developer.

The missing link is a trusted broker

One of the most interesting developments in agentic security is the emerging idea of a trusted broker that sits between an agent and the systems it wants to access.Some approaches are described as MCP proxies. Others use authorization services, gateways or different architectures. What they’re circling is the same fundamental problem: how do we decide which agents can access which resources, under what circumstances and for how long?Crucially, the agent cannot be responsible for deciding the limits of its own authority. Those decisions must be enforced by a separate system that can authorize individual operations without surrendering the credentials that make them possible.Imagine asking an agent to fix a GitHub issue. Instead of granting unrestricted repository access, the developer authorizes the task once. A trusted intermediary could then permit the agent to read the repository, push changes to a designated branch and open a pull request. Those permissions could expire after an hour, without exposing a broadly reusable developer credential.This is the core tension agentic security has to resolve. Grant too little access and developers abandon the controls. Grant too much and isolation becomes irrelevant to the damage an authorized agent can cause. The goal is to make secure delegation as frictionless as unrestricted access.Agentic security may be approaching a comparable architectural moment. Developers, open-source projects and commercial vendors are experimenting with approaches to identity, delegation, authorization and policy enforcement. Some organizations are building their own controls around existing IAM systems. Others are exploring dedicated intermediaries that evaluate requests before allowing agents to reach external resources.The trusted broker is not yet a universally defined component, and there’s no guarantee one implementation will become the equivalent of Kubernetes. Questions about policy decisions, credential custody, latency, availability and auditability remain open.But the missing function is becoming clearer. We need a dependable intermediary that translates human intent into narrowly defined, enforceable authority for autonomous software.

MCP servers have become a new software supply chain

MCP is one of the principal ways agents connect to external tools and information. That makes it both an important integration mechanism and a security boundary.A malicious MCP server can become an indirect route into an agent’s workflow. If servers or tools execute with access to shared filesystems, processes or credential stores, a compromised component may be able to read secrets belonging to another tool.But credential theft isn’t the only concern. A compromised server can return manipulated information that influences an agent’s subsequent actions even before the agent uses the tool. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise the agent—only the context it consumes.The familiar disciplines of provenance, signing and build integrity need to extend to MCP servers, agent tools and model weights. Organizations should know where these components originated, whether they’ve been modified and what authority they receive when introduced into an environment.The answer is layered security: strong isolation, independently managed identities, narrowly scoped permissions, controlled network access and sufficient observability to understand what agents actually do.

Why agent security belongs in the execution path

Containerization demonstrated that security works best when guardrails are baked directly into developer platforms without stripping away speed. Kubernetes eventually made it possible to enforce common security and operational policies across distributed workloads without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure expert. Agentic development needs a comparable shift.The longer-term opportunity is to move from granting persistent access to delegating task-specific authority. Developers need a way to authorize an agent to fix one issue or open one pull request without surrendering standing keys.Laptops are production endpoints now, and they won’t revert back to safe sandboxes. Security teams must protect developer speed by embedding the boundaries that human judgment used to handle manually directly into the infrastructure.

articles.title: Maersk Reveals Data Breach as Extortion Group Demands $5m
articles.context: The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect...
articles.full_text:
Maersk has disclosed a data breach involving one of its IT systems after an extortion group claimed to have stolen 100GB of logistics-related data from the company.

The shipping and logistics giant said in a November 11 statement that it “identified unauthorized access and data extraction,” although it didn’t clarify when.

The incident affected one of its “local legacy systems from a previous acquisition,” it claimed.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI [electronic data interchange],” the statement continued.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.”

Read more on Maersk: Cybersecurity Lessons from Maersk’s Former CISO

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, explained that ownership of acquired systems often gets muddled during M&A activity, and pen tests should be carried out during due diligence to highlight any potential weaknesses.

“Acquired systems arrive with their own credentials, their own patch schedule, and connections into the parent network that were set up during integration and rarely revisited,” he added.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at Ridge Security, said that investigators must determine what the attackers accessed, how they gained entry, and whether the boundaries separating that legacy environment from other systems held.

“The lesson for organizations isn't simply to replace every legacy system,” he argued. “It's to know what you own, understand how inherited systems connect to the business, and continuously validate that the security controls protecting them work.”

WhiteArmor Ramps Up Attacks

A relatively new extortion group known as WhiteArmor claimed responsibility for the attack, according to screenshots of its leak site posted to X.

The group demanded $5m in Bitcoin, claiming it has 100GB of data linked to Maersk’s OCF/LF logistics platform, including driver records and plaintext passwords, staff accounts, delivery receipts, purchase orders, inventory rows, and mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEIs.

WhiteArmor is behind a string of extortion demands ranging from $140,000 to $20m over the past month, according to Nick Harris, CISO at cyber-insurance specialist Assured.

Citing publicly available information on the attacks, he noted that several were aimed at the logistics sector, with victims including J.B. Hunt, Ryder, and Echo Global Logistics.

“The group describes itself as focused on data-theft extortion, intending to expand into ransomware, and says its encryptor is nearly complete,” Harris said.

“The protections include cycling credentials, strong access controls, data loss alerts and validating third parties. If they aim to recruit insiders, treat security as “assumed compromise” and set controls and alerts accordingly.

Maersk hasn’t experienced a serious cyber incident since the NotPetya campaign in 2017, which it claimed at the time may have cost the firm as much as $300m.

articles.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Flaws, Including HTTP/2 Bugs That Crash Servers and Leak Other Connections' Data
articles.context: Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22
articles.full_text:
A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines.

The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:

CVE-2026-123865: a client can make any default HTTP/2 server hold memory and file descriptors permanently, on all three lines.

CVE-2026-123874: a client can corrupt server memory on 24.x and 26.x when the server serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). On all three lines, canceling such downloads can also crash the server (CVE-2026-123875, rated medium).

CVE-2026-126051: a client can crash a TLS server on 24.x and 26.x if the server uses the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext().

CVE-2026-123872: on a TLS server with stricter client-certificate rules for some hostnames, a client approved for another hostname can switch to a stricter one during TLS 1.2 renegotiation without meeting its rules. All three lines are affected.

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.
