articles.title: Attacker Used 4,837 Hijacked GitHub Accounts to Run a CI Secret Stealer in 1,806+ Repositories
articles.context: Correction (November 12, 2026): An earlier version of this article said the stealer sent data only by HTTP POST to two addresses and that the attacker reverted each change...
articles.full_text:
Starting Tuesday, an attacker used stolen credentials for 4,837 GitHub accounts to plant a secret stealer in repositories those accounts could write to, according to Aikido Security, a security software company.

The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. It ran in at least 1,806 repositories, where the attacker has likely collected those credentials, the company says.

Each attack started with a pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, opened from a branch named wfx-docs to test whether the account could write to the repository. These test pull requests were opened in 61,764 repositories, and the stealer followed in some of them.

In a separate analysis, researchers at SafeDep, which sells software supply chain security tools, counted 8,093 repositories that received malicious commits between 12:46 UTC on Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today. That count covers every repository that received malicious commits, not only those where the stealer ran. Their search covered only the default branches of public repositories, so the true total is higher, the researchers say.

In 7,309 of those repositories, the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771, it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also runs on a developer's machine during npm install.

After pushing the stealer, the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes. Where the stealer ran, its logs were deleted, usually along with the run itself. In those repositories, every secret and cloud role available to the workflows should be treated as compromised.

More pull requests with the same title were opened early today, after the company's own GitHub search ended on Wednesday, a check by The Hacker News found. Three that were checked, opened between 05:04 and 05:38 UTC, came from wfx-docs branches. It is not clear whether the stealer followed.

Any account that opened one of the attacker's test pull requests is compromised, even if the stealer never ran, Aikido said in its technical analysis. The analysis does not explain how the attacker obtained the credentials.

SafeDep's researchers advise owners of affected repositories to revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH keys, and sessions, and to turn on 2FA. Owners should also rotate every secret and variable the repository can read. Anyone who ran npm install on an affected commit should treat that machine as compromised and rotate its keys.

In most other repositories that received a test, nothing was pushed afterward, or the stealer did not run due to the repository's settings or the account's permissions. The figures cover only the public repositories the company could see.

The tests also reached repositories that the compromised accounts did not own. Of the test pull requests, 10,431 were submitted via collaborator or organization access, and 92% of those were still open when the company checked.

Signs a Repository Was Hit

Check for these signs, from Tuesday onward, in any repository you can write to:

Branch: wfx-docs

Branch: chore/[a-z0-9]{8}, short-lived

Branch: ci-check-[0-9]{4}

Pull request title: docs: dependency audit notes

Commit message: ci: refresh build cache, which adds about 1,500 lines to an existing workflow

Commit message: chore: add ci helper, which adds a .ci-xxxxxx.sh script and a postinstall hook in package.json that runs it on any npm install

Commit message: chore: add dependency audit workflow, which adds .github/workflows/build-audit-xxxxxx.yml on a chore/ branch

Commit message: chore: initial commit, pushed before a new workflow file in an empty repository

Commit message: ci: restore

Commit message: ci: cleanup

SHA-256 (stealer script): 89695abb392d5cfd4972672961e644bb46baa98aa1ed7173c2a2816c762735cf

IP: 194.150.166[.]244:8080/exfil

IP: 18.143.168[.]96:8080/exfil

IP: 153.75.82[.]159:8080

A repository can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. A missing run number on the attacker's commit is the more reliable sign that the stealer ran.

The stealer sends data by HTTP POST to the addresses above or to a Telegram chat, the SafeDep researchers found. In a sample of 200 payload commits, about a fifth used Telegram only.

The stealer is built to collect credentials from every source on the runner, according to the company. They include GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, keys for AI services, and secrets in the memory of the runner's own processes. It reads credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, SSH, and other tools from their usual locations.

It also copies the repository, its last 100 commits, and recent workflow artifacts. On self-hosted runners, it takes cloud credentials from instance metadata as well as Docker container state and systemd units.

The stealer also has settings for private repositories, and the company says that suggests it may be running in them.

The stealer is designed to use those credentials to reach deeper into cloud accounts. It exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, and on AWS it can create long-lived access keys for IAM users.

Some of its steps are built to survive credential rotation. It can rewrite an AWS role's trust policy to open the role to any AWS account.

It can also add federated identity credentials with the prefix wfx-ci- to Azure AD applications. Workflows in the compromised repository can then sign in to Azure without a stored secret, even after all tokens are rotated.

To find these backdoors, the researchers suggest checking for:

Entra ID: federated credentials named wfx-ci-* that you did not create

AWS CloudTrail: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or AssumeRole sessions named wfx-*, followed by CreateAccessKey or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy

GCP: GenerateAccessToken and SignJwt calls from your GitHub workload identity pool

Vault: JWT logins from the GitHub OIDC issuer

The stealer reached at least one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers. At least 50 of the compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI, or crates.

The attacker appears to be after CI secrets rather than trying to spread through packages, the company says.

Version 3.14.3 of the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio is malicious, and the company advises treating any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. Its package listing shows the version was published on Wednesday. Early today, the version was still listed, under a notice that versions of the package had been flagged as malware.

A normal composer install does not run the stealer, but running npm install inside the package's vendor directory does, the researchers found. Users should block v3.14.3 and pin v3.14.2 or earlier.

Two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280, carry the stealer only in a GitHub Actions workflow file. The Go code and release binaries are unchanged, and Go builds never run workflow files, so users of the module may not have been affected. The company still recommends removing those versions.

The researchers also found the stealer in another Go module, github.com/vkuznet/gocurl, in pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da, inside a workflow that has never run. Users should block that pseudo-version.

The stealer also reached 28 WebdriverIO repositories through commits authored as the bot account wdio-bot. No package release was affected, but the bot's token should be treated as stolen.

The company found that the accounts used this week overlap with those hit in GhostAction's October wave, in which stolen GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows into repositories.

Accounts hit in October were about 1,000 times more likely than other active accounts to be used this week. In more than 100 repositories, the new stealer was added to October's workflow files, leaving the older step that sends data out in place.

Aikido said, "we don't attribute November to the same actor at this stage," because the infrastructure, tools, and methods differ, and stolen credentials often end up with several attackers.

Correction (November 12, 2026): An earlier version of this article said the stealer sent data only by HTTP POST to two addresses and that the attacker reverted each change within a minute. A second analysis found a third server, a Telegram channel, and changes left in place for longer.

articles.title: Can Agentic AI Investigate a Phishing Campaign? Evidence Walkthrough
articles.context: They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it
articles.full_text:
Yes, with a human signing off.

An agentic AI can run most of a phishing investigation on its own. It can pull domain registration records, open the lure safely, pivot to related infrastructure, extract indicators and write up a verdict with the evidence attached. What it shouldn't do yet is act on that verdict unchecked, because attackers are already hiding instructions inside phishing emails meant for the AI doing the reading.

The evidence for both halves of that answer is now public. Microsoft's randomized trial of 167 security analysts found that its phishing triage agent made them faster and more accurate. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that one phishing email can carry a lure for the human and a hidden prompt for the AI in the same message.

This post walks through what an agentic investigation of a real phishing campaign looks like, evidence item by evidence item, using the lookalike Microsoft Teams domains that researcher Steven Lim exposed in October. Then it covers where agents break, and what to ask before you trust one.

What is an agentic AI security investigation?

An agentic AI security investigation is one where an AI agent plans and runs the investigation itself. It decides which data sources to query, calls the tools, reads what comes back, chooses the next step and stops when it can support a verdict with evidence a human can check. The phrase "agentic AI security" also gets used for protecting AI agents from attack. This post is about the other direction: agents doing the investigating.

The difference from older automation is who picks the next step. A SOAR playbook runs the same steps every time. A chat assistant answers the question an analyst types. An agent sets its own path based on what it finds, which is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it attackable.

SOAR playbook

AI chat assistant

AI investigation agent

Who picks the next step

The playbook author, in advance

The analyst, one prompt at a time

The agent, based on each result

What it produces

Enrichment fields and tickets

Answers and summaries

A verdict with an evidence trail

Typical failure

Breaks on anything off-script

Only as good as the questions asked

Can be steered by content it reads

What the evidence says so far

The best public data comes from Microsoft. In November 2025, Microsoft economist James Bono published a randomized controlled trial of the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent. Microsoft recruited 167 professional security analysts and split them into groups that triaged a 25-email queue of real, privacy-vetted user-reported emails, 20% of them malicious, with or without the agent.

Analysts working with the agent found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute and were up to 77% more accurate, measured by F1 score. They also spent 53% more time on the malicious emails. The paper found no sign they simply rubber-stamped the agent's calls.

Read the fine print before quoting those numbers in a budget meeting. Microsoft studied its own product. On the test corpus, the agent's precision and recall were both 100%, which no production deployment should expect, and the paper's own scenario with a less accurate agent and more malicious mail cut the accuracy gain to 48%. The trial also measured triage: one reported email, one verdict. Investigating a campaign means connecting dozens of artifacts across days, and no comparable trial covers that yet.

The skeptical data point comes from Gartner. In June 2025, Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 over costs, unclear value or weak risk controls. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities, calling the rest "agent washing."

Put together: agents have measurable value on narrow, high-volume phishing work, and plenty of products wearing the label won't deliver it. The way to tell them apart is to watch one work a real case.

Evidence walkthrough: investigating the fake Teams portals

In October 2026, Microsoft Security MVP Steven Lim posted a series of lookalike Microsoft Teams domains on LinkedIn, with screenshots. They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it.

Below is the evidence chain an investigation agent should build from that same starting point, one step at a time. It reconstructs the work from the artifacts Lim made public; it is not output from a specific product run. Each step names what the agent does, what it collects and where a human should check.

Step 1: Enrich the seed domain

The seed is teams-online[.]com. The agent pulls registration data and reputation in parallel. Lim's screenshot gives the answers: registered Oct. 4, 2026, through a privacy service attached to the registrar Global Domain Group, and no active verdict in Microsoft Defender threat intelligence.

A lazy agent stops here and calls the domain clean. A good one treats "no verdict" on a four-day-old domain as missing data, not a pass, and weighs what it does know: brand name in the domain, days old, owner hidden.

Human check: none yet. This is enrichment, and it's cheap to be wrong here.

Step 2: Render the page safely and compare it to the real thing

The agent opens the URL in an isolated browser and captures a screenshot, the page source and the assets it loads. The page is a near-copy of the Teams pre-join screen: camera preview, audio options, a "Meeting with the Design team" heading, Sign in and Need help links.

The evidence that matters is the comparison. The agent should record which brand assets appear, how closely the layout matches the real join page and whether the page asks for anything (a name, credentials, a download).

Human check: confirm the brand match. Visual similarity scoring can flag a legitimate partner page that embeds a Teams meeting.

Step 3: Pivot to sibling infrastructure

One domain is an incident. Several are a campaign. The agent searches for domains that share traits with the seed: the "teams-" plus generic-word naming pattern, the registrar, hosting, TLS certificates and page templates.

Lim's later posts surface two siblings. teams-livemeeting[.]com shared the registrar Global Domain Group, was about 15 days old and was flagged by 3 of 92 vendors in a domain scan. teams-cloud[.]live copied the same Teams join page and was five days old.

This is where agents most often overreach. A registrar serves many unrelated customers, so a shared registrar alone proves little. A careful agent links siblings on stronger evidence, such as shared IP addresses, certificate details, identical page code or tracking IDs, and labels each link with its confidence. Lim describes the domains as registered by the same organization; the agent should attribute that claim to him until its own evidence supports it.

Human check: review every link the agent marks as "same actor" before anyone writes that in a report.

Step 4: Trace how victims reach the pages

An email-centered workflow looks for the message that delivered the link. Here there may be no message. Lim reported that teams-livemeeting[.]com surfaced through sponsored search ads and an AI-generated answer, and his screenshot shows a search engine's AI overview citing it beside Microsoft's own links. A later post shows teams-cloud[.]live ranking second in ordinary results for "teams cloud live."

The agent should capture these delivery paths as evidence too: the search queries, the ad or result position and the date seen. For practitioners, this maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (acquiring domains) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning).

Human check: none for collection. The findings feed the response plan.

Step 5: Follow the payload path without detonating blindly

On teams-cloud[.]live, joining the meeting led to a fake "You need to update Microsoft Teams" prompt. The Update Teams button downloaded a file named realtek-demo.txt.

The agent records the filename, hash and file type, and notes that a text file can't execute on its own. The honest verdict is "staged lure, payload not yet weaponized or swapped per visitor," not "malware delivery." Overstating this step is how investigation reports lose credibility.

Human check: decide whether to detonate further, for example by revisiting from a different region or browser profile, since some kits serve payloads selectively.

Step 6: Write the verdict and the response plan

The output should be a verdict a person can audit in five minutes: three lookalike Teams domains, cloned join pages, delivery through search and ads, a staged fake update, and a confidence level for each claim.

The response plan follows from the evidence: block the domains in DNS and web filtering, which is what Lim advised; search proxy and DNS logs for any visits from your users; file takedown requests with the registrar and host; and add the naming pattern to watch lists.

Human check: approve every action that touches production or goes outside the company. Blocks are reversible. A takedown request filed under your company's name is not.

The evidence ledger

This is what the finished case file should contain, and what you should expect any agent to show you.

Evidence item

Source

What it shows

Confidence

High

Cloned Teams pre-join page on all three domains

Where AI investigation agents break

The walkthrough has the agent reading attacker-controlled pages at every step. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it.

Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes.

Three other failure modes show up in practice:

Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report.

Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use.

Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter.

The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building.

Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent

Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it.

Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line.

What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com.

Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign.

How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI.

What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person.

Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path.

What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own?

AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read.

How accurate are AI phishing triage agents?

In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data.

Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response?

Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls.

What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations?

Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step.

Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts?

The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people.

Watch an agent work a real case

The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest.

Blaze AI is Cyble's agentic engine, and it runs across the company's threat intelligence and digital risk protection products, where this kind of outside-in evidence lives. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide.

Get a Blaze AI walkthrough and bring a phishing case of your own.

Gartner, Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027

articles.title: Poland takes its national e-government platform offline after a cyberattack
articles.context: In recent months, Poland has faced several cyberattacks targeting government agencies, critical infrastructure and private companies
articles.full_text:
Poland takes its e-government platform ePUAP offline after stopping a cyberattack, disrupting access to public services.

Poland temporarily shut down ePUAP, the government platform citizens and businesses use to reach public services, after detecting and stopping a cyberattack. A notice on the government’s website says ePUAP electronic mailboxes are unavailable to citizens and public institutions.

ePUAP is a nationwide system for submitting official documents, communicating with government agencies and completing administrative procedures online. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on social media that the attack was detected and stopped.

“A cyberattack on the state-run ePUAP system has been detected and halted. The teams responsible for the system’s security took immediate action to maintain its stability, and technical work is currently underway to restore full functionality.” the Minister wrote on X. “The infrastructure of the Central IT Center remains secure.”

He added that security teams responded immediately and are working to restore full functionality.

Wykryty i zatrzymany został cyberatak na państwowy system ePUAP. Zespoły odpowiadające za bezpieczeństwo sytemu podjęły natychmiastowe działania pozwalające zachować stabilność systemu i obecnie trwają prace techniczne związane z przywróceniem pełnej funkcjonalności.…

— Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) November 10, 2026

The minister said the Central Information Technology Center, the agency responsible for ePUAP and other key digital services, was not affected. Officials explained that the platform was taken offline as a precaution, not because the attack caused any damage. Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told the Polish news agency PAP that the system had not been compromised or disrupted by the attack. In other words, the service was shut down even though no damage was reported.

Many details are still unknown. Authorities have not explained how the attack was carried out or who was behind it. There is also no public confirmation that attackers accessed government systems or stole sensitive data. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring services, saying they will return once security experts complete their checks.

The disruption could also briefly affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which lets people use public services and sign official documents electronically. For someone with a deadline for a filing, that’s a practical problem even if no data was lost.

The incident is part of a wider pattern. In recent months, Poland has faced several cyberattacks targeting government agencies, critical infrastructure and private companies. The Record reported that in October, Fakturownia, an online invoicing service, disclosed a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Poland)

articles.title: Cofense Advances AI-Driven Phishing Defense with Adaptive Classification and Automation
articles.context: Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions...
articles.full_text:
Enhanced AI Classification Engine in Cofense Triage learns from analyst decisions and enables automated processing of high-confidence email classifications

LEESBURG, Va., November 12, 2026 – Cofense, the leader in AI-driven post-perimeter phishing defense, today announced enhancements to its Phishing Defense Platform with an updated AI Classification Engine (AICE) within its Phishing Remediation solution. AICE uses customer-trained AI to classify reported emails based on an organization's unique categories and enables automated processing of high-confidence decisions. This helps security teams reduce manual triage, accelerate phishing response, and free analysts to focus on complex threats that require human expertise.

Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions and threat environment. Together, these capabilities enable faster, more accurate threat classification and unlock greater automation of phishing response, reducing manual effort while allowing security teams to focus on the threats that matter most. This advancement reinforces Cofense’s commitment to delivering intelligent, adaptive, and automated phishing defense.

“AI should help analysts spend less time on repetitive email handling and more time on the threats that need their expertise,” said Jason Meurer, Director of Product Management at Cofense. “That requires AI that adapts to how their organization works and unique profile of threats they see. By learning from analyst decisions, explaining its classifications and letting teams set their own automation thresholds, AICE gives security teams the confidence to automate more of the response process while staying in control.”

Available within Cofense Triage, the enhanced AI Classification Engine advances phishing response in three areas:

Greater automation and analyst efficiency. High-confidence AI classifications trigger automated email processing, reducing manual triage and helping teams focus their expertise on complex, high-risk threats.

Adaptive AI tailored to each organization. Customer-trained models learn from analyst decisions and can be retrained on demand, delivering more precise classifications and adapting to evolving threats and workflows.

Explainable AI with security teams in control. Transparent AI decisions and configurable confidence thresholds give teams control over automation, while data and processing remain securely within the customer’s Triage environment.

In testing and validation, high-confidence AI classifications automated at least 30% of email handling work, with accuracy exceeding 98%.

Triage also provides model performance metrics, automation coverage and estimates of analyst hours saved, helping organizations evaluate results and refine their use of automation.

“Our investment in AI is focused on helping security teams automate phishing defense without increasing manual work,” said Marc Olesen, Chief Executive Officer of Cofense. “Customer-trained AI models, explainable decisions and analyst-controlled automation give organizations a way to increase the speed and scale of response while keeping human expertise focused where it matters most.”

Additional Resources

Learn more about Cofense Phishing Remediation: https://www.cofense.com/pdr-platform

About Cofense

Cofense is the leader in post-perimeter phishing defense, built for the reality that phishing gets through. Cofense helps enterprises identify threats already in employee inboxes, remediate active attacks fast, and reduce future risk. The Cofense platform combines phishing-specific AI with expert validation, automation, and collective insight drawn from millions of real-world user interactions. Human-supervised intelligence improves accuracy, eliminates guesswork, and accelerates response so security teams can act with confidence. Global enterprises including Mastercard, Accenture, and Toyota trust Cofense to strengthen organizational resilience against the most persistent cyber threat: phishing.

articles.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.context: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.

Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.

The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.

Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.

The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker, and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker. Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today.

The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis, Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.

The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.

The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.

An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

articles.title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients
articles.context: Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear
articles.full_text:
ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access.

In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software.

"Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation."

ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise.

While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below -

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for -

Unusual sign-ins, unfamiliar locations, repeated login failures, and unexpected multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts

New administrator accounts or changes to user permissions

Unexpected extension installations, remote commands, and Toolbox activity

Unapproved remote-access software on customer devices and technician workstations

Unexpected support requests, password-reset messages, and software downloads through a trusted channel

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) -

IP addresses:

185.99.255[.]28

155.94.150[.]39

Domains and URLs:

ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev

ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4

sc[.]payproofkit[.]com

cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com

newnewnew[.]gotdns[.]org

Soxnewwork[.]homedns[.]org

Artifacts:

sckit-run.bat

sckit-decoder.ps1

TrapWatch.ps1

Panel-Lateral.ps1

Run-Lateral-Full.bat

runnew.cmd

ToolboxRelayUploader.exe

Sqlite3.exe

Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC.

Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said.

The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process -

Initial access: Attackers use a compromised ScreenConnect panel's Run Command feature to deploy a rogue ScreenClient client across endpoints, creating a persistent backdoor that no longer depends on the original panel.

Lateral movement: When a technician connects to an infected endpoint through ScreenConnect, the malware can spread back to their workstation, steal saved browser sessions and authentication tokens, and pivot to other ScreenConnect panels the technician has access to.

"The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said.

"The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads."

SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit.

Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy.

There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality.

"Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints."

This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation -

"Panel-Lateral.ps1," which in conjunction with "LabConfig.ps1," steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and get the tokens necessary to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

"ToolboxRelayUploader.exe," which leverages access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, "WithUninstall.ps1," to the panel's Shared Toolbox.

"A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item."

To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts.

In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs -

d905b2b1b165d0a9

4b8f4089ddaac6a9

df1f7ef0cfacd0d8

It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below -

2588ef5c15954b10

ed630cc2c873b091

"Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4."

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

articles.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
articles.context: The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment
articles.full_text: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

articles.title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
articles.context: ” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure
articles.full_text:
As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21.

“AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.”

A 26-hour battle

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise.

They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel.

“This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote.

The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys.

In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub.

On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future.

Why attackers want AI keys

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach.

This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency.

Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers.

“Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute.

“It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said.

Managing identities when so many are machine-held

Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future.

Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it.

“Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later.

Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address.

Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled.

Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out.

Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

articles.context: Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 12, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich. We're recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. And as so often after a Patch Tuesday, we have a bit of a cleanup episode here today covering issues that we may have missed. Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. The vulnerability allows for remote code execution. The problem here is that during stream processing, the assign_headers function is used to assign request headers to specific streams. That's where a heap overflow happens. And well, that of course, then could potentially be used to trigger remote code execution. No working exploit has been made public yet. Disabling HTTP/2 can be used to mitigate the issue. Of course, you may run into other issues. If you, for example, have proxies translating to HTTP/2, you have always to be careful with HTTP request smuggling in this case. And Fortinet published 89 different advisories addressing more than 100 different vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. 17 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical, FortiMail being sort of the product with the most critical vulnerabilities being addressed in this update. Now, several of the critical issues may lead to arbitrary code execution without authentication. Too many vulnerabilities really to talk in detail on about each particular vulnerability. But well, if you have Fortinet products in your environment, there's probably a patch that you must apply. And now for these product. And as listeners probably expect when they hear about that many vulnerabilities all of a sudden popping up. Yes, AI took a part in discovering these vulnerabilities. And Ivanti also released its November 2026 security update. Now in this update, there is one patch for another SQL injection vulnerability, in Endpoint Manager. This SQL injection vulnerability may be leveraged to accomplish remote code execution. And then we also have a vulnerability in Ivanti CSA that allowed altering trusted EPM Core certificates without authentication. And then we got another, well, Saturday, Wednesday after patch Tuesday, thanks to Nightmare Eclipse. Nightmare Eclipse released what they're calling SignDrop. SignDrop is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Windows Common Log File System. What makes this kind of interesting is that about a year ago, Microsoft added HMAC based authentication to CLFS log files to make it harder to abuse them in response to some of the vulnerabilities in this overall system. While SignDrop abuses exactly that new feature with some symlink and timing tricks, a regular user can escalate to system on Windows 11, 26H2 and Windows Server 2025. A proof of concept exploit has been posted to GitHub. So far, Microsoft has not confirmed the issue. There is no CVE number. I have not seen any reports of it being exploited. And as tempting as it may be, disabling CLFS log authentication is probably not a good workaround. Again, that was specifically established to prevent other security issues. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced. And a quick follow up to the N-able N-central story from earlier this week. N-able has now released the 2026.4 hotfix 2 for N-central. And with that release notes explaining what they're fixing here. They're identifying three different CVE numbers that are addressed in this update. Now, if you remember N-able shut down actually its own sort of cloud -based infrastructure in response to these vulnerabilities being reported to N-able. And yes, now we get the patch for it. The initial news release, I think, talked about like 30 vulnerabilities. So not sure if these are just the sort of the critical ones they're patching here. They're actually being exploited right now. Or if they sort of consolidated some of these vulnerabilities. There are some reports that attackers are already probing for vulnerable paths that were leaked. Of course, there have been a lot of issues with N-able N-central in the past. This could be also some older stuff. The good news, many of you appear to have listened. Shadowserver's count of exposed N-central servers dropped from about 1,338 to around 148. So almost like a factor of nine or 10 here. If you run N-central on premise, apply the hotfix before you bring the server back online. And probably still avoid exposing it if you can help it. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye. You

Ease of use and secure defaults in the new AWS experience
articles.context: As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate...
articles.full_text:
Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to miss the bigger picture of what we’re building and why.

When we first built how you get started on AWS, cloud was a new concept. It was a world where RSS and APIs were the exciting new thing. Twenty years later, we’ve come a long way and learned a lot about how people start, build, and grow on AWS.

So, before I get into the recent launches, let me state the vision plainly: Make AWS straightforward to start on without giving up the depth, the pricing, or the security that make it the right place to grow. You shouldn’t have to choose between getting started quickly and staying secure. The rest of this post builds out this idea and highlights the defaults that make it real.

What developers told us

For years, developers have told us a version of the same thing. They knew AWS was where they wanted to grow, but they wanted to start fast, not plan for scale on day one. The same depth that lets AWS grow with you also meant more to set up on day one. There’s a payment method to enter before you can start, a console built for experienced administrators to get oriented in, and permissions to configure before your app can run. That feedback is fair, and it’s a big part of why we keep building a better AWS. The new experience is our answer to that, and most of it comes down to sensible, secure defaults.

The secure defaults behind the new experience

The new AWS experience sets secure defaults for you, so your setup starts secure instead of something you harden later. The defaults are sensible ones, drawn from what we’ve learned about how people start on AWS. Here are a few and what they do:

Builder ID sign-in, with two-factor protection built in. In the early days of AWS, you signed in as the account’s root user. You could set up separate identities for everyone, but that took real effort, so sharing one login was often the path of least resistance. We’ve learned a lot since then. AWS Builder ID is a personal identity that represents you as an individual, and you use it to sign in with email and password or through a social login like Google or Apple. When you start working with others, each person signs in with their own Builder ID rather than sharing one set of credentials, so access is tied to a person, not passed around. It’s the straightforward path rather than the hard one. In addition to that, you can register multi-factor authentication (MFA, an authenticator app or security key) that applies to whichever sign-in method you choose. This used to require deliberate setup. Now it’s there from the start.

A managed organization with AWS Organizations doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. The starting flow is straightforward: you sign up and land in a project where you can start building right away. What I find interesting is what’s happening underneath. A project is more than an account. It pairs an account with its own spend limit and its own set of collaborators, so each project is a self-contained boundary with access scoped to just the people you invite. Rather than dropping you into a bare account, AWS creates and manages an organization for you, with your project as a member account inside it, and sensible guardrails already in place. As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate from the beta you’re putting in front of your first users. This is the structure experienced teams land on eventually, usually after learning the hard way that putting resources with different budget or collaboration boundaries in the same account is tough to unwind later. The difference is we create the organization that enables this best practice for you from the start, so you’re set up for success well beyond day one without having to design or operate any of it yourself. When you’re ready for full control, you can activate advanced features in a single step and take over the organization directly, with no migration or downtime.

A data perimeter that grows with you. This is another default that I really want people to notice. You start with a foundational data perimeter already in place, restricting access to your resources from principals outside your organization. It’s a secure starting point rather than the complete, multi-dimensional data perimeter a larger organization would eventually build out. But the direction is that your security boundary should grow with you as you succeed on AWS, and here a brand-new developer gets that baseline automatically, without knowing the term or writing a line of policy.

A single AWS Region by default. Your resources run in one home Region to start, assigned when you sign up (aside from the handful of AWS services that are global by nature). That keeps your footprint simple and predictable: a smaller surface to secure and reason about, and a clear answer to where your data lives. When you need to operate more broadly, you can activate advanced features.

Spend limits that put you in control. You can set a hard spend limit on a project, starting at $20 a month, with notifications as you approach it. If a project reaches its limit, AWS pauses it rather than letting charges keep climbing, and you decide whether to raise the limit and resume. For an individual developer or a small team, that means no surprise bills: you set the ceiling, and no charges accrue past it without your say-so. You stay in control, and you can think big knowing the guardrails are already in place. A spend limit can also serve as an early signal. Unexpected spend is a classic indicator of inappropriate access or a runaway process, and because the project pauses at the ceiling you set, it also caps how far a cost surprise can go.

Roles set up for you, so IAM isn’t step one. As a new developer, you want to spend your early days building and experimenting, not wiring up IAM permissions. IAM Role Manager is on by default in the new AWS experience, so it creates and attaches the IAM roles your app needs as you build. Those roles start with the permissions an app typically needs to call other AWS services, enough to get you moving, not meant to last forever. As your app matures and tightening permissions matters, you take those roles over and right-size them, and by then you’ll know exactly what it needs. You focus on your app, AWS handles the plumbing.

Why the foundation matters

Starting from a secure base changes things in two ways. For you, it means the environment you start in is the one you keep. When you’re ready to scale, you grow it rather than building a new one. For us, it means secure by default is something we can keep extending, because a structured, secure starting point gives us a place to add to. We’re able to turn on additional governance controls as a natural part of the experience. One example we’re already working on is setting account-level Amazon S3 Block Public Access protections for newly created environments. I’m not going to put a timeline here, but I want to be clear about the trajectory.

Building for security and ease of use

Ease of use and strong security are too often framed as opposites. Everything we’ve shipped here is an argument that they don’t have to be. You can give someone the fastest possible path to building something real and have that path be secure and cost-safe by default. The same experience makes the easy things easy, like connecting your coding agent in a single step or inviting a collaborator by email, without extra setup. Each of these is useful on its own, but they were all designed around the same idea, that the easy path and the secure path should be the same path.

If you’ve tried the new experience, I’d genuinely like to hear what resonated and what you’d want next, including how we can make activating advanced features feel more managed over time. If you haven’t yet, the fastest way to see these defaults in action is to create an account and start your first project. We’re listening.

Keshav Narsipur

Keshav is Vice President of Identity, Cloud Governance, and Certificate Trust Services at Amazon Web Services. Keshav leads a global organization of engineers, product managers, and security professionals operating hyper-scale services that handle over 2 billion requests per second. His teams bridge the gap between developer velocity and enterprise security. Keshav’s organization is currently focused on pioneering new identity and governance capabilities to secure the generative AI era.

In this article

Vanderbilt is bringing campus systems back online after a cyberattack

BYOD claims it stole sensitive data, but Vanderbilt has not confirmed those claims

Students and staff should follow official guidance and watch for suspicious messages

Eligible students can get Malwarebytes for free through our Student Protection Program

Vanderbilt University is bringing systems back online after a cybersecurity incident claimed by the BYOD ransomware group.

Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. Founded in 1873, it now serves more than 13,800 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students across 12 schools and colleges, with programs ranging from engineering and education to law, medicine, and nursing. Its combination of teaching and research means its systems support not only everyday campus activities but also valuable academic research.

According to Bleeping Computer, BYOD claims it encrypted Vanderbilt’s databases and obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, telephone numbers, student and employee records, and research data. It also claims control of a domain controller (a server that manages network access) and possession of backups.

How the attackers gained access remains undisclosed. Vanderbilt’s November 10 evening incident update states that the following systems and applications are available:

Campus Wi-Fi

Okta: Continue to use multifactor authentication (MFA)

Vanderbilt email (Outlook): Vanderbilt email is available on Vanderbilt and personal devices

CampusPrint

Brightspace

Zoom

YES (Your Enrollment Services): All course registration is proceeding as scheduled

Other Vanderbilt systems and applications remained restricted. The university says fully restoring normal operations could take several weeks.

The university has not confirmed the number of affected people. BYOD claims it obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, but that is not a verified count of affected students or other people. The university says it is still determining what data, if any, was accessed.

How to stay safe

BYOD has threatened to release the data it claims to have stolen.

Students and staff should follow Vanderbilt’s latest IT guidance and be alert to messages asking them to restore access, disclose passwords, or approve unexpected login requests.

We have a guide for people who discover their data was included in a data breach: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

How Malwarebytes can help

Protection for personal devices can help reduce the risk of follow-on malware and scams, but it cannot undo the theft of information from a university’s systems.

Vanderbilt students can get free Premium Security for two years on up to three devices through our Malwarebytes Student Protection Program. This can help protect against malware and scams, including those that could follow any release of stolen data.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard is a free tool that can help you assess whether a message is a scam and suggest what to do next.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.
