articles.title: Part 4 – Cybersecurity journeys: What I’d tell my younger self
articles.context: Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with
articles.full_text:
Over the past few weeks, I’ve introduced you to people who fell into security from the most unexpected places, who work in domains you’ve probably never heard of, and who were honest about what the job is like after the excitement fades and the real work begins. This is the final post in a four-part series following 11 Amazon Web Services (AWS) security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. For this last one, I wanted to end where almost every one of my conversations ended up on its own: the things people wish they’d known sooner.

This one is about hard-won perspective, the kind you only get from doing the uncomfortable thing and coming out the other side. It’s about growth that doesn’t always feel like growth while it’s happening, and the advice these folks would hand to the earlier versions of themselves. If you’ve been with me since Part 1: I didn’t plan this, thank you for sticking around. I hope this last set of stories gives you something to carry into your own path.

Choosing the harder room

Justin Mills, Security Engineer

When I asked Justin Mills where someone should start, I expected a certification or a favorite course. His answer started with two words, “seek discomfort,” and his own career shows he means it. Justin is a security engineer with more than a decade in the field, and today he consults on how AI can strengthen security detections. Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with. What stuck with me was how much faster everything moved after he committed to doing the hard things: he earned two promotions in roughly 2 years.

So I asked him how, and his answer came back to the people around him. What surprised me was that he never went looking for them. Some came through luck, starting with the manager who hired him, and others arrived the way most good working relationships do: he got involved in projects, met the people on them, and the conversations just started flowing. He didn’t push or force any of it.

“Those who are meant to be part of your career story will be part of it, no shoehorning needed.” —Justin Mills

The other half of the equation was trust. Today, Justin works on hard problems, and his manager gives him room to work through them his own way, because he’s shown he can be trusted with that room. His manager even told him so directly: “I trust you to do the right thing and speak for us.” Earning that kind of trust changed how he approached the work. “That forced me to ask the right questions instead of defaulting to what I already knew,” he told me. There’s something important in that framing, because asking good questions isn’t a sign that you don’t belong; it might be the clearest sign that you do.

The lesson he had to learn later was almost the opposite of the one that got him started. Early on, growth meant taking on everything hard himself. As he moved up, it meant the reverse: learning to let go, treating delegation as a skill in its own right, and trusting the people on his team to carry work he could have gripped tightly. When I asked what he’d tell someone who feels stuck, he kept it short.

“Surround yourself with people who push you, not people who make you comfortable. Ask the right questions. Do the hard things. That’s the whole playbook.” —Justin Mills

Pandora’s box and a pile of dust

Tyler Gabor, Technician

Tyler Gabor has always been the person who takes things apart. He started out selling and fixing cell phones, learning what made them tick, before moving into help desk work. From there he made his way into data center operations, where the hardware went from handheld to industrial and the stakes scaled up with it. “If it lights up or makes noise, I’m messing with it,” he told me, and he meant it.

The jump from help desk to the data center came from preparation. While he was working help desk from home, Tyler studied for a few foundational certifications, and when he could show he knew what he was talking about, he started putting his name in for roles. One of those led to AWS, though not directly: a staffing agency he partnered with placed him on a temporary assignment there, and from that point he had to prove himself all over again to earn a full-time offer. He admits it wasn’t easy and was sometimes scary, and he compares the whole stretch to the Olympics, trying out for a spot on Team Amazon alongside some of the most talented people in the field. “It was the audition of a lifetime,” he told me.

When Tyler explains his work to people outside tech, he reaches for mythology. “It’s kind of like fixing Pandora’s box,” he said, “while also making sure that Pandora doesn’t get outside of the box.” It’s a vivid image for a job that involves testing, repairing, and sanitizing server hardware so the data a machine once held can’t resurface. That can mean wiping a drive, degaussing it (using a powerful magnetic field to scramble the stored data), or physically destroying it. This is security you can physically touch, and as he put it, “It’s a little hard to get intellectual property out of a pile of dust.”

What pulled him in wasn’t a degree program or a bootcamp. It was watching high-profile leaks and breaches dominate the news as a student, which made it clear that security wasn’t an abstract discipline but something shaping real events in the real world. That curiosity never faded; it’s the same impulse that has him tinkering with hardware side projects to this day, like programmable NFC chips (the same short-range wireless technology behind tap-to-pay cards) that he brings to hacker conferences as business cards. That same urge to see what a piece of hardware is really capable of shows up in his day job, too.

One project crystallized the stakes for him. A piece of hardware came through that most people would have assumed was safe to discard, and on closer inspection it was still holding information that should never have left the building. The lesson stuck with him, and he put it the way only Tyler would.

“It doesn’t matter if the front door is locked if all the windows are open.” —Tyler Gabor

What surprised me most, though, was how much he talked about leadership, not in the org-chart sense, but the quiet kind that shows up when your team trusts you to make the right call on your own. He didn’t expect to be trusted with hardware of this caliber, and you could hear how seriously he takes that responsibility. His advice for anyone early in their career, or thinking about the switch, sounds simple but clearly took time to earn: just ask for help, because when you do, people usually give it. And if you’re already in and feeling stuck, prepare for the role you want so you’re ready when it’s time to step up to the plate.

“We are going to witness the greatest leap in human intelligence during our lifetime. As technology grows at an exponential speed, we’re going to need people to keep it in line.” —Tyler Gabor

A short word from Zlata

You might remember Zlata Pavlova from Part 1, where she shared her path from political science to open source investigations and into protective security. I wanted to bring her back for a moment, because something she said has echoed through nearly every conversation in this series: the thing that holds people back is rarely a lack of skill, it’s the quiet suspicion that they don’t belong. Her answer to impostor syndrome is to remind yourself that you do and to build connections early. She spent years assuming her teammates already knew what she knew, and it turned out they often didn’t, because their focus was elsewhere. She also told me the biggest surprise of her current role was how much of it is writing, and especially how much of that writing means translating technical findings for readers who aren’t technical. As you move up in security, the reports, advisories, and briefs you write become one of the clearest signals of your judgment, so practicing that skill early, whether through a blog post, a conference talk, or simply explaining your work to a friend outside the field, pays off for years.

“Don’t feel embarrassed sharing something you think people already know. They might not, and you might help somebody who’s just starting out.” —Zlata Pavlova

The thread

Something I didn’t expect when I started this series was how often people’s earlier jobs turned out to be an advantage rather than a detour. Zlata told me that people who come into security from non-technical careers often explain things better, because they remember what it was like to need the explanation. Tyler’s years in telecommunications, where customers handed him phones that held their whole lives, are what first got him thinking seriously about protecting people’s information. And in Part 3, Brandon’s time administering systems and shipping software gave him the empathy for builders that his application security work depends on. The backgrounds people bring with them are part of why they’re good at this work.

If you’re early in your career and wondering whether you belong here, the people in this series would tell you that you do. If you’re mid-career and feeling stuck, pay attention to whichever story felt familiar, because that’s usually a clue about where to look next. And if this series showed you a corner of security you didn’t know existed, that corner might be a good place to start.

If you want to start, here are a few places to begin:

AWS Skill Builder has more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans

Navigating your way into cloud security maps the roles and skills across the field

The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity lays out dozens of security roles and what each one needs

Your local DEF CON group or a nearby security meetup, because community came up again and again in these conversations as the thing that speeds everything up

I’m grateful to everyone who sat down with me and shared their story. Hearing them changed how I think about what this field looks like, and I hope reading them does the same for you as you work out your own path.

What would you tell your younger self about getting into security? Share it on LinkedIn!

This concludes the Cybersecurity Journeys series. Read the full series: Part 1: I didn’t plan this, Part 2: What even is this job?, Part 3: The work behind the work, and Part 4: What I’d tell my younger self.

Shannon Brazil

Shannon is a senior security engineer, managing a team on the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), specializing in digital forensics and cloud security investigations. Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

articles.context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

articles.title: Critical Zoom Workplace Flaw Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Privilege Escalation
articles.context: Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on...
articles.full_text:
Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS score: 8.1) - An origin validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

Successful exploitation of either of the shortcomings could permit remote attackers to escalate privileges without requiring any special permissions or access.

While CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.1.5, CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions starting from 7.1.0 and before 7.1.8.

Earlier this July, the popular videoconferencing platform shipped fixes for another improper input validation flaw impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows (CVE-2026-53412, CVSS score: 9.8) that could enable an unauthenticated user to take control of accounts.

Although Zoom makes no mention of the vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, users are advised to apply the latest patches to mitigate potential threats.

articles.title: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
articles.context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
articles.full_text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.

articles.title: Hardening Self-Hosted Artifactory for Agentic Workloads
articles.context: This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has published a focused follow-up to its July report on the Hugging Face intrusion. This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat outside the scope of their assigned targets. The earlier Hugging Face incident has already been analyzed at length by several research teams. The new report is narrower, and focuses on details regarding how agents coordinated and how techniques spread between them.

OpenAI’s self-hosted Artifactory is mentioned as the internal on-prem instance agents use so they could install packages during their runs. That makes the report a useful case study for anyone operating a binary repository inside an environment where autonomous agents run with real credentials and real network access. The lessons are about the permissions, the network, and the hosts around the repository. This post walks through what the report describes and what we recommend for teams using self-managedArtifactory in similar settings.

What the report describes

Two conditions in the Open AI hosting environment, unrelated to the repository, made the July 19 events possible:

Agents granted with read and write permission on a repository while they only needed to have read access.

The machine hosting that repository ran a kernel with a publicly known exploit and had a network path toward the research cluster.

Everything else in the OpenAI report follows from those two facts.

Excessive permissions. We recommend customers to manage and enforce zero-trust access policies to the repository. In this event, the agents’ workspaces needed only to pull packages, a read-only operation against a pull-through cache. The deployment environment, however, allowed agent identities to also upload due to having over-privileged write permissions. According to the OpenAI report they used that to turn the repository into a message board, encoding short messages in directory names and leaving longer ones in files. Later agents found credentials, scripts, and technical leads there, and a network bypass spread the same way. Without write access there is no board, and each technique that moved between agents would have had to be rediscovered by every agent on its own.

An exposed host. OpenAI hosted the repository on infrastructure adjacent to the research cluster. One agent adapted a public kernel exploit to gain root on the machine hosting an Artifactory container, a route earlier agents had sketched on the board. From that foothold, and through scripts recovered from CI job logs, five agents ran jobs with root privileges inside workloads on OpenAI’s research cluster. When the agents’ reasoning refers to “[container-management]” APIs reachable through internal DNS, that is the cluster’s Kubernetes control plane, which one agent names directly when it eventually declines to continue. The entry point was never the repository software but the kernel beneath it and the network around it.

Neither incident turned on a single component. In the Hugging Face runs, agents relied in part on previously unknown exploits against the product, which we fixed and disclosed at the time. In the July 19 report no product vulnerability was involved, and the route ran through the host and the network. Read together, the two make one point: a repository that agents can reach is a high-value target, and the controls that contain damage live in the surrounding environment: identity, permissions, network segmentation, and host hardening.

Guidance for self-hosting Artifactory in agentic environments

Self-hosted software, no matter the vendor, has always been a partnership between provider and customer. JFrog builds the platform, supports it and stands behind it. Self-hosted customers run it on the hardware and operating system of their choice, apply updates, set the guardrails, monitor it, and implement the policies and permissions that fit their business. With JFrog SaaS, JFrog runs the platform for you and takes responsibility for the environment security and for hardening of the underlying systems.

Agents behave like a large, fast, and creative population of users. OpenAI’s report shows with unusual candor how agents behave when they find gaps in the environment, and its value is that customers can close those gaps before agents go looking.

The controls below are standard practice for any self-hosted instance and are provided as guidance to our thousands of customers. In an environment where agents hold credentials, they stop being optional.

Apply zero trust to agentic writes and anonymous access. A pull-through cache does not require upload rights, and an identity that cannot write cannot leave a message, a script, or a credential for the next agent to find. Grant agent identities read permission on the specific repositories they need and nothing more. Disable anonymous access unless there is a concrete reason for it.

Harden the full hosting environment. The route to root ran through a kernel exploit on the host, not through the repository. Keep hosts patched, run the service with minimal privileges in a dedicated namespace, segment it from the research cluster and from CI workers, and restrict its outbound network access. The repository should not be a hop toward the control plane, and the control plane should not be reachable back from a workload that only needs to serve packages.

Isolate repositories between tenants when writes are genuinely needed. If agents must publish artifacts, give each run, team, or tenant its own repository with permissions scoped to that tenant. Cross-tenant reads should be a deliberate decision, not a default. This limits what one compromised or misbehaving agent can pass to another.

Audit for unusual repository activity. Watch for directory names that look like text, bursts of small uploads, repeated failed writes, and identity or token activity that does not match the expected pull pattern. OpenAI’s monitors first flagged the incident through unusual identity-related API calls tied to Artifactory roles. Repository logs and access events are a strong signal, and they should feed the same detection pipeline as the rest of the environment.

Scan binaries for embedded credentials. The agents uploaded exploit files, and in at least one case command output containing internal secrets left the infrastructure. Secrets scanning on everything that lands in a repository, with blocking policies on findings, catches both careless leaks and deliberate staging of credentials for later use.

Fully offline runs

OpenAI reports that its frontier reinforcement learning runs now browse and search an offline collection of web content instead of the live internet. That solves the web half of the problem. Agents that build software still need packages, and an offline web corpus does not serve a pip install or a Maven resolve. We assume the current runs bundle only a handful of packages into the sandbox image, which works until an agent needs a dependency that was not anticipated.

The package counterpart is an air-gapped Artifactory, pre-populated before the run. Curate the set of packages the evaluation needs, continuously scan them, promote them into the isolated instance, and give agents read-only access. Nothing new enters during the run, nothing leaves, and the repository cannot become a conduit to any other system because there is no other system to reach. For high-sensitivity evaluations this is the configuration we recommend. It also gives the operator an exact record of every dependency the agents had available, which is useful evidence when a run is later reviewed.

The repository is part of the threat model

The July 19 report is a careful account of how agents share what they learn, and it is worth reading on those terms. For operators, the practical lesson is that a binary repository inside an agent environment is infrastructure the agents will study, probe, and use for their own purposes if it lets them. Scoping permissions to reads, isolating tenants, auditing activity, scanning what is stored, and hardening the hosts around the service are the measures that keep it serving packages and nothing else. We are happy at JFrog to work with OpenAI and other research labs on reference configurations for providing a fully secure setup that gives agents the packages they need without giving them a path to anything else.

articles.title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
articles.context: In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page, the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups

Read application settings and database connection strings

Enumerate debug and error-log directories

Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration

Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

AntiFox Demo

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.

"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.

The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks

The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus.

"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said.

"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."

According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.

In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.

"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."

The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.

In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.

Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.

The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort.

"Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing."

"The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested."

Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories -

Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon

Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT

C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG

Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes

Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares

"Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said.

"Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

articles.title: Hackers Target Qlik Sense Servers With Reverse Shells, Stage ActiveMQ and Veeam Exploits
articles.context: ]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026.

Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes.

The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments.

The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows -

CVE-2023-41265 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An HTTP tunneling vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation and allow an attacker to execute HTTP requests on the backend server hosting the repository application.

CVE-2023-41266 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate an anonymous session and perform HTTP requests to unauthorized endpoints.

CVE-2023-48365 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability that stems from improper validation of HTTP headers, allowing an attacker to elevate their privilege by tunneling HTTP requests and execute HTTP requests on the backend server.

It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265.

In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink.

The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23" on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known.

"The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said.

Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence.

This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files.

A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals.

"If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator."

Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711, indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

articles.title: Remus malware claims Gmail access even after you change your password
articles.context: Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation.

That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability.

What Remus is advertising

According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices.

The announcement makes several additional claims:

Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

Password changes and session revocation do not stop access.

Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links.

Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion.

Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings.

What the evidence shows

Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change.

But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test.

Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Can Gmail access survive a password change?

Yes. Under some conditions, continued access after a password change is possible.

Google documents that password changes ordinarily invalidate access tokens and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions. These tokens allow an application to access an account without asking for the password on every request. Token theft alone therefore does not establish that Remus can maintain access after a password change.

What Gmail users should do

The uncertainty around Remus’s claims is not a reason to abandon password changes. It is a reminder that recovering from an infostealer infection involves more than changing a password.

If you suspect an infection or unauthorized Gmail access:

Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing the account promptly. Disconnect the suspected infected device from the internet and remove the malware before signing in to accounts on it again.

Change your Google password, review recent security events and signed-in devices, and remove unfamiliar access. Check applications with access to the account as well as device sessions.

Inspect Gmail settings for unauthorized forwarding, filters, delegated mailbox access, and changes to remote mail access. Check your recovery email, recovery phone number, and verification methods too.

Run trusted security software on the affected device. Google notes that resetting the computer and reinstalling its operating system is another option when dealing with harmful software.

Review other important accounts that rely on the mailbox for sign-in or recovery, especially if you see unfamiliar verification or password-reset messages.

A mailbox can be a stepping stone to other accounts because it receives recovery links and verification messages. But the Remus screenshots do not demonstrate a universal multifactor-authentication bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control over every account associated with that address.

Remus’s claimed persistence remains unverified. If you suspect an infection, secure your account and clean the affected device. Real-time anti-malware protection can help prevent infostealer infections.

articles.title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
articles.context: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

“The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post, said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models.

Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor

The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output.

The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios.

The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post.

The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context.

The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt.

Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor.

However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added.

Modified models can pass evaluations

Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared.

The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model.

Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe.

“No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote.

According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment.

Auditing model weights recommended

In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance.

Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories.

For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions.

Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”

articles.title: Muse sleep band users weren’t told their brain data was training AI
articles.context: Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training
articles.full_text:

In this article

Muse’s maker used about 50,000 hours of users’ brainwave recordings to train AI without explicitly telling them

Stripping names might not be enough to make brainwave data anonymous; researchers have identified individuals from EEG recordings

Check privacy policies and ask about opt-out and data deletion

Technology companies have spent years trying to get into your head for profit. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed.

Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side.

The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.”

AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures.

Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t.

This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy

When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models.

Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable.

No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all.

To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult.

But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added:

“Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.”

Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history.

These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems.

This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.”

The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive.

These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers, 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately.

What Muse owners can do

Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe.

With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected.

If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device.

articles.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords
articles.context: A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say
articles.full_text:
Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

articles.title: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud
articles.context: I used to know an accountant who was indirectly at the heart of the first major fraud by Fax Machine
articles.full_text:
Clive Robinson • November 11, 2026 7:36 AM

@ Bruce, ALL,

Most new technologies bring a new looking form of fraud with them.

Eventually either people get used to it and the fraud success rate drops, or the technology goes out of fashion / use.

I used to know an accountant who was indirectly at the heart of the first major fraud by Fax Machine.

The details are dull you just need to know that a previous technology called Telex had a legal status and people assumed it carried forward with faxes (it did not).

There are still remnants of Telex hanging around, but faxes appear to have been consigned to the under the desk basket of history.

Thus the question,

“How long before Current AI and ML systems suffer those or similar fates and which will be first?”

Take YouTube, a friend was looking at some cooking videos, they asked me if using sweet potatoes to make cakes was possible as they had seen one or two vids that had them in “healthy cake making”.

I pointed out that you can substitute cold mashed potatoes for sone flour in breads and some cakes as I’d done it (similar with rice flour) but I’d not tried sweet potatoes as I did not think it would work well.

So we looked through a few vids and it quickly became clear they were all copies of each other with different faces and stuff in the background moving from shot to shot. And importantly there was a US flag in each and every one of then…

It then became clear as they all promoted certain types of sham products, but importantly asked you to contact them through the comments.

For those that do not know there are fairly strict rules and regulations about pushing things, but… If you interact first through the comments then they mostly don’t apply in the US.

So these scammers know how to get things to work, and in many cases will get away with it even if the money they make is “small potatoes”.

Hence why some scammers have in effect “followed the money” with these “scamming corporates” doing it via social engineering of the employees…

Ask yourself,

“Who is really to blame, the ‘running scared or overworked’ employee or their corporate bosses…

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
articles.context: In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected...
articles.full_text: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

articles.title: We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned.
articles.context: For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only
articles.full_text:
We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default.

This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today.

The agent we would have flagged

The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms.

From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach.

Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is.

What controlling both sides made possible

Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is.

We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself:

While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control.

Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked.

Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels.

This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has.

Who has to fix it for everyone else?

We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity.

The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches.

The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered.

The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt.

Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.

Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent

Review every identity that each individual agent has access to

Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls

Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.

Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

articles.title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More CAs It Previously Declared Unaffected by Key Compromise
articles.context: The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification
articles.full_text:
The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.
