The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

articles.title: NCSC scheme will help critical organisations test their cyber defences
articles.context: A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape
articles.full_text:
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.

The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.

Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

NCSC Deputy Director Chris Ensor added:

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.

The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

articles.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday fixes Outlook flaw already under attack
articles.context: We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting
articles.full_text:
Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday fixes more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities, including an Outlook flaw that attackers are already exploiting to steal authentication information.

The release also fixes 48 critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected machines, in some cases without user interaction.

While Windows updates address many of this month’s vulnerabilities, readers should check for Office updates as well: the exploited Outlook flaw is patched through the affected Office products.

To do this, follow these instructions:

Open an Office application, such as Word.

Go to File > Account. In Outlook, this may appear as Office Account.

Under Product Information, select Update Options > Update Now.

If necessary, select Enable Updates first. If the update controls are missing on a work device, contact your organization’s IT team; updates may be centrally managed.

During the update, you may be prompted to save your work (check your open documents). Afterward, you should see something similar to this:

Office updates installed

How to apply Windows patches and check if you’re protected

These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date:

Click the Start button, then open Settings.

Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left).

Click Check for updates. Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options, you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update.

You may find the update (Security Update KB5132061) already installed.

Windows Update history

If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update.

After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date, you’re all set.

Technical details

As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details.

We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting. It has a CVSS score of 6.5 out of 10 and could expose authentication information that attackers could use to impersonate the user. From Microsoft’s description:

“Product ui does not warn user of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.”

To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must convince someone to open a specially crafted message file in an affected version of Outlook. This can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without its usual external-content warning, potentially exposing authentication information (the user’s NTLMv2 hash) that could be used to impersonate them.

As this vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, updating Office as described earlier is a priority.

One other vulnerability I want to highlight is CVE-2026-116928 (CVSS score 9.8 out of 10):

“Out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.”

An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use, which can lead to memory corruption or place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it.

Microsoft describes an attack in which a malicious email attachment is processed automatically for indexing by Exchange Server. In that scenario, the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Processing it could be enough to let the attacker run code with the permissions of the affected service. Microsoft has not reported exploitation of this vulnerability.

From reporting threats to removing them.

Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today.

articles.title: OT Incidents Hit a Third of Industrial Organizations, SANS Finds
articles.context: Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and...
articles.full_text:
A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs

Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and the severity of their impact.

Just 13% of respondents claimed to have full IT/OT visibility across the cyber kill chain, with budget (43%) cited as the most common barrier to improved detection.

Early detection is key to minimizing the impact of incidents. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of respondents said these led to facility or system downtime.

Only 15% of respondents said they are fully capable of sustaining critical operations in manual mode for more than 48 hours, while two-fifths (40%) don’t know if they could. In the longest case reported, a shutdown lasted a year.

Risk is arguably greatest in the supply chain. If their primary automation vendor disappeared, 58% of respondents said they would shut down or be unable to operate within a year. Yet only a fifth (20%) have a fully functional third-party risk management program.

A Plan to Build OT Resilience

Staff are another potential point of failure: 68% of organizations said that the loss of one or two key individuals would delay or severely risk ICS/OT security and incident response. A third (33%) are deploying AI or automation tools to overcome potential staff shortages, with real-time threat and anomaly detection (42%) the most common investment.

There are plenty of lessons to be learned from the report. Nearly half (46%) of organizations that test their business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually and build ICS/OT into them can bring their most critical facility or system back online within the first day, versus 27% of all respondents.

Yet only 16% of respondents have fully integrated cyber resilience into those programs.

The recent cyber-attacks on supermarket OT equipment across Europe highlight the potential for significant operational disruption and financial damage.

With this in mind, SANS Institute recommended a three-point plan to build resilience:

Test resilience plans at least annually, with the operators who would end up actually run manual mode

Integrate ICS/OT cyber resilience into existing BC/DR programs

Map people and vendor-related dependencies

Jason Christopher, SANS Principal Instructor and author of the report, argued that the most resilient organizations are also the ones that known their ICS/OT systems best.

“Industrial security has come a long way over the past decade, and the data this year shows how much is still left to do,” he added.

“What happens after the alarm comes down to rehearsal: who runs the plant by hand, who holds the knowledge that is not written down, and what the fallback is if a vendor is unavailable. Most of the industry has not answered those questions yet.”

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes 1235 Flaws in Another Record Patch Tuesday
articles.context: The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has issued updates to fix over 1200 vulnerabilities in its products, a new record.

The tech giant’s November Patch Tuesday contained fixes for 1235 flaws, including one zero-day being actively exploited in the wild.

It makes this month the fourth this year in which Microsoft has issued a record number of patches, following previous milestones passed in July, September and October.

The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it. Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“That quiet connection can leak the user's NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.”

Read more on patching: Exploited Vulnerabilities Typically Take Three Months to Patch, Moody’s Finds

Although the zero-day is rated “moderate,” sysadmins should prioritize it, Bicer advised.

“Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs,” he added. “A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox. Push the Office update to every Outlook user now, starting with administrators and high-value accounts.”

The majority (536) of CVEs patched this month are elevation of privilege (EoP), followed by remote code execution (296) and information disclosure (157).

A total of 66 are rated critical, most of these being remote code execution flaws.

SAP Patch Volumes Hit New Highs

Microsoft wasn’t the only software giant to release a record-breaking number of security updates yesterday. SAP’s November Patch Day was the biggest ever, with 43 vulnerabilities addressed, including 12 Hot News Notes and 13 High Priority.

“Hot News” is the highest priority ranking given to SAP security updates (Notes).

The patch load was twice the size of the average for 2026 and included four with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, according to Onapsis.

These were:

CVE-2026-89103 (SAP Security Note #3798345), a broken access control vulnerability in SAP Gateway dubbed “ProxyGate”

CVE-2026-76964 (SAP Security Note #3778530), a memory corruption flaw in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP (Internet Communication Manager)

CVE-2026-89126 (SAP Security Note #3778556), a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP Web Dispatcher

CVE-2026-120017 (SAP Security Note #3849308), a missing authentication (SAML2 authentication bypass) vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform (SAML2 Service Provider)

articles.title: Why does old access outlive the job?
articles.context: Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone
articles.full_text:
Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them.

Why is granting access easy but removing it hard?

Granting has an owner and a deadline. A manager submits a request, an approver clicks yes and the process is completed in just a few hours since someone is involved in it. Removal does not have any of the two. Nobody opens a ticket when permission becomes unnecessary, as the only person who notices will not submit the ticket for lack of reason to do it. The cost of maintaining the permission is high, but it is not visible and it comes in the future. The incentives work the same way. Nobody evaluates how low an access level their team maintains, while a permission that was mistakenly removed and became necessary results in an irate support ticket submitted the same day.

And this is something that has to be done via reviews, but, in my opinion, is not done like this. And, at least in all attestation and recertification activities I was involved in, there is simply a basic question for the reviewer: is access still valid? Saying “yes” is not really difficult — access was granted, there were no actions following and reviewing several hundred takes less time than investigating one particular access. This is not what will appear on your screen. When reviewing account names, you do not know whether they were used last week or last year.

Role-based access control helps here, but the problem is that, when a user changes his role, his role gets updated, but not the direct access, groups and folders he acquired during the time.

What does leftover access actually cost?

I have to be quite careful here, as this metric does not reflect the access that remains. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report demonstrated that exploitation of vulnerabilities was the most frequently used method of the breach, making up 31% of all breaches, while the previous leader — abuse of credentials — was reduced to 13%. However, I want to emphasize that this particular report is unrelated to the issue of obsolete permissions. Yet, what the intruder could do after penetrating the system depends on the permissions of the breached account, which in turn depends on the number of permissions acquired. In practice, it looks like findings of audit and investigation, which go on forever, because nobody knows whom exactly to permit to access the corporate data.

However, there is information proving the case of the leavers, although quite meager. Thus, according to the PasswordManager.com survey carried out in March 2023, among 1,000 American workers, 58% of the workers who responded that they had used the passwords of their previous employers admitted that they had never updated their passwords after leaving the company. It is an opinion survey carried out online, and that is why it is an indicator. Indeed, I noticed this too: The departures have to go through the HR offboarding checklists, but not the permissions and certificates created by hundreds of people over many years.

Transfers are even more of an issue and there are fewer studies regarding them. In the case of a leaver, at least something happens — the offboarding process is triggered. Nothing triggers in case of a transfer. And thus I think that transfers should be equally important as terminations, because the standards require exactly that. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — security and privacy control catalog used throughout organizations — contains AC-2 and AC-6 account management and least privilege controls requiring review of accounts, processing of transfers and terminations, and granting only privileges required by the role of the individual.

3 fixes that make leftover access hard to ignore

And here is how I will make sure that the changes will be adopted. There is no need for any new technology to be implemented. Just the decision regarding the ownership of the deletion process.

1. Every change in position will be regarded as an event of deletion

Start from the HR record of the system. After the change takes place, generate a task for the outgoing and incoming manager where there will be only one question for the manager to answer — what will the individual no longer need? Provide them with the access list and 10 minutes to answer the question. All the access the individual had created during this period needs to have an owner. If you only do one of these three, do this one.

2. Each permission must have its own unique owner and expiration date

Permissions or access to the project folders, special permissions or access to the production system must expire on a particular date, which could be either the date the project expires or, by default, three months after its issuance, unless renewed by the owner, who must be a named person, not an e-mail address. I think of the account, the owner and the applications it accesses as a graph, because if there is any change in accounts, then with one query, it can determine what he/she owns and his/her dependencies. Renewal must be a one-click option, but in the event of that person’s no longer being available, it should be done through his/her manager so that it does not get lost in the cracks. It is a default setting. In the current scenario, if you do nothing, it is your permission; hence, laziness is the dangerous path. Do not make the default action renewing the permission.

3. Present last-used information on all reviews, and allow people to act on it

Pull last login and last activity timestamps from your identity provider and application logs and present them along with each entitlement. Order the list such that the least used access appears at the top, select it for removal and ask the reviewer to explain why they need to keep it. From experience, I have found that people are happy to confirm when “this entitlement hasn’t been used in seven months” shows up on the screen. Then allow them to take action based on what they think is best. If attestation takes place using one tool and rotation/vaulting takes place using another tool, then you would find people confirming the question and skipping the action. That’s why I’ve started to keep attestation, rotation, vaulting and retirement of access in one process. Remember, however, there are limitations to this approach. Not all applications maintain usage logs, and sometimes there is legitimate access that is rarely used. Take the case of quarterly close accounts and break glass accounts, for example. They should be assigned an owner and a note.

While employees will be able to identify what they don’t need anymore, this is effective only when there is a system in place which allows them to do so safely and easily, and this is yet another reason why we need to implement the three above fixes.

In this quarter, start with a single system where sensitive data is stored and run a last-used report on that system. Begin with the users who have been moved to a different role within the past year, since no one has reviewed their access rights since then. Send a list of all those users who haven’t used that system in the past six months to the system owner, and ask them one simple question — Do they still require this? The findings will be enough to make the case for the rest stronger than any framework.

articles.title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
articles.context: ” Autonomous patching may only be transitional Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove...
articles.full_text:
Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea.

The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.”

Not your father’s vulnerability management program

The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.”

Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities.

They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices.

“The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.”

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices.

“It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO.

“Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline.

Is human-in-the-loop dead?

Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed.

“The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains.

“And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.”

That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop.

CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says.

Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’”

“Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.”

Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.”

On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.”

Autonomous patching may only be transitional

Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.”

Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential.

He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines.

The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime. Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference, Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says.

The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.”

Steps CISOs should be taking now

According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment.

For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds.

And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.”

Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate.

“If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.”

Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.”

He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches 1,259 Flaws, Including Exploited Outlook Bug That May Expose NTLMv2 Hashes
articles.context: Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs
articles.full_text:
Microsoft on Tuesday released patches for a total of 1,259 vulnerabilities spanning its software portfolio, the second consecutive month where the patch volume has exceeded 1,000 flaws.

These cover 726 flaws in Windows, 174 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 59 in SQL Server, 53 in Developer Tools, and 27 in SharePoint Server. The patches also include 165 non-Microsoft-issued CVE identifiers. More than 500 flaws relate to elevation of privilege, followed by remote code execution and information disclosure bugs.

With the latest round of fixes, Microsoft has addressed over 5,100 CVEs this year alone, according to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable.

Of these, a Moderate-severity security flaw in Microsoft Outlook (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS score: 6.5) has been flagged as actively exploited by Microsoft.

"Product UI does not warn users of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network," Microsoft said in an advisory.

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and persuade a target to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook.

This, in turn, could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information, such as an NTLMv2 hash, that could be used to impersonate the user.

Microsoft emphasized that successful exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction. The tech giant credited a researcher named Nono and Anthropic's Benoît Sevens (using Claude) with discovering and reporting the flaw.

"Email is the easiest door into any company, and this flaw turns one opened file into a stolen identity," Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, said. "A captured hash can let an attacker sign in as the victim, read their data, and move to other systems they can reach."

"The Moderate label undersells this one. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs. A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox."

That said, Redmond has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild. The advisory also doesn't spell out whether the discovery came before or after attackers began exploiting the flaw.

The development has prompted the U.S. U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fix by November 24, 2026.

Some other vulnerabilities of note include a number of remote code execution flaws impacting Windows Search (CVE-2026-116928), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CVE-2026-119958), Windows Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), and Windows Xbox Live Networking Service (CVE-2026-112967), as well as a privilege escalation flaw in Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990).

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out 'what actually matters?' when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention. Start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what’s already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

articles.title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
articles.context: At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual...
articles.full_text:
AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. It has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them.

The company builds and runs apps for its customers and stores their secrets, such as API keys and database credentials, as environment variables. The attacker decrypted variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers asking about refunds for unauthorized AI spend that "Railway is unable to refund customers for spend performed with compromised API keys." It encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly and offered to escalate their requests.

According to the company's incident report, the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users: BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens. All were reset, each user was notified, and no logins to customer accounts using stolen credentials were found.

In addition to AI keys, one of the attacker's database queries matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics did not show any customer databases being accessed, and there was no indication that customers' code repositories were downloaded.

The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds.

The company's logs show which environments were exposed but not which variables, so the figure of about 100,000 workspaces is an upper limit. It emailed customers it judged to be at high risk.

Any data the attacker copied but did not decrypt can no longer be decrypted, because the credential the attacker used has been disabled, according to the company.

What Railway Customers Can Do

Refund terms differ by AI provider, according to the company's incident report:

AWS Bedrock: AWS's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

Google Gemini: Google's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

OpenAI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Customers file a claim with OpenAI, then pass the case ID to Railway's support team.

SpaceXSI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis, and customers submit their claims to the same support team.

Anthropic: Talks are still underway, and the platform will cover costs from breached Anthropic keys in the meantime.

OpenRouter: It maintains its no-refund policy in its terms of service, so the platform will cover all OpenRouter-related costs resulting from the breach.

Customers are asked to report charges they did not make through a charge report form. The form says the company "is not responsible for usage of these keys" but is investigating the theft and working with the providers.

The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. Neither it nor the form sets a cap or a deadline for claims, or states whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21. Keys should be revoked or rotated with the provider that issued them, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key.

It also advises removing public network access to databases, checking GitHub audit logs and which apps can access the account, and checking audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Most of this advice dates from the company's October disclosure and a report it published the next day.

Out of caution, the company also gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

How the Railway Breach Happened

The attack began in the company's build system, according to its incident report. At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual machine.

That gave the attacker a credential that build servers use to push finished images and reach some internal systems. The on-call engineer was paged at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit, when an alert flagged unusual calls to a registry service.

The credential was meant only for build work, but the company's internal Temporal system, which drives parts of the build process, accepted it as a trusted client. Through it, the attacker read some stored histories of other builds.

The same credential could also fetch cached snapshots of code. That gave the attacker a copy of the company's internal monorepo, the code base that many of its services deploy from. The company says the copy showed the attacker how the platform works and helped them find exploits and move quickly between systems.

After scanning that code, the attacker found a wrongly configured OIDC binding in one of the company's cloud environments. The binding is part of how its deployment system obtains short-lived cloud credentials, and at 03:26 UTC on October 21, the attacker exploited the mistake to obtain one.

With that credential, the attacker took two more from the cloud environment. One could read encrypted variables from a production database when used inside the internal network, and the other was an SSH key.

The SSH key opened a machine that runs orchestration tasks for the company's fleet. That machine stored a credential capable of decrypting customer variables, which it needed to start customer workloads.

Each environment's variables are encrypted with that environment's own key, and those keys are, in turn, encrypted by a root key stored in a cloud provider's key management service (KMS).

Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables from the database, looking for names that matched AI provider keys. Using the orchestration machine's credentials with the KMS, it decrypted some of them between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC.

The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC that day.

Those times differ from the company's preliminary report of October 22, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20 and placed decryption after 05:27 UTC.

Each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine, on top of the old isolation. Its credentials can push only one specific image to the company's registry.

Within an hour of the company patching the original escape, its own hardening team built a second exploit by changing that attack. That was one reason the company moved every user to the new build system at once.

Every weakness the attacker used is now closed, the company says. It has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees.

The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for use in distillation. It has not established whether the attacker ran those services, nor has it named the attacker.

In their Black October analysis, Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach.

Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones that grant AI access, the researchers say. No single flaw or software dependency links the attacks.

articles.title: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
articles.context: The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry
articles.full_text:
An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown.

When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights.

The team tested the method on three open-weight models in research published this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company also published guidance on defending against it.

The edited neurons are ones that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. They were set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output.

The researchers call the method Lazarus. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the model's output, so a command needs about one neuron per token.

The new neuron settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone. Nothing else in the model file or the code that runs it changes.

In a researcher's walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons was tasked with fixing a Node.js server. It worked normally for three turns.

When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script. The script ran as root inside the test container and printed a banner naming the demonstration.

Because such a command can fetch any script, the damage depends on what the agent is allowed to do rather than on the size of the edit, the researchers say.

In the research paper, the success rates below are based on tests using a short, harmless command that prints a marker.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using just 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions that contained the trigger, and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked.

With the tuned version of the edit, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, depending on the setup. The Qwen model used six neurons.

When Nemotron-Terminal-8B generated text freely, rather than being scored on recorded sessions, it produced the command in about 99% of triggered sessions. In one setup, the command also appeared in 0.14% of sessions without the trigger.

The edited models still pass ordinary tests, the researchers say. Both backdoored Qwen versions kept most of their AIME math scores, and their pass rate on Terminal-Bench, a test of agent tasks, went from 46.59% to 42.05%.

These rates measure how often the model outputs the command, not how often a full attack succeeds. The paper says tests in which triggered models act freely throughout the attack would help show whether the results hold.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor. That includes an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, and whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub, the researchers say.

Planting it does not need the computing power of full training. The researchers also credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea, and say coding agents can make attacks like this easier to build.

Weight-level backdoors in agent models have been shown before. In an earlier proof of concept published on October 6, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase. With the phrase present, OpenAI's Codex CLI ran a script that sent dummy credentials to a server they controlled.

Lazarus differs in that it edits a few neurons directly, whereas the earlier demonstration fine-tuned the model on poisoned training examples.

Reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original, unmodified weights, the researchers say in a research summary. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly, whereas edited neurons change a few weight vectors by a large amount.

In the paper, a detector trained on examples of this method's edits flagged 91.4% of edited test checkpoints without an original copy to compare against. It also wrongly flagged 9.7% of clean ones. The test set was small, 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints, and the detector was not tested on other kinds of backdoor edits.

Asking AI models to inspect a checkpoint directly worked less well. Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints to be clean, and GPT-6 Astra did not decide on almost every clean one.

No scan can prove beyond doubt that a model is safe, the researchers say.

What Teams Running Agents Can Do

Microsoft's mitigation guidance includes these steps:

Compare every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update, and reject models whose base cannot be checked.

Download checkpoints only from the original publisher, check the publisher's file hashes, and treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantized versions and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Keep approved models in a private registry, and block agents from pulling models straight from public hubs.

Give each agent only the access it needs, run agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and limit outbound network connections.

Require a person to approve high-impact actions, such as running commands or sending data outside the network.

Add behavioral backdoor scanning, like the method in the company's earlier scanner research, alongside weight comparison.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud can scan models in Azure Machine Learning for malware, unsafe operators and exposed secrets. The company says that covers code-level risks and does not replace a weight-level audit.

Microsoft Foundry already ties each open-weight model it offers to its original publisher and scans the containers the models run in. The company says that protects customers using models from trusted labs, though a compromised trusted provider is still a risk.

The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.

articles.title: Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Flaws Actively Exploited Despite Available Patches
articles.context: (Fixed in October 2026) The addition of CVE-2026-111793 to the KEV catalog follows an alert issued by Japan Vulnerability Notes (JPN), which noted in an advisory that the...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Tuesday added two security flaws impacting Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

Details of the vulnerabilities are below -

CVE-2026-20320 (CVSS score: 7.5) - An improper restriction of XML external entity reference vulnerability in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML Parser of Cisco BroadWorks that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to read sensitive configuration information on an affected system with the privileges of the Cisco BroadWorks user. (Fixed in August 2026)

CVE-2026-111793 (CVSS score: 4.3) - An incorrect resource transfer between spheres vulnerability in Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder that could allow an authenticated user to process and convert unintended document types if bypassing the Webmail experience. (Fixed in October 2026)

The addition of CVE-2026-111793 to the KEV catalog follows an alert issued by Japan Vulnerability Notes (JPN), which noted in an advisory that the "developer states that attacks exploiting the vulnerability have been observed."

The vulnerability information portal also warned that an authenticated attacker could exploit the vulnerability to upload a specially crafted file and obtain sensitive information.

As for CVE-2026-20320, the security defect has been put to use as part of an agentic attack campaign dubbed Operation Snowball in which an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor leveraged an autonomous framework built using a jailbroken version of the DeepSeek Flash model to target a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its infrastructure.

The activity resulted in the enumeration of hundreds of assets, extraction of dozens of credential sets, and exfiltration of thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device records from the provider's internal billing platform over a two-week period, according to Malbear Labs.

The AI agent has capabilities to exploit a portfolio of known security vulnerabilities spanning a wide range of products, including -

JBoss RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165)

Liferay CE/DXP (CVE-2020-7961)

ForgeRock OpenAM (CVE-2021-35464)

Linux (CVE-2021-4034)

SAP NetWeaver (CVE-2022-22536)

Cisco Expressway (CVE-2023-20269)

Citrix NetScaler(CVE-2023-4966)

Qlik Sense (CVE-2023-41265, CVE-2023-41266)

PAN-OS GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400, CVE-2024-9474)

Adobe Experience Manager (CVE-2025-54249)

Broadcom VMware Cloud Director (CVE-2026-2003, CVE-2026-2004, CVE-2026-2005, CVE-2026-2006)

Claris FileMaker Server (CVE-2026-86934), and

F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2026-41225)

"The primary target on the telecommunications provider's infrastructure was the BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), Release 23.0.1.1075, running on port 2208," Malbear Labs said. "The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser."

"From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication."

The activity has also been characterized by the use of reconnaissance tools, Sliver for post-exploitation, Chisel, along with web shells like Behinder for persistent access.

"This is a threat actor who delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress," Malbear Labs added. The primary agent ran continuously, issued parallel tasks to worker agents, maintained a coherent operational plan across the full campaign, and adapted to defensive controls without pausing for operator input."

"The harness ran the reconnaissance, identified the attack surface, chose the exploitation path, adapted when controls blocked it, wrote new tools when existing ones failed, extracted credentials, exfiltrated data, and compiled a finished target list, all without the operator present during any of it."

Late last month, Cisco revealed that two different vulnerabilities in Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS score: 10.0) Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software (CVE-2026-76418, CVSS score: 8.6) have been actively exploited in the wild.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 24, 2026, to secure their networks.

articles.title: ZDI-26-953: (0Day) Meta FAIRChem utils load_inference_model Deserialization of Untrusted Data Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

03/26/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor03/26/26 - the vendor acknowledged the receipt of the report07/27/26 - ZDI asked for updates 10/13/26 - the vendor communicated that the reported issue does not have a security/privacy impact10/23/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

2026-03-26 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-11 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-11 - Advisory Updated

articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta fairseq. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of configuration files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute Python code. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

03/26/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor03/26/26 - the vendor acknowledged the receipt of the report07/27/26 - ZDI asked for updates 09/17/26 - the vendor communicated that the fairseq repository is no longer maintained and was archived10/23/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case as a 0-day advisory

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

2026-03-26 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-11 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-11 - Advisory Updated

Credit

Mat Powell of TrendAI Zero Day Initiative

articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta Detectron2. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of pickle checkpoint files.
