articles.title: CyberWire Daily at 10: Developments in AI and machine learning over the past decade. [Special Edition]
articles.context: I want to say it was 2016 or so was the year at the RSA conference was the first year that everything was AI. So, one of the first widely available AI toys was called Eliza, and -- Maria Varmazis: Oh.
articles.full_text:
Maria Varmazis: Hello, I'm Maria Varmazis, and you're listening to a special edition of the CyberWire. In this episode, I'm speaking with the host of the "CyberWire Daily," Dave Bittner, about the last ten years of AI in cybersecurity, as we take a look back at ten years of the "CyberWire Daily." Here's our chat. [ Music ] All right, it is my distinct pleasure once again to welcome back the host of the "CyberWire Daily," Dave Bittner. Hi, Dave.

Dave Bittner: Hello, good to be back.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, thanks for joining me yet again. And we are as we have been all year talking about the ten-year anniversary of the "CyberWire Daily." Again, congratulations, Dave. That is a wonderful milestone.

Dave Bittner: Thank you.

Maria Varmazis: And we've been in these conversations eventually getting to a topic and ringing the bell of oh, we have to talk about AI. It just feels inevitable when we talk about cybersecurity nowadays.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: We're getting that out of the way real early in this conversation today because we're going to be talking about AI and cybersecurity as our topic for today. So --

Dave Bittner: Right, right.

Maria Varmazis: -- ding a ding a ding. Here we are. We're talking about it the entire time today.

Dave Bittner: Yes, it's a funny thing because I feel like in my interviews, you know, as a interviewer you always have go-to questions, right? I refer to it as a bag of tricks. You know, there are things that if you find yourself out of things to ask or for some reason distracted or flummoxed, you can reach into your bag of tricks and buy yourself some time in these days.

Maria Varmazis: You're giving away our secrets to people.

Dave Bittner: Oh, sorry. But these days --

Maria Varmazis: No, no, we're brilliant. We always think on our feet.

Dave Bittner: That's right.

Maria Varmazis: We don't have shortcuts. Yes, it's great.

Dave Bittner: Exactly. Spontaneous. Yes, but these days you can always say, "Well, how does AI affect this?" And off you go, right?

Maria Varmazis: Off you go. Yes, there's always a great answer to that one because inevitably it's doing something. So, when I was preparing for this chat, I think I'm having the same whiplash every human being is having with how much AI as a concept, as a broad umbrella of technology, has quickly progressed in just the past months, if not years. So, trying to go back ten years thinking about this, I'm not sure how much of my own recollection I can honestly trust. Just putting that out there.

Dave Bittner: Yes.

Maria Varmazis: But if -- I'm trusting you a lot more than I'm trusting myself, Dave, if you can go back ten years and remembering, we were talking about AI back then, but it to me seems like it was one day far off or very vague. We're not there yet tech. Maybe your recollection is different. What do you remember?

Dave Bittner: I think you're right. I was -- I think back then it was more the promise of AI versus the reality and much of the AI that was happening was happening under the hood and it wasn't anything that a regular user could really get their hands on. It was just this thing that the folks with technical expertise had included in whatever platform or package you had purchased and it was somehow going to help you do your work more quickly, more efficiently, more securely, all those good things. I want to say it was 2016 or so was the year at the RSA conference was the first year that everything was AI.

Maria Varmazis: Oh.

Dave Bittner: And it was that kind of AI. It wasn't large language models. It wasn't chatbots. It was just everybody. If you were selling a product, you had to say somewhere under the hood, there was AI. And --

Maria Varmazis: That hasn't changed in ten years. Yes.

Dave Bittner: It has -- no, it hasn't changed. But there was a lot of eye rolling back then because I think the notion of what it is and what it could do and like there are still people who get bent out of shape when you say AI versus machine learning and is it this, is it really that or you know, and you have those debates and conversations till the cows come home. But I guess the challenge back then was how much of this is real and how much of it is marketing, particularly when it's all under the hood and you really can't see it yourself?

Maria Varmazis: Were you seeing it in specific contexts at that time? I mean, I know it was sort of being spammed everywhere as the you know, marketing team has been given their directive. You have to include it. But were there certain defense or attack areas that were seeing you know more successful deployment? And if you remember any of this, what was the (inaudible)?

Dave Bittner: Yes, I mean I guess the promise was that these AI systems could recognize attacks that had never been seen before. Right? So, we were coming from the days of indicators of compromise and malware signatures. So, it was really built off of the fact that somebody saw something, documented it, reported it, and your antivirus software would then start scanning for that. And the idea was that these AI systems didn't need that, that they could just look for anomalies or they could even look at behavioral things and that -- what black magic was that? And so, raise alerts that your normal virus searching software would miss.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, I want to say there's also a confluence of you know, we were coming off of sims being a big thing that -- not that new at that time, but there was just -- we were well into that world of sims and the flood of alerts and that just became a huge problem also that I think AI was being promised as a potential solution for, but again, I don't remember as well as I'd like.

Dave Bittner: I think also, like just a fun thing to remember is like it was back in 2011, I believe, that IBM's Watson competed on Jeopardy and won.

Maria Varmazis: What? What?

Alex Trebek: And now the newcomer, developed and programmed especially for this moment, making its first appearance on our national television program, ladies and gentlemen, this is Watson.

Dave Bittner: Pretty sure that was 2011, and Watson you know, kicked Ken Jennings' butt on Jeopardy. Ken Jennings now the host of Jeopardy.

Maria Varmazis: I was going to say I think somebody might -- well, I mean who really won? Yes.

Dave Bittner: Yes, right, exactly. In the end, Ken got the last laugh. But what was so interesting about that, and I think what captured people's imagination was like we've been used to computers being able to play chess.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Which is very deterministic. You know, you could -- most people who know how to play chess can understand how computing power could be thrown at the problem of chess, because of the limited amount of things that chess pieces can do and all those kinds of things.

Maria Varmazis: It's basically an extremely complicated algorithm that the more you study it, you understand certain outcomes. I don't play chess, but this is also my understanding. Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right. And so, you could see that how you could throw computing problem at that and get good results. And so, computers had been competing for chess championships for long periods of time up to this point. You know, there -- you could go to your local radio shack, which still existed, and buy a computer chess set that would play against you. And depending on how good you were, well, if you were at my level, it would beat you every time. Right.

Maria Varmazis: Same. Yes, same.

Dave Bittner: By the way, I should add in preparing for today's episode, I went -- I found a clip of me at the 2016 RSA conference. I was being interviewed by Matt Stephenson, who was working at Cylance at the time. And so, we caught up at the Cylance booth, and we actually discussed this very topic about AI and playing chess. So, here's a clip from that interview.

Matt Stephenson: Any other kind of fringe technologies, maybe you personally, that are grabbing your attention? Obviously, AI and machine learning, big deals as that is maturing in the security market. But is there any kind of outlier that's worth keeping your eye on for the next year or two?

Dave Bittner: Oh boy, that's a good question. I mean, I think a lot of it is -- I think we have this huge problem with workforce issues. So, I will tell you, I heard an interesting interview last week with Garry Kasparov, the famous chess player, and he said that we are at the point where any computer, the best chess playing computers can beat any human. However, if he teams up with a chess playing computer, they can beat any machine. So, I'm really intrigued by that notion of not just the AI, but if you team up AI with a really smart human, how does that change the game? I think that's going to be something looking forward to really pay attention to. Do I sound ten years younger, Maria?

Maria Varmazis: Honestly, I didn't want to say it, but you --

Dave Bittner: Butter me up, flatter me. Tell me what I want to hear.

Maria Varmazis: The optimism and brightness in your voice and kind of how like "Isn't this going to be cool?" you know?

Dave Bittner: Right, right. No, the weight of the world had not yet crushed my spirit.

Maria Varmazis: I know.

Dave Bittner: So.

Maria Varmazis: But also, the tenor of which you speak about AI as a great potential thing as opposed to I think the existential dread most of us can't help --

Dave Bittner: Sure. Yes.

Maria Varmazis: -- but inject now.

Dave Bittner: Yes, the cynicism had not completely set in yet.

Maria Varmazis: No. It's a little wild, but it was also kind of sweet. I --

Dave Bittner: Yes. No --

Maria Varmazis: -- no but, how much things have changed in a decade though? I mean, truly.

Dave Bittner: Yes, and you know, of course, Matt was a great host and Matt passed away recently, so we miss him very much. But getting back to Watson playing Jeopardy, I think the thing that was so remarkable about that was that that was a natural language engine, and that I think was something that most of us hadn't really experienced before. At the time, that took the big compute that IBM's, was it Big Blue or whatever their Watson engine had that was able to do that to be able to just understand spoken word, interpret it and come back with a meaningful answer, that seemed magical at the time. But, now it's part of everyone's everyday thanks to the large language models we have. But it -- back then, it was magical.

Maria Varmazis: In that vein, that kind of capability and extrapolating out to going a bit back to what you talked about you know, signatures for example. On the defensive side, you could see how these kinds of capabilities would make a lot of sense as an you know, something that can help the defenders aggregate you know, things that are trending or you know, all the unbelievable amount of things that the defenders have to just comb through, but eventually I mean the attackers started figuring out how they could use these kinds of tools to their advantage, and not to sound too dramatic, but that's when everything changed. Okay, that was too dramatic. But I mean, eventually we did start seeing attackers using AI to their advantage, and I do feel like that was a bit of a shift. You could feel the cold winds blowing when we started seeing more of that happening. Can you paint a picture for us about what you remember from when these started appearing more and more, I guess, across your desk at the CyberWire?

Dave Bittner: Yes, I mean, there was the rise of adversarial machine learning. And as you say, sort of a way for the bad guys to parry against malware detection, you know, spam filtering, all those kinds of things, to be able to use this technology to morph your code so that it wouldn't trigger recognition from you know, something that was checking for viruses, just what -- things that are considered simple and maybe quaint by today's standards, but back then were pretty advanced things. You know, DARPA had their Cyber Grand Challenge back in 2016, I believe, which was -- they were looking to see how autonomous systems could work with all this for both discovery, exploitation, and patching of software vulnerabilities. So, they were kind of on the early edge of that. And then I guess around 2018, 2019, we saw SOAR platforms became the new hotness, right? Their Security Orchestration Automation and Response, and that was supposed to make life easier for the SOCs.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: And I think in many ways it did, but that was again looking to automate things to get rid of those repetitive security tasks, to take away the drudgery from the people running the SOCs to, you know, the phrase is always to "allow them to focus on more important things." Right?

Maria Varmazis: This is true. Although I do wonder, I mean that kind of work also, not that this is something you control, just that's also a lot of work for junior analysts and it's a shame for that to go away. But I understand it is the volume that we're talking about. It's just human beings can't keep up with it at a certain point.

Dave Bittner: Yes, and I mean it's an interesting point you bring up because one of the things that I've heard from many folks in security leadership is how do we take junior analysts and turn them into senior analysts when they're not doing the work anymore?

Maria Varmazis: Yes. Ten years ago, you were talking about workforce concerns. Here we are ten years later, I don't think those concerns have gotten any better. In fact, they've gotten a lot worse in many ways, but that is a totally different conversation, but --

Dave Bittner: No, it's weird. I mean, you're right. It's weird. I mean, on the one hand, back then there were all these, oh -- there's so much talk about how are we ever going to fill all these empty positions in cybersecurity? How are we going to ever find enough qualified people? And now, we're talking about Microsoft looking for voluntary layoffs or voluntary separations with 25% of their workforce. So, things have changed. I think there's still demand for folks who know a lot, but sort of to what we were just talking about, it -- it's really tough out there for those folks who are looking for entry-level positions.

Maria Varmazis: It is, yes, and you know what? Every conversation we've had this year, AI has been part of that conversation, so I say it's only fair that workforce comes part of the AI conversation. The tables have turned a little bit. It's only fair. Yes, so all right. So, you were in 2018, 2019. And then COVID hit and we were all stuck at home looking at really funny videos coming across our devices that were in some cases AI powered, and they were a bit of a novelty, but there was of course a security implication of these things as well. And I'm remembering Will Smith eating spaghetti as --

Dave Bittner: Right, right, right, and of course --

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: -- we're talking about deepfakes.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes, what deep fake -- I'm -- there have got to be deep fake stories from back then that you remember that made you go "uh-oh." There've got to be.

Dave Bittner: I guess so. I mean, I think a lot of the conversation was about the uncanny valley, and I remember as a huge Star Wars fan, I remember Rogue One coming out, and of course at the end of that film they have the AI-generated version of Carrie Fisher playing Princess Leia, and it was okay. It wasn't great. You know, it was one of those things where you could see, all right, where's this going? How interesting that the -- and clearly this is the future. But what I remember specifically about that is, not long after the movie came out, people were homebrewing versions that were way better.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right?

Maria Varmazis: I was wondering if you were going to mention that because that was my recollection, too. That was my oblique moment was the homebrew versions are way better. I mean, not a surprise. Nerds, we're awesome like that. But at the same time that home capabilities were able to beat Lucasfilm.

Dave Bittner: Yes, exactly.

Maria Varmazis: I mean --

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: -- this just was a sign of this is -- it's going to pop off real fast and boy, did it ever.

Dave Bittner: Right, and how quickly it was changing to go from the probably, you know, the most well-known special effects company in the world, ILM, doing a fine job, but only you know, let's say a year later, people being able to do a better job just at home.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right? And so, again, you sort of recalibrate what your expectations are and what does this mean for the future if we can no longer trust our eyes, what we see, that's a big deal.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, I remember on a personal note around that time just the biometrics and identity verification procedures for so many things having to evolve extremely rapidly to keep up with just how well deepfakes were evolving and how effective they were becoming. And I was seeing that as you know a consumer in my day to day, and I remember thinking and wondering, what is this like for people who are actually, you know, are defending against something like this? This has got to be crazy. This fire hose. And truly around that same time, not that long ago, I mean four, five, six years ago, instead of AI being sort of this magical under the hood, magical, but under the hood thing for people who really knew what they were doing, it became a thing that a lot of us could homebrew and start using at home and then I mean, I think that's really when, I mean, not to use that again cliche phrase, but a lot of things changed when we started being able to play with it ourselves.

Dave Bittner: Right. ChatGPT comes out 2022 or so, '22, '23, around that time. Yes, it was late '22 was when it came out, and suddenly the world had a new toy, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes.

Dave Bittner: And you -- are you -- I'm sure you remember, and I'm sure our listeners are vigorously nodding their heads at the avalanche of articles and podcasts and everything that at the end of it they said, "In fact, this article was written by ChatGPT. Ha ha ha ha."

Maria Varmazis: Got you, humans.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: That em-dash didn't give it away? No.

Dave Bittner: Yes. Yes.

Maria Varmazis: And in a security context, also, it couldn't not -- it couldn't not change things. All the double negatives, triple negatives going on there. Things like intellectual property, you know, code bases, all sorts of stuff leaking out through ChatGPT. People putting things into these public tools that they really shouldn't. But also, how do you use these kinds of things in a secure way at work? And then all of our advice, I'm thinking you know on "Hacking Humans," a lot of our advice for people on how to detect phishing campaigns, for example, almost overnight became ineffective. You know, the old tells gone.

Dave Bittner: Just supercharged it, right? No longer do you look for clunky English that was oddly translated from whatever the mother tongue was, but no, there -- all of a sudden, you can take anything, run it through one of these large language models. Say "Clean up my English, make it flawless," and it was so.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, it's almost quaint now when I get something that has broken English in it. It's like, "Oh, oh, don't you know about AI, my friend?" Yes, but in terms of, you know, the really heavy-duty lifting of you know, the work that defenders are doing every day in their organizations, I mean, people are using AI in their workflows now in all sorts of creative ways, but also, it's -- you can't ignore its capabilities now, too. So, what have you seen in the last few years as you know trends in that direction?

Dave Bittner: Well, I think similar to what we were talking about from back in the early days of 2016 when it was under the hood but still part of everyone's marketing pitch. Here we are again, right? History may not repeat itself, but it sure does rhyme. And are there any cybersecurity companies out there who do not have AI as part of their marketing pitch? You have to. It's required. And I think it's easy to be cynical and poo-poo that. But on the other hand, it may be required. It may -- like to keep up with because the adversaries are using it, so why not? It's part of the toolbox now, and it's expected. I think it's just a matter of what are you using it for? Who's using it? How much does it include the human in the loop? You know, getting back to the clip of where -- from the old clip of me talking about chess, how the human plus the computer was the real chess champion. And I think a lot of folks are settling into that that you want the AI to handle the stuff that requires high speed analysis, but at the end of the day, you still need a human to sign off on it. The analogy I use all the time is that AI is like a tireless intern, which is great, but you're not going to bet the company on the output of an intern.

Maria Varmazis: And on the attacker side, to me, AI has been like pouring gasoline on a fire in terms of just what -- the volume that attackers have been able to you know, pump out what they do essentially, and the effectiveness and the way that they can iterate and the speed at which they can iterate. And we haven't even touched on things like prompt injection attacks. That's like a whole other world. But in terms of you know, what defenders are seeing coming across their worlds from the attacker side, AI has been an incredible tool in the arsenal for attackers and it also has, I mean to me, I don't know about you, but I'm sure in the conversations you've had, it has significantly lowered the bar for how technically sophisticated an attacker needs to be. You know, you don't even have to be a script kitty.

Dave Bittner: No.

Maria Varmazis: And that's alarming.

Dave Bittner: No, and to anyone who's experienced the joy and delight of vibe coding, you know, which I personally held off on for a long time because I just -- I don't know, it didn't -- didn't really see how it applied to me. It's not really part of what I do, but a friend of mine, I was asking a friend of mine who knows a lot about developing websites. I said, "I want to make some updates, but I feel like I'm you know, out of my realm here," and he said, "Well, just vibe code it." And I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "Just tell -- ask one of the language models what you need to do, and it'll do it for you." And sure enough, I tried and it did.

Maria Varmazis: Yes. Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right? My point being that, as you say, the bar is on the floor now for being able to create technically sophisticated things quickly, without having that technical expertise. And I think that's another big part of the story here is how much AI is a velocity engine, how it allows you to iterate quickly and just hammer away at things, set the system out on a task, and all the AI engines want to do is please you. And as we've seen story after story, they will do whatever it takes to please you, even if that means escaping their sandboxes.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, and we've -- that's been really the story of the last year, is exactly what you just said, and that has felt extraordinarily consequential, I'm sure, for everybody listening. And not that you have a crystal ball, Dave, but you know, given again the conversations you've had over the years and the trends that you've been following, where could you imagine this going?

Dave Bittner: Boy, that is the big -- that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? But it -- to be fair, it's a question I get to ask people all the time, as do you.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: And it's been very interesting to me to hear the question -- the reactions that people have, the responses that people have to that question. I was asking someone recently, I was at a conference and had the opportunity to speak off the record with someone who was a very, very high -- high level person when it comes to all of these things. This is someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity and has been at leadership positions at the highest levels. And I said, "What do you think? What's the future hold?" And this person said, "I think like sort of like California wildfires, it has to burn down before it can be rebuilt." In other words, there's so much deadwood, there's so much brush, inflammable material at the ground level, and by that I think they meant just pre-existing bugs and vulnerabilities, all of these things that we're seeing being discovered at machine speed, and that all has to be cleared out before we can build the next thing. So, I think it's a interesting possibility that the next few years are going to be those wildfires making their way through the ecosystem, burning out all the dead wood, but then after that there won't be as many fires because all that kindling, all that tinder is gone. And then hopefully, it'll put the defenders in the better position of being able to spend their time on new novel things rather than having to clean up all the messes that were left behind.

Maria Varmazis: That is an oddly optimistic and I mean that it's a really optimistic take actually. It -- more optimistic than I would have guessed.

Dave Bittner: I'm hopeful. I'm buoyed by how many people I've talked to, people who I respect who believe that ultimately the defenders are going to have the advantage. It may take us a while to get there, but it seems like there are plenty of people who think that that's how it's going to play out. And here's hoping, my friend, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yes, yes. I mean, this is one of those things like I trust people with much greater technical expertise than I certainly have. If you had asked me to guess how people would feel, it would not have been that. Which -- so that does -- that honestly gives me a lot of hope as well. Dave, in your capacity as host of the "CyberWire Daily," doing a daily cybersecurity news show, talking to so many people and just watching these trends, especially with AI, when did it crystallize for you that AI was going to be basically a required component of any major cybersecurity news story? Was there an incident or a year, a date, anything like that where you went, "Yes, this is real, this is permanent."

Dave Bittner: I think it was the release of the large language models when those became publicly available, I'd say the year after that, when anybody who was paying attention could project out where this was going, right? Because the models were only going to get better and they have. The GPUs have only gotten fast -- or were only going to get faster and they have. People learning how to apply these things effectively gotten better, right? These tools have gotten more powerful. If you just look at the answers that you get back from these systems compared to what we did four years ago, they're so much more capable than they were. And the -- again, the folks I talk to who are working on the cutting-edge versions are saying, "You ain't seen nothing yet," right? Like they're -- it's just -- we've got a long way to run out. Like Moore's law isn't going to run out for AI for a little while. Like don't -- we don't seem to be up against that wall. Obviously, there are concerns about the toll that may play on our economy, our -- the environment, you know, all of those things which I think are legitimate concerns of -- as a civilization balancing out our needs and the advantages versus the resources that they demand. So, that's a whole other conversation for another day, but they're here to stay. I do believe that the release of the large language models was an inflection point in history. There was before and there is after, and now we're in the aftertimes. And so, we'll see how it plays out. I try to stay optimistic. I try not to get overly cynical about it. Some days it's easier than others. Some days it's harder than others. I think we're all fighting that fight and particularly folks who have an inside view of this, it's hard to know what ground truth is sometimes from day to day. It's hard to know what to believe, who to believe, and so hopefully, you know, something that we're really focused on is trying to provide that ground truth and you know, pre-filter things so that our listeners don't have to. But hasn't gotten any easier. I'll tell you that.

Maria Varmazis: Well, Dave, it's been an honor and a joy speaking with you, as always, and I want to make sure that if there's anything you want to leave the audience with before we conclude, that we -- I give you that chance.

Dave Bittner: So, just for fun --

Maria Varmazis: Okay.

Dave Bittner: -- if you have not done so, and I suspect a lot of people out there who are younger than me, and that would include you, Maria, go online. There are a million different versions of this online and search for Eliza. Maria, have you ever played with Eliza?

Maria Varmazis: As in like Eliza Doolittle, Eliza?

Dave Bittner: Just it it's -- yes. So, one of the first widely available AI toys was called Eliza, and --

Maria Varmazis: Oh.

Dave Bittner: -- it was written in BASIC back in the late 60s, and it's a therapist basically.

Maria Varmazis: Oh, my goodness.

Dave Bittner: And it's very clever, but I first came across it in the 70s, I think. It was running on like on a TRS-80 or an Apple II, but it's interesting to look back at something like Eliza, which is from a different time, but how Eliza can capture your imagination, how Eliza can make you feel like you're interacting with someone and not something. You know, I know Eliza doesn't pass the Turing test, but it's a really early indicator of how these sorts of things have the capability to delight and capture our imagination. So, if you're not familiar with Eliza, it's everywhere. Just go search for Eliza. I'm sure there's one -- run in your browser, and just poke around at it, see what it can and can't do, and remember that this was created probably before most of you were born.

Maria Varmazis: Oh, that is super fun. Well, I know what I'll be doing this afternoon.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: So, thank you, Dave. Appreciate it. And as always, Dave, thank you so much for taking the time to speak with me and share your insights with me and all of our listeners. And again, congratulations on a wonderful ten years and to many more.

Dave Bittner: Yes, thank you. This was great fun. Talk to you soon.

Maria Varmazis: Thank you for joining me for this special edition. See you next time.

articles.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
articles.context: The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a...
articles.full_text: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post. The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

articles.title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
articles.context: The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania
articles.full_text:
There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

“Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.”

Sophisticated tradecraft

ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk.

The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part.

Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained.

“This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote.

They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual.

The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said.

The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla.

Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected

Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode.

“ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic.

“Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said.

This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted.

Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory.

Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said.

A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy.

Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said.

His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process.

But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described.

“A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.”

‘A level above’

And, said David Shipley, CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.”

Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow.

However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability.

“They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.”

Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.

articles.title: One Identity Unveils Active Roles 8.6 with Enhanced Security and Administration
articles.context: 6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8
articles.full_text:
Active Roles 8.6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades

One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8.6, strengthening secure and streamlined Active Directory administration with cumulative platform improvements, expanded API capabilities and greater authentication flexibility.

Active Roles 8.6, updated July 27, 2026, focuses on security and cumulative platform improvements. It fixes an RSTS configuration security issue and supersedes versions 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Compared with Active Roles 8.2.1 SP6, One Identity says 8.6 incorporates the features, enhancements and resolved issues delivered across that intervening release line. See the Active Roles 8.6 Release Notes.

The recent improvements are therefore best described as an administrator and integration experience upgrade, rather than a new visual redesign. The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication.

Active Roles 8.6: Familiar Administration Meets Greater Flexibility and Consolidation

Those upgrades complement one of Active Roles’ most recognizable usability strengths: a flexible, configurable UI that can be tailored to individual users and personas. Its thick-client interface is designed to resemble the familiar Microsoft Active Directory experience, helping reduce the learning curve for experienced AD administrators.

The broader experience centers on consolidation, with a single console spanning Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 helping administrators avoid constantly switching between separate management environments. Together with PowerShell and VBScript support, the product keeps familiar tools and interaction patterns at the center of the administrator experience.

This combination of configurable views, familiar administration and centralized control supports Active Roles’ position among top Active Directory management solutions.

#1 Peerspot Position Strengthens the Ease-of-Administration Story

PeerSpot currently ranks Active Roles by One Identity #1 in Active Directory Management, with an 8.5/10 rating based on 92 reviews. It also reports the largest category mindshare at 11.7%, up from 10.4% year over year, and identifies Active Roles as the category’s most popular solution by searches. [peerspot.com]

The PeerSpot assessment highlights automated user provisioning, lifecycle management, role-based access control, password resets and streamlined account management among capabilities that reduce manual effort.

Feature in focus: Administrator experience with Active Roles 8.6

Active Roles 8.6 is an administrator-experience evolution, combining cumulative security, API and authentication improvements with the product’s established configurable UI, familiar Microsoft-style experience and consolidated hybrid administration.

About One Identity

One Identity delivers trusted identity security for enterprises worldwide to protect and simplify access to digital identities. With flexible deployment options and subscription terms – from self-managed to fully managed – our solutions integrate seamlessly into your identity fabric to strengthen your identity perimeter, protect against breaches, and ensure governance and compliance. Trusted by more than 11,000 organizations managing over 500 million identities, One Identity is a leader in identity governance and administration (IGA), privileged access management (PAM), and access management (AM) for security without compromise. One Identity is recognized as one of the best cybersecurity companies for agentic AI security and NHI management solutions.

Users can learn more at www.oneidentity.com.

articles.title: Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
articles.context: ” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported...
articles.full_text:
Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.”

Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current.

Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization.

Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.”

It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said.

Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings.

It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.”

The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported resources in the runbook to identify compromised areas and inform recovery decisions before returning services to production.”

Commvault did not provide a spokesperson to offer further details before publication.

Depends on IT awareness of the environment

A number of factors will influence the effectiveness of the solution, analysts said.

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out, “nothing in Commvault’s announcement describes a generative model making recovery decisions. This is runbook automation. A runbook is a recipe: do this, then this, then this. It does not hallucinate. It does exactly what it is told.”

“That is the real risk. A flawed runbook gets executed flawlessly, at machine speed,” he said. “Automation does not make a bad plan good. It makes a bad plan fast.”

That means, said Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, whether Recovery Studio ultimately helps or hurts enterprise restoration efforts depends on how aware IT is of everything going on in its global footprint.

“How much it solves depends on something no vendor controls, which is the accuracy of the dependency map underneath it. A runbook is a prediction about your environment and every change since it was last tested makes it a little more wrong: a new application, a rotated certificate, a firewall rule added on a Friday,” Mahapatra said.

“Most enterprise dependency maps are aspirational,” he noted, “and CMDBs in particular tend to describe the environment someone intended to build. Commvault’s figure of 28 days to reach minimal operations is plausible, but the gains will go to organizations that refresh and rehearse their runbooks continuously. For everyone else, automation will execute an outdated plan faster.”

Abbas Jaffery, principal advisory director at Infotech, agreed.

“My concern is that automation can execute the wrong recovery sequence just as efficiently as the right one. Enterprise environments change constantly,” Jaffery said. “Applications are upgraded, infrastructure moves, identities change and integrations are added or removed. If the dependency information behind a recovery workflow is outdated, automation could restore systems successfully but leave the business service broken.”

Defined recovery

Mike Leone, a VP and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, added that Commvault is still advancing the space.

Recovery Studio “follows defined recovery runbooks rather than a model inventing steps on the fly. That’s much more deterministic and structured,” Leone said. “Sure, automation can repeat a mistake faster than a person can, and a runbook that’s gone stale is a fair concern. But Commvault is validating each piece as it rebuilds and scanning for threats before anything goes back into production. Those are the kind of safeguards and checks everyone should want. The alternative is people rebuilding systems by hand in the middle of an outage, and that isn’t exactly mistake-free either.”

But Dickson stressed that automation is not necessarily the perfect fix.

“Commvault says the runbooks validate components and can scan supported resources for threats before services return to production. Good,” he said. “But the honest comparison is not automation versus perfection. It is automation versus exhausted people working from a spreadsheet at 3 a.m. Humans get the order wrong, too.”

Johnny Yu, an IDC research manager, is not as impressed by the components of the solution as he is by the way Recovery Studio organizes them.

“I do see Commvault Recovery Studio as significant, but not from a capability standpoint,” Yu said, adding that all of the product’s components, including recovery runbooks, threat scans, and recovery testing, are already offered by Commvault, as well as by various competitors. “I think the significance comes from how Recovery Studio organizes different recovery workflows for different applications onto a single platform or hub, kind of like a library of validated recovery runbooks to be used for all kinds of scenarios.”

He explained that he liked how Studio standardizes recovery runbooks to follow a similar workflow to that of manually rebuilding the environment, recovering the components, such as data, applications and agents, and “validating the recovery before bringing it back into production, but allows recovery nuance for each runbook, such as if you want to do in-place vs secondary-site recovery or whether threat scanning is necessary, such as DR scenario vs cyber recovery scenario.”

Jaffery noted, however, that while the promised Commvault cybersecurity controls are attractive, they may also be insufficient.

“Following a cyberattack, organizations need to be confident they aren’t restoring compromised identities, configurations or malicious persistence mechanisms,” Jaffery said. “I would not advocate fully autonomous recovery for every scenario. There needs to be appropriate human authorization for high-impact actions, particularly those involving identity, security controls and reconnecting systems to production. And organizations need to test the entire recovery process, not just whether the backup can be restored.”

An AI agent recovery plan

Commvault on Tuesday also introduced AgentRecover capabilities to help track and control autonomous agents. It would specifically “help organizations audit agent activity, restore agents, and recover the data and systems they affected across environments.”

Mahapatra noted that AgentRecover addresses a potentially more difficult problem than system restorations.

“Restoring an agent’s configuration is straightforward. Unwinding what it did is not, because an agent’s actions land as side effects in other systems, and some of them, such as an email sent or a payment initiated, cannot be restored at all,” Mahapatra said.

“Traditional recovery rolls back to a point in time,” he explained. “Rolling an environment back to 9 a.m. erases everyone’s legitimate work since 9 a.m., while rolling back only what the agent changed requires knowing causality: which agent, acting under which identity, changed which record. Commvault’s mapping of agent activity and the identities agents act through points in the right direction.”

Jaffery added that rollbacks of an autonomous agent can be especially daunting.

“Restoring the agent itself doesn’t necessarily undo what it has done. An agent might modify customer records, change permissions, invoke APIs or trigger downstream transactions,” he said. “You need to understand what actions it performed and what the consequences were before deciding what to reverse or restore.”

Leone also noted that agents can complicate system restoration, partially because of their speed.

“Agents don’t wait for anyone to confirm things are safe. The moment a system comes back, agents start hitting it, far faster than any person would,” he said. “If an agent comes back before the data and identities it relies on are verified, it starts acting on stale or incomplete information at machine speed. Get the order wrong and one outage quickly turns into a second one.”

Jaffery also observed that Commvault is far from alone in the automated restoration space, and may even be a tad late.

“I don’t think Commvault has an uncontested position here. Rubrik, Cohesity and Veeam have all been investing in cyber recovery, application recovery and orchestration,” he said. “Rubrik, in particular, has been pushing toward automated business application recovery and dependency mapping. Cohesity has capabilities around cyber recovery orchestration and cloud application reconstruction, while Veeam has an established disaster recovery orchestration offering.”

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

articles.title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product Security
articles.context: The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and...
articles.full_text:
Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates

Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains.

The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it.

In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability.

Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see.

“Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund. “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking. “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.”

Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. articles.title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
articles.context: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday...
articles.full_text:
A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases.

Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing.

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed.

Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password.

Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang, senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.”

Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network.

Microsoft patches

Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical.

Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119958) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk.

The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-118207) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-112967) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system.

The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119990), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft.

Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks.

Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.”

CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.”

Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said.

SAP patches

The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126. Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested.

To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said.

The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data.

Other patches

Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google.

Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9.

Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350, which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later.

Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907, a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Wednesday, November 11th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10174, (Wed, Nov 11th)
articles.context: Of course I have to start with the one vulnerability that's already being exploited. Nothing too serious and Microsoft also does not rate this vulnerability critical.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Wednesday November 11th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington DC. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu, Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Leadership. And of course today Microsoft Patch Tuesday is at the top of the news and the AI induced patch surge continues with Microsoft. Microsoft is addressing 1260 different vulnerabilities this month. 68 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical. Now out of these vulnerabilities there are 167 vulnerabilities that are actually Chromium vulnerabilities. And yes they affect Microsoft Edge. That's why Microsoft is including them in their patch lists. But not really sort of a Microsoft product per se. And we haven't always included them. Depends a little bit on how Microsoft is representing them in their vulnerability feed. But still a lot of vulnerabilities sort of in line with what we had the last couple months from Microsoft. Now I picked a couple vulnerabilities here that I considered somewhat more significant. Of course I have to start with the one vulnerability that's already being exploited. That's an Outlook spoofing vulnerability. And apparently Outlook will not really tell you the risk of a particular file when you're opening it. So probably one of those Mark of the Web style vulnerabilities that is being exploited here. Nothing too serious and Microsoft also does not rate this vulnerability critical. And definitely something that you want to take care of. Now as far as the critical vulnerabilities are concerned. There are sort of three groups really that I'm paying a little bit more attention to. One is remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft LDAP. LDAP of course they're used throughout the sort of Active Directory ecosystem. So there's certainly some at least internal exposure here. And something that you have to watch out for. Yes and please don't expose it to the internet. And then we have a number of different vulnerabilities. I listed five in the diary. These are all critical vulnerabilities that relate to Microsoft Queuing, Queue Manager. This sort of a group of issues that keeps coming up around Queue Manager. Definitely something I haven't seen a lot of exploit out there yet. But haven't really been looking that much at it either. Definitely something that tends to be exposed at least internally. Something that you must pay attention to. And then we do have sort of interestingly Windows TCP/IP remote code execution vulnerability. Has a fairly low CVSS score, 7.5. But Microsoft still rates it critical. Will be interesting to see a little bit more detail about this particular vulnerability. Given all the issues we had sort of in the Linux world. With like the Multipath TCP option issue and such. So maybe there's something related going on in Windows as well. Other than that, yes lots and lots of vulnerabilities. So too much to really talk about them all in detail. But again only one that's already being exploited. And otherwise, yes just a lot of them. Nothing really that sort of in my opinion sticks out that much. Just apply those patches before the next month's release comes out. But then we also got patches from Apple. iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS are being addressed in these patches. Only nine different vulnerabilities. We're not yet seeing sort of that AI surge from Apple as we're seeing from Microsoft. There's of course always a possibility of some silent patching happening here. But yeah, a fairly small patch set. What Apple however is doing that we are seeing more sort of of these incremental updates. So that may be hiding a little bit the total number of patches. But last time I checked really it didn't go up like by orders of magnitude. It's like what we're seeing with Microsoft. Now for iPadOS we are getting patches back to 18. Same for macOS. watchOS we only get sort of one version back. And visionOS just for the current version. Now as far as the older versions go. One of the vulnerabilities actually only affects the older version of iOS. And this is a vulnerability when an attacker may be able to pair your device with an AirPlay receiver. The attacker must have physical access to the device. But this works even if the device is locked. Interesting there are a couple of vulnerabilities that affect Bluetooth. That's sort of the majority here of the vulnerabilities. And the idea behind these vulnerabilities is that these vulnerabilities weaken the handshake procedure with Bluetooth. So essentially someone would be able to pair a device with your phone or your Mac. There's also some rate limiting issues for example here with AirPlay. That also you know could make it easier to kind of brute force connection with your device. And then we also have a vulnerability that sort of leaks sensitive data. And probably some of the more interesting vulnerability from this set is a vulnerability in iMessage. Where someone may be able to actually join an iMessage group. And then receive its messages without you actually sort of inviting them or adding them to an iMessage group. Not sure if they would still show up as a member in that group. Anyway, apply the patches. Nothing sort of outrageously dangerous here or critical. Nothing exploited at least as far as Apple states it in their advisory. Well we also have a patch day from SAP. Now SAP typically does have a patch day in sync with Microsoft. I often don't cover them because not too many people are using SAP. But if you're using SAP and SAP NetWeaver which is one of the affected products here. Well you certainly care about these vulnerabilities. And earlier this week I wrote about it. So figured I'll at least mention the patch Tuesday for SAP. There are four vulnerabilities that have a perfect 10 as their CVSS score. And then an additional three with a 9.9. And two more in the nines. And so certainly something to pay attention to. There is one vulnerability that's broken access control in SAP Gateway. Onapsis, a company that does research in ERP security, has reported this vulnerability and published a blog post about it. They're luckily not going into too much detail. So it's not sort of a blueprint for exploitation of the vulnerability. But it gives a couple of hints. Like for example the proxy's access control list. Here is apparently sort of one of the culprits in enabling this vulnerability. So that one actually sounds like it's once the details are out. Not that terribly difficult to exploit. We also have memory corruption vulnerabilities. Again Onapsis has details about at least one of these vulnerabilities. It affects WebSockets. This one is likely a little bit more difficult to exploit. Onapsis is only talking about sort of how they exploit it for denial of service. But yes, remote code execution is possible via that vulnerability. Just of course as many of these memory corruption vulnerabilities may not be that easy sort of to exploit reliably. So definitely get your SAP products updated. And as all of these complex systems of course, take also look at which components you are actually running in your environment. Well, that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing to this podcast. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.
