articles.title: Introducing JFrog Threat Hub: Turning Vulnerability Intelligence into Blast Radius Analysis
articles.context: A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment
articles.full_text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

articles.title: Cloud Vulnerabilities Surge Fourfold in Less Than a Year
articles.context: ” Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds
articles.full_text:
The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

articles.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
articles.context: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar
articles.full_text: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

articles.title: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting
articles.context: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available
articles.full_text:
On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available.

Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update.

Technical details

Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.

Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.

XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do.

articles.title: Before you buy an advent calendar, check these warning signs
articles.context: Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller
articles.full_text:

In this article

Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent

Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order

AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information

Learn how to check an online seller before you buy

Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page.

We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them.

Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand

Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.”

None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day.

Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35.

The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself

The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone.

These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it.

The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings.

The stores are copies of one another

Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools.

The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.”

The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number.

The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t

Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon.

A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores.

How to spot a questionable store before you pay

In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.”Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs.

Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal.

Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there.

Don’t arrive through a link. These stores sell largely through social video. Search the brand name separately and look for history, press, or customers outside its own website.

Treat partnership claims as claims. A video saying a brand is stocked by a retailer isn’t evidence that it is. Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller.

Look for a real business. A postal address, company registration and working phone number are easy for a legitimate seller to provide and were absent from these.

Reverse-image search the photos. Generated images usually have no history anywhere else online. A complete absence of results is itself informative.

Read the small print against itself. If a calendar’s warranty talks about inflatable costumes, the page wasn’t written for the product you’re buying.

Check the spelling, including on the box. We found a misspelled artist name in a product title, a mangled savings line, and a calendar with the word spelled “calindar” on the packaging artwork itself. A real manufacturer proofreads its own box.

Pay with a method that offers buyer protection. A credit card or payment service with buyer protection gives you a route to a refund. Bank transfers can be harder to reverse.

Tools that help

Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam sites, which can help when a link appears in your feed before you’ve had a chance to look up the seller.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard lets you check a suspicious link, message, or screenshot when something feels off but you can’t say why.

If a purchase leads to follow-up texts or calls about delivery fees, customs charges, or a refund, Malwarebytes Scam Number Check can tell you whether the number has been reported. A follow-up message can turn a bad purchase into something worse.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.

articles.title: Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack
articles.context: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware...
articles.full_text: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD. Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests. Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message. "You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one." By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted. "We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation." Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally. Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday. BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site. "Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess." Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen. BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database. BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®

articles.title: Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
articles.context: Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory.

The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling.

“The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post. Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely.

The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system.

Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers.

Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote.

Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees

Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify.

Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. Microsoft said these APIs must meet a strict soundness requirement: “no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.”

Microsoft grouped the findings into three categories: unsafe code that assumes operations will not panic, code that trusts user-provided implementations to behave correctly, and code that makes incorrect assumptions about the underlying system.

The first involved a panic-safety problem in Rust’s MapWindows::clone implementation. The function created a buffer before fully initializing its contents and then called a user-provided clone operation to populate it. If that operation triggered a panic, Rust’s unwinding mechanism could invoke the buffer’s destructor, which would attempt to access uninitialized memory. Microsoft said the reported fix prevents the partially initialized buffer from being destroyed before initialization is complete.

Another finding involved str::replace. The researchers found that the function could make an incorrect assumption about a custom implementation of the nightly Pattern trait. A custom implementation could supply a non-ASCII byte where the code expected an ASCII character, causing the replacement operation to produce invalid UTF-8 data. Subsequent string operations could then trigger undefined behavior, Microsoft said.

System-level bugs affect stable Rust

Microsoft said the first two categories of weaknesses were already being studied in 2021 through Rudra, a static analyzer developed by members of the research team. The standard library had also addressed panic-safety problems as far back as 2015, but similar weaknesses continue to appear in its implementations.

The third category involves interactions between Rust and underlying operating systems and C libraries. Besides the process::exit issue, researchers identified a problem in Rust’s CommandExt::exec functionality involving the process-wide environment variable array.

Microsoft found that the function could modify this shared state while holding a read lock, potentially allowing other threads to access inconsistent data. Under certain conditions, concurrent operations could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory.

Microsoft said both the process::exit and CommandExt::exec findings affect stable Rust. A proposed fix for the environment-variable issue, which avoids modifying the shared array by calling execve directly, was under review when the blog was published.

Two issues reported by Microsoft’s team remained open at publication. The blog also discussed related reports from other researchers and fixes still under review.

Findings feed into Microsoft’s security products

Microsoft said the research findings can also feed into Microsoft Perception, its multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work across broader security workflows. It would therefore help the company improve the development of MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender.

For example, Microsoft’s Web App Pen Test Agent can use MDASH findings to prioritize testing, assess exploitability against live applications, and provide information to support remediation, the researchers wrote.

“Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs,” the researchers wrote, but to identify meaningful issues and improve the safety of foundational software developers and organizations depend on. The Rust project had not responded to a request for comment from CSO at the time of writing.

articles.title: Your Artifact Repositories Need a Firewall
articles.context: Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise
articles.full_text:
Most organizations spend a lot of time looking for vulnerabilities in the software they build. But what about the malicious packages that enter before development even begins?

Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise. Malicious packages can run code during installation, when a developer or build system may already have access to source code, tokens, cloud accounts, or publishing credentials.

CI pipelines and AI agents add to the volume of package requests. They can resolve and install dependencies automatically, often without a human reviewing each request. That makes the point where packages enter the development workflow an important place to evaluate risk.

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests against threat intelligence and policy before components reach developers, agents, or builds. The protection depends on the quality of that intelligence and where the firewall can evaluate a request.

Recent Attacks Show How Much Can Hide in a Package

In October 2026, a hijacked release of the TensorLake TypeScript SDK used an install hook to search for credentials and accept remote commands.

Sonatype's analysis found code that could modify repositories accessible to the compromised account and could expose collected data through a GitHub fallback. The investigation did not confirm that data was published, repositories were modified, or downstream systems were affected.

Other campaigns used different routes into the same workflows:

Hijacked packages and new malicious packages: Six npm packages delivered the same malware. Three appeared to be hijacked legitimate packages, and three were published with the malicious payload already included. The malware used Ethereum transactions to find infrastructure hosting additional payloads.

Large-scale package flooding: Sonatype identified nearly 850 components in the Flooding Dropper campaign. The packages downloaded and launched additional payloads on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Credential theft and propagation: The Mini Shai-Hulud wave affected more than 2,200 component versions. Malicious releases of legitimate packages used install hooks to steal credentials and, where publishing access was available, compromise more packages.

Install-time execution: Miasma waves abused binding.gyp and node-gyp to execute during installation, rather than relying only on familiar lifecycle scripts. The Leo Platform compromise report tracked 23 malicious package versions.

These incidents show why package risk is not limited to suspicious names or newly created projects. Malicious code can arrive in a familiar package, run as part of installation, and act with the access available to the developer, build, or agent that requested it.

What a Repository or Package Firewall Does

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests as they pass from a development environment toward package sources. It evaluates a requested component against security intelligence and, depending on the product's capabilities and configuration, can block or quarantine components that appear malicious or violate policy.

Once a package has been installed, teams may need to investigate the affected machine, identify exposed credentials, check for persistence, and determine whether the package reached other systems. Blocking a known malicious package at the point of entry can help prevent that cleanup from starting in the first place.

A firewall is one layer of software supply chain protection. It does not replace endpoint security, code review, or other controls. It addresses a specific risk: malicious or policy-violating components entering through package requests. And like any control, its coverage depends on which developers, pipelines, agents, and package sources route through it.

What to Look for in a Package Firewall

A repository or package firewall should do more than sit between a repository and a registry. As you evaluate options, consider whether or not it can:

Block malicious components before download, at the point where a package is requested.

Use current, in-depth threat intelligence that can help identify more than known vulnerabilities or suspicious package names.

Protect requests from developers, CI pipelines, and AI agents that can access public package sources.

Fit your repository tools and package sources without requiring a change to established workflows.

Cover the package ecosystems your teams use, and make clear which registries, mirrors, and private sources are included.

Strong firewall protection helps teams stay ahead of threats by identifying and blocking malicious components before they enter the development process. By evaluating package requests at the point of intake, it can reduce the risk of compromised builds and the investigation and rework that follow, while helping teams keep development moving.

How Sonatype's Intelligence Informs Firewall Decisions

A firewall's decision is only as useful as the evidence behind it. Sonatype Firewall combines machine-learning signals with AI-powered analysis, alongside the expertise of Sonatype's security research team, to identify suspicious packages and investigate if they contain malicious code.

By analyzing release behavior, examining package contents, and correlating findings across multiple sources, Sonatype can detect threats earlier, uncover additional affected packages, and turn new discoveries into actionable intelligence that informs Firewall's blocking and quarantine decisions.

That work can involve several kinds of analysis:

Activity and release patterns can help surface packages that behave differently from their project's history or from typical ecosystem activity.

Behavioral analysis can flag unusual signals around a package or release. Researchers can investigate those findings to confirm whether a component is malicious.

Payload analysis examines what the code actually does, including behavior such as credential theft, code injection, or downloading another payload.

Secondary expansion follows the code beyond the original package. Advanced Binary Fingerprinting can help identify embedded or renamed code that may not appear in a package's declared dependencies. In one investigation, Sonatype researchers found code associated with the flatmap-stream incident in 12 additional npm components.

Together, these methods provide context that a package name or manifest alone cannot. That context helps a firewall make a more informed decision about whether to allow, block, or hold a request for review.

Give Every Package Request a Safer Path

Every dependency starts with a request. A developer adds a package, a pipeline pulls it into a build, or an AI agent selects it for generated code. That request is an opportunity to assess a component before it becomes part of your software.

Sonatype Firewall helps teams bring security and development together at the moment open source enters the software supply chain. Backed by Sonatype's research and designed to work with supported repository environments, it helps organizations block malicious components earlier before they reach developers or workflows. That gives teams a chance to stop known threats at the point of entry, reduce avoidable disruption, and keep development moving with greater confidence.

Even if your existing repositories support secure component selection, malicious packages can still make their way into development. The difference comes down to how threats are identified, how quickly new malicious activity is detected, and whether that intelligence can stop a package before it's downloaded. Sonatype Firewall is that difference. Since it's designed to work with a wide range of repository managers, you can add an additional layer of protection to block known risks and avoid downstream work.

See how Sonatype Firewall can help protect your repositories from malicious packages.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
articles.context: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that...
articles.full_text: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register. Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI." As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years. AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens." "The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited. "So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out." Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general. "We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

articles.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability

CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data
articles.context: It’s the reason we have detections in the first place
articles.full_text:
At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

After the alert

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Data vs. data

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:

Are full transaction details provided or just a summary?

Is packet content or file extraction available?

How far back can we search, and how fast?

Can I follow a connection across hosts and time?

AI <3 data

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

Unfamiliar territory is the test

When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

Look at the transactions behind the alert

Ask what packet content or extracted files are available

Follow the activity backwards and forwards in time

Ask a question that wasn’t anticipated

These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions.
