articles.title: New Supply Chain Attack Compromises Tens of Thousands of GitHub Repositories
articles.context: Security researchers at Socket have uncovered a new software supply chain attack that has affected tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, including organization-owned ones
articles.full_text:
Security researchers at Socket have uncovered a new software supply chain attack that has affected tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, including organization-owned ones.

Uber is mentioned as one of the businesses that runs compromised packages. The kill chain is reminiscent of GhostAction, a malicious campaign discovered by GitGuardian in September 2025 and reappeared in October 2026.

Malicious Workflow Spread Via Two GitHub Accounts

On October 8, 2026, two GitHub accounts, ‘henrywoo’ and ‘kitao,’ pushed a malicious GitHub Actions workflow to hundreds of repositories they had permission to modify.

A GitHub Action is an automated task that runs in a GitHub repository to handle activities such as testing code, building software or deploying applications whenever specific events occur.

The workflow, named “.github/workflows/security-audit.yml,” was added through a single-file commit designed to look routine, “Add security audit workflow” and “Update security audit workflow.”

Despite its name, the workflow does not perform any security checks. Instead, it steals credentials from affected repositories and sends them to an external server at 193.32.204[.]199 over HTTP.

Because the workflow looks like a legitimate security tool, it can go unnoticed while running as part of the repository's automated processes.

According to Socket researchers, the malicious file was found in tens of thousands of repositories, which include ones where ‘henrywoo’ or ‘kitao’ have write access.

Infection vectors include the following repositories:

henrywoo/pyllama and henrywoo/chatllama, AI GitHub projects created by ‘henrywoo’

kitao/pixel, typically distributed through both Python Pacjkage Index (PyPI) and crates.io, online repositories where developers publish and distribute software packages written in Python and Rust, respectively

uber/athenadriver, an Uber-owned project where ‘henrywoo’ has write access as its original author

Even repositories that had been inactive for a decade were affected, suggesting the attackers systematically enumerated every repository they could access instead of choosing targets based on their activity or value.

The activity appears automated rather than manually targeted.

Expanding GhostAction’s Secret Theft Capabilities

While the incident is a new variation of the GhostAction campaign, Socket researchers noted that this latest version expands what the attackers can steal.

Earlier GhostAction attacks primarily targeted secrets stored in GitHub Actions, such as API keys and access tokens configured for automated workflows.

The new variant also searches the repository's files and complete Git history for credentials using regular-expression patterns. This means it can find sensitive information that developers accidentally committed to source code, configuration files or earlier versions of files, even if those credentials have since been deleted from the latest version of the repository.

The additional search targets credentials for cloud providers and AI services, potentially exposing access to infrastructure, hosted applications and third-party services.

Malicious Workflow Still Active in GitHub Repositories

As of October 9, 2026, Socket reported that the malicious workflow was still present on the default branches of the repositories it examined, including uber/athenadriver and kitao/pyxel.

The workflow had also successfully executed in affected repositories, meaning the credential-stealing activity was not limited to an attempted injection.

However, the researchers had not observed any malicious package versions published to PyPI or crates.io as a result of the campaign at the time the Socket report was published.

This does not mean the stolen credentials have not been used for other purposes, only that Socket had not identified evidence of follow-on malicious package releases on those two registries.

Image credits: Poetra.RH / PJ McDonnell / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed
articles.context: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the...
articles.full_text: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register, the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement, Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed. Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications. "The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email. While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions. Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

articles.title: Email Addresses of 2.2 Million Sega Customers Leaked in Vendor Breach
articles.context: Sega has revealed that around 2
articles.full_text:
Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

Image credit: Bangla press / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
articles.context: In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day
articles.full_text: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required. Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

articles.title: 13.3 million people’s medical data exposed; companies pay $300,000
articles.context: The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment
articles.full_text:
The New York attorney general (AG) has reached a settlement over a medical data breach that affected 13.3 million people after basic security failures.

Perry Johnson & Associates (PJ&A) and four related companies have agreed to pay $300,000 and implement extensive security reforms following a breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 13.3 million people. They face another $9.7 million in penalties if they fail to meet the settlement’s terms.

New York AG Letitia James announced the agreement on November 6, alongside the attorneys general of Connecticut, Michigan, and New Jersey. Approximately 4.2 million of the people affected were New York residents.

The investigation describes a series of failures: remote access without multifactor authentication, nearly identical passwords circulated by email, sensitive files without file-level encryption, and security software that detected malicious activity but did not alert security staff.

The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment.

How many people were affected?

The stolen database files contained records associated with more than 13.3 million people, including approximately 4.2 million New Yorkers.

Earlier reporting put the number of affected patients at approximately 8.95 million. The settlement documents now give the larger figure of more than 13.3 million. The total could be higher, since the AG found that attackers also accessed files in shared network storage containing personal and health information, but the companies did not review those files to identify additional affected people.

The information included:

Names, dates of birth, and home addresses.

Social Security numbers.

Medical record and hospital account numbers.

Insurance information.

Admission diagnoses and dates of treatment.

Clinical information from medical transcriptions, including test results, medications, treatment facilities, and healthcare providers.

See if your personal data has been exposed.

SCAN NOW

Notifications were also slow. PJ&A began contacting clients about the stolen database files in July 2023, and its clients notified affected individuals between October 31, 2023, and February 8, 2024. The New York AG found that the companies violated state requirements to disclose a breach as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay.

The settlement

Although the announcement describes a settlement worth up to $10 million, the companies must pay $300,000 in penalties to the states. The remaining $9.7 million is suspended and could become payable. New York will receive $100,000 from the initial payment. These are payments to the states, not an announced compensation payout to patients.

The exposed information could be valuable to criminals. Our research found stolen identity packages selling for as little as 95 cents apiece on the dark web.

The settlement also requires extensive security changes for the relevant active companies, including:

MFA for individual user accounts, including administrator accounts, and remote network access.

Stronger password management and access restricted to what employees need for their jobs.

Encryption of personal and protected health information.

Monitoring that automatically alerts security personnel to suspicious activity.

Annual risk assessments and penetration testing.

Network segmentation and measures to detect and prevent unauthorized data transfers.

Written incident response procedures and clearer rules for retaining and securely disposing of sensitive information.

Given the carelessness, number of exposed records and people, do you think the companies got off cheap? Let us know in the comments.

How to stay safe

A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details:

Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to your healthcare provider or insurer’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust.

Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer.

Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com.

Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing.

Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse.

articles.title: Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk
articles.context: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7
articles.full_text: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

Two weeks ago, I attended the [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. It was an excellent event: three days of very dense talks about all aspects of AI security. (My talk was about integrous AI, and I will post it when it is online.)

AI security can be divided into three broad topics. It’s important for researchers to understand which one they are working on. And it’s important for us as a community to work on them all. They are: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. [un]prompted had good talks about all three.

articles.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Targeted in Reported $133m Heist
articles.context: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out
articles.full_text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.

articles.title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
articles.context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
articles.full_text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

articles.title: Anti-Money Laundering Watchdog FATF Targets Scam Compounds
articles.context: Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment...
articles.full_text:
A leading anti-money laundering (AML) organization has called for global action to disrupt the scam compounds responsible for a considerable volume of transnational fraud.

AML watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned in a new report that large physical scam compounds are a major driver of a global fraud economy estimated to be worth $500bn annually.

Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment platforms, money mules, social media, messaging services and AI-enabled content, FATF said.

The trend is increasingly one of smaller and more mobile operations, with compounds created out of repurposed casinos, rented rooms, apartments, coffee shops and even moving vehicles, the report warned.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

The FATF report noted that countries are generally better at tackling scam compounds through downstream action such as asset tracing and targeting victim payments.

But it called on FATF member nations to combine these efforts with upstream disruption targeting things like fraudulent advertising, recruitment activity, malicious domains and suspicious phone numbers and telecom indicators,

“With criminals weaponizing AI and other technologies to intensify their scam operations, we need to urgently modernize and accelerate our response,” argued FATF president, Giles Thomson. “This means focusing on dismantling the criminal networks behind scam compounds, working proactively with technology, social media and communications sectors to prevent and disrupt more scams before they happen, and quicker intervention to freeze and seize the proceeds of scams once they’ve happened.”

Six Principles to Combat Illicit Money Flows

With this in mind, the FATF report promoted six pillars to its approach:

Shift the focus from physical compounds to criminal leaders, recruiters and traffickers, and other supporting players

Disrupt the infrastructure and services, including stopping, tracing, freezing and recovering victim payments

Share information between financial institutions, technology companies, telcos and authorities

Act at speed across borders, as the first 24-72 hours after a scam are critical for freezing funds and recovering assets

Ensure investigations put the protection of trafficked and scam victims front and center

Continuously update approaches as scam operations decentralize and adapt

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory at BioCatch, welcomed the focus on compounds and the need for action by platform providers.

“Those platforms need to act on what they can already see. But when push comes to shove, banks are often the last and sometimes the only line of defense,” he added. “Funds can leave an account in minutes, and customers are often groomed into trusting the scammer over their bank. Banks must detect the manipulation itself, not just the transaction, and intervene before the money moves.”

A CybSafe report published last month found that over a fifth (22%) of Brits have received a scam call impersonating a familiar person’s voice or appearance. Over a third (36%) of these reports have led to their employer losing money or data.

articles.title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
articles.context: That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI
articles.full_text: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

articles.title: Huawei says it’s made a 100 percent Chinese PC
articles.context: Japan announces emergency response package after wave of cyberattacks Japan’s government last Friday announced emergency funding to help local organizations strengthen the...
articles.full_text: Huawei claims it’s built a desktop PC that uses only parts made in CHina. The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes. A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs. The Register mentions that uncertainty as many non-Chinese companies continue to operate factories in China. Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren’t entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. China’s government is an enormous buyer, and losing the chance to bid for its business is unlikely to be helpful. Japan announces emergency response package after wave of cyberattacks Japan’s government last Friday announced emergency funding to help local organizations strengthen the nation's cyber-defences. The ¥10 billion ($63 million) package follows a wave of cyberattacks that have disrupted railways, retailers, KFC’s logistics provider, and cloud computing operators. The emergency package aims to help Japanese government agencies to use AI to nail infosec basics, and to build tools that let the National Cybersecurity Office aggregate information about cyberattacks. Some funds will also go towards supporting victims. Lenovo’s APAC boss shifts to lead Motorola Lenovo is looking for a new leader of its Asia-Pacific operations after shifting the boss, Amar Babu, to a role as mobile business group general manager and global president at Motorola. Amar led Lenovo in the region for over five years and the company credited him with turning it into “a more balanced and diversified business and a key growth engine.” “Across the portfolio, AP maintained its #1 PC position, while our mobile business achieved notable growth, with Motorola reaching nearly 9 percent market share in India and the #2 smartphone OEM in Japan,” according to a company announcement. “Our infrastructure business achieved profitable growth and nearly double-digit market share, while Solutions & Services continued to strengthen its best-of-breed industry position and significantly increased its advanced services business mix to over 50 percent.” Lenovo has not named a new leader for its APAC outpost. Vietnam hails homegrown USB storage chip Vietnam’s government last week announced the nation’s first domestically-designed security chip - a 28-nanometer device that apparently integrates encryption algorithms in silicon. The chip is already in use on secure USB storage devices that Vietnam’s government employs to store info for government and defense agencies, plus the Communist Party. The nation hopes to use the chips to secure storage of the national digital signature certification system, and critical infrastructure systems in electricity, water, oil and gas, and telecommunications. Hanoi says the chip needs more testing before the government will trust it to protect state secrets, but hailed the chip as an important step towards development of sovereign security capabilities. Apple’s biggest ever education deal Apple last week quietly announced it has won its biggest-ever sale of Macs into the education market in the Philippines. Speaking on the company’s Q4 earnings call, CEO John Ternus said Apple sold 172,000 MacBook Neos to the Department of Education in the Philippines, which will deploy them to teachers and staff. ®

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Monday, November 9th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10170, (Mon, Nov 9th)
articles.context: Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 9, 2026 edition of the SANS Inline Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington, D.C. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cloud Security. Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. And yes, indeed, it is being exploited. Now, this investigation had a couple of hiccups. First of all, in order to exploit sshole, you must use a password that's larger than 256 characters. Well, we only record passwords up to 256 characters because, well, that's usually for brute forcing and so all that matters. On the other hand, there are sometimes passwords that are longer than 256 characters that are being recorded by our honeypots that are not related to sshole. What usually happens here is that simple scripts that are doing brute forcing are actually not checking if the login succeeded or not. So what they're doing then is they end up entering whatever bash command they would like to execute in the password field of the login. Sometimes also the username, that's where we also see them often showing up. But here, of course, the password field was what matters. And if you're looking at the data that I published as part of the diary, we saw a number of long passwords like this on November 1st. So what I'm calling here is the actual sort of exploitation of passwords that I would associate with sshole started on November 5th in our honeypots. Now, what I'm calling here an sshole password is one that basically is just letters, no recognizable bash commands or anything like this, and fills the entire 255 bytes that we are recording. The only ones that I've seen so far being used is either all uppercase letter A or all lowercase letter A. Of course, the actual content of the password shouldn't really matter when it comes to exploiting this vulnerability. I hope to follow this up maybe later this week with a look at what commands are being executed by these attacks after they're logged in. These attacks should actually work as far as our honeypot is concerned. They should sort of randomly allow some of these login attempts to log in. And on Friday, SonicWall released patches for seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS. This is significant because one of these vulnerabilities is already being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins. Apparently, the problem here is if you have multiple authentication methods defined, and one of these authentication methods does not require multi-factor authentication, then an attacker essentially can use that to bypass the multi -factor authentication requirements that you may have set up for SSL VPN access. So this should be patched now. And again, it's already being exploited, which should tell you to please expedite release rolling out this particular update. In particular, of course, with SSL VPNs, we often had issues where people didn't use multi-factor authentication because, well, we all know passwords don't work. And Microsoft this weekend patched an authorization bypass vulnerability in Entra. This vulnerability would allow a user to essentially gain elevated privileges. The attacker in this case doesn't even have to be authorized. Now nothing you have to do. Microsoft already took care of it for you since this is an Entra vulnerability. So it really only affected Microsoft's cloud services and they released the advisory as they state to be more transparent about these vulnerabilities. They also say there was no exploitation happening at the time when they patched this vulnerability. Now they say exploitation is less likely, so more complex vulnerability. And hopefully now after the patch supplied, exploitation should be impossible. And a agentic coding security company, Apiiro, found that Anthropic's Claude Code under certain circumstances will add secrets to a hidden file in GitHub. The way this works is if you're requesting Claude Code to connect to an API or such, it may need credentials. And there is an option when you provide credentials to Claude Code where it basically asks, well, do you want me to ask you again about these credentials, about accessing this API? If you say no, then of course it has to remember those credentials somewhere. And the way it does so is by saving them to a .claude folder and inside there a file settings.local.json. We've actually seen in our web honeypots this weekend an increase in actually for the first time requests for this .claude directory. So attackers are definitely looking for it and Apiiro as part of their blog states that they found sort of around 1500 or so of these credential files on GitHub. There's still work in progress into how to exactly fix this. Essentially what they're proposing is to check automatically for secrets before anything is being sent to GitHub. But of course that may still keep those credentials in any other Git repositories. So not quite clear how this will be fixed. Definitely be aware of this and check with Anthropic and as a Claude Code user with any updates that you may be receiving that will fix this problem for you. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending and subscribing to this podcast. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

articles.title: On the hunt for ARTEX: understanding agentic attacks in AWS environments
articles.context: In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in...
articles.full_text:
Key points

In October 2026, Datadog observed in-the-wild activity from ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework, against several AWS environments, with a focus on accessing financial data.

Using compromised long-term IAM access keys, ARTEX searched through CloudWatch using FilterLogEvents, hunting for financial information, file paths and secrets such as long-lived AKIA access keys and passwords.

We also observed unauthenticated abuse of public Amazon Cognito user pools, including anonymous sign-ups, token collection, and follow-up AWS account enumeration attempts.

In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin and hosted with providers in locations including Singapore and Hong Kong.

Background on ARTEX

ARTEX is an AI-native penetration framework in which an operator supplies a target and an objective, and a team of LLM agents plans and runs the attack. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 and made it closed-source on October 8, after it had passed 12,000 forks.

Microsoft tied it to Storm-0940, a China-aligned actor behind a recent supply-chain compromise. In recent months, ARTEX has been documented attacking Okta, Entra ID and Cognito across IT and software vendors.

Those reports center on identity providers and web application logs. In this post, we provide more details on the cloud control-plane view, in particular how ARTEX behaves once it has compromised an initial set of AWS credentials, through leaked long-lived access keys or following a successful anonymous sign-up on a public Cognito pool.

First, we will dive into ARTEX as a platform. Then, we'll describe specific behaviors and indicators we identified in the wild.

Inside the ARTEX console

ARTEX started as a repository and has grown into a platform running on live infrastructure. Operators run it as a hosted web console, and many of those consoles face the internet. We found hundreds of hosts serving the same Chinese-language login page, titled ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台 (ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console). We've also seen the same platform appearing under other names:

Page title

English translation

ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台

ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

ScopeWeaver — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

(original in English)

LUCK — 自主资产控制台

LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console

观澜SEC渗透测试平台

Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform

A similar console is rendered across many of these hosts.

The platform user supplies API keys to chosen AI inference providers and points ARTEX at almost any provider through three request formats:

openai: OpenAI Chat Completions and any compatible gateway, which covers OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, OpenRouter-style resellers and self-hosted models.

openai-responses: OpenAI's newer Responses API.

anthropic: Anthropic's Messages API, plus vendors that expose an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, such as DeepSeek.

When one provider bans or cuts off a key, ARTEX moves to the next to continue activity. Therefore, a single campaign can be spread across several providers and keys.

An agent planner directs a small team of workers. The planner sends "intents" to workers, which run three at a time by default. A main agent handles chat with the operator, with a /btw command for side questions.

Everything is recorded on a "blackboard" graph of tasks, goals, intents, facts, findings, hints and compression digests. Each task carries operator-defined allow and deny constraints, a timeout with a wrap-up step, and a planner heartbeat of at least 10 minutes. A fixed task timeout would explain bursts that end at a consistent length, though we have not confirmed the value operators set.

Command interception rules, written as regex or plain strings, can allow, deny or ask a human for a judgment. In some versions, a global asset blocklist excludes .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn by default.

API paths expose core routes, such as:

/tasks /exploration/findings /exploration/graph /exploration/intents /traffic /companies /llm/profiles /llm/pool /intercept /mcp /skills /agents /notify

One version we observed shipped with a sample demo engagement. It walks through a full external-to-internal compromise, from a public web app to a DMZ foothold, internal lateral movement, and finally the Active Directory domain controller.

We often found the agent reading the front end of web apps hosted in S3, looking for build manifests and runtime configurations.

Wiz noted that before each fuzzing run, ARTEX requested a path that should not exist (/zzz-nonexistent-xyz123) to learn what "not found" looks like. We saw the same habit against S3, with keys such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt and Notexist-xyz. A request for an object named like a placeholder, right before a burst of guesses, is a useful signal to hunt on.

This behavior is one example from agentic pentesting tools, which continue to evolve whether they're used directly as a tool or hosted as an interactive platform.

ARTEX sightings in AWS environments in the wild

In this section, we share some activity we've identified in real-world AWS accounts, and that we have attributed to ARTEX usage.

The two initial access vectors we've witnessed ARTEX start from are:

Compromised long-term AWS access keys

Public Cognito user pools

Before either, every session we reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 requests. In CloudTrail, these show a userIdentity.type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs.

Activity cluster 1: Post-exploitation following compromised access keys

In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents. The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like Fund, Invoice, Billing and LLC.

Every FilterLogEvents call was set with a limit of 1000, below the API's 10,000-event maximum. That constant shows up across sessions.

On October 20, the same long-term key was used again from 103.54.154[.]40, an address associated with zeofast[.]cn. This session widened the search, looking for file and storage links, internal secrets, internal IP addresses, and database information.

Files and storage links

Databases, internal IPs and secrets

Errors

"s3://" || "presigned" || ".pdf" || ".xlsx" || ".csv" || "rawData_" || "transformedData_"

?mongo ?172. ?10. ?password ?AKIA

?Error ?❌ ?⚠

Activity cluster 2: Self-registration through public Cognito user pools

In an instance where no long-term access keys were obtained, ARTEX went after public Cognito user pools. Wiz reported account-recovery abuse through InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode. We saw the agent go further, registering an account, collecting tokens, trading them for AWS credentials, then enumerating resources.

One example came as a spike on October 26 and 27 from 154.64.252[.]77. The observed SignUp calls sometimes named the tool in the user agent such as Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX, while other user agents included curl or typical browser user agents.

Getting through sign-up was noisy. The pool had a PreSignUp Lambda trigger that checked a tenant domain, and the agent iterated against it and continued probing. For example, below are errors generated as the agent continued attempting to sign up:

PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: api[.]github[.]com. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: example[.]com PreSignUp failed with error tenantId does not match tenant domain. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenantDomain format: hxxps[://]artex-hqheizfk[.]invalid/x. Attributes did not conform to the schema: Type for attribute {custom:isAdmin} could not be determined

Once registered, it walked the standard user pool flow: SignUp, InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken, followed by Get* requests and attempts to call ListUserPools.

In CloudTrail, that session appears under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name with short-term AWS credentials. The agent used it to try nearly every read-only discovery call it could, such as:

ListBuckets

GetBucket*

ListSecrets

DescribeParameters

ListTopics

DescribeLogGroups

GetRestApis

DescribeRepositories

ListFunctions20150331

In this case, all of them failed because the identity pool's authenticated role did not grant the required permissions.

Hunting for ARTEX activity

In this post, we've shared some in-the-wild sightings of ARTEX-attributed activity in cloud environments. It's important to remember that while ARTEX is an offensive AI-native orchestration framework, distributions we analyzed don't appear to have an opinionated methodology for targeting or performing post-exploitation in cloud environments: the playbook is therefore left to downstream AI inference, and can vary greatly depending on the model in use.

In this context, research such as "I Gave 14 LLMs AWS Keys. Here’s What They Wanted to Do Next" by Adan Alvarez is valuable for gaining a broader understanding of how LLMs tend to behave when faced with compromised credentials.

When hunting for ARTEX activity in your environment, we recommend following the methodology below.

Start with quick wins, namely ARTEX user agents (see IOCs), to identify noisy ARTEX probing or exploitation requests. Note that user agents can easily be changed, but they aren't always updated to a stealthier value.

Review your environment for activity originating from IP addresses known to be associated with ARTEX activity (see IOCs).

We've seen ARTEX behave noisily in a number of cases: identify large volumes of permission denied errors, enumeration of objects in S3 logs, unusual access patterns (for instance, credentials vended from an EC2 instance role being used by a non-AWS IP), and CloudTrail events that relate to known cloud attack techniques (Stratus Red Team, Datadog's Cloud Security Atlas and TrailDiscover are useful resources for these).

How Datadog can help

Cloud SIEM

Datadog Cloud SIEM contains several out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules that can detect ARTEX-related post-exploitation and initial access in your AWS environment:

A user received an anomalous number of AccessDenied errors

Enumeration from multiple regions using a long-term access key failed

Anomalous number of S3 buckets accessed

Anomalous S3 bucket activity from user ARN

AWS ListResources by long term access key

AWS ListResources executed by new principal identity

AWS Cloudtrail possible secret enumeration in multiple regions and secret retrieval

Temporary AWS security credentials generated for user

Unfamiliar IAM user retrieved secret from AWS Secrets Manager

Tor client IP address identified within AWS environment

Cloud Security Misconfigurations

Datadog Cloud Security Misconfigurations ships with out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules to help you identify risky long-lived AWS credentials proactively:

Access keys should be rotated every 90 days or less

IAM access keys that are inactive and older than 1 year should be removed

Unused credentials should be deactivated or removed

articles.title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
articles.context: Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

articles.title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
articles.context: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review...
articles.full_text: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. How the spreadsheet slipped through Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023. This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records. Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses. The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets. The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed. Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped. For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations. This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache. Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible. At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache. The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review. The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time. Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count. The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses. A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it. The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations. A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved. "An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability. "The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses. "The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again. "We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

articles.title: Stealing more than the spotlight. [Research Saturday]
articles.context: " Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting...
articles.full_text:
This week, we are joined by Matt Poto, Associate Triage Analyst at Huntress, discussing their work on "Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware." Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting gamers.

Huntress identified malicious ISOs promoted through search engine poisoning, gaming forums, torrent sites, and social media that contain multiple types of malware, including remote access trojans (RATs), an infostealer, and ransomware. The malware can steal credentials and personal information, give attackers control of compromised systems, and encrypt or destroy files, with evidence suggesting the campaign may be targeting Russian-speaking gamers.

The research and executive brief can be found here:

⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware
