articles.title: The components of agent memory
articles.context: It loads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY
articles.full_text:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.

As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.

Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest, the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.

Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).

We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.

Memory notes

By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).

In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.

Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?

Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need

Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.

Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0, a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.

Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.

We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents. Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.

Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.

Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.

Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).

Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.

Claude has learned to judge salience

We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red, a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).

We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).

Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md, and earned four badges.

Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.

Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.

Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”

With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.

Steering Claude to write memory

We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).

We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.

We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.

In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

Dreaming can correct memory

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.

Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.

In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.

At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.

We then tested whether dreaming could help Claude avoid this trap. We ran dreaming on the memory folder that contained the wrong location for the PokéCenter: Claude checked the note against the session transcript, caught its error, and rewrote it. The transcript gave Claude a ground truth to validate its memory against. With the corrected memory note, Claude went straight back into Mt. Moon and eventually reached Cerulean City.

In the run with the uncorrected note, Claude dropped back onto that earlier route three times. After the third failure, Claude seemed to give up, writing, “I’m going to stop rather than keep looping.” Our setup’s automatic reply instructed it to continue. So it did, all the way back to Pewter City, the town before the mountain, where it hoped to heal and restock. The run ended without Claude ever reaching Cerulean City.

Dreaming can build new memory representations

With dreaming, Claude can build representations to help navigate memory (Figure 9). One type of memory representation it uses is called a wiki, a collection of pages written and maintained by Claude that gathers what Claude knows about one subject and links it to other notes. These links effectively provide Claude with a map it can use to sift through its memory and efficiently locate memories when they’re needed.

Representations like wikis can help Claude traverse its ever-growing knowledge base. We explored the benefit of wikis as a memory representation using a corpus of internal documents—about 350,000 files, roughly 420M tokens—from Stainless, a software company we acquired in May. We created an evaluation set of 25 questions about this corpus and gave Claude a search tool to explore it. We also instructed Claude to build a wiki based on these files using dreaming. Over 128 sessions, we prompted Opus 5 agents to explore the files, write or correct linked wiki pages, merge duplicates, and check claims against the sources.

Each session built on the progress that agents made in prior sessions, using a shared log to coordinate work. As we scaled dreaming from two sessions to 128, performance on the 25 questions grew from 13% to 48% of graded criteria (Figure 10).

Claude builds its wikis incrementally. After creating an initial wiki, it uses subsequent rounds of dreaming to add to, edit, or prune it. In the early rounds of dreaming, Claude’s knowledge is like that of a new employee, and its ability to answer questions based on the wiki alone is limited. The more it dreams, the richer its knowledge map grows, like that of a seasoned employee. In our tests, we found that the wiki helped Claude the most when we also gave it access to a search tool. When it used both search and the wiki, Claude’s aggregate score rose from 54% to 61% as that wiki grew, compared with 53% when it had access to the search tool alone. Claude’s best score was 48% when it used only the wiki to answer questions. Using search and the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question.

We wanted to test which kinds of tasks benefited from Claude having a wiki. To do this, we used the Harvey LAB benchmark along with a collection of documents about a merger. The benchmark gives Claude a set of documents and asks Claude to generate a legal brief based on their content. The benchmark then grades the brief against a list of criteria. While a tad less engaging, perhaps, than a Pokémon run, these evaluations give us diverse collections of documents to build wikis from.

We instructed Claude to build a wiki from the documents. We then asked Claude to answer questions (about the merger) or generate legal briefs (the LAB benchmark) both from the wiki and from a direct file search. One test asked 24 questions about the merger (Figure 11, left), more than half of which needed Claude to find information across several documents, and many of which also needed Claude to use judgment or do math. On those items (red and orange lines), Claude scored 87% when it consulted the wiki, compared with 73% when it used search alone.

In other cases, the wiki was less useful. On one LAB task (Figure 11, right), brief criteria often could be retrieved with a text search from a single document, and the wiki showed no clear gain in performance relative to search. On another LAB task, the wiki grew larger than the documents themselves (Figure 12). Like the mapmakers in Borges’s one-paragraph short story “On Exactitude in Science,” who drafted a map so detailed it was as large as the empire it represented, Claude had made an extremely detailed wiki that effectively abstracted nothing.

Dreaming can promote notes up the memory hierarchy

Dreaming can also float notes to the top of the memory hierarchy, and the agent harness can preemptively load them into Claude’s context at the start of every session (Figure 13). This means Claude doesn’t need to search for them, or even to know there’s something to search for.

Promoting memories into a new session (a form of context injection) must be done carefully. Injected memories use up valuable tokens, and an incorrect note can be carried into every session. Loading a note also doesn’t guarantee that Claude acts on it: our documentation on Claude Code warns that longer instruction files reduce adherence. So the top layer of the memory hierarchy has to stay relatively small, and much of dreaming’s work here is keeping it that way—by moving some details down the hierarchy and leaving links behind.

Claude Code’s auto memory keeps its injected layer small in the same way, with Claude maintaining it during the session. Claude doesn’t load all of its auto memory into every session’s context window. It loads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md. This header serves as an index, which shows Claude what it knows and where to find it.

Dreaming can focus memory on a specific goal

Dreaming can also shape how memory grows. An assistant like Claude Duet, for example, often benefits from having memories that are organized around the person it’s helping, and dreaming can be tuned to build memory in service of a particular goal.

The instructions that guide how memory grows differ by task and tell Claude what information actually matters. For example, one task in the LAB benchmark simulates a company acquisition and provides a set of contracts. The brief is graded on whether it correctly describes the contract terms.

We started with basic instructions for generating the wiki that didn’t tell Claude how to use the wiki. This task relied heavily on contract terms. While the wiki was being built, several agents wrote to a shared table of contract terms at the same time (Figure 14, left).

The result was a wiki that was missing key facts. When we graded a brief generated from the wiki, Claude had included only 41 of the 57 facts (72%). When we looked at what had gone wrong, we found that the shared table summarized the contract terms poorly and was missing some of them altogether, because agents had overwritten one another’s work.

The contract terms were the most important part of the wiki, but the instructions didn’t say that. To find better instructions, we ran a loop in which Claude reflected on its failures, proposed a change to the instructions, and rebuilt the wiki. This loop allowed Claude to discover how important it was to follow the contract terms, and it rewrote the instructions for building the wiki accordingly.

Each contract got its own page in the wiki, written by a single agent, which quoted the terms word for word rather than summarizing them into a shared table. When we graded the brief generated from this improved wiki, 100% of the criteria could be met, up from 72%.

Dreaming can fill in gaps a session leaves behind

When Claude writes memory notes, it sees only the context in that particular session. Dreaming can search across many sessions to find common patterns or correct common mistakes.

When building the wikis for the LAB benchmark (as an example, see Figure 14), sometimes Claude would link to pages that hadn’t yet been created. A second dreaming pass closed many of these gaps. On one task (Figure 15), dreaming found nine links to a missing page in the wiki and repointed them to an existing page for the same document. It also added three new pages, including an index, to improve the wiki.

Thinking backward, looking forward

There are many open questions about how to design memory systems for agents. One is when Claude should create memory. When Claude works on a task, it can write to a memory store (e.g., a folder, file, or database), capturing salience at the source and making important details immediately available for future turns or sessions. But logging notes in the moment inevitably draws Claude’s attention away from its main task. In contrast, dreaming can push memory creation to the background, but any outputs from dreaming may not be immediately accessible to Claude.

Another question is how to keep memory reliably up to date. Claude can make incorrect predictions or write rules to memory that are wrong from the start. Memory can also drift and become irrelevant as the environment changes. Dreaming is one way to fix these mistakes (Figure 8), but it requires compute. Directing Claude to continuously check all its memories might not be practical. It may be important instead to focus dreaming on information that’s likely to change or to carefully tune the cadence of dreaming (e.g., based on how often memories are accessed).

It’s also reasonable to consider transcript search as the foundation of Claude’s memory. Combining representations (e.g., wikis) with search (Figure 10) can sometimes be effective. But Claude needs to use compute to maintain memory representations and make sure they don’t accumulate errors or hallucinations.

Even though Claude’s judgment about salience has improved, no model can really know what will happen in future turns. Dreaming gives Claude an opportunity to look backward and use compute to organize its memory, correct mistakes, and maintain representations that allow future sessions to access memory more readily. Memory systems will evolve as Claude gets more capable, and we still have a lot to learn about designing Claude’s memory systems.

See our cookbooks for getting started with dreaming and knowledge wikis.

articles.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
articles.context: The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data
articles.full_text:
In 1951, Cambridge University’s computer went out of action for six months. This was inconvenient for physiologist Andrew Huxley, who, alongside his colleague Alan Hodgkin, had just built a set of equations to describe how a particular squid nerve cell fired. The scientists wanted to understand the “action potential” of these nerve cells: the electrical pulses they use to communicate, which underlie everything brains do, from perception to intelligence. The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data.

Huxley had hoped to use the newfangled computer to solve the equations. Instead, he was forced to solve them using a hand-cranked mechanical calculator. It took him over three weeks.

The basic structure of their model was dictated by known facts about the cell. Hodgkin and Huxley modeled its membrane as an electrical circuit. One part of the model, however, was just an educated guess. In order to make the curve fit the data they had measured, they found that they had to raise one variable to the fourth power—that is, to multiply it by itself three times. At the time, they did not know why. They just knew that otherwise the model didn’t predict the observed data as well.

They did offer a hypothesis, however. They cautiously suggested that the variable in question, which governed how particular gates in the cell membrane opened, might require the fourth power because multiple charged particles in the membrane had to move into place before the gate would open.

Decades later, long after both Hodgkin and Huxley had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963, another team found the structure of a related potassium channel protein. And they discovered that, yes, it had four identical pieces arranged around a central pore. The model was fit to the data in 1951. Even then, it predicted how fast the impulse travels relatively accurately. More than that, it turned out to have helped predict the structure of potassium ion channels themselves, which it had never been fit to.

Today, an AI system could plausibly find an equation like Hodgkin and Huxley’s in an afternoon, and perhaps it would fit the experimental data even more closely. But the point of the story is that simply knowing the fourth power did the job was not enough; what mattered was knowing that a simpler version of the model did not work. An AI system that merely hands you the model might give you an answer, but it does not give you understanding. Reproducing the data with a model is insufficient, because any number of models could do the same. What matters is being able to make claims about the real-world system itself, and ideally about other, similar systems. To do so, you need to know which features the model shares with other models that work, and which set it apart from models that don’t. As the mathematician Richard Hamming wrote in 1962, “The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.”

A three-step program

More than 70 years on, the Hodgkin-Huxley model remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons. The same kinds of equations, with different constants, describe nerve cells across the animal kingdom, from squids to humans, even though our evolutionary lineages separated more than half a billion years ago.

Even more important than its longevity, however, is what the Hodgkin-Huxley model tells us about how models work. Hodgkin and Huxley’s approach can be broken down into three steps, and most scientific modeling involves some version of them.

The first is building the model. This means deciding what the model is made of and what shape its equations take. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s case, that meant the parts of the electrical circuit—the membrane and the gates—and the form of the equations, such as raising the underlying variable to the fourth power.

The second is constraining the model—tuning its adjustable parameters to fit real measurements. For Hodgkin and Huxley, that included settings like how often the gates open under different voltages.

The third is interpreting the model—asking what the model says about the real system, such as suggesting that the fourth power meant the gate had four moving parts.

In practice, scientists go through these steps repeatedly. If the numbers fail to fit the measurements, or if the interpretation makes no sense, they go back and revise.

All three steps were once done by people, but AI systems are increasingly involved in each of them. Machines have arguably made the most progress in constraining models, so we’ll start there.

Splitting the bill, or how to constrain models

When Hodgkin and Huxley constrained their model by eye and intuition, they ended up with a single set of numbers. This told them that the model could match the data. It didn’t tell them whether other numbers would have worked just as well or even better.

Imagine you know that a group dinner added up to $120, but not who ordered what. Many different combinations of orders could have added up to that amount—perhaps everyone ordered a mid-priced burger, or perhaps one person had steak and lobster while everyone else had soup. Models of nerve cells work on the same principle: different combinations of gate parameters can produce near-identical electrical activity. Simply showing one combination that fits well hides all the other plausible parameter settings, and other combinations might have led to different predictions. This is true of almost any phenomenon being modeled. Many different sets of parameters can explain the observed data equally well.

The solution is a statistical method called Bayesian inference. It gives you every set of numbers that works reasonably well, as a probability distribution that takes into account their fit to the data and your prior knowledge about the parameters. The distribution takes the shape of a curve, with the best fits at the peak and the weaker ones at the fringes.

But this method has usually been impractical for complex models, because it involves calculating how likely your measurements would be under every possible set of numbers. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s model, that would still be feasible, but for anything more complicated, it would be computationally impossible. For example, if each of the thousands of ion channels opens and closes at random, you would have to work out every combination. Returning to our restaurant bill analogy: it would be easy to answer, “If person A had the burger and person B had the steak, what would the bill come to?” but much harder to show which combinations could have led to the final bill, especially as the number of people and menu options grows.

A different approach called simulation-based inference (SBI) overcomes this reverse-engineering problem with sheer computation. You pick random parameters, run the model, and record the output. You do it again and again—perhaps 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley, and millions of times for larger, more complex ones. Then you train a neural network on the results so that, given an output, it can return the range of parameters that could have produced it.

All SBI requires is that you can run the model: put in a set of parameters and get back the kind of data you would expect to see. A model you can run like this—parameters in, data out—is called a simulator, hence the name “simulation-based inference.” You never need to use a formula to calculate how likely your measurements are, which is the step that makes standard Bayesian inference often impractical. These days a simulator is usually a computer program, but it doesn’t have to be: Huxley, cranking through the equations by hand, was running one. Many simulators are easy to run forward but impossible to reverse. Some can’t even be written out as a tidy equation—their assumptions are built into the rules they follow—but they are models nonetheless. For many complex phenomena, from networks of neurons to colliding galaxies, simulators are often the only kind of model we have. SBI lets us constrain those models with data.

Running all those simulations is expensive and can take weeks. But once it is done, a trained network can perform inference on new data in seconds, without requiring further simulations. That speed has changed what’s possible. When two neutron stars collide, SBI can work out roughly where in the sky the collision happened, fast enough to point telescopes at it while the signal is still detectable. The same approach has been successfully applied to problems in cosmology, structural biology, geophysics, and many other domains.

And SBI has been applied to nerve cell models, including the Hodgkin-Huxley model. Because it returns a distribution rather than a single fit, we can see which parameters are well constrained by the data, where more than one explanation is plausible, and where more data—and thus another experiment—is most needed.

The bill, one level up, or how to build models

Before you can constrain a model, you need a model to constrain. The equations of the Hodgkin-Huxley model were not derived from first principles. Instead, the fourth power of the underlying variable emerged empirically from the scientists’ biological insight, and from finding that simpler versions didn’t work as well.

For most of the history of science, this is how models have been built. Scientists used their expertise and assumptions to write down a candidate model. Then they tested it, revised it, and tried again. The problem is that the space of possible models is essentially infinite, and a scientist proposing a handful of models from experience will very likely miss models that could have explained the observational data equally well.

AI systems can now help with, or even take over, this step. Given some data and a natural-language description of a system, an LLM-based agent writes code for a candidate model or a set of candidate models. Then it runs the model, constrains its parameters, compares the output to real-world data, and revises it, perhaps by modifying the form of an equation. This loop repeats until the model replicates the data accurately enough. Several such systems have appeared in the past two years.1 The details vary, but all use an LLM to design the model itself. Until recently, this was thought to be something only humans could do.

But the fact that a model replicates data doesn’t mean that it provides insight. As with the restaurant bill, or the Hodgkin-Huxley parameters, many different combinations of parameters within a single model can provide the same output. The same is true one level up, for the model itself: many different models, with differently shaped equations, can explain the same data equally well. Run an agent twice on the same data, and it might return two different, and equally good, models. An agent that returns only one of them is hiding the rest, just as a single best-fit set of numbers does.

So it is better to treat building a model the same way we treat constraining one: you ask for the whole range of models that could plausibly explain the data.2 The AI system proposes many candidates. Each is then weighted by how much it is supported by the data, and the ones that need a lot of flexibility to fit are given less credit than those that fit naturally. The weak candidates drop out, and the AI system proposes new variations on the stronger ones.

AI agents can thus provide a distribution of plausible models, rather than a single best fit, and that distribution tells you things a single model can’t. If every surviving model shares a feature, the data likely favors it. If the survivors disagree, that shows where the evidence is thin, and points researchers in the direction of the next experiment.

We shouldn’t get too far ahead of ourselves. So far, these systems have mostly been tested on rediscovering models that scientists already know. Evidence that they work on problems with no known answer is sparse. Still, newer LLMs perform better at research tasks than older ones, and we expect these systems to keep improving.

Lost in translation, or how to interpret models

Once a model has been built and constrained, it still has to be interpreted. What does it tell us about the real system being studied? Hodgkin and Huxley’s four-particle hypothesis came about because equations involving the fourth power are what you would expect if four separate things all had to happen before a gate could open. So they suggested that this might be what was happening inside the membrane. As we saw above, they turned out to be largely right.

That interpretation only carried weight because of what they had ruled out. If a simpler model had worked just as well, there would have been no reason to think the gate had several moving parts. It was the failure of the alternatives that allowed them to make that claim. There was some uncertainty about the exact number: Hodgkin and Huxley noted that a third or fourth power was needed and settled on four. They wrote that higher powers might even have fit slightly better, but that the potential “improvement was not considered to be worth the additional complication.”

The equations also let Hodgkin and Huxley reason out several other implications. For instance, the equations explained why nerve cells have a voltage threshold below which they don’t fire and above which they do, and why nerve pulses all have the same shape. They also predicted that a current rising slowly enough would never make the cell fire. Philosophers of science call a theory “intelligible” if it lets you work out its consequences without having to run it. That test works for a model with a handful of variables, like Hodgkin-Huxley. For a larger model with perhaps thousands of variables, the equivalent might be whether we can boil it down to a few crucial mechanistic ideas that are enough to rebuild it. The larger the model, the harder that becomes.

Of the three steps, interpretation is the hardest to hand over to AI. The goal is harder to pin down: we can measure how well a model fits the data, but not whether it leads to a better understanding of the system, and it’s not clear how to tell an AI system to make “understanding” its objective. One proposal is to judge an AI system’s understanding by seeing how well it predicts what a system does when you disturb that system. Another is to sidestep the question altogether, and instead ask whether the agent’s outputs help human scientists better understand the problem. One example is an AI system for designing quantum experiments. Rather than providing a single setup, it was trained to write a short program that generates the setups for a whole family of related experiments. A physicist can then read the underlying design principle straight off the program instead of reverse-engineering it from one experimental setup.

In both approaches, having access to a full distribution of suitable models, rather than a single best-fitting one, is crucial for interpretation. A single model cannot tell us which of its parts are actually constrained by the data, so it’s easy to read meaning into parts that are not. In Hodgkin-Huxley, as we’ve seen, the hypothesis about four particles only makes sense if you know that lower powers don’t work as well. A range of models also makes predictions more robust. Say you ask your models what happens when you disturb a system—for instance, by blocking all, or only some, of the sodium gates on the cell membrane. If all the models that fit the data return the same answer, as you would expect when every gate is blocked, then you can be fairly confident in it. If they disagree, as they might when only some gates are blocked, that can provide ideas for the next experiment.

Cells and scales

Most famous models, including Hodgkin-Huxley, are compact. They consist of a handful of variables and equations, small enough for a human scientist to write down and reason about. That’s no coincidence: they needed to be compact, because people had to build, constrain, and interpret them. Their smallness is also what made them intelligible. But as AI takes over more of the work, the size limit will start to lift. We can begin to model systems that are far too complex to write down by hand, even if we can no longer understand them just by reading the equations.

Brains are an obvious use case. The Hodgkin-Huxley equations describe a single nerve cell. But a fruit fly’s brain contains more than 100,000, and a human brain tens of billions. And it is the interplay between those neurons that gives rise to behavior and thought. For the fruit fly, we now have something that was impossible for previous generations of scientists: a complete wiring diagram of its brain, showing every neuron and how it connects to the others.3 Researchers have started building large-scale models on top of it, including one that predicts the activity of neurons across the fly’s visual system. That opens up questions nobody could sensibly ask before. How does a whole brain turn its wiring into behavior? How much of an animal’s behavior can be predicted from its wiring alone? And which connections actually matter?

But at these scales it will not be possible to find a single correct model. Indeed, in most cases there is no such thing. As the statistician George Box wrote, “All models are wrong but some are useful.” The data will always be compatible with many models. The question will no longer be which model is the right one, but which properties all data-compatible models share, and which predictions can be derived from them. The most useful experiments will be those that rule out the greatest number of remaining models, even if they are not always the ones a human scientist finds the most interesting.

This isn’t unique to neuroscience. Climate scientists already work like this: they build many gigantic numerical simulations, each based on slightly different assumptions, and report their projections as the spread across all of them. Particle physicists at the Large Hadron Collider work in a similar spirit: when they look for a new particle, they don’t just declare whether a particular theory worked or not; they produce a map of which versions of the theory are ruled out by the data and which remain open.

The painstaking work Hodgkin and Huxley did—building the model, fitting each curve by eye, trying the powers that didn’t fit, and, in Huxley’s case, spending three weeks hand-cranking the mechanical calculator—is not something we want to go back to. But it was not wasted. Much of the insight that a model provides comes from the process of creating it; Hodgkin and Huxley understood what the model was telling them because they had built it themselves, and they knew what hadn’t worked. This understanding let them formulate their interpretation of gating variables—part of the discovery that ultimately earned them the Nobel Prize.

An AI system could now plausibly do much of the same work in an afternoon. But to offer understanding, it needs to deliver what the two scientists’ slow work produced: not just the model that fits, but an account of which parts are pinned down by the data, which are still open, which alternatives failed along the way, and what new puzzles were uncovered in the process. A scientific model may provide an answer, but it is the process of constructing it that provides the insight.

Other VPNs We’ve Tested

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

VPNs to Avoid

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

How We Test VPNs

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

On the privacy front, the top-recommended services included on this list have been independently audited, and they all maintain some sort of transparency report. In most cases, there's a proper report, but in others, such as Windscribe, that transparency is exposed through legal proceedings.

articles.title: Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up
articles.context: Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds
articles.full_text: If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement. Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires. The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets. But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue. Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands. Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks. The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter. In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said. Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures. How to stay frosty To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet. Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities. “Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise. Other recommended tactics include: Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks. Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible. Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer. Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list. Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline. And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

articles.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
articles.context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
articles.full_text:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

How phone return scams works

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

How to stay safe

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and deliberate whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.

A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.

A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.

Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.

A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help explain what happened to support a billing complaint and fraud report.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

articles.title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
articles.context: Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client
articles.full_text:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

Run programs and system commands.

Browse folders and download files.

Take screenshots.

Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.

Collect browser passwords and cookies.

Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.

Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.

Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.

Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.

If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

From reporting threats to removing them.

Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
articles.context: Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the...
articles.full_text:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.

The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.

They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment.

They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard:

“We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.

Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.

Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

How to stay safe

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.

Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.

Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.

A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.

If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.
