articles.title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
articles.context: The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose...
articles.full_text: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks. News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool. “The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email. For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year. The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent. Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained. According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said. Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem. “Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while. “Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.” Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them. Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems. Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over. “Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed. The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

articles.title: APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users
Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
articles.context: The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions
articles.full_text: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions. The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled. If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration. That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not. Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration. Dawn of the *sshole The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually. In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account. Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out. The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk. Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going. In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times. On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack. Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set. There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

articles.title: October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed
articles.context: In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of...
articles.full_text: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time. In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company. Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials. Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials. In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work." These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page. Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5). Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords. "We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary. "We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely." Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30. "Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems." In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed. Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base. It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations. Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews. It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

articles.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber, and promises this one stays within 'rules of engagement'
articles.context: This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute...
articles.full_text: OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement." The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do. The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately." In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests. "In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise. OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things. The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing. The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review. OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework. This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks. As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming. Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well. The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products. Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments, and added new bonuses for independent researchers. This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®

articles.title: SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era
Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
articles.context: He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential
articles.full_text: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture. Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets. Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it. "I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here." Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client. "My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes." Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company. He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside. The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share." “I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file. Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated. But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all. He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all. "And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe." He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it. "The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

articles.title: Residential Proxy Traffic Traced to White House Network
articles.context: Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4
articles.full_text:
Residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network 236 times over a 30-day period, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses.

Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4. Residential proxies are services that sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from each device's network.

The addresses sit in AS2650, the block of internet addresses (autonomous system) registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Layer3 spotted the exits, recorded on 26 of the 30 days between October 5 and November 3, in its newly launched Residential Proxy Observatory.

Layer3 cross-checked the addresses against public lookup pages from proxy detection services Spur and Synthient, which independently identified them as residential proxy exits.

Evening Pattern Suggests a Single Device

Layer3 said anyone could route traffic out through the same addresses by signing up to a public residential proxy service and paying a few dollars. It found the activity by chance, while requesting ordinary global rotating access through these services.

About half of the activity fell between 5pm and midnight Eastern Time, with almost none in the early morning.

Layer3 said that pattern suggested a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device was infected with a proxy software development kit (SDK).

"Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them," the firm wrote.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk said: “The most recent activity was recorded in the evening of November 4; hopefully, it stops soon!”

Read more on residential proxy networks: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet

No Compromise Reported, but Proxy SDKs Carry Risk

Layer3 did not report any compromise of White House systems. It said it has backed up the raw logs of the activity and has shared their finfings with a US federal agency.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow access to internal networks and lateral movement, which is how past botnets have spread.

Layer3 cited Synthient research showing the Kimwolf botnet reached at least two million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed Android Debug Bridge (ADB) service, through residential proxy networks.

If an SDK on the White House network had the same kind of flaw, Layer3 said, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

Infosecurity has contacted the White House for comment.

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Patch Missed Flaw Behind Wave of Attacks
articles.context: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks...
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks on 996 switches in 48 countries.

Firmware security company Binarly detailed the finding in research published on November 3, linking it to an exploit that threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had described in September. The vulnerability now carries a new identifier, CVE-2026-107441. It is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management program that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run operating system (OS) commands with root privileges.

The attacks had originally been tied to CVE-2026-7273, which Zyxel fixed on June 16 and described as a stack-based buffer overflow in the same program, rated 8.8. On September 21, GreyNoise reported that an attacker had exploited that flaw against 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, taking switch configurations, hashed root credentials and networking information.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day.

Read more on network device zero-days: Critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day Under Active Exploitation

June Fix Left Vulnerable Code in Place

Binarly analyzed an obfuscated Python exploit that matched the one GreyNoise described. On September 28, the researchers confirmed that all 10 firmware releases shipped as the June fix remained vulnerable to it.

Binarly said the June change added a check, but the check ran only after the unsafe copy had already occurred. The researchers wrote that the change "does not address the vulnerability."

The firm offered two explanations. Either the June patch, its description and its Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score were incorrect, or the attacks used a different flaw and CISA's link to CVE-2026-7273 would be wrong.

Either way, Binarly said, all 10 releases advertised as fixes contain the vulnerable code.

Severity Disputed as Zyxel Ships New Firmware

Zyxel rates CVE-2026-107441 at 8.8 and says an attacker must be on the local network to exploit the vulnerability, while Binarly rates it 9.8 and says exploitation requires only network access to the switch's management service.

Binarly said it notified Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel confirmed the flaw on October 11, released a fix on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models. On the GS1900-8, for example, firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier is affected and 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 contains the fix.

Zyxel told users to install the updates "for optimal protection." Its advisory lists the June releases among the affected versions, so switches last updated in June still need the new firmware.

articles.title: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses
articles.context: Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some...
articles.full_text:
Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some previously attributed to Chinese hacking groups.

In a new security advisory published on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that non-banking financial companies, including digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators, payment services providers and cryptocurrency exchanges, have reported falling victim to repeated cyber-attacks.

Some of them received a restricted-distribution advisory in early October warning them of cyber threat actors exploiting application programmable interfaces (APIs) traditionally used for payment and disbursement transactions to make unauthorized transfers.

Despite undertaking remediation after receiving this previous warning, these financial organizations were attacked again, with CERT-In noting “incomplete remediation” on their part.

Attacks were typically observed during holiday periods, on weekends and “other low-monitoring windows” to delay detection and response, CERT-In added.

Crafty Falcon’s Attack Lifecycle

According to CERT-In’s Finance branch (CERT-Fin), Crafty Falcon is a previously undocumented threat actor that uses a range of AI and agentic AI penetration testing tools to breach the systems of its victims.

Typically, Crafty Falcon gains initial access through internet-exposed non-production environments, such as user acceptance testing (UAT), staging and testing environments.

Once inside, the threat actor moves from non-production environments into production systems by exploiting shared credentials, authentication tokens or network paths between the environments.

The actor reverse-engineers the organization's application codebases to develop tailored exploits. They then use altered or modified application packages to initiate unauthorized API calls, bypassing security controls that assume only the legitimate client application will communicate with the APIs.

The actor also bypasses IP allow-listing restrictions by routing traffic through whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools, such as content-acceleration services and app-store review fetchers. These shared services can be instructed by any internet user to fetch arbitrary URLs, allowing the actor to originate traffic from IP addresses already trusted by the organization.

Another Crafty Falcon characteristic move is to target the victim’s cloud infrastructure, including compute, serverless and management services. Cloud management services, such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda, are abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, allowing malicious activity to blend into legitimate cloud management operations.

Before executing large-value transfers, the actor performs micro-value test transactions, such as transactions of Rs. 1, to validate that unauthorized fund flows are possible. They exploit or abuse merchant settlement APIs belonging to payment aggregators to move funds.

The actor targets cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds from cryptocurrency wallets.

CERT-In noted that Crafty Flacon also exploits newly published vulnerabilities as soon as they become publicly available. These include file-upload and deserialization exploit chains, leading to the deployment of web shells in PHP and Node.js applications.

Throughout these activities, Crafty Falcon creates large numbers of custom, tailored scripts on the fly. Functionally identical variants are refined in rapid succession, a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.

Notably, CERT-In and CERT-Fin observed the use – and combination – of several AI-powered offensive security tools against affected entities. These include:

Penetration testing tool ARTEX, based on PentAGI, an autonomous, multi-agent framework that can be plugged to large language models (LLMs)

Penetration testing framework CyberStrikeAI

Attack search engine Cairn

These tools allow attackers to “execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses,” CERT-IN indicated.

While these tools are publicly available and could be used by many threat actors, most previous malicious campaigns where they were deployed were linked to China-based actors.

Read now: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

CERT-In Provides Crafty Falcon Threat Mitigation Recommendations

In its latest advisory, CERT-In provided a long list of recommended security measures organizations can take to mitigate the threat. These include:

Maintaining heightened 24/7 security monitoring, increased staffing and lower alert thresholds during holidays, weekends and periods of reduced monitoring

Centralizing real-time monitoring of cloud audit logs and alert on high-risk events, including remote command execution, serverless function code updates and creation of roles, users or access keys

Restricting cloud management and serverless execution to approved principals and accounts

Implementing instance metadata service protections, least-privilege roles, restrictions on wildcard egress and default-deny internet egress for serverless functions

Separating UAT, staging and testing environments from production, ensuring no shared credentials, tokens, API keys, databases or direct network paths

Making application deployment directories read-only for application runtime users and implement file-integrity monitoring to detect web shells

Treating client applications and packages as untrusted and enforcing server-side transaction validation, API request signing using nonces and timestamps, application attestation and certificate pinning

Establish rapid patching SLAs for Internet-facing applications, prioritizing file-upload and deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js. Use WAF virtual patching as an interim measure

Extending real-time transaction monitoring to identify small-value test transactions to new beneficiaries followed by high-value transfers. Treat these as strong indicators of potentially unauthorized fund transfers and hold or review such transactions

Storing cryptocurrency wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold custody

Prohibiting unauthorized security and attack tools, including publicly available AI-driven offensive frameworks, on corporate infrastructure

Monitoring and governing LLM API usage and keys. LLM API traffic originating from servers or non-development hosts may indicate an attack infrastructure or planted operator console

Adjusting SIEM correlation to identify machine-speed, multi-technique attacks, parallel attack threads, adaptive payload changes and continuous activity outside business hours. Implement automated SOAR-based containment

Adopting zero-trust principles, micro-segmentation, identity-based access controls for every user and service and inspection of east-west traffic

The agency also urged organizations to report any suspicious activity that could be related to Crafty Falcon to incident@cert-in.org.in with all relevant logs and to contact the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) and its Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS).

Read now: AI-Powered Cybercrime Tools Surge on Dark Web

articles.title: New York's Queens Public Library battles ransomware crims: Wi-Fi, checkouts, and website go dark
articles.context: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly
articles.full_text: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials.) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild. Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library. In its 2025/26 annual report, published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

articles.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
articles.context: Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery...
articles.full_text:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

Authentication bypass;

Arbitrary code injection; and

Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

Change of temperature, which could:

Affect the service life of the system;

Create a fire hazard;

Cause loss of inventory; or

Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.

Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.

Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].

Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.

For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.

Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:

Date, time, and location of the incident;

Type of activity;

Number of people affected;

Type of equipment used for the activity; and

Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.

Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

Disclaimer

The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. The authoring organizations do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favor by the authoring organizations.

articles.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
articles.context: To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-...
articles.full_text:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

articles.title: Chinese Nation-State Threat Activity Falls Sharply in Q2 and Q3 2026
articles.context: The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state...
articles.full_text:
Despite the sharp fall in China-aligned detections, observed PRC cyber activity remained “substantially higher” than nation-state cyber activity from Russia and Iran during the period, the researchers noted.

“The decline may reflect changes in targeting, infrastructure or detection visibility rather than a reduction in activity. The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state actors,” they wrote.

A number of Chinese nation-state espionage campaigns have gone undetected for long periods in recent years. For example, in 2025, the Chinese-nexus actor Weaver Ant was found to have infiltrated the network of an Asian telecommunications service provider and remained undetected for more than four years.

Such cases highlight that there may be significant ongoing Chinese nation-state activity occurring that has not yet been detected.

US and Turkey Primary Targets for Nation-State Actors

The Trellix report, published on November 4, found that nation-state targeting primarily focused on two countries, the US (38%) and Turkey (37.1%), which collectively represented over three-quarters of all detections from April to September.

The researchers noted that the US represents a valuable target due its status as the world’s largest economy and the concentration of high-value technology, defense and government infrastructure. Meanwhile, Turkey also represents a key strategic target given its location at the intersection of Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, as well as its NATO membership.

The third most targeted country by nation-state actors was Germany, representing 4.4% of such activity.

articles.title: Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
articles.context: " The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations
articles.full_text: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues. Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it. "We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said. "They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to." Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it. Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question. The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal. It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously." The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world. Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. The issues Norad and the Norwegian government support, however, are wide-ranging – from access to healthcare for transgender people worldwide and Kenyan incubators for innovative transport solutions, to delivering aid to war-torn Gaza. ®

articles.title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
articles.context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
articles.full_text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

articles.title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
articles.context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
articles.full_text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
