articles.title: My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
articles.context: On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours,...
articles.full_text:
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.

For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.

When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.

Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?

For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.

James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.

The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.

In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.

I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.

Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.

An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.

Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.

Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.

Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.

FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.

The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.

Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.

“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”

Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.

“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.

Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.

I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.

That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

articles.title: FBI Attributes Binance Heist to North Korea’s TraderTraitor
articles.context: “At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3
articles.full_text:
North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last week, according to the FBI.

A brief statement from the Bureau published on October 31 attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor group (aka Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces).

“The FBI, together with partners at the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH),” it read.

“It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using decentralized finance products (DeFi) and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.”

Read more on TraderTraitor: US and Japan Blame North Korea for $308m Crypto Heist.

The FBI and its partners urged crypto entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to “block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”

According to Blockchain analytics company Elliptic, around $2.9bn of the stolen funds have been frozen or seized, but that still leaves almost $3.3bn outside the reach of issuers.

“At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3.25bn of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, spread across more than 800 addresses. This includes around 584,000 ETH ($1.32bn), 18,327 BTC ($1.42bn) and 233 million XRP,” Elliptic explained.

“The ETH includes TRX laundered through bridges, which arrives on Ethereum and is split across hundreds of fresh wallets. Almost all of the stolen TRX has now been laundered. The XRP, SOL and NEAR, worth around $439m, have not moved at all since they were stolen.”

Binance Investigation Continues

Binance has said it will cover the costs of the incident, so customer funds are not in danger. However, it continues to investigate the actual cause of the breach.

Originally, the firm claimed that a compromised DevOps laptop may have been the source of the incident, but later added that it “uncovered additional points of breach” in what it is describing as a “complex attack.”

The attack was carried out by more than one individual, and used a “self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as it ran,” which has made forensic analysis harder, according to Elliptic.

TraderTraitor, which also has links to the Lazarus Group, APT 38 and AppleJeus, has been pegged for a string of historic crypto heists.

These include attacks on Japanese firm DMM, which cost the firm $308m, as well as Alphapo ($60m), CoinsPaid ($37m) and Atomic Wallet ($100m). TraderTraitor was also blamed for the previous record setter for biggest ever crypto breach, when it stole $1.5bn from Bybit.

articles.title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
articles.context: At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator
articles.full_text:
At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.

All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Hidden Behavior

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

articles.title: Chainalysis Warns Customers After “Offensive Agentic” Security Incident
articles.context: ” Read more on agentic attacks: AI Agent Carries Out Multi-Stage Data Theft Attack
articles.full_text:
A leading blockchain analytics company has revealed details of a security breach involving an AI agent.

Chainalysis said in a post on October 30 that an external actor used “offensive agentic techniques” to gain unauthorized access to undisclosed internal systems and tools.

“Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users,” it continued.

“We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.”

Read more on agentic attacks: AI Agent Carries Out Multi-Stage Data Theft Attack.

Chainalysis clarified that the incident is unrelated to the Binance heist last week. It also claimed to have no evidence that the threat actor was able to access investigation content like graphs, notes or cases, or transaction query results.

These sensitive pieces of data could allow an unauthorized third party to snoop on blockchain investigations carried out by Chainalysis customers. The firm has been busy this week helping the community to understand who carried out the Binance raid, for example.

The firm also said that it had no evidence that clear-text passwords, multifactor authentication (MFA) secrets or user session tokens had been accessed, meaning customer accounts should be safe.

A Warning for Customers

However, Chainalysis did warn customers about possible follow-on attacks.

“Chainalysis users should continue to be hyper-vigilant of unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts,” it said.

“If your organization has not yet enabled two-factor authentication, we strongly recommend doing so. Your Chainalysis account manager can help you complete that process.”

The firm said it has been working “around the clock” to investigate the unauthorized activity, patch any affected vulnerabilities and harden its systems.

“We have engaged world-class third-party cybersecurity experts and are using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform’s security and strengthen our defenses,” it added.

“This work extends beyond the exploited vulnerabilities to enhance our security posture across the platform.”

articles.title: ZDI-26-850: Microsoft Qlib MLflowRecorder Deserialization of Untrusted Data Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Microsoft Qlib
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Microsoft Qlib. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the MLflowRecorder class. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

Additional Details

Fixed in v0.9.8https://github.com/microsoft/qlib/releases

Disclosure Timeline

2026-07-17 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-02 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: Inside a successful AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise to demonstrate independent operation
articles.context: The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany
articles.full_text:
On Saturday, October 24, 2026 we conducted a successful exercise demonstrating that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate without depending on any infrastructure outside the European Union (EU). This was the first public technical exercise demonstrating the independence of a sovereign cloud Region.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany. It is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and all customer content and customer-created metadata remains in the EU.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is managed through dedicated European legal entities established under German law and operated entirely within Europe. My fellow Managing Director, Stefan Hoechbauer, and I called for the exercise. We are EU citizens residing in the EU, responsible for its management and operations, including its infrastructure, technology, and services. Only EU residents located in the EU control its operations and support, and AWS is gradually transitioning the AWS European Sovereign Cloud to be operated exclusively by EU citizens located in the EU.

What we did

In standard operations, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, and a dedicated system operated by the local EU team to manage limited, controlled transfers of operational AWS data. As we explained ahead of the exercise, neither is critical to running the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. During the exercise, the team switched off both systems, and traffic that normally travels across the AWS Global Network backbone rerouted securely over the public internet.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently at any time, and for several hours on October 24 the team showed exactly that, running it on only its own software and hardware resources, operated by EU-resident staff within the EU.

Workloads continued running, and customers could still access their data. The exercise did not affect service availability within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, other AWS Regions, or private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect. When the exercise finished, traffic returned to its normal path.

Why we ran it

Transparency is at the core of our digital sovereignty commitment, so we ran the AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise openly and reported back on the outcome. The exercise produced verifiable technical and operational evidence that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can continue to operate independently within the EU. It turns a design claim into a verified result. Organizations in regulated industries and the public sector can take this result to regulators and their boards as evidence for their compliance and assurance documents.

What customers and partners are saying

“Digital sovereignty is ultimately about trust and safeguarding business continuity. The successful demonstration of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud’s operational independence is an important proof point for European organizations with the most stringent sovereignty requirements. Combined with Capgemini’s European heritage, presence and AWS capabilities, we can deliver a sovereign proposition in Europe, for Europe, by Europeans, enabling clients to accelerate secure and resilient cloud and AI transformation at scale whilst assuring business continuity.” – Fernando Alvarez, Chief Strategy and Development Officer and Group Executive Board Member, Capgemini

“Autonomy, resilience and operational control are foundations driving digital sovereignty concerns across the public sector and regulated industries. Achieving sovereignty requires more than a sound and consistent architecture; it demands operational evidence to build trust. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud team has provided evidence, supporting organizations on the transformation of their critical data and digital assets toward greater sovereign control. Having engaged with this team since the inception of the project, and as a Launch Partner of the AWS Digital Sovereignty Competency, Atos helps customers define their sovereignty roadmaps, adopt the appropriate graduated solutions, and confidently operate and govern their target sovereignty posture.” – Michael Kollar, Digital Sovereignty Leader and Head of Cloud & Modern Infrastructure and Digital Workplace, Atos Group

“For organizations in regulated industries, meeting strict data and operational requirements cannot come at the cost of a great customer experience. Running on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, Genesys can help European organizations deliver exactly that, with their data and operations kept in the EU. Seeing the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operate independently under real conditions helps give our shared customers added confidence to move their most sensitive workloads to the cloud.” – Daniel Karadza, Senior Director, Partners and Alliances, EMEA Central and Benelux, Genesys

“Operational independence is a defining pillar of digital sovereignty, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud has shown what that means in practice. It runs without reliance on any infrastructure outside the EU and is operated entirely by EU residents, which makes it a strong fit for Europe’s regulated industries and public sector. As an early collaborator with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud team before its launch, Accenture is uniquely positioned to help clients navigate sovereignty requirements and scale with greater confidence and control.” – Emanuele Baldassarre, Managing Director, Accenture

Learn more

To learn more about the design and digital sovereignty controls of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, visit aws.eu. If you have questions about this exercise or want to discuss your workloads, reach out to AWS Support or contact your AWS Account team.

Stéphane Israël

Stéphane is the leader and Managing Director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. He is responsible for the management and operations of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, including infrastructure, technology, and services, in addition to broader digital sovereignty efforts at AWS. Prior to AWS, he was the CEO of Arianespace, where he oversaw numerous successful space missions, including the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope.

articles.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
articles.context: An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and...
articles.full_text:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.

For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.

Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6. Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;

A technical report explaining the details of our system;

A (Claude-written) protocol specification document;

Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and

Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.

Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

Challenge 3: text provenance

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

Challenge 4: model approval

Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

Our system: FlashProve

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:

In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase.

In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:

The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

Guarantees

A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:

A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier.

A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden.

A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure.

Evaluation

We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

Prover. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.

Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.

Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

Engineering the system

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

The prover's work is proportional to the experts that actually ran. In a MoE model a token uses ~17B of the 400B parameters, and the prover's work per token is proportional to those ~17B instead of all parameters (the proof still hides which experts were chosen).

Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request.

The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices.

Post-hoc versus in-line

When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.

Trustworthiness from formal verification

Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?

The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:

Completeness: if the statement is correct, the resulting proof is accepted by the verifier.

Soundness: any fake proof is rejected by the verifier (except with negligible probability).

Zero knowledge: the proof reveals no information about the weights of the model, beyond what the verifier can infer from the response itself.4

These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.

Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.

Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.

For soundness, we only need the verifier code to be correct (the entire value of having “proofs” is that you can fully distrust the prover if you trust the verifier). We provide an executable Lean verifier, alongside the C++ verifier. The Lean verifier runs more slowly, but Lean proves that it accepts only what the verifier in our soundness theorem accepts. Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests.

For completeness, the threat model does not assume adversarial attacks (the prover and verifier are honest). Therefore, a Lean verifier lets us gain confidence through standard software testing that the honest prover produces accepting proofs: run the prover on a correct statement, and then the Lean verifier on the resulting proof.

For zero knowledge, we only need the prover to be correct. However, unlike the verifier, the prover is an expensive procedure, and it would be impractical to run a Lean prover. We do not provide facilitations here: we expect that any prover that wants to hide the weights of a model they are serving has access to enough resources for careful agentic and/or human security audits to ensure equivalence to the Lean prover.

Prior work

Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.

Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. In 2025, zkGPT reduced GPT-2 to 21.8 s (≈0.05 tok/s), zkPyTorch proved Llama-3 8B at ~150 s per token on one CPU core (≈0.007 tok/s), and ZKTorch proved GPT-J (6B) in about 20 minutes (≈0.001 tok/s). VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. DeepProve, a current peer-reviewed state of the art, certifies an entire generated sequence with a single forward pass. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100.

Recently commercial efforts have reached impressive numbers, with Attestable proving Gemma 4 31B at 53–77 tok/s on a single H100; at the time of writing, Attestable has not released a corresponding open source library.

The above numbers speak to the precipitous progress of provable inference in the past years. They should update our priors on what it is possible to prove in zero-knowledge.

In 2024, zkLLM proved a 13B model at about 2.5 tokens/second on one A100. The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify.

FlashProve proves the same model at 110 tokens/second on a single H100, with 19 MB proofs that can be verified in seconds. Attestable independently reports 53–77 tokens/second for a dense 31B model.

We believe that the progress should transfer to more models and architectures, yielding a flexible and powerful tool with overhead over native computation of roughly 2 orders of magnitude (about 70 to 95 times in our measurements), much less than previously expected.

Limitations

This release is a research prototype, and has the following technical limitations:

No formal guarantees on fast executable code. We provide a Lean implementation of the protocol (including an executable “slow” Lean verifier), along with security properties proved in Lean. The paper and the fast executable code are derived from the Lean protocol, but we do not guarantee that all three (Lean, paper, code) match each other.

The proof is about an integer model under greedy decoding. We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved. The integer version is generally expected and empirically tested to be within some small error rate of true floating-point inference generically (even taking into account non-determinism of floating-point computations), though this does not cover adversarially designed prompts.

Architecture hiding. Our system assumes the served model uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, in which each transformer layer’s feed-forward block is replaced by multiple expert sub-networks and a router that activates only a small subset of experts for each token and our system uses the MoE structure for efficiency gains. Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model.

Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release.

Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens).

articles.title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
articles.context: With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT)
articles.full_text:
Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions.

How message threads works

A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT).

With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%.

To use message threads, add the thread parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.

Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including:

Long-running coding agents, where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation.

Computer use agents, where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn.

Document and image-heavy workflows, where requests are made smaller.

The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token.

Getting started

Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the documentation to get started.

articles.title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
articles.context: Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

articles.title: The long road to root. [Research Saturday]
articles.context: " A Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Red Heron exploited a critical Gitea remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-60004, within days of its public disclosure,...
articles.full_text:
Today we are joined by ⁠⁠Subhajeet Singha⁠⁠, Senior Security Researcher at ⁠⁠Acronis⁠⁠ Threat Research Unit, discussing their work on "Red Heron exploits Gitea n-day flaw in multinational campaign, exposing new Linux rootkit." A Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Red Heron exploited a critical Gitea remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-60004, within days of its public disclosure, compromising organizations across five countries and stealing source code, credentials, and sensitive infrastructure data.

The campaign involved deploying persistent backdoors and a newly identified Linux implant called JITTERLY, which contains an undocumented rootkit, SIXZUT, capable of hiding files, processes, and network connections while protecting the malware from removal. Acronis assesses with moderate confidence that Red Heron operates within a PRC-linked context, highlighting how quickly attackers can weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities and turn exposed development platforms into gateways for broader network compromise.

The research and executive brief can be found here:

⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Red Heron exploits Gitea n-day flaw in multinational campaign, exposing new Linux rootkit⁠
