articles.title: Crypto's biggest withdrawal.
articles.context: Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts.
articles.full_text:
Binance suffers a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. Russian disinformation targets U.S. elections. Treasury sanctions North Korean IT worker operations. A cyberattack halts Polymarket trading. GCHQ loses track of thousands of storage devices. An abandoned Mac app leaves security risks behind. Japan Airlines reports a third-party breach. An AI-powered command-and-control framework emerges in the wild. Our guest is Josh Devon, Co-founder & CEO of Sondera, winner of the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

Today is Friday October 30th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Binance suffers the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered a staggering $6.3 billion theft, reportedly the largest cryptocurrency hack on record. Researchers at TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the October 29 attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation. Attackers moved funds across ten blockchains, with most of the theft occurring in just 20 minutes. Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which may have provided access to systems authorized to move funds. The company found no evidence that private wallet keys were stolen. Instead, attackers apparently manipulated transaction-signing infrastructure, including an Ethereum feature that allowed them to automate withdrawals. Cryptocurrency issuers and networks have frozen billions in stolen assets, but estimates suggest attackers still control between $2.4 billion and $3.3 billion. Binance has promised to reimburse affected customers, while significant questions remain about the security controls protecting its wallets.

A maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA has added the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler, allowing attackers to execute malicious code through specially crafted CI/CD configurations. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts. The Shadowserver Foundation reports nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable. The latest discovery follows several serious GitLab security issues this year, including another recently exploited vulnerability that could expose sensitive credentials and other secrets.

A Russian disinformation group targets U.S. elections.

Researchers say a covert Russian influence operation is targeting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas with fabricated allegations of misconduct. Analysts at Alethea and Clemson University attribute the campaign to Storm-1516, a Russian disinformation group that spread similar false accusations during the 2024 presidential election. The latest attack involved videos that researchers at Graphika believe were AI-generated. Initially attracting little attention, the videos gained traction after several influential accounts on X amplified them. One received more than 850,000 views in its first 24 hours. U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Russia has recently intensified its election interference efforts, particularly in competitive Senate races. While much of the activity targets Democrats, intelligence officials haven’t concluded that Moscow is explicitly favoring either party.

Treasury officials sanction Russian and North Koreans over fraudulent IT worker operations.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russian and North Korean nationals and companies accused of supporting Pyongyang’s fraudulent IT worker operations. Two Russians allegedly laundered millions in cryptocurrency earned by North Korean operatives working remotely for American companies. Treasury also targeted North Korean managers overseeing IT workers in Russia, along with a company accused of using artificial intelligence to help operatives secure U.S. jobs. The broader scheme involves North Koreans using stolen identities to obtain lucrative technology positions, then funneling earnings back to Pyongyang. Some workers have also stolen sensitive information and extorted employers. U.S. officials say the proceeds help fund North Korea’s weapons programs. The sanctions follow a Justice Department operation targeting laptop farms used to disguise workers’ overseas locations.

Polymarket suspends trading following a cyberattack.

Prediction market Polymarket temporarily suspended trading Thursday after a cyberattack involving a third-party service provider disrupted its international platform. The company says trading has resumed and promises to reimburse affected users, but hasn’t disclosed the extent of the losses or identified the attacker. Blockchain security researchers traced more than $2.1 million in suspected cryptocurrency theft to a single account. Security firm Hudson Rock identified the compromised provider as website performance company DebugBear, which separately acknowledged a security incident and urged customers to remove its embedded code. Researchers discovered malicious code apparently designed to identify cryptocurrency wallets and transfer their assets to an attacker-controlled account. Polymarket removed DebugBear’s code from its website. There’s currently no evidence that other DebugBear customers were compromised.

GCHQ laments missing storage devices.

Britain’s intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of storage devices potentially containing sensitive information. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner says USB drives, hard disks, and memory cards remain unaccounted for years after the problem was first identified. Some devices may contain intercepted communications and other highly sensitive intelligence data. The watchdog expressed frustration over GCHQ’s slow investigation. The agency acknowledged shortcomings in its tracking system but says it has implemented corrective measures. Officials are still determining how many devices are actually lost.

An abandoned Mac app causes security headaches.

An abandoned version of the once-popular Popcorn Time streaming app left hundreds of thousands of Macs potentially vulnerable to attack. Researchers at Eye Research discovered that Time4Popcorn installed a persistent update checker that could download and execute code with elevated privileges, even years after users stopped opening the app. With the developers long gone, attackers could potentially hijack expired update domains to distribute malware. Researchers found no evidence of exploitation, but estimate 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. They took control of an abandoned domain and used the update mechanism itself to disable the vulnerable checker on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. Other vulnerabilities remain, however, and some update domains are still uncontrolled. Researchers recommend uninstalling Time4Popcorn entirely.

Japan Airlines suffers a third-party data breach.

Japan Airlines says a breach at its technology provider, Amadeus IT Group, exposed personal information belonging to 92,000 customers. Compromised data includes names, reservation codes, and flight details. For approximately 2,000 passengers, attackers also obtained passport numbers, contact information, and frequent flyer numbers. The airline says payment card information and flight operations were unaffected.

The disclosure comes amid a wave of cyber incidents in Japan, including breaches affecting millions of customers at a Sony-owned internet provider, Burger King Japan, and gaming company Capcom. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called for emergency cybersecurity measures, warning of growing risks from stolen personal information. Japanese and American defense officials have also discussed strengthening cooperation against cyber threats as the country grapples with the recent attacks.

An AI-integrated command-and-control framework is found operating in the wild.

Cisco Talos researchers have discovered an AI-integrated command-and-control framework called NIK C2 operating in the wild. The Windows-based malware combines credential theft, keylogging, surveillance, and remote access with direct access to OpenAI’s API. Attackers can use AI to analyze stolen information during an active intrusion, potentially accelerating their operations. The malware can even use a victim’s own OpenAI API key, potentially charging them for the attacker’s AI requests. NIK C2 also includes screen-locking ransomware that demands cryptocurrency payments without encrypting files. Its capabilities extend to lateral movement, security evasion, and persistent access. Talos observed active infrastructure and multiple versions of the malware, suggesting ongoing development. Researchers warn that integrating AI directly into malware could significantly reduce defenders’ opportunities to detect and interrupt attacks.

We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

We say goodbye today to Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.

His was a remarkable life. From a difficult childhood in a working-class Yorkshire home, he found his way to the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he spent decades mastering his craft. And then, approaching 50, he took a chance on a science fiction television series that he wasn’t entirely convinced would succeed.

And in doing so, he became Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

For those of us who grew up with Star Trek, it’s difficult to overstate what Patrick Stewart brought to that role. Picard was thoughtful, principled, intellectually curious, and deeply committed to the idea that humanity could become something better. He valued diplomacy over violence, reason over impulse, and the dignity of every individual. He was a leader who listened, who questioned his own assumptions, and who understood that having the authority to give an order didn’t necessarily mean it was the right order to give.

And there’s something else worth remembering. Star Trek inspired generations of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technology professionals. People who watched those shows as kids and went on to build the technologies that shape our world today. The communicators, the tablets, the voice-controlled computers, the extraordinary networks connecting people across unimaginable distances. For countless young viewers, Star Trek wasn’t just entertainment. It was an invitation to imagine what technology might make possible, and then go out and make some of it real.

Patrick Stewart helped make that future feel worth pursuing.

He also reminded us that intelligence and kindness weren’t mutually exclusive, that leadership could be compassionate, and that even in a universe filled with extraordinary technology, the most important questions were still fundamentally human ones.

Now, you might reasonably ask, “What does this have to do with cyber security?”

Well, as it happens, Captain Picard was something of an early adopter of multifactor authentication. Whenever the Enterprise’s auto-destruct sequence needed to be activated or canceled, the ship required authorization codes and confirmation from multiple senior officers.

Even in the 24th century, apparently, you couldn’t just blow up the Enterprise with a single password.

Sir Patrick Stewart gave us many wonderful performances over a long and extraordinary career. But for generations of us who looked to the stars and imagined a better future, he’ll always be our captain.

Thank you, Sir Patrick.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: “Are We Exposed?” What CISOs Need to Know About Their Software Risk
articles.context: Curl When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer
articles.full_text:
Recent events have once again highlighted the need to quickly answer the question, “Are we exposed?”

We now face threats to businesses and governments from vulnerabilities and compromises in three fundamental components used in software development: Curl, PHP, and LiteLLM.

Curl

When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer. With libcurl embedded in many enterprise environments – from backend microservices and container runtimes to automated CI/CD pipelines and shell scripts – this vulnerability carries potential systemic risk. The core threat centers on high-severity flaws disclosed in October 2026, notably a high-severity HTTP/2 use-after-free issue (such as CVE-2026-92392) where a malicious upstream server handling an upload can corrupt client-side memory and, under specific conditions, trigger remote code execution or application crashes on the machine initiating the transfer. Because libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for HTTPS URLs when the server supports it and applications rarely inspect what libcurl does under the hood, development stacks and automated deployment pipelines that have not upgraded to a fixed version can remain exposed to hostile external endpoints.

LiteLLM

Regarding LiteLLM, JFrog Security Research detected the problem within 2 hours, and the errant LiteLLM package, version 1.107.0, has already been removed from PyPI. Reflecting the open-source community ecosystem’s continually improving maturation, the package maintainers have already published a report. But from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on October 21, 2026, software developers, agentic agents, or your build systems could have downloaded that package from PyPI, and affected Docker images remained available until 14:20 UTC. The ripple effect of a compromised package or vulnerable component getting into an environment doesn’t just impact the developers or security team. It also impacts IT Ops and, down the line, auditors. Every change impacts the whole organization. Executives, the business decision makers who determine where to invest and allocate resources, need a way to understand where they sit in this maturity. Do they have complete visibility or not?

PHP

In the case of PHP, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), were disclosed and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, according to public advisories. Within days, news outlets reported on the vulnerabilities, and CISA issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately, including CNBC and the BBC, CISA.

“Are We Exposed?”

When a CISO wrestles with the question of “Are we exposed?”, their triage process should focus on these key issues:

Is it really a threat?

Where is it being used?

What is the business impact?

Do I have a reporting or disclosure obligation under rules or standards that apply to my organization, such as those of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), PCI DSS, or, for product manufacturers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?

Did we block it?

How do we fix it?

The CISO’s ability to answer these questions with confidence depends on how well they’ve integrated their tools, people, processes, and security program to provide that visibility and respond quickly to security incidents. The ability to do this, in turn, is a reflection of the maturity of their overall security program and how well they can protect, monitor, and govern the full gamut of software development operations – whether it’s on the developer’s workstation, in agentic workflows, or implemented directly by AI coding agents.

A true assessment of your organization’s abilities to determine your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats is critical to providing a full 360 view of your risk posture.

Hands-On Assessment Experience

As a CISO, I’ve done these assessments on a number of occasions, for both new deployments and as an ongoing protective measure to help keep the business protected as new threats and vulnerabilities evolve.

These assessments should be broadly based and take into account business objectives, employee capabilities, workflows, data usage, and the maturity of the infrastructure. Covering these bases should give you an accurate compass of where you are and where you need to improve.

This should, of course, include your tools, but should not lead to one of the classic mistakes organizations make, which is over-focusing on tools, simply because they’re the easiest thing to measure. The other areas mentioned above are easy to overlook, but extremely important to a realistic assessment, as tools without the right people and processes won’t achieve the objective of protecting your business.

JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment

Based on JFrog’s experience working with many of the Fortune 100 customers and through the expertise of our in-house security research team, we’ve actually built our own Security Maturity Assessment. It lets organizations self-assess their software supply chain security program maturity across 11 domains, based on their answers.

I strongly recommend taking a few minutes out of your busy day to complete the questionnaire, as it assesses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and risks in your software development operations and could help you identify where to start when it comes to ensuring you can truly answer the question: “Are we exposed?”

Takeaways

The question of “Are we exposed?” can be complicated and difficult to assess, but recent high-profile security incidents don’t give CISOs the luxury of taking days to come up with a reply. Corporate executives and board members need fast, accurate answers.

Having complete visibility into your people, processes, workflows, tools, and dependencies gives you the leverage to protect your business under the pressure of the latest attacks. Take the first step in securing your applications by evaluating your operational maturity with JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment or speaking with one of our domain experts today.

articles.title: New Framework Puts Ransomware Resilience for AI Systems in Focus
articles.context: Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks.

The tool is the Ransomware Assessment and Incident Defense Framework for AI Systems (RAID-AI) and is fully available for anyone to use online for free.

Behnaz Karimi and Yuvaraj Govindarajulu, both co-leads of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s (OWASP) AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) initiative developed RAID-AI over the past two years.

They had initially planned to introduce the framework at the ISC2 Security Congress, held in Denver, Colorado, between October 26 and 28. Unfortunately, visa issues prevented Karimi from attending.

A Manual Ransomware Readiness Assessment for AI Systems

Speaking to Infosecurity, Karimi said RAID AI focuses on ransomware attacks against AI systems, whether or not an attacker uses AI. The framework’s approach is hands-on, asking security teams to assess their own controls rather than connecting to or scanning their systems.

“Right now, we are slowly seeing that ransomware attacks targeting AI systems are happening,” Karimi said.

She highlighted a April 2025, a report by Zoran, Mitrovic head of engineering at Kintra Health, which detailed how ransomware actors used data poisoning techniques, as well as an alleged cyber-attack on Novo Nordisk in June 2026, where hackers claimed to have stolen AI models used by the pharmaceutical company.

The RAID-AI assessment covers general cybersecurity measures alongside risks specific to AI models, data and supporting infrastructure.

The framework is delivered through a web console aimed at CISOs, cybersecurity officers and security engineers.

Users assess controls manually, selecting maturity levels on a scale from zero to five. The controls are organized into general and AI-specific categories, with levels such as basic, advanced and high.

General controls include recovery, training and sensitive-data protection. AI-specific areas include data, tools and runtime.

RAID AI maps controls to two voluntary security frameworks, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) and the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Cybersecurity Performance Goals 2.0 (CPG 2.0).

It also allows users to map adversarial attacks through three attack mapping frameworks, MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS and NIST Adversarial.

Karimi and Govindarajulu have provided comprehensive documentation, including guidelines for using the tool and an explanation of how it was developed and how maturity levels and various security scores are calculated.

Future Plans: Extend Ransomware Assessments to Agentic AI Systems

Organizations do not need to connect their internal systems or upload company documents to complete the assessment.

Therefore, the RAID-AI assessment is not an automated audit: results depend on users’ evaluations and the tool does not independently verify an organization’s security posture.

Instead, teams review their practices and enter their assessments themselves.

“Ideally bringing security managers, engineers and AI-security specialists together in workshops,” Karimi told Infosecurity.

The console displays the results in dashboards, including maturity views and mappings to other frameworks. Users can also download PDF reports that highlight weaknesses and help teams set priorities.

Karimi said the dashboard can give senior leaders a high-level overview, while technical teams use the underlying controls to guide more detailed discussions.

In the future, Karimi hopes to provide practical implementation resources, including videos and blueprints to help security engineers apply individual controls, and develop a similar tool for ransomware threats targeting agentic AI systems.

articles.title: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit
articles.context: The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9...
articles.full_text:
A suspected Chinese nation-state actor chained the PHP2Shell exploit with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access to 25 Palo Alto Network (PAN) firewall and management servers.

The campaign rooted 25 PAN servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, according to an investigation by cyber defense platform provider Dream.

There was a particular focus on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment, resulting in persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

The Dream researchers noted a number of indicators of Chinese nation-state involvement in the campaign, including the narrow focus of the targeting.

“Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts,” they commented.

In addition, a number of tools used in the campaign, such as the large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi, and the internet reconnaissance platform FOFA, are Chinese-based services.

The Dream researchers highlighted the “automated and efficient” nature of the exploits, which took place from 23-24 October, including the targeting of specific PAN-OS versions.

“This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing,” they said.

“There was a clear-cut focus on government targets,” the researchers added.

Palo Alto Networks Confirm Compromise

Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 verified Dream’s findings in a blog published on October 29. It said that around .02% of its global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and were impacted by the campaign.

All the affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

“Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available,” Unit 42 wrote.

Palo Alto Networks has recommended that customers review its mitigations for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and apply patches immediately.

Chained Exploits Achieves Access in Under 15 Minutes

The attackers developed two separate exploits and chained them together into one request to target the PAN-OS servers. One of these was the widely reported ‘PHP2Shell’ exploit, made up of two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The exploit, which affects the PHP server-side programming language used by around 70% of websites, was leaked in October before a scheduled disclosure and release of patches. This resulted in many websites being taken down, including by governments, while emergency fixes were applied.

Read now: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

In the campaign identified by Dream, the threat actors tailored the exploit specifically for PAN-OS, targeting PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server.

This was chained to a second exploit, a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem known as Fragnesia and tracked as CVE-2026-46300. The attackers used this flaw to overwrite authentication rules, allowing root access to be achieved without a password.

“Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes,” Dream explained.

Threat Actor Narrows Focus to US Government Servers

Once the exploit was ready, the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. It narrowed down its targeting through a number of stages, using scanners to identify which devices were connected to the internet, their geographic location and what PAN-OS version they were running. The latter was focused on the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30.

This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls located in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.

These targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target.

Of the 240 targets, 24 firewalls were successfully rooted. For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker only planted a webshell and did not carry out any further post-exploitation activity.

However, the two other firewalls, which belonged a US government-affiliated environment, saw the attackers establish persistent access. This included building an 8-port reverse SSH tunnel, which connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure.

The attackers quickly used its access to one of the government servers to compromise a third government server via same PHP2Shell and Fragnesia exploit chain. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

As this third server centrally managed all of the government organization’s firewalls, compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials and network settings.

This allowed the threat actor to exploit the server’s connectivity to Active Directory to steal data such as credentials, although the researchers cannot determine the full extent of the accessed data.

“What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure,” they warned.

Dream said the campaign demonstrates that finding a vulnerability is only one part of identifying weaknesses across an organization’s systems, particularly with the growing use of chained exploits.

“Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise,” the firm added.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability

CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
articles.context: “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says
articles.full_text:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

Neither Binance or law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers, but researchers say there are overlaps with previous cryptocurrency attacks from TraderTraitor. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

articles.title: Binance Hit by Record-Breaking $6.3bn Hack in Largest Cryptocurrency Heist in History
articles.context: Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6
articles.full_text:
Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6.3bn of cryptocurrency being stolen.

The Chinese-founded, Dubai-headquartered and Delaware-registered company said it has frozen $3bn of stolen funds and that it will cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

According to a company statement on October 30, its investigation suggested that an attacker's entry point may have been a compromised Binance development and operations (DevOps) engineer's laptop.

This allegedly allowed the attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

However, Binance has since revised that assessment and said its subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach.

"This was a complex attack," the company said, adding that it was working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other industry partners to establish the full circumstances as well as identify and recover affected assets.

Binance has not yet provided a definitive account of the attack, saying it is still gathering the facts and will publish a comprehensive technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete.

The company has said it has found no evidence that any wallet private keys were leaked.

In its many updates on social media, the exchange has repeatedly stressed that customer funds remain safe, despite the scale of the incident. It has also promised to publish an updated proof of reserves once remediation work is complete, providing customers with an updated view of the assets held against user balances.

Three world-leading cryptocurrency analysis firms, TRM Labs, Elliptic and Chainalysis have attributed the attack with “high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.

articles.title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
articles.context: More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings
articles.full_text:
More than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents, have had their details published online by a group of hacktivists.

As TechCrunch reports, the leaked records include the names, job titles, work email addresses, phone numbers, abd office locations.

More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Around 10,000 ICE employees have had their records breached, and almost 1,000 members of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

WIRED reports that the massive leak includes staff who work undercover, as well as in other sensitive areas such as those engaged in wiretapping and the interception of communications.

A hacktivist group calling itself "Department of Peace" says that the data was taken from an Okta single sign-on system that staff use to log onto the central network of the US Department of Homeland Security. Okta for its part says that it has not seen any evidence that its own systems have been compromised.

The data reveals which tools and services particularly individuals can access. Alongside everyday office software, these include Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, the phone and social media analysis tool PenLink, and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by immigration agents.

Explaining its justification for the data breach, "Department of Peace" wrote:

"They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs."

The leaked data has been published online, under the title "Icepick", and can be either downloaded via a torrent or accessed via a web interface - making it significantly easier for curious parties to search.

One threat intelligence expert told WIRED that, if authentic, the leaked data was "an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS," and could help adversaries identify vulnerable personnel or compromise ongoing investigations.

An obvious concern is that the leaked contact details could be used in phishing attacks that target employees, or could potentially put agents in physical danger. Clearly anyone whose details have been exposed through the incident would be wise to treat unexpected emails, texts, and phone calls with caution - and be particularly wary of any communications that claim to come from IT support or ask for a login to be approved.

Earlier this year the same group of hacktivists claimed to have breached the US Department of Homeland Security and accessed contracts between DHS, ICE, and more than 6000 firms including the likes of L3Harris, Raytheon, Palantir, Microsoft, and Oracle.

Explaining their motivation for that breach, the hackers referred to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by federal agents in Minneapolis.

"Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I'm releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they're working on."

There has been a long string of cybersecurity incidents affecting US government personnel. For instance, in September the notorious ShinyHunters hacking group claimed to have stolen personal details related to nearly every employee of the FBI, and the records of millions of serving and former US military personnel were reportedly stolen from the Pentagon's human resources unit.

articles.title: A leak in the chain of command.
articles.context: Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs.
articles.full_text:
DHS suffers a massive data leak. Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods. Cisco patches a firewall zero-day. A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories. Online scams overtake phishing. NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance. CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation. The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline. A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations. Our guest is Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center (TAC), discussing securing operational technology in our critical infrastructure. Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

Today is Thursday October 29th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

DHS suffers a massive data leak.

A massive leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed information on more than 41,000 employees and contractors, potentially providing adversaries with a detailed roadmap of the department’s operations.

The archive, dubbed “Icepick,” was published by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets. It reportedly contains data from DHS’s Okta identity management system, including employee contact information, reporting relationships, and access permissions for sensitive systems.

WIRED’s analysis identified references to undercover operations, surveillance programs, facial recognition tools, and investigative platforms. The records cover roughly one-seventh of DHS’s workforce, including thousands of ICE and Customs and Border Protection personnel.

Security experts warn the information could facilitate targeted phishing, impersonation, and intelligence gathering, particularly when combined with other leaked datasets.

DHS says it’s investigating a potential breach. Okta maintains its systems were not compromised.

The hackers, calling themselves the Department of Peace, framed the release as an act of government accountability.

Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods.

For years, U.S. officials have warned that China’s Volt Typhoon hacking group poses an extraordinary threat to American critical infrastructure. Now, researchers are revealing the sophisticated methods behind those warnings.

As Kim Zetter writes in her Zero Day newsletter, Lumen Technologies’ Black Lotus Labs has uncovered what it calls Silent Train, a covert network of compromised routers, servers, and internet-connected devices that Volt Typhoon uses to infiltrate sensitive American networks.

The attackers construct elaborate chains of compromised devices, sometimes in less than two minutes, routing their activity through multiple countries before reaching their targets. Each chain is typically used for a single intrusion, then dismantled. The hackers erase logs, remove evidence, and disappear, sometimes after spending just minutes inside a network.

Researchers tracked more than 27 classes of compromised devices and identified at least four exploited zero-day vulnerabilities.

The targets include government agencies, defense contractors, telecommunications providers, military research institutions, and operators of energy, water, and transportation infrastructure.

Many victims are concentrated in Hawaii, California, and Texas, locations strategically important to U.S. military operations in the Indo-Pacific.

Researchers believe the campaign combines espionage with preparations for potential disruption during a conflict involving Taiwan. They’ve observed attackers stealing military-related documents, mapping networks, and collecting credentials that could provide future access.

And that access can persist long after the initial intrusion. Volt Typhoon sometimes returns weeks later using stolen credentials and entirely new routes.

The result is a carefully maintained network of potential access points into critical American systems, built to remain largely invisible until the attackers decide they need it.

Cisco patches a firewall zero-day.

Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. The high-severity flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash vulnerable devices with SSL VPN enabled, causing unexpected reboots and service disruptions. Cisco confirmed exploitation earlier this month but hasn’t identified the attackers or their targets. The company urges customers to install security updates immediately. Administrators unable to patch can mitigate the vulnerability by disabling secondary authentication on affected VPN tunnel groups.

A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories.

Radware researchers have uncovered a suspected coordinated supply chain attack targeting 61 public GitHub repositories, including projects from Google, Brave, and Trivy. They identified 83 malicious submissions, most posted within just 43 minutes, using 74 GitHub accounts, many potentially compromised.

The attacker concealed malicious commands inside HTML comments in issues and pull requests. When vulnerable CI/CD workflows processed that content, the commands could execute automatically, attempting to steal environment variables, credentials, and access tokens.

Researchers confirmed malicious command execution in two cases but found no definitive evidence of stolen repository permissions or compromised downstream software.

The suspected objective was to gain access to repositories and potentially distribute malicious code through trusted open source projects.

Researchers recommend restricting workflow permissions and treating externally submitted content as untrusted.

Online scams overtake phishing.

Online scam detections doubled over the past year, overtaking phishing for the first time, according to Akamai’s latest State of the Internet report. Researchers recorded 6.4 million scams during the second quarter of 2026, including fraudulent stores, investment schemes, and payment scams.

Phishing also increased 61%, with AI helping criminals create convincing lures and launch shorter, more agile campaigns.

Meanwhile, a separate report from the Identity Theft Resource Center highlights the devastating human consequences. More than 80% of surveyed U.S. scam victims reported suicidal thoughts, while nearly nine in ten who sought institutional assistance received no response.

Many victims subsequently paid supposed recovery services, potentially exposing themselves to further fraud.

The findings illustrate both the growing industrialization of online scams and the troubling lack of support for their victims.

NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance.

NIST has released guidance to help federal agencies meet deadlines for transitioning sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography. Under a June executive order, agencies must adopt quantum-resistant key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. The guidance recommends prioritizing sensitive, long-lived data vulnerable to future quantum decryption, while allowing hybrid encryption approaches for particularly critical systems. NIST also urges agencies to assess their cryptographic supply chains, warning that meeting the deadlines will require immediate, coordinated action.

CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-41709, has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. CrowdStrike attributes earlier exploitation to the China-linked group Warp Panda, which reportedly used the zero-day to conceal activity during intrusions targeting U.S. organizations, including law firms. Despite its low severity rating, the vulnerability can significantly hamper forensic investigations. Federal agencies have two weeks to apply patches.

The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline.

The Federal Election Commission has taken several systems offline following reports of an attempted cyberattack, just days before the U.S. midterm elections.

The disruption affects electronic filing, campaign finance searches, and reporting tools, preventing organizations from submitting required disclosures detailing political spending. The FEC says it has identified an issue and is implementing a fix, but several services remain unavailable.

The timing is particularly sensitive, with record amounts of money flowing into congressional campaigns. Security experts warn that interruptions to financial disclosures could undermine transparency and public confidence.

Importantly, the FEC regulates campaign finance but does not administer elections. The incident has no direct impact on voting systems or how ballots are cast.

The agency says it’s working to restore services.

A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations.

A Ukrainian national has been sentenced to nearly six years in a U.S. prison for his role in the Nefilim and Hive ransomware operations. Thirty-six-year-old Artem Stryzhak pleaded guilty to participating in attacks that encrypted victims’ systems and demanded ransom payments, including attacks against healthcare organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Stryzhak joined Nefilim in 2021, agreeing to surrender 20% of his ransom proceeds in exchange for access to its malware. He later became an early Hive affiliate, participating in attacks against seven organizations, including healthcare providers and law firms.

The FBI helped one victim recover its files without paying.

Authorities are still searching for alleged Nefilim administrator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. The State Department is offering up to $11 million for information leading to his arrest, conviction, or location.

Stay with us, after the break we have Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center (TAC), discussing securing operational technology in our critical infrastructure takes more than traditional I.T. cybersecurity skills.

On our Industry Voices segment, we are joined by Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center (TAC), discussing securing operational technology in our critical infrastructure takes more than traditional I.T. cybersecurity skills. Here’s our conversation.

That was Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center, if you enjoyed this conversation and want to learn more, check out the show notes for the full interview.

Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

A company that previously turned space heaters into bitcoin miners now wants to bring cryptocurrency into your shower.

Heatbit has introduced Bitwater, an $899 replacement heating element that uses twenty bitcoin-mining chips to heat household water while generating cryptocurrency.

The idea is straightforward: Bitcoin mining produces heat, so why not put that heat to work? The company says Bitwater fits many conventional electric water heaters, operates without noisy fans, and sends mining proceeds directly to the homeowner.

The economics, however, are a little less refreshing.

A conventional heating element costs less than $30. Heatbit has shared estimates suggesting mining could generate roughly a dollar a day, potentially recovering the premium in about three years. But those returns depend on volatile cryptocurrency economics, hardware longevity, and household hot-water demand.

Shipments are planned for early 2027.

Our return on investment desk reports it would take over three hundred years of bitcoin mining to break even.

Whether Bitwater ultimately saves money remains uncertain. But at least your morning shower might finally contribute to your retirement portfolio.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Drei Tage it-sa und eine Frage, die uns nicht loslässt: Wer hat Zugriff auf was?
articles.context: Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet,...
articles.full_text:
„Wenn Sie uns fragen würden, wie viele Service Accounts oder KI-Agenten wir in der Organisation haben, bekämen Sie je nachdem, wen im Security-Team Sie fragen, eine andere Antwort.” Ein CISO sagte uns das auf der it-sa 2026. Und wissen Sie was? Er war nicht der Einzige. Drei Tage lang drehte sich in Nürnberg alles um KI, Regulierung und Souveränität. Doch die Gespräche, die blieben, drehten sich um etwas viel Grundlegenderes: Welche Identitäten haben in der Organisation Zugriff auf was, und wie wird dieser Zugriff abgesichert?

Diese Frage ist der rote Faden, der sich durch viele Gespräche zog, nur jedes Mal in anderer Verkleidung: mal als KI-Thema, mal als Compliance-Thema, mal als Souveränitätsfrage.

Was wir über die Trends und Herausforderungen gehört haben, die die IT-Security-Welt gerade beschäftigen, wollen wir Ihnen nicht vorenthalten.

Silverfort, it-sa Expo&Congress 2026

Drei aktuelle Trends von der it-sa 2026

1. KI-Angriffe: Wer sie nicht erkennt, hat sie trotzdem.

Jeder CISO beobachtet genau, wie Angreifer KI als Waffe einsetzen. Die Zahlen bestätigen das: Laut der Bitkom-Studie „Wirtschaftsschutz” gehen 82 % der Unternehmen davon aus, dass Angreifer verstärkt KI einsetzen. Gleichzeitig bestätigen Schlagzeilen, dass KI-Angriffe zunehmen. Tempo und Umfang, in dem sie sich entfalten, machen sie für Verteidiger derzeit so herausfordernd.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet, dass SIEM- oder SOAR-Erkennungen etwas Verdächtiges melden. KI-Angriffe spielen sich in Minuten ab, schneller als jede Triage und schneller, als ein Mensch etwas rechtzeitig korrelieren kann. Das Einzige, worauf jeder Angriff weiterhin angewiesen ist, ob KI oder nicht: der Missbrauch von Identitäten. Auch der beste KI-Angriff braucht am Ende einen Zugang, ein Passwort, ein Token, einen Service Account. Auf der Identitätsebene wird ein Angriff sichtbar, wenn man jede Anmeldung und jede Zugriffsanfrage im Blick hat und in Echtzeit entscheidet, ob sie fortgesetzt werden darf.

2. Compliance & NIS2: Ein Dauerprojekt.

Auf die Frage, was die EU-Richtlinie NIS2 bei Security-Teams konkret verändert hat, kam am Stand am häufigsten diese Antwort: „Wir arbeiten dran.” Das Gesetz gilt in Deutschland seit Ende 2025. Laut einer TÜV-Rheinland-Umfrage haben aber nur 14,3 % die Pflichten vollständig umgesetzt. Fast jeder Dritte (30,8 %) antwortete auf die Frage nach dem Umsetzungsstand sogar mit „weiß nicht”.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Unternehmen müssen bald nachweisen können, dass sie die Pflichten einhalten. Ein Großteil der NIS2-Compliance beruht auf starken Identity-Security-Kontrollen, etwa: alle privilegierten Konten identifizieren, MFA einführen, nicht-menschliche Identitäten wie Service Accounts prüfen, Remote-Zugriffe wie RDP und SSH schützen, granulare Zugriffsrichtlinien für alle kritischen Systeme und Anwendungen etablieren und mehr.

Die gute Nachricht: An der Einsicht fehlt es nicht. 60,3 % der Befragten halten NIS2 für wichtig oder sehr wichtig für mehr Resilienz. TÜV-Rheinland-Experte Michael Silvan sagt: „NIS2 ist kein Bürokratieprojekt. Es ist eine Chance, Sicherheitsstrukturen so aufzubauen, dass sie im Ernstfall wirklich tragen.” Wer jetzt auf der Identitätsebene gründlich Bestandsaufnahme macht, hat bei der Umsetzung einen Vorsprung.

3. Souveränität: Wer abhängig ist, kann nicht souverän entscheiden.

„Digitale Souveränität” war auf der it-sa an jeder Ecke Thema, und fast jeder wünschte sie sich. Aber: Der Bitkom „Cloud Report 2026″ zeigt, wie weit Wunsch und Wirklichkeit auseinanderliegen: 85 % halten Deutschland für zu abhängig von US-Cloud-Anbietern. 71 % beziehen heute Cloud-Angebote aus den USA, bevorzugen würden das nur 8 %. Als größtes Hindernis für einen Wechsel nennen die Unternehmen Lock-in-Effekte. Und das ist ein Sicherheitsthema, nicht nur ein Infrastrukturthema: Laut demselben Report sagen 87 % der Unternehmen, dass es souveränen Cloud-Angeboten internationaler Anbieter an Transparenz bei Datenverarbeitung und Zugriffsrechten fehlt.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Ohne diese Transparenz lässt sich die Frage, um die es in diesem Beitrag im Kern geht, nicht beantworten: Wer hat Zugriff auf was? Souveränität ist im Kern eine Frage der Kontrolle: über Ihre Daten, Ihre Schlüssel und Ihre Logs und darüber, wer entscheidet, wenn es darauf ankommt. Unsere Einschätzung: Jede Abhängigkeit ist auch ein Zugriffspfad und ein potenzieller Single Point of Failure. Wer nicht weiß, wo seine Abhängigkeiten liegen und wie schwer ein Wechsel wäre, kann im Ernstfall nicht entscheiden, sondern nur reagieren.

Die gute Nachricht: Die Bereitschaft wächst. 37 % würden für eine Cloud, die Daten ausschließlich in Deutschland und geschützt vor ausländischem Zugriff verarbeitet, inzwischen Nachteile in Kauf nehmen. Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst sagt: „In den Cloud-Markt könnte in den kommenden Jahren mehr Bewegung kommen, wenn sich Unternehmen einen Wechsel zutrauen und gezielt nach Alternativen mit klarem Souveränitäts-Profil suchen.”

Der gemeinsame Nenner: Unternehmen erkennen, dass die Basics wichtiger sind denn je

Auf den großen Bühnen ging es wie zu erwarten um KI, in den Gesprächen am Stand jedoch um Basics. Auf die Frage nach alten Konten begegnete uns Ehrlichkeit: Das bleibt eine Daueraufgabe, die Security-Teams lösen wollen, um identitätsbezogene Lücken zu schließen. Das deckt sich mit der Bitkom-Studie: Angriffe richten vor allem deshalb Schaden an, weil sie nicht erkannt werden (59 %), Systeme falsch konfiguriert sind (57 %) und das Identitäts- und Zugriffsmanagement Lücken hat (55 %). Die häufigsten Schadensursachen seien „keine besonders ausgefeilten oder exotischen Angriffe, sondern blinde Flecken im eigenen System”, so Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst. Oder, wie es unser CISO vom Anfang sagte: „Wie viele Service Accounts wir haben? Kommt drauf an, wen man fragt.”

Aus Identity-Security-Wahrheiten werden Prioritäten für 2027

Bei allem Gerede über neue Kategorien und neue Lösungen: Die Konzentration auf die Basics bringt viel, während Security-Teams erst lernen, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen. Die meisten Sicherheitsstrategien setzen auf klassische Detection-and-Response-Szenarien und auf Schwachstellenmanagement. Doch in einer Welt, in der Angreifer KI als Waffe nutzen, müssen Organisationen verhindern können, dass Angreifer überhaupt erst eindringen und Schaden anrichten. Und so bleibt jedes Mal dieselbe Grundfrage: Wer hat Zugriff auf was, und was kann diese Identität tun, sobald der Zugriff gewährt ist? Das sind Ihre Prioritäten für 2027:

Jede Identität sichtbar machen, auch die nicht-menschlichen (NHIs) und KI-Agenten. Erfassen Sie Service Accounts, API-Schlüssel und Tokens, die Ihre KI-Agenten nutzen, und löschen Sie, was niemand mehr braucht. Beginnen Sie mit Sichtbarkeit und erweitern Sie von dort aus um Kontrollen, die zur Laufzeit durchgesetzt werden.

Jeden Zugriff prüfen, und zwar in Echtzeit. Gemeint ist wirklich jeder Zugriff: ob Mensch oder Maschine, in der Cloud und on-prem, auch auf Altsystemen. Und Echtzeit heißt wirklich Echtzeit, denn KI-Angriffe arbeiten in Maschinengeschwindigkeit, ihr Angriffsweg schrumpft auf Minuten. Nur eine Prüfung, die mithält, hindert Angreifer, ob KI oder Mensch, daran, mit dem Zugang, den sie zu missbrauchen versuchen, etwas anzurichten.

Nachweisen können, wer worauf zugreifen darf. Dokumentieren Sie Zugriffe so, dass Sie Ihren NIS2-Stand belegen können, und kennen Sie Ihre Abhängigkeiten. Das ist Ihre Roadmap für Geschäftsleitung und Budgetrunde.

KI-Angriffe auf der Identitätsebene stoppen: So geht es nach der it-sa 2026 weiter

Wir haben uns gefreut, Sie in Nürnberg zu treffen, und wollen das Gespräch darüber fortsetzen, wie Sie Ihre Identitätsebene zur stärksten Verteidigungslinie machen. Es mag abgedroschen klingen, zu sagen „Identität ist der neue Perimeter”, aber es stimmt: Einen Perimeter gibt es eigentlich gar nicht mehr, und Angreifer haben nur dann Erfolg, wenn sie in Ihre Umgebung gelangen.

Bei Silverfort erforscht unser Team, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen und warum KI-Angreifer Identitäten so gern ins Visier nehmen. Wir teilen unsere Erkenntnisse gern ausführlich mit Ihnen, ob wir uns auf der it-sa gesprochen haben oder diesmal nicht zusammengekommen sind.

Vereinbaren Sie ein Gespräch, um den Austausch fortzusetzen, oder stöbern Sie in unserem AI Attack Readiness Kit, um selbst loszulegen.

The post Drei Tage it-sa und eine Frage, die uns nicht loslässt: Wer hat Zugriff auf was? appeared first on Silverfort.
