articles.title: OpenCode User Hit with Hostile Backlash After Reporting Free AI Loophole
articles.context: Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration
articles.full_text:
An OpenCode user who reported a loophole in its free AI usage limits became the target of harassment, including comments encouraging suicide, from people who blamed the disclosure for cutting off their supply of free AI. The GitHub thread has since been deleted, although an earlier version remains available through the Wayback Machine.

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that helps developers write, edit, and run code from a terminal, IDE, or desktop app. The MIT-licensed software can connect to commercial AI providers or locally hosted models. Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration. The reported bypass concerned the allowances on the free hosted models.

The report drew a flood of hostility in the project’s public issue tracker, with warm pillow wishes among the mildest responses. Other participants unleashed the kind of abuse that would ordinarily get someone banned from an open source project, openly encouraging suicide and pressing the reporter for identifying information.

A Call for a Fix Turned Into a Pitch for the Bypass #

The report, opened on June 28, described limits tied to an IP address. Switching to a different address through a VPN allegedly restored access while preserving the coding session. The author claimed to have automated the process and kept DeepSeek V4 Flash and MiMo V2.5 running for weeks. They proposed tying limits to accounts and detecting rapid IP changes. The account was created 13 days before the report and has no public repositories, a sparse history consistent with a throwaway account.

In an odd reversal, the author inexplicably closed the issue as completed on July 31, then reopened it on August 24 to promote the very workaround they had originally proposed fixing. They complained about the available free models and said they wanted people who could not afford subscriptions to build more with them.

Three days later, the reporter claimed to have run 130 agents across concurrent sessions, hitting usage limits six times in four to five hours and continuing by changing IP addresses. By then, the author was advertising the same behavior they had initially proposed preventing.

The same technique was being discussed elsewhere. A September 5 Hacker News commenter described OpenCode’s per-IP limits and told readers that “if you get some high-quality proxies you can get basically unlimited agent compute.” The comment did not reference the GitHub issue, but it shows the workaround had circulated beyond that thread before the late-October backlash.

On October 1, OpenCode collaborator rekram1-node responded that enforcing limits without authentication was difficult and that abuse undermined the effort to let anyone try a coding agent at no cost.

“Broadcasting this isn't very helpful, it only serves to harm,” the collaborator wrote before closing the issue. The response did not announce a fix.

Commenters Attacked the Reporter and Kept Trading Workarounds #

In late October, users traded conflicting accounts of whether changing IP addresses still restored access. Some said it had stopped working, while others offered additional workarounds. The attacks on the reporter escalated alongside those exchanges.

One GitHub commenter accused the author of gaining nothing from the disclosure, adding, “thanks for ruining it for us.” Other commenters wished suffering on the reporter, and at least two encouraged suicide.

The pile-on also included a supposed million-dollar reward. A commenter claiming to represent OpenCode offered the money if the reporter supplied their address. Replies joined in requesting identifying information, including the reporter’s “government name.” There is no evidence that the offer came from OpenCode.

Later replies quoted a participant telling others to stop harassing the reporter, only to accuse that person of being the author posting from another account. Other commenters challenged the reporter’s reversal, pointing out that they had first recommended closing the loophole, then reopened the issue and described using it extensively.

The discussion became a mix of personal attacks, arguments over the reporter’s motives, and requests for help keeping the bypass working. Some blamed the disclosure for losing access even as others continued to claim success. It’s unclear whether OpenCode changed its enforcement in response to the report.

The blame also spread to Reddit. In a post titled “The End of Long Free OpenCode Sessions”, the author complained that sessions had shrunk from hours to one or two prompts and claimed IP-switching workarounds no longer worked. “I didn't even know about this VPN bypass stuff, people like you ruined it for us,” one commenter told the Reddit poster. A reply redirected the blame with a link to the aforementioned deleted GitHub issue.

Others welcomed the prospect of tighter restrictions. “Well, if this helps my paid subscription to work much better, then it’s more than welcome,” another participant wrote.

The thread offered no settled explanation for the restrictions. Its author asserted that OpenCode now tracked hardware IDs and account metrics, without supplying evidence, while another commenter said changing a cellular IP still worked.

VPN Users Reported Access Problems #

Reports of disrupted access predated the October 27 release. In an October 22 Reddit thread, users said free models were blocked after little activity, including users who said they were not using a VPN. An October 23 post described changing IP addresses successfully for two months before the workaround recently stopped helping.

In another Reddit discussion, a user said a longstanding VPN setup now produced a daily-limit message immediately upon opening OpenCode.

“I think the IP detection may be a bit over zealous?” the user wrote. After another participant attributed the restrictions to VPN-based abuse, the original poster asked why the offering was described as a free tier when it appeared available only to people without VPNs. Another commenter said changing servers still worked.

OpenCode contributor Tarquinen addressed network-level blocking in a separate GitHub issue, explaining that the restriction applied to the connecting network address.

“Shared VPN addresses are often flagged, and we can't make exceptions for individual users,” the contributor wrote.

The experiences remained inconsistent. In an October 27 Reddit discussion, one commenter reported usable access through a dedicated-IP VPN, while another described very low limits without using a VPN.

The Fix Status Remains Unclear #

OpenCode made several infrastructure changes in October, including routing free-model requests through a newer inference service and tightening how it handles client IP information. An October 13 change addressed spoofed IP headers, but that is different from switching to a genuinely different IP address through a VPN. Whether those changes closed the reported loophole remains unclear.

The October 27 v2.2.0 release added visibility into usage and budgets but did not announce a fix for the reported bypass. Enforcement could also have changed on the hosted service independently of an application release.

The final comments preserved before the thread’s deletion still offered conflicting accounts of whether the workaround functioned. The thread remained accessible on October 28, after the release, and was subsequently deleted without a public explanation.

Socket contacted OpenCode for comment on the reported bypass and the thread’s removal but had not received a response at publication time.

Demand for AI Compute Accelerates #

The rush to code with AI has reached a fever pitch, with developers chasing more capable models, longer sessions, and enough compute to keep fleets of agents running. AI demand is squeezing memory supplies and driving prices higher. At the high end of the local hardware market, Apple’s newly available 512GB Mac Studio configuration reached an eye-watering $29,799 with 16TB of storage.

In the OpenCode thread, that hunger for compute curdled into a pile-on. The reporter went from proposing a fix to boasting about running 130 agents through the loophole. Other users blamed them for spoiling the arrangement, hurled abuse, and kept asking how to get the free models working again. The thread captures the AI coding gold rush at its most frantic, with users scrambling to keep their agents running and searching for the next route around the limits.

articles.title: NIK C2 Malware Can Use Victims’ OpenAI Keys for AI Queries
articles.context: Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays...
articles.full_text:
A new AI-enabled malware framework has been found that can fall back on victims' own OpenAI API keys for artificial intelligence requests, charging the usage to the victim while obscuring who made the requests.

Cisco Talos observed the command-and-control (C2) framework, dubbed NIK C2, in the wild, according to research published on October 29.

Its Go-based implant gave attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging and surveillance capabilities, while an integrated OpenAI client let them send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.

NIK C2 Routes AI Requests Through Victim Machines

The AI capability is built into the implant rather than requiring operators to process collected information separately. Talos said attackers could supply a prompt and model choice through the C2 panel, with the implant sending the request to OpenAI from the victim's machine and returning the response to the operator.

If the operator supplied no key, the malware read an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable on the infected machine instead, which Talos called a deliberate design. An organization with an OpenAI API key configured on a compromised Windows system could therefore end up funding the attacker's AI requests.

Read more on AI API key abuse: Attackers Steal METR API Key and Burn $600,000 in AI Credits

Talos said OpenAI's billing system would charge the victim's payment method and its access logs would show the victim's key as the one making the requests, leaving no trace attributable to the attacker.

Malware Framework Combines Theft and Ransomware

Beyond its AI functionality, the Windows malware supported more than 52 commands covering credential theft, browser data collection, cryptocurrency wallets, Wi-Fi credentials, keylogging, screen capture and remote access. Talos said it also offered lateral movement and multiple defense-evasion capabilities.

The framework also contained a screen-locking ransomware module that displayed customized ransom demands in Bitcoin or the Tether stablecoin (USDT). Talos said the module encrypted no files, leaving no forensic trail of file-modification timestamps or encryption markers, and that a screen lock is considerably faster to deploy than file-encrypting ransomware.

The company said it observed at least three versions of the implant and found its infrastructure active during the research. That led it to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is a fully functional framework rather than a proof of concept.

Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows."

articles.title: CREST Urges Whole-Ecosystem Approach to Financial Cyber Resilience
articles.context: CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and...
articles.full_text:
Cyber resilience in financial services should be built across the wider ecosystem of institutions, supervisors and specialist providers rather than treated solely as each institution's own responsibility, a new framework has argued.

CREST, the global non-profit accreditation body for the cybersecurity industry, said its whitepaper, Cyber Resilience in Financial Services: A Whole Ecosystem Approach, provides a maturity pathway for jurisdictions to assess their capabilities and coordinate improvements across three domains.

The paper, published on October 29, argued that weaknesses in shared infrastructure, technology providers, cyber firms or public authorities can undermine resilience across the wider financial system.

CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience

Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and demonstrating their controls work under pressure.

Financial supervisors are tasked with setting proportionate expectations, overseeing individual firms and understanding systemic risk, while cyber service providers are expected to deliver specialist advice, assessment, threat intelligence, testing and response capabilities.

The framework maps each domain through five stages of cyber maturity, with the three pathways planned together. Institutions progress from incomplete basic hygiene to advanced, threat-led assurance and continuous improvement. Supervisors move from mapping their sectors and establishing mandates to adaptive, cross-sector oversight, while providers progress from unvalidated services to specialist financial-sector capabilities.

CREST said the pathways are illustrative, not a new compliance standard. Its three priorities were ecosystem-wide measurement of maturity, a common language across the three domains and faster development wherever one part of the ecosystem lags.

Read more on financial-sector cyber regulation: FCA Updates Cyber Incident and Third-Party Reporting Rules

Framework Calls For Multi-Year Cyber Maturity Programs

CREST suggested supervisors or other market participants set out multi-year programs so the three domains develop in parallel, warning that requirements outpacing readiness can produce limited assurance. Its roadmap begins in years one and two with institutions mapping critical services and closing urgent hygiene gaps while supervisors publish a baseline and strategy.

Years three to five would bring independent assessment and risk-based testing for institutions, tiered requirements from supervisors and independent accreditation for providers. Years five to 10 would focus on threat-led penetration testing where proportionate, system-wide exercises and a diverse community of accredited specialist providers.

The whitepaper also warned that moving prematurely to mandate the highest international accreditations could shut out local providers where no route to accreditation exists. It pointed to measures including mentoring, partnerships, training and CREST's Cyber Accelerated Maturity Programme (CREST CAMP).

"Financial institutions, supervisors and cyber service providers each have a distinct role, and the strength of the system depends on their capability developing together," said CREST CEO Nick Benson.

articles.title: Shadow AI Across Government: It's Three Problems, Not One
articles.context: That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking
articles.full_text:
Most agencies and contractors now have a generative AI (GenAI) policy. Far fewer can tell you what their people are actually running.

That gap has a name. Like shadow information technology before it, Shadow AI is what happens when AI tools, services, and components enter an organization outside the processes meant to govern them. The difference is that shadow IT mostly showed up as an unapproved application.

Shadow AI can create risk at three points:

Data that leaves your environment.

AI-generated code your developers commit.

AI models and other components your builds pull down.

Those three are usually discussed as one risk. They are not. They have different failure modes, different owners, and almost no overlap in the controls that address them. An organization can have an excellent acceptable-use policy and still have no idea which AI models are running inside its own software.

None of which is an argument against adoption. The productivity gains are real, and the organizations getting the most from these tools are not the ones that tried to ban them. They are the ones that made the sanctioned path the easiest path to take. That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking.

Here is what each problem is, who owns it, and what closes it.

The Adoption Already Happened

Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that 45% of employees are now regular users of AI on corporate devices, authorized or not — up from 15% a year earlier. Two thirds of those users accessed AI services through non-corporate accounts, which means the activity is largely invisible to the organization paying for the device.

Shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action in the report's data loss prevention findings. And the most common category of data sent to external AI services is source code.

That last detail is the one worth sitting with, because it connects all three problems. Source code leaving is a disclosure problem. The same assistant that received it returns code and dependency choices that come back in. And the models behind these tools increasingly arrive as components inside your own applications.

One behavior, three exposures.

Problem One: What Goes Out

This is the problem most policies already address, and the one most people mean when they say Shadow AI. An employee pastes contract language, personnel data, or controlled unclassified information (CUI) into a public chatbot to summarize or rewrite it.

Ownership: Security and privacy teams, records officers, and acceptable-use policy owners.

Controls: Provide a sanctioned platform people prefer, use data loss prevention and network controls, name approved services, and give staff practical guidance.

Verizon's findings show why prohibitions alone may not work: employees may turn to personal accounts, moving AI use further out of view rather than stopping it.

For Department of War (DoW) components, this is already written down. DoW Instruction 8430.01 bars entering non-public departmental information into generative AI services unless the service resides on departmental systems and is approved for departmental use. Both conditions, not either.

What does not close it: anything in your software supply chain toolchain. No repository control, bill of materials, or scanner sees a developer paste code into a browser. If a vendor tells you otherwise, press on exactly which telemetry they are reading.

Problem Two: What Comes Back In

Your developers are using coding assistants. The output is unverified input, and the accountability for it does not transfer to the tool that produced it.

DoWI 8430.01 is explicit on this point for defense work: AI-generated code is treated as unverified, and developers and their teams remain fully accountable for what they ship. It also asks software efforts to maintain a record of the models, versions, and significant datasets used to generate or test software, kept with the software evidence package and treated as analogous to a software bill of materials (SBOM).

The subtler issue is that a coding assistant does not only write code. It chooses dependencies. An assistant suggesting a package is making a supply chain decision on your behalf, at a speed and volume no review process was designed for, which is a different problem from whether the code it wrote is correct. We covered that specific question in more depth earlier this month.

Who owns it: engineering leadership and application security.

What closes it is treating assistant output as you would a pull request from an unfamiliar contributor. Human review, software composition analysis (SCA) on everything it introduces, and a record of which models were in the loop, which is both a DoW requirement and the only way to answer the question later.

Problem Three: What Your Builds Pull Down

The third problem is the least discussed and the hardest to see after the fact: AI models and machine learning packages entering your environment as components.

Sonatype calls components retrieved straight from public repositories, bypassing the repository manager, shadow downloads. Sonatype Research Labs audited 9,658 Hugging Face requests across a set of customers in the first half of 2026, as part of our Beyond Traditional Packages report. Nearly 7% were blocked or rejected by policy. Of the 674 models blocked, 55% were stopped on model acceptability and 18% on security grounds, which says models are raising governance questions traditional policies were not built for.

A model is not like a library. It arrives as opaque weights, it may carry a license with terms on how its output can be used, and its published name tells you very little about what it was built from — open models are routinely fine-tuned, merged, quantized and re-released under a new publisher. Three federal exclusion orders now name a single model developer and reach products "developed using" its implementations, which makes model provenance a procurement question and not only an engineering one.

Who owns it: platform engineering and whoever runs your repository manager.

What closes it: one governed path in. Route model pulls through a proxy repository so every request is visible in one place, block direct downloads from the corporate network, and lock client configuration so the path cannot quietly be bypassed. Sonatype Firewall can then audit or quarantine models at that boundary before a developer gets them. Start in audit mode to see what your teams are actually pulling, then move to quarantine. At scan time, Sonatype Lifecycle flags a model as a derivative and names the foundation model it came from, and the AI Models Usage dashboard shows which applications are using models, with lineage, commit hash and publishing date.

That last piece matters for a reason beyond engineering. Joint guidance on AI and machine learning supply chain risks, co-sealed by the National Security Agency and seven other national agencies, tells organizations to require an AI bill of materials from vendors as a condition of procurement. Asking your suppliers for something you cannot produce yourself is a difficult position to hold.

What To Do About It

Pick your lane. These are three different jobs and they rarely belong to the same person.

If you own policy. Name specific sanctioned services rather than categories, and pair the policy with a platform people prefer to the alternative. Then confirm your inventory obligation is being met. OMB Memorandum M-26-05 makes each agency head responsible for the security of software on the agency network and directs agencies to maintain a complete inventory. Models are software.

If you own compliance. The obligations people associate with the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) did not go away when Phase 2 was suspended. DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171 and Supplier Performance Risk System scoring are unchanged, and annual affirmations remain in effect. An attestation that does not match the environment is the exposure, and that gap is exactly what undeclared AI tooling creates.

If you own the platform. Start with visibility, not enforcement. Put a proxy in front of model pulls, turn Sonatype Firewall on in audit mode, and spend two weeks looking at what comes back before you block anything. Most teams are surprised, and the surprise is the business case. Then make it continuous — an inventory taken once begins decaying the day it is produced, and the reason to route intake through a single path is that the record maintains itself rather than becoming an annual exercise.

Shadow AI is no longer a question of whether people will adopt these tools. They already have. The question is whether you can identify:

Which services receive your data.

Which models help write your code.

Which models run inside the software you ship.

Three questions, three owners, one answer: you can only govern what you can see.

See how Sonatype helps federal teams govern the AI models and open source components entering their software.

Written by Tom Tapley

Tom Tapley specializes in securing software supply chains for Federal environments, bringing deep expertise in aligning agency security, compliance, and operational requirements with modern technology solutions. With a proven track record in supporting mission-critical systems, he bridges the gap between evolving federal mandates and scalable, secure software practices.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability

CVE-2026-76418 Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure FTD Software Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
articles.context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
articles.full_text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

articles.title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
articles.context: In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at...
articles.full_text:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.

It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.

Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.

He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.

The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.

An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.

With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.

Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.

articles.title: ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach
articles.context: Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to...
articles.full_text:
A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

articles.title: NIST Publishes Guidance to Meet Federal Post-Quantum Deadlines
articles.context: For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to...
articles.full_text:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has published official guidance designed to help federal government agencies meet the 2031 deadline to transition post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

President Trump’s Executive Order 14412, published in June 2026, mandated that all US federal agencies transition “high value assets” and “high impact systems” to use PQC for key establishment by December 31 2030 and for “digital signatures” by December 31 2031.

NIST’s new document sets out a transition plan for agencies and organizations that work with the federal government to meet this deadline. The guidance references the post-quantum algorithm standards that NIST published in 2024.

“These deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend,” NIST wrote.

How to Prioritize the PQC Transition

The NIST report emphasized the logistical complexity that comes with the PQC transition. It outlined the approaches that can be taken for different types of systems and data to ensure security teams to take a risk-based approach to the transition.

For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time, due to the risk of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks.

The NIST guidance also accommodates a hybrid option for particularly sensitive systems, which combines conventional encryption with PQC – essentially providing two layers of security. However, this approach would demand more computational resources.

It also sets out how long less critical systems can continue to use conventional encryption protocols.

NIST mathematician Dustin Moody commented: “We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out. It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.”

The report also urges federal agencies to look beyond their own system components and at its entire cryptographic supply chain.

Post-Quantum Preparations Ramp Up

The new NIST guidance follows a series of pledges around PQC transition from other governments and across the tech world.

Governments like Canada, Australia, Japan, and the UK have set deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2030 as milestones for ensuring critical government systems are quantum safe.

While many of these mandates are focused on government and critical infrastructure organizations, they generally come with a push for other sectors to follow suit and set a roadmap for PQC migration.

Large tech firms, including Cloudflare, Google and Microsoft, have set a 2029 deadline for full PQC migration. Meanwhile, Apple, AWS, IBM and Meta, have officially started rolling out NIST-approved PQC algorithms into their products.

Read now: How Cybersecurity Vendors Are Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era

The situation has been made more urgent after warnings from tech companies like Microsoft that advances in quantum R&D mean that cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) capable of cracking asymmetric encryption could appear sooner than anticipated – potentially within the next five years.

articles.title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
articles.context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
articles.full_text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

articles.title: Searchjacked: Hidden Browser Extensions Hijack Searches for 13 Million Users
articles.context: This investigation expands on previous research with 264 newly identified extensions which exist only to capture users search queries impacting 8
articles.full_text:
You may have come across ads on webpages promoting "manual finder", "safe search", "PDF converter", or "AI search" tools which often end up as easy to install browser extensions. What are these extensions actually doing and who is behind them? This investigation expands on previous research with 264 newly identified extensions which exist only to capture users search queries impacting 8.7 million more users. This brings the total number of distinct extensions to 319 installed by roughly 13.4 million users across a decade of time.

These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID… but that might not be all.

These are not extensions users normally search for. In fact many of them are hidden in the Chrome Web Store. They are pushed into browsers through paid advertising (Google Ads, Bidbrain and more), often use shared landing pages tracking conversions, and are on the Chrome Web Store under shallow branding like Safe Web Search or PDF Manual Finder.

Why this is more important than just a potentially unwanted program:

Every search you make is captured. Because your searches pass through the operator's server first, the operator sees your complete search history, often tied to a unique identifier.

The redirect could be dangerous. The operator decides, per request, where your search actually ends up (similarly to a Traffic Distribution System). Today it leads to real results on Yahoo or Bing, but given enough time, a specific search string, or client geography, the results could show a phishing page, a fake results page, or a malware lure selectively.

The Chrome Web Store hasn’t kept up. Even if extensions are taken down, there are new domains and lures popping up quickly after. We’ve seen evidence of this technique running continuously for a decade.

An extension whose only function is to intercept searches users could have made anyway, that is purposefully hidden from indexing, promoted through low-value advertising listings, and provides no additional value should be considered malicious by definition.

Search syndication monetization #

Yahoo and Microsoft operate search syndication programs where partners who bring search traffic get a revenue share on the resulting ads. The partner bringing the searches is assigned tracking IDs. For Yahoo it is the hspart=/hsimp= parameters. In Bing it is the PC= partner code and PTAG= partner tag sub-ID.

In browser extensions, there is a simple setting in the manifest file to change the default search provider. This is built into the framework for browser extensions, it is not even code that executes! For example, this manifest (plus three icon files) is the entirety of one of the extensions analyzed in this report.

{ "update_url": "https://clients2.google.com/service/update2/crx", "manifest_version": 3, "version": "1.1", "name": "Safe Game Search", "short_name": "Game Safe Search", "description": "Real-time safety alerts for game searches and risky game websites", "default_locale": "en", "icons": { "16": "icon16.png", "48": "icon48.png", "128": "icon128.png" }, "chrome_settings_overrides": { "search_provider": { "name": "Safe Game", "keyword": "Safe Game Search", "is_default": true, "encoding": "UTF-8", "favicon_url": "https://safesearchgame.com/favicon.ico", "search_url": "https://search.safesearchgame.com/query?q={searchTerms}", "suggest_url": "https://suggest.safesearchgame.com/querying/autocomplete?query={searchTerms}" } } }

How to get more installs of extensions in order to generate more search revenue? Advertisements of course! The cost of promoting an advertisement which in turn generates search result revenue perpetuates the listing of more advertisements and extensions. Ultimately, Google can benefit from more advertisements being run and more extensions being listed in the marketplace so there may not be an urgent reason to police this activity too broadly.

Anatomy of a hijacker

Above we saw a manifest for a search hijacker, but how is that really different from any other extension? Most of what people think makes up an extension is missing from that configuration:

No permissions: what capabilities the extension requests access to

No background service worker: the logic brains of any extension

No content scripts: JavaScript injected into pages the extension requests access to

No UI: the toolbar popup or options page

There is no utility in the extension outside of changing the default search provider. Changing the default search provider will trigger a prompt to the user during installation, but it will not clearly state where your searches end up going.

Many analyzing these extensions may incorrectly assume that since they request no permissions, there is no risk and move on. Here we make the case for why that is wrong.

Why a proxy?

You might’ve noticed that your searches don’t actually go directly to Yahoo or Bing for search referral capture. As configured in the extensions that ship code, the actual flow is something like the following:

This is probably done for a few reasons:

A record of search referrals: measuring if search referrals match up with partner compensation.

A complete search capture point: every search query is captured and potentially monetized as trend or sentiment data. It could be geographically segmented or tied to specific IP sources.

A programmable redirect: this is the core "searchjacking" idea and builds on the previous two reasons. All redirects are decided server-side per request so the proxy operator can selectively serve different outcomes.

Through this research, most server redirects only appended partner tags to search results, but we did identify instances where a repeated search was redirected to Google's homepage without partner tags while other searches still went to Bing. This means redirects are chosen per request based on the search itself. The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads.

Predator Search (odkcfoohjiicbelloepgcomekdknchjh, 50,000 users) shows how much a single proxy can vary. Six identical searches sent through its proxy search server ended in four different places: straight to Yahoo with partner tags (hspart=sz&hsimp=yhs-026), a landing page on searchlio.net, a hop through searchtosearch.com to a second results domain (mcftink.com) before Yahoo, and a Cloudflare non-responsive error page. The extension never changed; the proxy chose each destination as the search came in.

It is only an assumption that these redirects could be malicious, but outside of needing to keep an accounting of all searches, the extensions could simply put the partner tags in the search provider override directly.

How extensions are “hidden”

The Chrome Web Store includes an option for publishers to keep their extension unlisted from both the web store search and other indexers. The pages are accessible to anyone for viewing, but you either need to know the exact extension ID or be linked to it from another page. There can be good reasons why an extension would be unlisted, but we’ve seen it used by attackers to keep their malicious extensions from being easily discoverable.

A majority of the search hijacking extensions we found are unlisted in the Chrome Web Store. Why is it important for such a simple extension to be unlisted? How do 13.4 million users end up finding them?

These extensions are often promoted through advertisement networks. Most often they are shown as “pop overs” or “pop unders” on webpages. Generally these advertisements are of the “junk” advertising quality which is the most cost effective and lowest converting. When a user loads a web page, a quick “auction” is run deciding what advertisements to show a user and these end up being shown on some of the less desirable and signal poor parts of the internet like small monetized blogs and content farms. Ultimately, a lot of users do end up on these sites and get shown popovers to help them “Search PDFs” or “Find Manuals”. It only takes a few clicks to end up with the extension installed and forgotten about quickly after.

A decade of hijacks #

The extensions tracked in this report date back to 2016. To help understand the scale, if we thought of these as a single extension configuring a search provider, 13 million users would rank within the top 25 Chrome extensions by popularity currently. There have likely been many more extensions which fall into this pattern of behavior but have been removed or have gone undiscovered to this point.

“Yandex search” published in 2016. A Russian-language MV2 extension that forced Yandex as the default search through the still-active extension-search.online. It had 200k users before it was taken down.

HermesTab published in 2017 was a Yahoo new-tab hijacker across two extensions that totaled 400k users.

Since 2018, Intango LTD has published about 111 extensions that reached roughly 2.2 million installs, spread across about 279 domains. Each extension got its own domain and its own admin@ mailbox, so every listing looked like an independent small publisher. Often several domains led to the same extension like newtabsearch.net and newtabhub.net. Domains often stay active even as their extensions are removed. Most send searches to Yahoo under Intango's partner account, but 15 send them to Bing (PC=INES*) instead. Intango's verified Google Ads account carries only 16 ads (October 2026), mostly for its "Search Direct" extension, so most of its installs come from somewhere else.

Tightrope Interactive ran about 200,000 Google ads across 307 domains. The advertising account also features advertisements for iOS apps, Microsoft Store apps and Windows browsers.

2024 included the SecuryBrowse wave which was covered in previous research. 58 extensions with plausible security brands (”Fire Shield”, “Wise Ghost”, “Securify”, “Protecto”, “WatchTower”) reached ~4.9M users total. They often requested many sensitive permissions in addition to hijacking search.

During 2025 and 2026 extensions appeared which focused on Bing redirection, usually pushed through Bidbrain advertisements, and difficult to attribute due to hidden domain registrations and lack of identification in privacy policies. Starting in April 2025, the same month previous research was released, 37 extensions were published. The group is clearly one actor. Fifteen seemingly independent extension publishers pushed updates within the same four days in June 2026. All use the same Bing partner account tags.

319 extensions · ~13.44M users across a decade

Identified Operators

Finding the source of these extensions

Unless you are served these ads for extensions, you practically can’t find them and identifying the owners of them can be even harder. We’ve developed a hunting methodology using a combination of the Chrome Web Store page, the extension’s landing page and Google Ads Transparency to gain insight into who may be behind these advertisements.

Identification

After being served an extension through an advertisement, you can click through the ad which sends you to a branded landing page with a single button requesting the user to install the extension with instructions for doing so. Sometimes it will redirect automatically to a Chrome Web Store page after a couple seconds.

Once at the Chrome Web Store listing, you can get the extension ID from the URL. While you cannot evaluate the extension code, you can attempt to search the ID in the Chrome Web Store search function. If you do not get a result back, the extension is a “hidden” one unlisted from search and indexing.

Privacy policies

When on an extension’s Chrome Web Store page, there is often a link to the extension’s privacy policy. Clicking through this you’ll be taken to the extension’s landing page which usually hosts the policy. In the privacy policy you may be able to identify a registered name for the company which made the extension, but it can be left out. Google usually reviews privacy policies prior to publishing an extension, but the requirements are loose and the privacy policy hosted outside of the web store can change at any time after review.

Ad transparency

Revisiting the branded landing page, you may be able to take the URL given and search Google Ads Transparency to find the organization posting the advertisement. Look for ‘Ads in anywhere’ to search all countries where an advertisement could be posted for full results.

While you cannot visit the links the advertisements go to from Google Ads Transparency, you will be shown the advertisement with the name of the company paying for them, in this case BrightWorks Technology LLC. Once you have the company’s advertiser ID, you can then pivot to see what other advertisements they post. From 400 advertisements related to the domain getsimplepdfsearch.com we are able to see that BrightWorks has over 3000 advertisements total for other types of extensions to download showing clear intent.

Systematically finding search hijackers #

Using a combination of Censys, Urlscan, and DecryptAds, we’ve developed a methodology that allowed us to pivot off of individual ads, fingerprint landing pages, and map out larger campaigns tied to real companies.

Censys searches

Censys crawls the web and indexes contents on web pages. When you click on an advertisement and get sent to a landing page pointing to a browser extension for installation, Censys has often already visited and collected information from that page. Here are some Censys search queries that are helpful for finding landing pages.

Query

Why it works

web.endpoints.http.body:"chrome.google.com/webstore/detail" and web.endpoints.http.body:"default search"

Searches for Chrome Web Store links and text involving ‘default search’

web.endpoints.http.body:"powered by Yahoo" and web.endpoints.http.body:"Add to Chrome"

Often finds extensions which change new tab behaviors and search funnels monetized through Yahoo

web.endpoints.http.body:"chromewebstore.google.com/detail" and web.endpoints.http.body:"default search"

A variant of Chrome Web Store link format

web.endpoints.http.body:"chromewebstore.google.com/detail" and web.endpoints.http.body:"search provider"

A variant of default search which often finds theme extensions that switch search providers

web.endpoints.http.body:"addons.mozilla.org" and web.endpoints.http.body:"default search"

A search for Firefox extensions. Edge extensions have been seen also.

Urlscan

What Censys doesn’t record is a website’s behavior like where a link actually takes someone, what JavaScript adds after the page loads, and which domains are sending visitors to which install pages. Urlscan records each page as a browser loads it, so a single scan links the submitted URL, every redirect along the way, and the final rendered page. Urlscan depends on users to actively ‘scan’ websites in order to register them, but due to the prevalence of these advertisements and the fact that many web proxies submit to Urlscan automatically, there is a great corpus of data.

Query

Why it works

page.redirected:off-domain AND links.domains:"chromewebstore.google.com" AND text.content:"default search"

Finds scans that were redirected from another domain onto a page linking to the Chrome Web Store and mentioning 'default search'.

page.redirected:* AND links.domains:"chromewebstore.google.com" AND text.content:"default search"

A broader variant that includes redirects within the same site, such as to a subdomain.

page.redirected:* AND text.content:"powered by Yahoo" AND text.content:"Add to Chrome"

Finds redirects into new tab and search install pages monetized through Yahoo.

page.url:"gclid" AND text.content:"default search"

Finds install pages reached from Google Ads clicks. Often surfaces downloadable suspicious browsers and search tools as well as extensions

page.url:"utm_source" AND links.domains:"chromewebstore.google.com" AND text.content:"default search"

Finds install pages reached through tracked campaign links.

content.globalNames:"MRAID_PATH"

A unique signature for many of the download funnels

content.identifiers:"html-id.already-installed-btn"

JavaScript that checks if an extension is already installed or not.

DecryptAds

DecryptAds is a new service that collects the public files that record how ads are bought and sold: ads.txt and app-ads.txt (which sellers a site authorizes) and sellers.json (which company owns each seller account). It then connects them across the web. A search hijacker ad seen on a site can only have come through one of the few dozen exchanges and resellers listed in that site's ads.txt, which narrows the possible routes. sellers.json then names the companies behind those accounts. The same data can link operator-run sites, new-tab pages and typo domains that share a seller account, which is a strong ownership tie and harder to rotate than a domain. DecryptAds can help identify and link where these search hijack ads can run across the web.

Today DecryptAds covers only the selling side, so it can't name the advertisers buying the install ads. This gap is clearly an important one to discover malvertising in the industry and one I’m hoping they are able to help with!

Thank you #

This research would be much weaker without access to key platforms.

To Andrew Northern, Silas Cutler, Aiden Holland and more from the Censys team for providing research access.

Johannes Gilger of urlscan for research access helping to find additional pivots and historical records.

Zach Edwards at DecryptAds for filling in gaps in how malvertising, software and advertising networks operate.

articles.title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
articles.context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Product

Affected

Node.js 22, 24, and 26

Before 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1

1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1

Bun

1.4.4
